World.title: Chad Ochocinco warns Browns' Deshaun Watson has 'very short' leash, could lose starting job by Week 3
World.content:
The Cleveland Browns made their quarterback decision entering the 2026 NFL season, but football fans are still trying to process why Deshaun Watson is getting the Week 1 start against the Jacksonville Jaguars over Shedeur Sanders.

The decision by first-year head coach Todd Monken may have answered the question on everyone’s mind for the Browns this preseason, but the debate still rages on throughout the football world considering Watson’s track record in Cleveland and how the $230 million man hasn’t lived up to his contract in the slightest.

In fact, fans booed Watson during their home preseason against the Buffalo Bills, to which he called them "disrespectful" and "personal" rather than a reaction to his performance on the field.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Either way, Watson heads into the new campaign – his first regular-season play since tearing his Achilles in 2024 – with an immense amount of pressure. However, one former NFL star believes the leash will be quite tight for the veteran signal caller.

Maybe to the point where he doesn’t start under center come Week 3 – the Browns’ home opener against the Carolina Panthers.

"If they start the season 0-2 – you open with the Jaguars. Then, you have Tampa Bay, then you come home. I’m not sure you play the third game, but you’d have to start that season off either 1-1 or 2-0. Either 1-1 or 2-0. One or the other. If you start off 0-2, they’re making a move. They’re making a move before the season gets too far away from them," Chad Ochocinco told OutKick in a recent interview while highlighting his partnership with DraftKings ahead of this NFL season.

DESHAUN WATSON SAYS 'EMOTIONS GOT THE BEST OF ME' AFTER RIPPING CLEVELAND BROWNS FANS FOR BOOING

Ochocinco has been very vocal about the Browns’ quarterback conundrum on his "Nightcap" podcast with Shannon Sharpe, where he’s noted on numerous occasions that there was never really a position battle between Watson, Sanders, Dillon Gabriel and anyone else on the quarterbacks' depth chart.

"It was never a quarterback competition. It never was. At no point in any game is the $46 million man competing for a job and would lose to the younger player based on salary," Ochocinco said. "As an owner and person writing the check, Deshaun Watson was always going to be the starting quarterback no matter what. Now, it’s his job to lose now going forward, and his leash is going to be very short."

From the fan perspective, Ochocinco also understands why the Browns faithful feel the way they do about Watson.

Since he came over in a now-infamous trade with the Houston Texans, Watson, who was given a whopping $230 million, fully guaranteed contract over five years, has started just 19 games across three seasons, with injuries and his lengthy 11-game NFL suspension coming in 2022. In those games, the Browns have gone 9-10, including the most recent in 2024 where he went 1-6. Watson has thrown 19 touchdowns compared to 12 interceptions, competing 61.2% of his passes for 3,365 yards and a passer rating of 80.7.

For comparison there, in his four years with the Texans, where he earned three Pro Bowls and led the NFL with 4,823 yards in 2020, he had a passer rating of 104.5.

"The fans are upset, the fans are booing because they have nothing to cheer for," Ochocinco said. "You haven’t given them anything to cheer for in general. So, the bad taste that’s left in their mouths are the issues that came with you from Houston on top of coming here to Cleveland. You’ve given them nothing to cheer for, therefore that’s why they’re gonna feel the way they feel."

So, what do Watson and the Browns do if even their home crowd seems to be against the most important player on the field for them come Week 1? As the saying goes, the shortest way through a storm is straight.

Watson is going to have to face the music, and Ochocinco is hoping he can do it.

HALL OF FAMER JOE THOMAS ON SKIPPING THE NFL DRAFT TO FISH, RAISING WAGYU AND TRANSFORMING HIS HEALTH

"But one thing can happen: performing and winning cures all," he said. "Listen, they come out the gate, somehow find a way to beat Jacksonville, find a way to beat Tampa, and you go into Cleveland the first home game 2-0. Man, they will cheer their a—off. You’re gonna hear cheering and eruptions of cheering for Deshaun that he’s never heard before. Honestly, I’m hoping he does.

"Winning cures all. It doesn’t matter what you did. You’re the quarterback of their team. If you start out the gate 1-1 at best – 2-0 best scenario – they’re going to love you in Cleveland despite what you’ve done. They’ll love you because you’re winning – something they haven’t had consistently for a very long time."

It will be a tough task for Watson and the Browns to get those wins against playoff hopefuls in Weeks 1 and 2. But Ochocinco sees no other way for Watson to hang on to his job even if it is just the start of a new campaign.

OCHO LOVES DRAFTKINGS GAMEDAY

College football is already underway, and the NFL is right around the corner, which has Ochocinco very excited about football being back. Also, he’s excited to impact the fan experience with DraftKings.

"DraftKings Gameday," which will take place on Sept. 2, was announced on Monday with quite the activation as it celebrates the first football season with DraftKings Sports & Casino available in all 50 states. As a way to fuel fans with the return of football, DraftKings will be offering free gas, while supplies last, to passenger vehicles at select gas stations in Los Angeles, Miami, Dallas, Atlanta and Detroit. Specific locations and event times will be announced separately.

"For me, I think it’s fun because who else would do something like this outside of DraftKings. This is a great touch for NFL fans to start the season," Ochocinco said. "We’re giving you free gas, so when your respective team plays, you’re fueled up to go. And word of mouth will be, ‘You won’t believe this? You know what DraftKings did? I was able to save money and get tickets to go to a game because they paid for my gas.’ That makes sense."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There will also be exclusive DraftKings Gameday promotions for customers, a customized in-app experience, in-person activations, a charitable donation through the DraftKings SERVES program, and a new campaign featuring Kevin Hart and Nick Jonas this season.

"It’s all about the fan experience, so some of the offers and luxuries throughout the season is what sets us apart from everybody else. I’m happy to be a part of them," Ochocinco said.

World.title: Gen Z Democratic lawmaker spars with Baby Boomers over whether American Dream is dead
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Rep. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., engaged in a fiery debate with a group of Baby Boomers this week on the web series Surrounded, arguing that Generation Z faces economic hurdles their generation did not experience.

The 29-year-old congressman appeared in the viral debate on the Jubilee YouTube channel, where a single public figure faces an entire room of challengers.

In the debate, Frost argued that young Americans were raised with the expectation that going to college — even if it required taking on student debt — would lead to a good job, allow them to repay that debt and provide a pathway toward the American dream. He argued that this bargain, and the American dream prospect itself, no longer holds for many young Americans.

Frost cited his working-class family background and noted that he worked as an Uber driver to make ends meet while running for Congress.

VANCE WARNS THERE WILL BE A SOCIALIST PRESIDENT IN THIS COUNTRY IF GOP DOESN'T FIX ECONOMY FOR YOUNG PEOPLE

"So that’s the American dream! You lived it!" his debate opponent, comedian Geno Bisconte, responded in a clip that went viral on Monday.

"The American dream isn't driving Uber to barely make ends meet," Frost replied. "The American dream is upward mobility and being able to have success."

"You went from driving an Uber to being a politician!" Bisconte shouted. "Is that upward!? What am I missing?"

"But it's not about one person. It's about the totality of a generation," Frost replied. "That's part of the reason that I have the claim that I have. The majority of my generation is struggling and having a hard time to just survive. Just to survive. The American dream isn't survival, my friend. Is the American dream survival or is it thriving? The American dream is thriving. The fact of the matter is the vast majority of young people feel like they're not able to put aside enough money to have mobility."

Another participant named William argued that many of Frost’s complaints can be attributed to population growth from mass immigration.

BIDEN'S ILLEGAL IMMIGRATION SURGE CAUSED HIGHER RENT AND HOME PRICES, FED STUDY FINDS

"When we started school, there was less than 157 million people in America today. Now there's 340," William responded. "More people needing homes means home prices go up. More people needing food means food prices go up. We can't correct that until we get rid of all the foreigners that have come in here. And your party is refusing to do that, even if they’re illegal!"

Frost pushed back, saying immigrants provide a net economic positive and share more in common with everyday Americans than billionaires do.

He added that entry-level wages haven't kept pace with living costs, making the prospect of buying a home on a retail or service job "a fantasy." Frost also pointed to competition in real estate, noting young buyers now face off against private equity firms.

Analysts and policy experts offered mixed takes on the generational exchange in comments to Fox News Digital.

Judge Glock, director of research and a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, argued that in general young adults have a much higher net income than Baby Boomers did at the same age, but agreed that housing affordability is at its "worst it's been in decades." However, Glock disputed Frost’s contention that institutional investors or older generations are to blame, attributing price spikes to regulatory constraints that limit new housing construction alongside high mortgage rates.

CEO UNDER FIRE FOR MASS LAYOFFS AMID FOREIGN WORKER HIRING SPREE NOW APPOINTED TO FED'S TASK FORCE ON JOBS

"Frost is wrong that higher housing prices are due to competition from Baby Boomers or Wall Street," Glock said. "The fundamental reason housing prices have gone up is that we are building less than we used to. And we are building less than we used to because of ever-increasing regulations, from zoning to environmental mandates. When combined with high mortgage rates due to both inflation and high levels of government debt, homeownership is becoming increasingly out of reach."

Glock also noted that "This generation also has much higher student debt levels than earlier ones. Due to their high student debt, and lack of wealth in housing, older Millennials have a lower net worth than Gen Xers at the same age. That's not because of a lack of jobs, but because colleges have been handing out ever more low-quality degrees at an ever higher cost."

Elizabeth Pipko, a former Republican National Committee national spokesperson, agreed that Gen Z faces certain major challenges, but argued they should not overestimate the luxuries the Baby Boomer generation had.

"Nobody is arguing that young Americans have it easy. And it is true that housing prices in many parts of America have risen much faster than incomes, particularly in desirable cities and suburbs. But, with that being said, times have changed and the comparison to baby boomers is not exactly fair," she said. "Households back then consumed much less. Today’s family is purchasing a much higher material standard of living. What is considered 'normal' today would have been a dream to many a few decades ago. For example, the material things that improve our quality of life which were mere dreams are now not only attainable by most, but vastly cheaper. Think about computers, televisions, household technology, air travel, etc. Times have changed, yes, and with that comes difficulties, but also incredible advantages and benefits."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Pipko added that immigration, artificial intelligence, and post-pandemic work shifts are compounding the tough entry-level job market for recent graduates. She cautioned against abusing H-1B visas for cheaper labor, warning that such practices put "American graduates in direct competition for the entry-level jobs that traditionally gave them their start."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Link Lauren, an influencer and former senior advisor to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., also told Fox News Digital, "For years, I’ve recommended trade and technical schools. If you go to college and major in queer theater or LatinX literature, don’t be shocked when there aren’t tons of jobs waiting for you. Unless you really need that four-year degree to go on to medical school or law school, you really have to think twice about spending all that time and money on a college campus. The American dream is certainly attainable. But the landscape has shifted. This is something Charlie Kirk spoke about often."

Fox News Digital also reached out to Frost's campaign and did not receive an immediate reply.

World.title: Army Secretary submits resignation to White House after tensions with Pete Hegseth
World.content:
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is expected to step down in the coming days after the White House accepted his resignation, according to a person familiar with the matter and a White House official.

NBC News reported last week that Driscoll had told close associates that he wanted to leave the administration by Labor Day. Driscoll visited the White House last week to discuss his future, according to three U.S. officials, but it wasn’t clear what came of the meeting.

Driscoll, who has been well regarded by many Republicans and Democrats, has been rumored to be leaving the administration for months. He has served in the role since February 2025, and has been a close associate of Vice President JD Vance.

Driscoll is the latest high-profile official at the Defense Department to depart; Navy Secretary John Phelan and the Army chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, were pushed out this spring.

Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll on May 23, 2026 in West Point, N.Y. Adam Gray / Getty Images file

The Wall Street Journal first reported Driscoll’s resignation.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly praised Driscoll in a statement Monday evening.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” Kelly said.

“The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

Driscoll had differed over a number of issues with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who removed George, Phelan and other high-ranking Pentagon officials. He has also blocked the promotions of several senior Army officers.

“Driscoll brought up concerns with the administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible,” a source familiar with the matter told NBC News on Monday.

The Pentagon directed any questions about Driscoll to the Army, which didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Trump calls for federal tax incentives to benefit TV and movie industry
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Monday called for bipartisan tax incentives to help a domestic TV and movie industry that has seen large chunks of its business move overseas in recent years.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that meetings were “being set up with the Leaders of both Parties in order to get this done.”

“It should be Bipartisan, especially since so much money is being lost in California, and other largely Blue States,” he wrote. “I am going to suggest that Republicans and Democrats get together, and immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America.”

Trump indicated that his call to help Hollywood — an industry that Republicans often rail against and one that resides in solidly blue California — was influenced in part by actor Jon Voight, who was a 2024 campaign surrogate for him.

Voight, whom Trump has called his “Hollywood ambassador,” has helped shape Trump’s policy toward the entertainment industry during his second term. In May 2025, Trump met with Voight before he proposed tariffs on films produced overseas.

Voight did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night.

President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House on Monday. Annabelle Gordon / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Trump’s Truth Social post drew immediate support from Democrats who are usually critical of him and his administration’s policies.

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., a frequent Trump target, said he was in “strong agreement” with Trump on this one.

“Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we’ve lost to other countries,” Schiff wrote on X. “Let’s work together — Republicans and Democrats — to get this done, and bring the movie magic back to America.”

Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Calif., praised the proposed measure and called for swift passage.

“For more than a year I’ve been sitting down with Jon Voight, Congressional colleagues, the unions, studios, and producers to build the case for a national film and television tax credit,” Friedman said in a statement. “There’s no reason Canada, the UK, or Australia should be taking our jobs. We still have the best crews on the planet. It’s time we made it possible for them to stay where they belong: in America.”

Friedman said last September that the proposed tariffs on foreign films were recognition from Trump that the U.S. was losing its domestic film and TV industry but that the path forward was a tax credit, not tariffs.

Trump’s announcement Monday was also embraced by the industry itself.

Charles Rivkin, the CEO of the Motion Picture Association, the trade group representing major film studios in the U.S., said in a statement that the group applauded Trump’s support for tax incentives.

“For over a century, American studios, casts, and crews have produced the films and series that the world wants to see. A federal incentive would be a landmark step toward bringing more production to local communities in all 50 states, strengthening our nation’s economy, and making our country a more competitive place to produce, create, and tell great stories,” Rivkin said in his statement.

While Trump did not lay out any financial details in his post, he predicted that the money spent on the tax incentives “will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers.”

World.title: Former gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis found guilty of murder in Tupac Shakur’s death
World.content:
The man accused of orchestrating rapper Tupac Shakur’s killing was convicted Monday of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon in the 1996 Las Vegas slaying.

Following a nearly two-week trial, jurors unanimously found Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of the murder that for nearly 30 years has gripped rap fans, true-crime experts and conspiracy theorists alike.

Clark County prosecutors had argued that Davis was a “shotcaller” for the South Side Compton Crips in Los Angeles and that he sought revenge on Shakur after he attacked Davis’ nephew.

Davis was not accused of pulling the trigger, but under Nevada law, someone who helps another person commit murder can be convicted of the crime. Davis is the only person alive who rode in the same car as the shooter 30 years ago, prosecutors said.

Davis, dressed in all black, stood silently next to his counsel as the verdict was read. He took a seat, hands clasped on the table in front of him, as the jurors were polled one by one, each affirming the guilty verdict.

Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, Tupac’s sister, cried and reached back to a person behind her. Davis’ son covered his face with one hand, The Associated Press reported.

District Judge Carli Kierny ordered Davis, who faces a life sentence, to remain in jail until his Oct. 13 sentencing. Davis indicated he intends to file an appeal.

Shakur, who was 25 when he died, was revered as one of the most influential rappers of all time and continues to bring in new generations of listeners.

The prosecution said Monday that the state would dismiss the gang enhancement part of the charge because of witness logistics.

Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal said in his closing statement that Davis “went hunting” for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight after they were spotted at the MGM Grand Hotel beating up Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, also known as the “prince” of Compton in California because of his relationship to Davis.

Tupac Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight circa 1996. Nitro / Getty Images

Jurors watched grainy VHS security video and heard multiple former law enforcement officers testify about the fight that broke out a few hours before Shakur and Knight were wounded in a drive-by shooting.

Knight survived his injuries, but Shakur died six days later.

In 2008, Davis entered into an agreement with federal investigators who were looking into the death of Marion Wallace, the rapper known as Notorious B.I.G.

Davis believed the deal, called a proffer, gave him immunity, but he was not shielded from future prosecution if he confessed to being involved in Shakur’s murder.

Because of the proffer, Davis described details of Shakur’s killing that only a witness could provide, Bilal said. They included the positions of people inside the car in the drive-by shooting and previous gang fights that culminated in Shakur’s death.

Davis’ 2019 memoir, “Compton Street Legend,” was the final piece of evidence needed to convict him, Bilal said. In the book, Davis writes that he played a role in Shakur’s murder, and its publication prompted a renewed investigation into Shakur’s killing.

Tupac Shakur in 1996. Steve.Granitz / WireImage file

“For nearly 18 years, Duane Davis has told the police, television, books, YouTube interviewers, anybody that will listen,” Bilal said in his closing statement. “He has told you he is responsible for the murder of Tupac Shakur. Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty.”

Defense attorney Michael Sanft argued that Davis fabricated or embellished his accounts of the killing for money and notoriety and that investigators failed to independently corroborate his claims.

During his closing, Sanft repeatedly pointed to a lack of physical evidence that could place his client at the crime scene. Detectives never found records — including receipts, phone logs or photos — that proved Davis was in Las Vegas at the same time as Shakur or that he provided the gun used to kill him.

Retired Las Vegas homicide detective Dan Long, the defense’s final witness, testified that he tried unsuccessfully to verify several details Davis provided during a 2009 police interview, Sanft argued.

“When you think about Mr. Davis’ statements, they all conflict,” Sanft said in his closing statement. “They conflict with the book, and they conflict with the past. And the only thing that we have is that we can agree on is that Tupac Shakur was shot and killed on Sept. 7, 1996, in Las Vegas, Nevada.”

Shakur’s killing triggered a decadeslong investigation that took Las Vegas investigators from the Strip to Compton, near Los Angeles, where rival gangs were embroiled in a violent war that erupted immediately after Shakur was shot.

Uncooperative witnesses and conflicting statements made it difficult for police to draw a straight line from Las Vegas to Compton, where everyone associated with the shooting lived, officials testified.

Las Vegas detectives traveled to Southern California a dozen times and were continually stymied by unreliable informants and a culture of silence, former law enforcement officers testified.

“I think it made the case more difficult, and I think the 30 years made the case more difficult, as well,” Sanft told reporters last week.

World.title: A look at search, rescue and recovery efforts in Nepal
World.content: A look at search, rescue and recovery efforts in Nepal On Monday, search, rescue and recovery efforts continued in Nepal after the devastating floods last week. Around 4,200 people are still missing and at least 903 people have been killed, according to Nepal's national disaster agency. Videos show some of the efforts.

World.title: U.S.-Venezuela oil deal will rely on North American Blue Energy Partners
World.content:
The Trump administration's plan to take a stake in tens of billions of barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves will hinge on a private company called North American Blue Energy Partners, the White House announced Monday, offering more details on the agreement.

Under the deal, the Venezuelan government granted 100-year concessions to NABEP to drill in 17 oil fields, the White House said in a fact sheet released late Monday. Those oil fields contain about 65 billion barrels, roughly one-fifth of Venezuela's total proven oil reserves.

The U.S. Defense Department will be granted a 35% stake in the company, according to the White House. The State Department will then have the right to buy 20% of NABEP's output at the cost of production, and it will have the right of first refusal to buy everything else.

Run by Venezuelan executive Alejandro Betancourt, NABEP describes itself as Venezuela's second-largest private oil producer, pumping more than 200,000 barrels of oil per day.

In a statement confirming the structure of the deal, NABEP said it is aiming to increase daily production in the near-term to over 1 million barrels. (By comparison, the U.S. consumed about 20.6 million barrels of petroleum daily last year, according to government figures.)

"Venezuela is blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential," Betancourt said in a statement thanking President Trump and interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez. "This transaction will unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans."

Rodriguez said in a speech over the weekend the ultimate goal is to produce more than 1.5 million barrels per day. She described it as a 25-year deal.

The White House said NABEP has "developed an ambitious plan to rapidly scale production by investing up to $100 billion in new oil infrastructure in Venezuela." It also said the deal will be executed at "no cost to the American taxpayer."

Mr. Trump has argued the deal will bring more oil to the U.S. market, pushing down energy prices and allowing the government to replenish its Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Since the U.S. military removed former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Mr. Trump has sought to ramp up oil production in Venezuela, which claims to have the world's largest oil reserves but has languished for years due to underinvestment.

"This deal secures our energy dominance for the next century—all at zero cost to the United States," the White House said.

Rodriguez has celebrated the deal, calling it a "historic agreement" that will bring scores of private investment to Venezuela's oil industry and draw hundreds of billions in tax revenue. She has said that Venezuela will retain control over its natural resources.

Some oil industry experts are skeptical that the deal will lead to lower prices at the pump any time soon. It could take years — or more than a decade — for new Venezuelan oil production to start reaching the U.S. market and impacting prices, according to analysts.

The country's energy infrastructure needs to be rebuilt, and Venezuelan oil tends to be "heavy" (or dense) and "sour" (or high in sulfur), making it harder to refine than the light, sweet crude often found in the United States.

The deal has also drawn pushback from both American and Venezuelan political figures. Some Rodriguez opponents have called it an "asset grab" and questioned the legal basis for handing the U.S. government a stake in a large share of the South American country's oil reserves.

Democratic Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, called the plan to give the Pentagon a stake in the Venezuelan oil venture "a blatant abuse of power and taxpayer dollars."

"President Trump has been explicit about his desire to extract Venezuela's oil," Reed said in a statement. "His administration removed Nicolás Maduro from power, threw its weight behind the unelected leadership that replaced Maduro, and is now attempting to use U.S. military assets and taxpayer-backed financing to boost a private oil venture."

World.title: 3 friends went hiking in the Grand Canyon. 1 died, 2 were reported missing.
World.content:
A hiker from Texas was among at least two people killed in flash floods that swept through parts of the Grand Canyon over the weekend, and two of his friends were missing, the group's family members said in a statement Monday.

Dr. John Giusti, a 46-year-old chiropractor from Granbury, Texas, described by his family as a devoted father of three daughters, was killed in the flooding.

"To the community, he was a gifted healer. To his friends, a powerhouse of life. To his daughters, he was their ultimate hero. To me, he was my whole world," Giusti's wife, Janet Giusti, said in a statement.

John Giusti, 46, died in the flash flooding at the Grand Canyon, his family confirmed. Family photo

Giusti was hiking with two friends, Brent Rosenkranz and Timothy Allen Smith, their families said. Rosenkranz has a wife and three sons and is a "lifelong martial artist who has dedicated much of his life to teaching and mentoring young people," his family said.

"As an ATA martial arts instructor and school owner, Brent has made an impact on generations of students, but his family says the role he prizes most is simply being there for the people he loves," the joint statement said.

Smith, also a husband and father of three, "loves the outdoors, exploring and helping others. Hiking and camping with his family are among the things he loves most," his family said.

The three men entered the Grand Canyon on Friday and hiked to Bright Angel Campground, the families said. Their plan was to spend two nights exploring trails near the bottom of the canyon and go fishing before moving on to Havasupai Gardens, which the park says is a "frequent stop for hikers and mule trains traveling up and down the Bright Angel Trail," before finishing their hike, according to the families' statement.

Brent Rosenkranz, left, and Timothy Allen Smith, right. Courtesy of the Rosenkranz and Smith families

"Our families are profoundly grateful to the search-and-rescue personnel working to bring our loved ones home and to everyone who has prayed for us, reached out, offered help and surrounded our families with love," the families said Monday in a joint statement. "We ask that you continue praying for Brent and Tim, for everyone searching for them, and for all of the families affected by this tragedy."

Authorities initially said about 15 people were missing but as of Monday night, that number had dropped to one. The families did not provide an update on the two missing hikers later Monday.

Dozens of people had to be rescued after heavy rain caused flash flooding in Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch areas of Grand Canyon National Park. But more heavy rain on Monday hampered continued rescue efforts. In just the past two days, the Grand Canyon was hammered by almost half a year's worth of rain.

Rolling bands of rain pummeled the South Rim of the Grand Canyon on Monday, preventing the Arizona Department of Public Safety, which rescued 61 people over the weekend, from using its helicopters for rescue flights all day.

An Arizona DPS official told CBS News that two reasons they've had trouble making contact with the missing are a lack of cellphone coverage and possible language barriers. Many of those believed to be missing or unaccounted for are believed to be foreign tourists, and their family members may not know exactly where they are or be able to contact authorities here.

Another complicating factor is the remoteness of the terrain. There are no roads inside the park. The only ways to get around are by foot, mule or helicopter.

Over the weekend, as creeks began to swell and masses of muddy debris clogged rivers, rangers ordered dozens of hikers to run. Among those racing to safety were Erica Viola and her boyfriend.

"He's yelling at me, 'Run, run,' and I'm going, 'I can't run any faster. I'm going to just die.' I knew if I didn't run, we weren't going to make it," Viola told CBS News. "Five minutes later we would have been washed."

Remnants of stone bridge pylons remain along Bright Angel Creek following a flash flood in Grand Canyon National Park that destroyed the footbridge on Aug. 29, 2026. Handout/Grand Canyon National Park

Ten minutes later, the footbridge they had used to reach safety was gone. It was among the infrastructure within the park that was wiped out by the floods.

"Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, eliminating pedestrian access across the creek," the National Park Service said Sunday.

Viola and her boyfriend were airlifted to safety a few hours later.

Steve Kramer managed to hike out, but he was exposed to yet another danger: falling rocks.

"All the people down in the canyon there, there's just nowhere to go and nowhere out," Kramer said. "No way out."

World.title: St. Louis becomes the latest battleground in fight over data centers
World.content:
As tech companies pour trillions of dollars into new data centers as part of the ongoing AI boom sweeping the globe, communities across the U.S., including St. Louis, are finding themselves in the middle of a high-stakes fight.

A million square feet of old warehouse space in the Missouri city has turned into a mountain of controversy as David Daneshforooz, CEO of TerraWatt, plans to develop a data center there.

"St. Louis has a lot of old, kind of decaying infrastructure that's being underutilized," Daneshforooz told CBS News. "And so data centers have the opportunity, if done responsibly, to bring back industry into those communities."

But for many in the community, the sales pitch has fallen flat. And they're not alone. A recent Gallup poll found that more than 70% of Americans don't want data centers in their area.

Kasey Fowler-Finn, a biologist at Saint Louis University, is a plaintiff in a lawsuit, filed on Friday, seeking to halt the development. She's concerned about noise, water use, electricity use and more.

"There's been no environmental impact assessment and no low-frequency sound study," she told CBS News.

"A lot of claims are being made that don't actually have data to back it up," she added, saying there's "a lack of transparency about the environmental impact, about the noise impact."

Looming over the debate is the technology that data centers help support.

"The AI side of it, I think, is just really out of fear. It's the unknown," Daneshforooz said.

But Fowler-Finn disagrees.

"It is not a baseless panic," she said. "It is a worry that's based in real scientific evidence. We have to be very careful about where and how we install these large data centers."

Daneshforooz, however, claims that not putting data centers in the U.S. could compromise Americans' data.

"Where is that information and data going to be stored? Would you rather have it be in a place like this in the middle of America, or would you rather have that information be stored in a country that we can't regulate or control?" he said.

The developers are promising to pay for their own electricity, use a closed system for water and invest hundreds of millions into the local school system. It's a playbook that's worked in other cities, but not yet in St. Louis.

World.title: 2 dead, at least 1 missing after Grand Canyon hit by flash floods
World.content:
Two deaths have been confirmed after parts of Grand Canyon National Park were hit by major flash floods over the weekend, but most of the people who were believed to be missing have now been accounted for, authorities said Monday evening.

At least one person is known to still be missing, incident commander Dave Black said at a news conference. Earlier, authorities said about 15 people were missing, based on the park's permitting system, but as of Monday night, all except one are accounted for, Department of the Interior spokesperson Elizabeth Peace said.

The raging waters swept boulders, infrastructure and other debris into the Colorado River after a storm dropped a huge amount of precipitation in a very short period of time, officials said.

The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered Sunday night near Crystal Rapids on the Colorado River, the National Park Service said. Family members identified him as Dr. John Giusti, a chiropractor from Granbury, Texas, who was hiking with two friends.

On Monday, the park service said a second body had been recovered, but released no other details.

The NPS called for anyone who knew of hikers or backpackers who were in Bright Angel Canyon or the Phantom Ranch area on Saturday afternoon, when the flash floods hit, to provide information to park authorities.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

"Grand Canyon National Park staff, in coordination with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, are continuing evacuation and response efforts and working to account for individuals who may have been in the affected area," NPS said in a statement.

Authorities were also searching for anyone who may have been on the North Kaibab Trail, between the trailhead and Phantom Ranch, staying at Bright Angel Campground, or traveling or staying in the area known as "the Box," north of Phantom Ranch.

Dozens evacuated amid "extensive damage" to infrastructure

At least 82 people were evacuated from the hard-hit areas in the sprawling national park after the flooding caused significant damage, Black said.

"Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, eliminating pedestrian access across the creek," NPS said in an earlier statement.

Officials said Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, Phantom Ranch Canteen, the North Kaibab Trail, the Black and Silver bridges and traffic to the Colorado River in the area would be closed until further notice.

Rafting trips on the Colorado River later reopened Sunday after authorities determined it was safe, according to Black.

Grand Canyon National Park Deputy Superintendent Brian Drapeaux said Monday night that the park is still open and accessible to both the North and South rims.

About half an inch to an inch of rain fell within just half an hour in the rocky area, where there's a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Justin Johndrow in Flagstaff.

Remnants of stone bridge pylons remain along Bright Angel Creek following a flash flood that destroyed the footbridge on Aug. 29, 2026. Handout/Grand Canyon National Park

"Most of it ran off instantly," Johndrow told The Associated Press.

The National Park Service said the flooding caused "extensive damage to infrastructure in the inner canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, which supplies water from the canyon for use in the park."

"The waterline is currently not operational, leaving the park with limited water reserves and requiring significant water conservation measures to ensure available supplies can be maintained," NPS said. On Monday, it reported that about 40% of the waterline has been destroyed.

Drapeaux told reporters Monday night that the park's Transcanyon Waterline, a 12 1/2-mile water pipeline constructed in the 1960s, was "battered, bruised and decimated in certain areas," adding that officials anticipate "miles of pipeline" might be destroyed.

"One of the indicators that allow us to track in terms of water use here on the South Rim ... We currently have approximately two weeks of water available in storage," Drapeaux said.

Teams on the ground still have to assess the full extent of the damage, and water usage will vary depending on the number of visitors and staff, he said.

Phantom Ranch is a historic and extremely popular lodge close to the bottom of the Grand Canyon by Bright Angel Creek.

Park officials asked people to stay away from the closed areas and said the operator of the lodge, which is usually fully booked months in advance, will inform guests about the state of their reservations.

Grand Canyon National Park is ranked the fourth-most visited national park in the U.S., with 4,430,653 recreational visits in 2025.

Lucky escapes: "It would have been game over"

Gabe Bergemann was with his family at Phantom Ranch when he said what looked "like a whole monsoon basically hit the campground in the cabins area."

They were among about 60 people told to flee from their cabins and across a footbridge as the water rose.

"It was just like these brown, almost like black waters, filled with debris," he told CBS News. "On that bridge, that was when it hit … I actually became scared and I didn't know — I didn't know it was gonna happen."

Flash flooding hit parts of Grand Canyon National Park, prompting the evacuation of dozens of people. Grand Canyon National Park

David Gregory was traveling with Bergemann's family and said the flood destroyed the footbridge only about 10 minutes after they all managed to get across. Hours later they were flown to safety by a helicopter.

If the park ranger hadn't ordered everybody to evacuate when they did, Gregory said all the campers could have been left trapped on the other side of the swollen creek.

"It was like a whirlpool in there, with all the debris circling around, cabins and other equipment from the maintenance work site," he said. "I don't think we would have made it out alive … I think it would have been game over."

Grand Canyon weather forecast: "Raging killer currents"

Officials also warned that additional thunderstorms and heavy rainfall are possible Monday, which could "result in additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and rapidly changing trail and river conditions."

"This is a reminder of what a dynamic and active landscape [the] Grand Canyon is," Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University, told AP.

A flood watch has been issued by the National Weather Service for all of northern and central Arizona through Monday evening, NWS Flagstaff said.

"Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas," the NWS alert said. "Raging killer currents will be possible in side canyons and narrow slot canyons. Low-water crossings may be flooded."

Showers and thunderstorms are also expected through Monday. The area's already-saturated soils and "deep monsoonal moisture" increase the risk of flash flooding, according to forecasters.

The monsoon, or rainy season, can make the Grand Canyon a dangerous place to visit in the summer, as it increases the risks of flash flooding. Even clear days can suddenly produce thunderstorms and downpours.

There were three initial waves of rain that "primed the drainages and already had creeks flowing at minor levels" when the deadly fourth wave arrived, the weather service said in a statement.

Forecasters were also concerned about additional flash flooding from rain that fell on part of the Dragon Bravo fire scar, a huge burn area caused by a wildfire in July 2025.

World.title: Supreme Court continues to allow construction of Trump's White House ballroom
World.content:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday continued to allow construction of the new White House ballroom, clearing the way for the massive new structure that President Trump has championed.

In a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court halted lower court rulings that would have temporarily blocked the construction of a new 90,000-square-foot ballroom where the East Wing once stood.

The high court said in an unsigned opinion that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which filed a lawsuit to block the project, likely did not have the legal right to sue. It did not address the legality of Mr. Trump's East Wing project.

Chief Justice John Roberts joined with the three liberal justices in dissent.

Roberts had temporarily allowed work on the ballroom to continue earlier this month, giving the Supreme Court more time to weigh the Trump administration's bid for emergency relief.

In its unsigned opinion, the court ruled that lower court judges "likely exceeded" their authority by blocking the ballroom. The majority pointed to sworn declarations from top administration officials, including the director of National Intelligence and heads of the Secret Service, Army and the State Department, who said the ballroom was necessary and had warned that any significant pause in construction would harm the government because of the national security facilities being built underground.

"Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government's East Wing project," the court said. "We conclude only that, based on the submissions before us, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks Article III standing to challenge the project in federal court and that the remaining stay factors favor relief."

But Roberts, writing in dissent, said that construction of the ballroom is "likely unlawful." Joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, the chief justice said that Congress has not authorized the East Wing project.

Roberts also said the injuries asserted by Alison Hoagland, one of the Trust's members, are sufficient to allow the lawsuit to go forward.

"The White House is not just any building, and — when it comes to historic preservation — Hoagland is not just any person," he wrote. "In failing to appreciate as much, the Court misconceives the plaintiff's injury, allowing the Executive's likely infringement of the Legislature's power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue. Today's decision is no victory for the separation of powers."

Mr. Trump praised the ballroom project in response to the Supreme Court's decision.

"We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.," he wrote on Truth Social. "When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of."

Brent Leggs, president and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, said it is "deeply disappointed in the Supreme Court's ruling today and respectfully disagree with the majority's opinion on standing. It is noteworthy that the majority did not weigh in on whether the ballroom project was in fact legal."

"We are pleased with Chief Justice Robert's strong dissent, which reiterated what we have maintained from the start of our case — that construction of the White House ballroom is unlawful," Leggs said in a statement. "In addition, this is not the final decision on the merits of our case and does not resolve our fundamental argument — that each President is a temporary steward of the People's House and does not have the unilateral authority to demolish and redesign it without the approval of Congress."

The Trump administration requested emergency relief from the court earlier this month after a federal appeals court ruled the White House lacked authority to build the $400 million project without congressional approval.

The divided U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit concluded that Congress — not Mr. Trump or the White House — has "full constitutional control over federal property and the funding of its maintenance and development," and noted an "absence of any express or implied authorization" that grants Mr. Trump the ability to construct the ballroom.

In a filing with the court, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the justices to pause the lower court ruling that blocked above-ground construction while the legal battle over the project plays out. The overhaul also includes an underground bunker, medical facilities and other features, and judges have allowed that work to continue.

"This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security," Sauer wrote.

Sauer wrote that the renovations are "absolutely required and should not be enjoined" because any delay threatens Mr. Trump's safety after recent domestic and international assassination plots against him.

Construction on the project is 65% done, Sauer wrote in the filing, because the initial district court order halting the construction has never gone into effect. He revealed that a 250-person crew is working "20 hours a day, 7 days a week."

Described as a "superstructure" made of concrete and steel, Sauer told the high court that it rises up to 70 feet high in some places, stretches five stories deep and has a footprint of nearly 50,000 square feet. The ballroom is funded by private donations, and $335 million of an expected $400 million has been raised, Joshua Fisher, director for White House Management and Administration, said in a declaration.

"Given the current progress, the superstructure is beyond the point of return," he said.

The White House anticipates the structure will be "substantially" completed by November, and the full project is expected to be wrapped by August 2028, when Mr. Trump will have just five months left in his term.

In April, the appellate panel granted an administrative stay sought by the Justice Department that allowed all White House ballroom construction to continue while the court considered briefs and heard arguments. Below-ground work on the presidential bunker and other security upgrades has continued as well during the legal back-and-forth. The D.C. Circuit then upheld the district court's injunction.

Attorneys for the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which filed suit to block the ballroom project late last year, argued in their response to the Trump administration that the organization would be irreparably harmed if the ballroom construction is permitted and accused the White House of attempting to "outrun judicial review."

"In the end, the question is not 'whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy.' Nor is it even whether Petitioners may ultimately construct the ballroom," they wrote in a filing. "The question is simply who decides whether a ballroom can be built on federal property. Our constitutional system and federal law commits that choice to Congress."

Lawyers for the Trust accused the White House of shifting positions regarding the nature of the project, including its stance that the ballroom was necessary for national security, when previously it said the ballroom could be built independent of the below-ground facilities. They reiterated that the lower court orders allow work on the subterranean bunker to continue.

Mr. Trump has been deeply involved in the project, frequently raising the ballroom during public events and in posts on Truth Social. In a social media post Friday, the president called the Trust "treasonists" and accused them of revealing "top military secrets."

Portions of some legal filings submitted by the Justice Department to lower courts have been written in the style of the president's social media postings, including with misplaced capital letters and exclamation points, raising questions as to whether Mr. Trump himself participated in the brief-writing process.

World.title: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigning after friction with Hegseth
World.content:
Washington — Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is resigning, the White House confirmed Monday, after months of friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

"Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CBS News. "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War."

A U.S. official told CBS News the secretary spoke to President Trump about the current state of the Army and submitted his resignation.

Deputy Army Undersecretary Dave Fitzgerald is also expected to step down this week, according to a U.S. official.

CBS News reported last week that Driscoll was considering stepping down from his post by the end of the year.

An Iraq war veteran and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll has served as the Army's top civilian leader since his Senate confirmation in February 2025.

His tenure has included the U.S. operation that captured former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro — which involved members of the Army's elite Delta Force — and the ongoing war with Iran. Driscoll has also met with Ukrainian and Russian officials as part of Mr. Trump's push to end Russia's war against Ukraine, and his time leading the Army coincided with a plan to cut the number of U.S. forces in Germany.

But there have been behind-the-scenes tensions between Hegseth and Driscoll, CBS News has reported.

Earlier this year, Hegseth ousted Gen. Randy George — a close friend of Driscoll — as Army chief of staff, asking him to retire. Gen. Chris Donahue, commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, also filed for retirement.

Donahue and George were supporters of a newly formed Army drone battalion that was tasked with gleaning lessons from the intense drone warfare in Ukraine. However, the Army began making plans to phase out that unit earlier this month, following friction between the Army officers who supported the new battalion and acting Army chief of staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve, CBS News has reported.

George and Driscoll also rolled out a broader plan last year called the Army Transformation Initiative, which focused partially on introducing more unmanned systems.

A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Driscoll had brought up to the Trump administration his concerns surrounding the Army's transformation efforts and the fact that Hegseth has pushed out some of the generals who were responsible for the transformation.

Driscoll is the latest high-level military official to exit. Navy Secretary John Phelan left his role earlier this year, with Mr. Trump saying Phelan "had some conflicts with some other people." Several officers have also retired in the last year, including George, Donahue and U.S. Southern Command commander Adm. Alvin Holsey.
