Background: Fintechs and Digital Banks in Brazil 2026: Market Guide.

Background: Brazil Inflation Rate 2026: IPCA, Selic and What’s Next.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Pix and how does it work?

Pix is Brazil’s instant-payment system operated by the Central Bank. It allows real-time, fee-free transfers between any registered accounts 24/7 using a phone number, email, or QR code. It processed 79.8 billion transactions in 2025 and roughly 6 billion per month in early 2026.

Is Nubank profitable?

Yes. Nubank has been profitable since 2023, reported net income of US$2.9 billion for 2025, and earned a record US$1.1 billion in Q2 2026. It serves 139 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia.

Do traditional Brazilian banks still dominate?

Yes. The five largest banks (Itaú, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil, Caixa, Santander) control roughly 80% of total banking assets. Fintechs have gained ground in payments and consumer credit but not in commercial lending or mortgages.

World.title: Charles Carr remanded after allegedly holding baby mother hostage at gunpoint and assaulting her
World.content:
Charles Carr remanded after allegedly holding baby mother hostage at gunpoint and assaulting her

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 23-year-old Belize City man employed as a technician at Belize Water Services has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged with aggravated assault with a firearm following allegations made by his ex-girlfriend.

Charles Carr appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, where he pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated assault with a firearm. He was remanded until November 3, 2026.

The charge stems from an alleged incident at a residence on Electric Avenue on August 28.

According to the police report, Carr’s 22-year-old ex-common-law partner visited the residence with their three-year-old daughter so Carr could spend time with the child.

The woman alleged that when she told Carr she was ready to leave, he became upset and told her she would not be allowed to leave until she had sex with him “one last time.”

She further alleged that Carr locked the front door, kept the key and later pointed a firearm at her after she began packing her child’s belongings.

The woman told police that she feared for her life and asked Carr to put the firearm down, but alleged that he refused and struck her several times to the forehead.

She reportedly managed to knock the firearm from his hand and kick it toward a couch, but said Carr retrieved it. She further alleged that he later removed the magazine, causing a bullet to fall to the floor.

The woman told police she continued asking to be allowed to leave but Carr refused. She eventually managed to send text messages to an aunt asking for help, and police arrived at the residence about 15 minutes later.

Following her report, Carr was arrested and charged.

During his arraignment, Carr reportedly told the court that the complainant was outside the building and intended to withdraw the charge. The court did not entertain a withdrawal at that stage.

Because the charge involves an alleged firearm offence, the Magistrate’s Court did not grant Carr bail, and he was remanded to prison pending his next court appearance.

World.title: Police detain 18-year-old for theft of $4,500 motorcycle
World.content:
Police detain 18-year-old for theft of $4,500 motorcycle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained an 18-year-old man in connection with the theft of a motorcycle from Belize City over the weekend.

A 21-year-old man told police that at about midnight on Sunday, August 30, he parked his black Lifan motorcycle outside a friend’s residence near the corner of Elston Street and the George Price Highway because the motorcycle could not fit through the property’s gate.

When he prepared to leave at approximately 3:30 a.m., he discovered that the motorcycle was missing.

The motorcycle, fitted with a black storage box behind the seat, is valued at approximately $4,500.

Police say an 18-year-old Belize City mechanic has since been detained in connection with the investigation.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: 15-year-old robbed of iPhone and injured in Belize City alley
World.content:
15-year-old robbed of iPhone and injured in Belize City alley

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the robbery of a 15-year-old student who was attacked while walking through an alley in Belize City on Sunday night.

According to police, the student was walking from Kut Avenue through an alley leading to Fairweather Street at about 7:50 p.m. when two unidentified men dressed in dark clothing attacked him from behind.

The teenager reportedly suffered an injury to the right side of his head and scratches to his right hand during the attack.

His red iPhone 11, valued at approximately $400, was stolen before the attackers fled.

The teen ran to the Fairweather Street police booth for assistance and was later taken to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Police noted that both residential and police surveillance cameras are located in the area and investigations are continuing.

World.title: Woman charged for bursting sanitation worker’s lip after swinging machete through window louvres
World.content:
Woman charged for bursting sanitation worker’s lip after swinging machete through window louvres

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City woman, Angelique Mejia, has been charged with aggravated assault and wounding following an altercation at a Cet Site residence over the weekend.

According to police, 38-year-old sanitation worker reported that at about 7:30 a.m. on Saturday, August 29, Mejia, whom he knew, arrived at his home carrying a machete and confronted him over allegations concerning a missing laptop.

He told police that Mejia initially rode away but returned shortly afterward and began swinging the machete outside his house.

He said he attempted to speak with her through a front window to de-escalate the situation when she allegedly pushed the machete through an opening created by two missing louvres, striking him on the upper lip.

Perez suffered a bleeding injury which was later medically classified as wounding.

Police subsequently arrested and charged Mejia with aggravated assault and wounding.

World.title: Police investigate suspected arson after SUV set on fire on Rasta Street
World.content:
Police investigate suspected arson after SUV set on fire on Rasta Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a suspected case of arson after a vehicle was damaged by fire early Monday morning in Belize City.

At about 5:00 a.m. on August 31, police responded to Rasta Street, where they found a black 2011 Nissan Rogue with fire damage to its rear passenger compartment, including the rear seat and passenger-side window.

The vehicle’s owner, a 26-year-old security officer, told police that he had parked the SUV in front of his yard at about 9:00 p.m. Sunday before going to sleep.

Initial investigations indicate that at approximately 4:15 a.m. Monday, a grey Caravan van without licence plates arrived in the area. Shortly afterward, the Nissan Rogue was seen engulfed in flames, and an individual was reportedly observed entering the Caravan before it sped away toward Central American Boulevard.

The Belize Fire Service extinguished the blaze. The value of the damage has not yet been determined.

Police are investigating.

World.title: 30 Years Later: Keefe D found guilty of murder in 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur
World.content:
30 Years Later: Keefe D found guilty of murder in 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly 30 years after the fatal shooting of rap legend Tupac Shakur, a Las Vegas jury has found Duane “Keefe D” Davis guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon.

The jury returned the unanimous verdict Monday after less than three hours of deliberations, marking the first conviction in one of the most notorious murder cases in hip-hop history.

Prosecutors argued that Davis, 63, orchestrated the September 7, 1996 drive-by shooting in retaliation after Shakur and members of his entourage attacked Davis’ nephew, Orlando Anderson, at the MGM Grand earlier that night. While Davis was not accused of firing the fatal shots, prosecutors said he obtained and provided the gun used in the attack. Under Nevada law, a person can be convicted of murder for aiding or facilitating the killing.

The prosecution relied heavily on Davis’ own accounts of the shooting, including statements made during interviews with investigators, media appearances and his 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend. His defense maintained that those accounts were exaggerated or fictionalized and argued there was insufficient physical evidence tying him to the murder.

Shakur was shot while riding in a BMW driven by Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight near the Las Vegas Strip. He died six days later at the age of 25.

Davis now faces a potential life sentence. His sentence will be determined by a judge at a later date.

World.title: Belize mourns the passing of longtime children’s healthcare advocate Milagro Garel
World.content:
Belize mourns the passing of longtime children’s healthcare advocate Milagro Garel

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Milagro Garel, the woman behind two decades of children’s medical missions in Belize, has died.

Her family confirmed her passing in a statement, saying she went peacefully with her loved ones at her side.

“It is with broken hearts that we share that our beloved Milagro passed away peacefully this afternoon, surrounded by love.”

Garel collapsed on July 28 with a ruptured cerebral aneurysm. Doctors stabilised her here before an air ambulance took her to Guatemala, where surgeons operated and she remained in intensive care for weeks. Her husband Joe kept the country updated as she regained consciousness in stages.

Belizeans raised the money that made the treatment possible, covering transport, surgery and hospitalisation costs running between $95,000 and $140,000.

As country director for World Pediatrics, Garel spent more than twenty years getting Belizean children onto operating tables they would never otherwise have reached, working alongside Friends of Pediatrics and other groups.

“Your beautiful smile, your incredible spirit and the light you brought into so many lives will remain with us forever,” her family wrote.

World.title: Court orders psychiatric evaluation for accused thief after questions arise about identity, ability to understand proceedings
World.content:
Court orders psychiatric evaluation for accused thief after questions arise about identity, ability to understand proceedings

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 33-year-old man accused of stealing a cellphone was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Monday after a magistrate ordered that he undergo a psychiatric evaluation amid concerns about whether he understood the court proceedings.

The man, known to police and the court as Raymond Moody and also as Lavender Kendale, appeared before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison on a single charge of theft.

Moody is accused of stealing a dark blue Samsung cellphone valued at $650, on Wednesday, August 26.

His arraignment was initially halted because he could not provide identification and questions again arose over his true identity. The matter was briefly stood down while prosecutors sought further information.

Later in the day, a woman identifying herself as his mother, Maria Moody, appeared in court and told the magistrate that the accused is her 33-year-old son, Raymond Moody, who was born at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital. She did not have documentary proof of his identity with her.

When the theft charge was read and Moody was asked to enter a plea, he reportedly responded, “I nuh know which is correct.”

Senior Magistrate Dennison subsequently ordered a psychiatric evaluation, with the court expressing concern that Moody may not be in a position to properly understand the proceedings or enter a plea. He was remanded until September 30, 2026.

Outside court, Maria Moody became emotional over her son’s remand. She said her son has experienced memory problems since suffering a blow to the head approximately three years ago.

“He is not crazy. Things come and go,” she said, explaining that he had previously been treated at the Port Loyola Clinic and KHMH following the injury.

Moody previously came before the court in 2025 after attorney Audrey Matura reported a burglary. During those proceedings, questions also arose over his identity after the man police knew as Raymond Moody told the court his name was Lavender Kendale.

That burglary case was eventually dismissed after the court was unable to establish with sufficient certainty the identity of the person before it.

Moody is scheduled to return to court on September 30.

World.title: Tents? No Way!
World.content:
The tent at Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth where some classes were held

MIDDLE QUARTERS, St Elizabeth — Describing tents as heat traps, Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett is insisting that all of her 252 students must be housed in ventilated classrooms when the new academic year opens next Monday.

“The tent cannot be used; it is extremely hot. We tried to use the tent last academic year. We had grade one initially in the tent and after the [Primary Exit Profile] exam we had grade six going to the tent and giving grade one a feel of a classroom space,” she told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“However, due to the heat the children were not able to use the tent for the entire day. They had to be out of it by midday. Right now it is hotter than what we were experiencing last academic year, so I don’t see where I can use that tent to host the classroom,” she added.

Last week, the Caribbean Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology and The University of the West Indies Climate Studies Group Mona advised governments, businesses, farmers and households across the region to step up preparations for potentially severe climate extremes as El Niño conditions are and set to intensify the hot and dry conditions already affecting parts of the Caribbean.

Both entities warned that the region should remain particularly vigilant as August to October marks the peak of the Caribbean’s heat season.

This year’s El Niño is on track to be the strongest on record, threatening to unleash extreme weather across the globe and make 2027 the hottest recorded year by far.

Under such severe heat, tents would not be suitable to serve as classrooms for children.

On Monday, when asked how all her students would be accommodated, Principal Watson-Barrett said the National Education Trust (NET) had promised to deploy temporary wooden classrooms, but up to Monday afternoon there was no structure or even foundation to give assurance of the buildings.

“I am yet to see them. Between the Ministry of Education, NET, and the contractor, they promised that we would be getting two buildings each holding two classrooms, so that would be a total of four classrooms. Up to this morning (Monday) there was no updated information. The contractor said he is waiting on NET to give approval for the building of the [wooden] classrooms,” Watson-Barrett told the Observer.

She said the school is exploring two options to accommodate students if the temporary buildings are not erected in time.

“We will have to look at rotation and/or merging of classrooms into one room. For instance, last academic year I had a classroom with two grade two classes and they were placed in one room and then the teachers team-teach,” she said.

“Because of the heat, also, I am not considering a shift system. Imagine coming to school at 12 o’clock to start classes in this heat on a shift system,” added Watson-Barrett.

She said the school is expected to have seven accessible classrooms based on ongoing construction work.

“Currently, we have one block that is 85 per cent complete. That block can host two classrooms. The other two blocks that are available are currently being worked on and we are hopeful that by this Friday those two blocks will be completely cleaned and ready for the opening of school, September 7,” she said.

A deteriorating building had to be demolished last week at the school.

“That would leave me wanting five more classrooms to accommodate the other students, because as of last week I lost a building that had four classrooms, the guidance counselling room and the library on it,” said Watson-Barrett.

She said Middle Quarters Primary and Infant will be receiving students from the now shuttered Giddy Hall Primary School, three-and-a-half kilometres away.

“Even without the inclusion of the Giddy Hall Primary children I would be short of classrooms. I have 170 students expected to attend school in the primary department with an additional 29 from Giddy Hall Primary School, seeing that the school was consolidated and we are the receiving school,” she said while pointing out that five academic and two auxiliary staff were moved to her school from Giddy Hall.

“The ministry has made the decision to close down smaller schools based on the enrolment there… For the infant department we are expecting to have about 52 students,” she added.

When asked about the availability of potable water, Watson-Barrett said the school has been getting reliable water supply from the National Water Commission.

“Currently, I am seeing where improvement has been made on the water system; it is still being worked on, but whenever it is locked off we purchase water,” she said.

“During Hurricane Melissa [last October] the drums were blown off the building. However, we have a large metal tank that we store water in. Those drums that were blown down are yet to be replaced,” she added.

World.title: Tough guardrails
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen (second left) gestures while speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. Flanking him are CGC executives (from left) Caleigh Reid, legal officer; Damion McKenzie, senior director, investigations and enforcement; and Shainee Myles, director of human resource. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

WITH Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator set to commence operations by March next year, once all outstanding conditions are met, the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) is assuring that stringent guardrails are in place to keep criminal elements out, with operators required to verify players, monitor suspicious transactions, and protect vulnerable gamblers.

Speaking during this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange, both CGC Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen and Senior Director of Enforcement and Investigation Damion McKenzie outlined a multi-layered system of checks that will follow casino operations from the moment a player registers to the regulator’s ongoing monitoring of the business.

The safeguards include know-your-customer (KYC) checks, scrutiny of suspicious transactions and sources of wealth, anti-money laundering controls, surveillance systems, responsible-gaming interventions, and direct regulatory access to the casino’s operations.

The officials were speaking as Adamas Grand Casino Limited, Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator, moves towards opening at Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover. The CGC granted the operator its licence on July 29, but the licence is conditional and does not yet authorise the casino to begin operations.

CGC Legal Officer Caleigh Reid said the operator must first satisfy all remaining requirements, with March 31, 2027 set as the deadline to commence operations.

“They have a specific time frame in which to open. There are certain deliverables that they have to satisfy us with, certain things that they have to provide us with before they get the go-ahead. Right now they have the licence, but they are not authorised to begin operations until all of those other deliverables are satisfied, which is all outlined in their conditions of licence,” she said.

The safeguards are intended to address several risks associated with casino gaming, particularly money laundering, organised crime, problem gambling, and the potential exploitation of vulnerable players.

At the heart of the CGC’s financial crime controls will be requirements for casinos to know who their customers are and to scrutinise the money moving through their operations.

According to McKenzie, the regulator will not simply assess an operator’s anti-money laundering system once and walk away.

“A part of our legislation requires us to do ongoing monitoring as it relates to money laundering and proceeds from illicit means. We will continue to monitor, but the training that we provided to our officers… allow them to understand the different typologies that are related to money laundering in the gaming sector, to understand the myriad things that happen that can be classified as money laundering,” McKenzie said.

The commission will also examine whether an operator has properly carried out those checks and whether the financial profile of a player makes sense.

“Our audit plan also allows us to go in and check on persons who have signed up, if you did the proper KYC and anti-money laundering check against this person: What does this person do? How did they come about the cash? The source of wealth? So all those checks continue throughout the lifecycle of the licence,” McKenzie added.

Furthermore, Allen noted that the commission is designated as the competent authority for casino gaming under the Proceeds of Crime Act, with responsibility for anti-money laundering, counter-financing of terrorism and counter-proliferation financing compliance in the casino sector.

He explained that casino gaming in Jamaica is restricted to approved Integrated Resort Developments, meaning a casino cannot operate as a stand-alone gambling establishment.

Therefore, this creates a two-stage screening process.

“At the first stage of the development of it, the Government wants to be satisfied that the operators, the financiers, their funding is from good sources, they have good standing in other jurisdictions, not just for the development but for the operations of the casino… and when you come to stage two, when you come to us, we then conduct our own due diligence, specifically in respect to the conduct and operations of a casino,” Allen said.

He also noted operators will be required to maintain surveillance systems capable of supporting regulatory monitoring, as well as provide space for commission officers at the premises.

“In Las Vegas, on any one casino property, there are about 5,000 cameras. These cameras can zoom in and read the serial number on a note at a table four miles down the road. We have similar surveillance and monitoring requirements for the casino. More than that, the operator is required to have facilities on its premises for the commission and our officers to be able to have access to and at any time go on site and monitor,” Allen said.

The CGC’s guardrails are not limited to criminal activity. Allen explained that the regulator’s responsible-gaming framework is designed to identify people who may be developing harmful gambling habits and provide avenues for intervention.

That framework includes staff training, player information, behaviour monitoring, exclusion and self-exclusion mechanisms, as well as controls on advertising. The commission has worked with the Responsible Gaming Council of Ontario and signed an MOU with RISE Life Management, which has experience in counselling and self-exclusion relating to gambling.

“The mechanism behind responsible gaming is that the staff will be trained to spot persons who have a problem, persons who sit all day and gamble. There’s some form of intervention from the staff to allow some kind of cooling-out period for this individual. Also, because Jamaica will be a cashless system, they’ll also be able to track the pattern of a player to see his betting patterns and some form of intervention can be implemented because of that pattern of constant gambling, constant topping up, constant chasing, constant losses,” he added.

Allen also assured that responsible-gaming controls will extend to how casinos advertise and promote their services.

He said s should not target children or young people and should not rely on influential figures who children might look up to.

He also noted that the CGC intends to leverage existing responsible-gambling programmes, including initiatives involving schools, while keeping casino-related promotion within the resort environment.

World.title: Sheree Martin named first female CEO of NCBJ, effective Sept 1
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — After months of acting in the post, Sheree Martin has been appointed chief executive officer by the Board of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), effective September 1, 2026.

She will be the first woman to hold the post.

Martin served as interim CEO since January 19, 2026, leading the bank’s strategic and operational priorities with a focus on efficiency, governance and the customer experience.

In a statement, the bank said her appointment provides continuity as it continues to work on the same priorities. Group Chief Executive Officer of NCB Financial Group Limited and Chairman of NCBJ Robert Almeida said Martin’s leadership during the interim period reinforced the board’s confidence in her ability to lead the bank.

“Sheree brings deep institutional knowledge, a strong understanding of our customers and a clear appreciation of how the different parts of the Bank must work together to deliver,” Almeida said.

“She combines strategic judgement with practical, hands-on leadership and a strong focus on execution. These qualities will serve NCBJ well as it builds on the progress already underway.”

Martin said she was honoured by the appointment and energised by the opportunities ahead.

“NCBJ has an extraordinary legacy, talented people and a vital role in the lives of our customers and in Jamaica’s development,” she said. “I look forward to working with our board and teams to build on that foundation – accelerating our progress, strengthening the customer experience and bringing the full capabilities of the bank together more effectively.”

She added, “Our priorities are clear: empower our people within the right culture, improve the way we deliver and earn our customers’ confidence through the quality and consistency of the service, financial solutions and platforms they experience every day.”

Martin brings more than 20 years of executive leadership experience across the financial services and energy sectors. Before assuming the role of interim CEO at NCB, she had leadership responsibility for several functions including retail banking, operations, credit underwriting, marketing and enterprise information management.

World.title: Former gang member found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Rapper Tupac Shakur attends a voter registration event in South Central Los Angeles, August15, 1996. (AP Photo/Frank Wiese, File)

LAS VEGAS, United States (AFP) — Duane Davis, a former Los Angeles gang member, was found guilty on Monday by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur.

Thirty years after the rap legend’s death at a Las Vegas casino, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.

World.title: Crackdown on care
World.content:
TUFTON...people must play their part...or they make way for someone else to do itPhoto: Garfield Robinson

SPURRED by more than 1,000 patient complaints in the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s Client Care Connect report, portfolio Minister Dr Christopher Tufton says efforts to expose system failures and hold negligent medical professionals accountable will intensify.

The move comes as the ministry prepares to publish its accountability data in September, which Tufton says highlighted various client complaints of poor communication, professional conduct, and overall patient experience.

“We’re looking to transform the health workforce. We are taking an inward look, recognising that a highly qualified health system cannot exist without sound governance, and that transformation requires effective leadership, which will be essential to managing the critical components of health.

“So when we speak about an accountability framework, it’s about delivering service with compassion, with empathy and, of course, ensuring that every patient is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness at every point of care,” said the minister as he delivered the keynote address at the Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston in St Andrew last Friday.

According to him, the report’s data aims to isolate departments and individuals responsible for poor patient experiences rather than allowing the failures of some to tarnish the reputation of the wider health-care system.

“Where there is a problem, we need to identify the institution, the department, and who is in charge. You have to start with all the names, because you can’t allow one bad apple to spoil the whole lot…Tell me where the worst experience takes place, the bad experience; tell me which department, and tell me who is in charge.

“And what leadership ought now to do is to address the specifics of a problem. Stop generalising the problem, because we’re letting down people who make sacrifices every day to do the work, and that’s a new modus operandi…People must play their part, and we must emphasise and insist on it, or they make way for someone else to do it,” charged Tufton.

The minister’s push for greater accountability comes amid heightened public scrutiny of the health-care system after the death of 33-year-old Kenise Dunn gained widespread media traction. The eight-month pregnant mother of three passed away at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days post-delivery.

When asked if his call for accountability extended to the contentious incident, Tufton told the Jamaica Observer that he cannot comment conclusively while the investigation is ongoing. Still, he emphasised that health-care professionals are always bound by a duty of care. “What I’ve heard, preliminary, is that, clinically, there was a diagnosis of the problem, but it appears, based on some of the feedback — including from persons who are on the ward — that maybe the management of the customer care and the empathy to the patient may have been less than desired. Now, I don’t have the final report, so I prefer not to conclude on that,” he said. “But the truth is drawn from what I said about the complaints report, the 1,000, which I spoke to, it’s quite clear that while we have excellent health workers, we have to work harder at delivering service with compassion and with empathy. And it’s not good enough to just have technical competence. If you treat people badly, if you don’t listen to them, if you don’t respond to them, if you don’t give them a sense of comfort when they’re in distress, then it hampers the healing process,” said the minister. In the meantime, Tufton urged the 141 recipients of the Barry Wint medical grant, valued at over $190 million, to be the difference once they enter their respective fields of practice. “I say this at the risk of offending some, that money is not the primary issue in health care, currently public health; the primary issue is how we conduct ourselves within the system. People who are in the system only for a pay cheque are not sufficiently willing to give the commitment and show care. You cannot afford to be like that. You have to show a better way, and that’s what Barry Wint is investing in. Not just in your capacity as a technical and competent person, but in moving the process forward,” the minister said. Pointing to what he identified as the major weaknesses of the system, Tufton noted that health care in Jamaica lacks a sufficient number of practitioners — specifically specialised individuals — and professionals with the capacity to show empathy to patients. He reiterated that that was not the type of behaviour that he expected from recipients of the Barry Wint scholarship, and challenged them to become “a catalyst for change”. “If you just want to be a nurse, a doctor, a biotech engineer because at the end of the month you’re going to get a fat pay cheque, and that’s the only driving motivation to apply and to pretty up the application for this money, do not accept it. There are too many people in the profession who see the profession only in financial terms, and not enough as a passion and commitment to enhance service delivery for those who need it, Jamaicans who are in distress,” he said firmly.

World.title: Jamaicans loud and proud!
World.content:
Trinidad and Tobago’s High Commissioner to Jamaica Deborah Thomas-Felix shares her admiration for the manner in which Jamaicans display pride in their country while speaking at the Jamaica Observer Press Club last Friday. Photo: Naphtali Junior

FROM schoolchildren in the country’s colours to packed cultural events, Trinidad and Tobago’s new High Commissioner Deborah Thomas-Felix says the unapologetic pride Jamaicans display in their identity is one of the things that has impressed her most since taking up her post.

Having lived in several Caribbean countries, Thomas-Felix said Jamaica’s expression of national pride stands out to her because of how openly it is displayed in everyday life, from the workplace to sporting and cultural events.

She was particularly struck by the way Jamaicans embrace national occasions, including Jamaica Day, when people turn out in the country’s colours, adding that the celebration of national identity extends beyond the traditional observances of Independence and Emancipation.

“You all have a national day — schoolchildren, big people going to work in Jamaica colours. I was so struck by that when I experienced it… Don’t get me wrong, because Trinidad and Tobago has a deep sense of pride and love, but it’s the way, the open way in which it’s displayed in Jamaica,” she expressed during the a Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s Beechwood Avenue, St Andrew, headquarters last Friday.

For Thomas-Felix, the pride is also visible in how Jamaica celebrates its culture, with Reggae Month — commemorated in February — providing an entire month of activities centred on one of the country’s most recognisable cultural exports.

She said that visible enthusiasm has helped her better understand Jamaicans in the Diaspora.

“Everywhere you go within the country, they say, ‘Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica, Jamaica,’ and I think that is so encouraging, and it gives me a better understanding of the Jamaicans I know who don’t live in Jamaica,” she said.

Thomas-Felix, whose parents are Grenadians and who has lived in St Vincent, Barbados, and Trinidad and Tobago, stressed that she was not suggesting that Trinbagonians lack national pride, but said she was particularly impressed by how visibly Jamaicans express theirs.

“There’s this open display of pride, and I think you all should keep that. I think that is just an excellent way to let [future] generations inherit that and continue with that, because I really, really like that,” she said.

Her comments come as Thomas-Felix seeks to strengthen ties between Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago across areas including trade, culture, and people-to-people relations.

She said the relationship between the two countries extends well beyond governments, pointing to Trinidadians who have built lives and careers in Jamaica and Jamaicans who have done the same in Trinidad and Tobago.

For Thomas-Felix, those personal connections are part of the Caribbean relationship that she wants to strengthen during her tenure.

“So the relationship is way beyond government to government, it’s really about people, and we interact through music, we interact in terms of culture, and so I want to really strengthen those bonds,” she said.

World.title: Slow movement on Spring Mount road repairs
World.content:
Residents of Spring Mount listen keenly as manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw (left) provides an update on plans to rehabilitate collapsed roads in the area.

SPRING MOUNT, St James — A soil test is among the items to be done before the State-run National Works Agency (NWA) can finalise a design to rebuild Spring Mount road in south St James. Last October’s Hurricane Melissa caused two major breakaways on the heavily trafficked route, leaving commuters with the choice of engaging in risky road use or a much longer, more costly journey.

With schools about to reopen, residents of Spring Mount and neighbouring areas have become increasingly anxious for an update on what is being done to fix the road. They were given the clearest signal, Thursday evening, that the road will likely be rebuilt in the same location; but there was no timeline on when work will start.

“We are looking to build back the road. We have looked at different possibilities and I can tell you straight up, one of the things that we are looking at is to take down the hillside and acquire [those] two houses on top of the hill,” manager of communication and customer services at the National Works Agency (NWA) Stephen Shaw told residents during a meeting held at Spring Mount Basic School.

He said the goal is to rehabilitate the roadway as soon as possible, restoring the vital connection between the north and south of the parish. The damage has made safe passage by vehicular traffic impossible just beyond Spring Mount Police Station. Residents have established a pedestrian path which is sometimes utilised by motorcyclists.

Shaw made it clear that there will be challenges in executing the project, given its scope and magnitude.

“It is not the normal run of the mill [approach of] looking at it as a breakaway, put up a wall, backfill it, and move on. No. We are going to have to do what are called bore hole tests,” he warned, adding that this falls outside the technical capabilities of the NWA and a private sector firm would have to be engaged.

These tests, he explained, will provide laboratory-based information on the soil in the area that will guide the designs on which work has already started.

“That testing of the material beneath there will inform us as to what else, if required, needs to be done to ensure that… when we build up that road, you have it longer than all of us inside here will live,” Shaw told the audience.

“Based on the survey that was executed, a design is being worked on but that design will not be finalised until the boreholes are done,” he added.

He explained the importance of the soil tests.

“A crucial factor in this area is the springs. It’s called Spring Mount for a reason. We have to design with that in mind to ensure that we don’t see a situation where we build a big wall, costing a lot of money… and then, [as seen in other locations] rain came, and the entire retaining wall just moved like… it was plastic,” Shaw outlined.

“We have that kind of experience and historical knowledge on which to build or not to build. We are not taking anything lightly in ensuring that the design solutions that we come up with, they are adequate, they are appropriate, are sufficient, and necessary for the particular areas that we are going to be working,” he added.

Responding to residents’ questions about timelines, the NWA representative said he was unable to provide one as it depends on the soil testing which is being done outside of the agency. He did, however, promise to explore ways in which alternate routes — such as the journey through Kempshot, up the treacherous Charlie Mount — may be improved.

Councillor Uvel Graham (Jamaica Labour Party, Spring Mount Division) was at the meeting and while he acknowledged that the project is complex he expressed frustration that it is moving too slowly.

“To be honest, I was looking for more of a timeline and that these tests would be done already and people would be hearing that the next two to three months, the work would start,” he told the

Jamaica Observer after the meeting.

World.title: ‘I’ve run my leg’
World.content:
GREENE...I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AFTER a brief but impactful two-year term as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Health and Wellness, Errol Greene is ready to pass the baton, proud of his legacy but acknowledging that critical work remains.

“As we gather to award students pursuing courses in public health, I am filled with mixed emotions. I’m filled with mixed emotions because this is my last time serving within the context as permanent secretary here at the Ministry of Health and Wellness,” said Greene, as he formally announced his retirement from the role — which takes effect Monday, August 31 — while delivering greetings at the Dr Barry Wint Memorial Scholarship Awards Ceremony at S Hotel Kingston last Friday.

Under the scholarship, named in honour of the former chief medical officer, recipients are awarded up to $1 million annually for health care-related studies in priority fields such as nursing, biomedical engineering, and medicine.

For this year’s staging, 141 awardees were selected from more than 700 applicants to benefit from over $190 million in scholarships, with the Government having spent approximately $900 million towards the initiative to date.

“While there’s a sense of nostalgia, there’s also a sense of tremendous pride and optimism as I look out at this room filled with talented, ambitious, enthusiastic, and determined persons who represent the future of health care in Jamaica,” said Greene, who noted that he would continue to watch their progress as professionals in the health field from the sidelines.

When asked by the Jamaica Observer if his retirement signalled a complete departure from public service, Greene offered a cryptic, “We’ll see how it goes.” However, he maintained that he is ready to hand over the reins to a capable professional who can drive the remaining work forward.

“We have done well, and we can do better. I certainly want to be a part of the journey because I know my minister is passionate about health, he’s passionate about service delivery, and I would have run my leg of the race and I have handed over the baton, so I’ll just go in the pavilion and watch the race finish,” he said.

Before his two-year stint as permanent secretary, Greene led a career spanning decades. His life as a public servant began when he assumed the role of town clerk of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) and also served at the St Thomas Municipal Corporation.

He then pivoted to begin service in the health sector, serving as regional director of the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), which oversees health services in Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, and St Catherine.

He was also a former regional director of Western Regional Health Authority and a former chief executive officer of the Kingston Public Hospital.

Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton, who delivered the keynote address at the scholarship event, used the opportunity to acknowledge Greene’s contributions and bid him farewell.

“Our permanent secretary, who is not riding off in the sunset, but is closing one chapter to start another, Mr Errol Greene…give him a round of applause, please. I believe he has done 50 years, thereabout. I don’t want to tell his age, because he is still young,” joked Tufton. “But he has done a whole heap of years, whole heap of decades to public service, and I just want to recognise him and thank him for his services.”

World.title: Europe gears up for its China counterpunch
World.content:
Brussels is getting increasingly worried about its economic relationship with Beijing … but the bloc doesn’t want to bring out the big guns just yet.

While the EU already has the infamous ‘trade bazooka’ at its disposal, the Commission is considering a new tool to address Chinese overcapacity and dangerous dependencies. Our colleague Camille Gijs has spoken with EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to learn more. Hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss what he said in the interview.

Next, EU defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today, and Ukraine is right at the top of the agenda. The big question will be whether the bloc can help ease Kyiv’s shortage of missile interceptors.

And finally, is Europe’s most prominent right-wing think tank, MCC Brussels, imploding … or is it morphing into something new?
