World.title: Labour’s new housing model comes from California’s backyards
World.content:
Experts think the tweaks could help the government stretch towards its target of building 1.5 million new homes before the next general election, but note the risk of a political backlash among local residents worried about their neighborhoods losing their character and green spaces and becoming overwhelmed.

“It could be significant and it’s certainly creative,” said Simon Creer from the Royal Town Planning Institute. “But it’s hard to say definitively what the increase in housing delivery could be, and whether it will be popular. There’s always a fundamental tension between the need for more homes and the potential local backlash about where those homes are and what they look like, which is why early, meaningful communication with communities matters.”

Indeed, planning changes around garden use during the previous Labour government in the 2000s led to public outrage about homes being demolished so speculators could cram properties into available land, as well as fears about destruction of green spaces. Labour was forced to intervene on what was dubbed “garden grabbing” as the 2010 election loomed, then the successor Conservative-Lib Dem administration was quick to change the rules.

Now the government has tweaked them again to fuel development on and around existing buildings, instructing planning committees via national guidance to favor upward extensions to homes and commercial buildings and filling gaps around houses.

The aim is densification: increasing the number of homes on a designated land mass.

“These changes are in line with our push for urban and suburban intensification, aiming to unlock private land and speed up small-scale construction alongside major transport-hub and grey-belt redevelopment,” said a government official who was granted anonymity to speak about the plans.

World.title: Britain’s Liberal Democrats get a new think tank
World.content:
The think tank is not formally affiliated to Ed Davey’s party, but at least 50 of his 71 MPs attended a presentation promoting its work during one of their regular parliamentary meetings in July — with many indicating they want to get involved.

Tim Leunig, the group’s policy director, who recently became a Liberal Democrat peer in Britain’s unelected House of Lords, said: “We are here to help them.”

“But we’re also here to ask them tough questions because: who knows? They might be a minister one day, and then the civil service will ask them tough questions.”

While in public the Lib Dems refuse to countenance any future deal with Burnham’s Labour, in private their MPs are frank that the opinion polls — which anyone can read — point to the two parties’ combined seat totals being an obvious route to a post-election majority.

Luke Tryl, executive director of More in Common, a think tank which tracks public opinion, said the “ever more acrimonious” battle for the right now makes a pact between the Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK “less likely.”

“The Burnham bounce and consolidation of the progressive left vote makes a Lib-Lab pact a more likely prospect,” he said.

World.title: Marine Le Pen’s risky economic gamble
World.content:
She also said she would soon present a plan to cut some €125 billion in spending, including on budget items associated with migration, “useless” public agencies, and France’s contribution to the EU. Le Pen will present her detailed platform in the fall, but Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a member of Parliament for the National Rally, told POLITICO this would be accomplished in “less than five years.”

But Le Pen has yet to explain in detail how those savings would be achieved, and rivals are already questioning whether the numbers add up. “Marine Le Pen will ruin France,” Bruno Retailleau, a conservative candidate from Les Républicains, told reporters shortly after the Medef event.

Marine Le Pen and François Durvye visit the VivaTech technology startups and innovation fair at the Paris Expo Porte de Versailles, in Paris on June 19, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images

The tension has also surfaced inside her own camp. As Le Pen was outlining her economic agenda at the Medef event, news broke that François Durvye, one of her key economic advisers and a leading advocate of greater fiscal discipline, was leaving the campaign.

Internal cracks

Durvye, who has informally advised Le Pen for five years, has been credited with building bridges between her party and the business world. A former fund manager, he was a key voice in the party on economic issues.

But his push for more fiscal discipline and economically liberal policies ran against the instincts of the party’s old guard, which remained wedded to the party’s populist positions. He was also a special advisor to National Rally President Jordan Bardella, Le Pen’s protégé who was expected to take the campaign’s reins if Le Pen had been judged ineligible to run because of her guilty verdict for embezzlement of EU funds.

Bardella has been working to move the party toward the center on economic issues, including softening Le Pen’s pledge on the pension age — something that Durvye had been advocating for internally.

World.title: What 248 books reveal about Kaja Kallas
World.content:
EU's top diplomat is a noted bookworm. But what can her bookshelf tell us about the politician leading Europe's diplomacy?

While actively running the EU’s foreign policy on the world’s most demanding issues, Kaja Kallas still finds time outside work to read about … more foreign policy.

The top EU diplomat and former Estonian prime minister frequently talks about her love of reading, citing her favorite authors in speeches and meeting with them privately to discuss their work. Since taking up her most recent post in December 2024, she has read at least 52 books she has shared publicly — all of which she has posted on her Instagram — most of them related to international affairs. In total, she has shared more than 200 titles since 2017.

“You know, my reading list is quite long,” said Kallas, who officially serves as the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, at a press conference in January. “By the end, when I finish this job, I will be very smart,” she joked.





The collection closely tracks the subjects Kallas is most involved with in her role, evolving alongside her professional remit: 24 books on Russia and Ukraine, nine on China, and seven on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Further-flung regions pop up only rarely, with just three books on the rest of East Asia and none on South American politics beyond Venezuela.

“Reading books is a valuable advantage, especially as it is not so common nowadays,” an official from Kallas’ team told POLITICO. “The Middle East wars, Russia’s aggression and China’s growing influence are major geopolitical issues, so naturally they feature on the High Representative’s reading list.” Noting that she meets with ministers, officials, staff and experts daily and receives countless briefing papers, memos and other sources of information, “books are a nice addition on long-distance flights,” the official added.

The reading lists alone have not shaped the full contours of Kallas’ foreign policy, of course. But they provide a view into which political subjects Europe’s chief diplomat is interested in learning more about and where she goes looking for answers.

So, what does Kallas’ bookshelf reveal about the person shaping Europe’s diplomacy? To find out, POLITICO reviewed the 248 titles she has included on public reading lists since 2017 and spoke to 24 of the authors.

Noted bookworm

Kallas is not the only avid reader in Brussels, but few politicians talk about their love of literature quite as often. Since 2023, she has released reading lists twice a year on Instagram, and before that, she blogged about her latest reads monthly.

“I read a lot, but you’re always influenced by the books you’ve read most recently,” Kallas told POLITICO in 2025.

Political scientist Ivan Krastev, who co-authored 2019’s “The Light That Failed: A Reckoning” on why liberalism failed to spread in Eastern Europe, said Kallas had reached out to him after reading his book. She was trying to find a publisher to translate it into her native Estonian, he told POLITICO. The translation was eventually released in 2022.





While Kallas was prime minister, her government had similarly pushed for the translation of political scientist Mark Leonard’s “The Age of Unpeace: How Connectivity Causes Conflict,” which she said she would “often cite.”

“It’s interesting, particularly when a politician in a high position reads a book,” said Krastev. “They’re trying to make sense of their own experience” and “trying to answer some of the questions that [they] are struggling with.”

Indeed, Kallas’ book choices appear to closely reflect her scheduled diplomatic trips. Visiting Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in June this year, the top diplomat had read the memoirs of Richard Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton Accords in Bosnia, and Martti Ahtisaari, the former Finnish president and mediator of the 1999 Kumanovo Agreement forcing Serbia’s withdrawal from Kosovo.

“A lot to learn also today, and actually a lot of parallels,” said Kallas of Holbrooke’s book in July.

Ahead of her trip to Sarajevo a month later, she then contacted former Swedish Prime Minister and High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina Carl Bildt about his 1998 book “Peace Journey: The Struggle for Peace in Bosnia,” a memoir about his work in the region.

“She sent me a text and said, ‘I’m reading your book, and I like it very much.’ And I said, ‘How on earth did you get hold of that one?'” Bildt told POLITICO, joking that the book was published nearly three decades ago. “She wanted to go down into the weeds of the history … and that could be useful.”





Earlier in the year, after the U.S. forcibly captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Kallas picked up two books about the South American country, too: “Comandante: Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela” and “Things Are Never So Bad That They Can’t Get Worse: Inside the Collapse of Venezuela.”

“She is one of the best-read people I know,” said Marietje Schaake, a friend and former liberal MEP who served with Kallas in the European Parliament. “That depth has shaped her thinking and her career.”

What’s in the library?

Six of the authors who spoke to POLITICO for this article specifically cited Kallas’ hawkish stance on Moscow as echoing the messages in their books — perhaps unsurprising given Kallas warned of Russia’s threat to Europe back in 2021, during her first term as prime minister.

“What is happening in Ukraine right now is what I was reading about in our own history books,” she told Vogue Greece in 2023.

Sylvie Kauffmann, author of 2023’s “Blindsided” (Les aveuglés) — which argues that Germany and France failed to recognize the Russian threat — told POLITICO her book “confirms everything that Kallas thinks” about how others downplayed Moscow’s aggression.





Speaking to POLITICO about his 2018 book “Identity,” famed political philosopher of liberal democracy Francis Fukuyama said the work contained “a kind of ideological roadmap to be able to better explain what it is that … we’re fighting for.” Noting that Ukraine’s fight against Russia was one of the reasons he wrote it, Fukuyama then praised the chief diplomat’s support for the country.

Kallas has also read extensively on Israel-Palestine, a conflict on which her stance has attracted both attention and controversy in Brussels.

Far more critical of Israel than her peers in the European Commission, Kallas reportedly compared the situation on the ground to South Africa under apartheid during a closed-door meeting in June, causing Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to sever contact.

Kaja Kallas at the E5 defence ministers meeting in Krakow, Poland on Feb. 20, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images

Two of the authors on the subject who feature on Kallas’ reading lists told POLITICO her reported comparison mirrored the arguments made in their books, with 2024 Pulitzer Prize winner Nathan Thrall saying his “aim in writing [“A Day in the Life of Abed Salama: Anatomy of a Jerusalem Tragedy”] was to influence people like her.”

“The fact that she has come to the conclusion that Israel is practicing apartheid is most welcome as far as I’m concerned,” he said.

“I explain the aspects of apartheid, and I hope she’d see that her judgment is well founded,” echoed Michael Scott-Baumann, author of “Palestinians and Israelis: A Short History of Conflict.”





But not every author on Kallas’ lists approves of her foreign policy decisions when it comes to their topics of specialization.

Kim Ghattas, who wrote her book “Black Wave” on the Middle East, for example, said Kallas has been too passive on the Israeli-U.S. war with Iran. “That is not good policymaking. I would hope that reading books like mine can help prepare policymakers like her, specifically for moments like the one that we find ourselves in right now.”

Former U.S. National Security Adviser John Bolton, who has long advocated for regime change in Iran, said he, too, wished Kallas had become more involved — though in support of President Donald Trump’s military operation.

He also noted that Kallas’ blunt style risked further alienating the U.S. from the EU, with her comments advocating for the bloc’s sovereignty “giving [Trump] the excuse to do what he probably wants to do anyway.”

Criticism extended beyond the Middle East as well. Robert D. Kaplan, author of 1993’s “Balkan Ghosts” — which heavily influenced former U.S. President Bill Clinton’s initial reluctance to militarily intervene in the region, according to his biographers — told POLITICO that Kallas’ impolitic moments “may be things that she’ll come to partially regret over time.”

“When you get far quick, you tend to make mistakes. Because you’re confident, you’re even arrogant,” said Kaplan.

Booking ahead

It’s not all about world affairs and global diplomacy, though — some of Kallas’ more recent political predicaments lie a little closer to home.

Recent months have seen the top diplomat losing a turf war with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the bloc’s foreign policy, while her diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, has struggled to build consensus across a divided Europe.

So with the rentrée almost upon us in Brussels, there may be no better time for Kallas to get through a few more books — a strategy she has turned to previously.





While serving as prime minister, during a 2023 podcast, Kallas recalled how she once considered foreign policy to be her greatest political weakness — until she turned to books.

“It’s not my weakness anymore because I’ve read so much about this,” she said.

Perhaps this time it will be Brussels that sends her back to the stacks.

World.title: Two dead and one still unaccounted for in Grand Canyon flash floods, officials say
World.content:
The number of people unaccounted for after a deadly flash flood hit part of the Grand Canyon has fallen to one as US Park Rangers said they had managed to make contact with over a dozen people who had been missing.

 

A monsoonal downpour that lashed the northern side of the huge canyon sent torrents of water, rock and debris down a popular hiking course on Saturday, washing out campgrounds in Bright Angel Canyon and around the historic Phantom Ranch.

Two men are known to have died in the sudden flood whose bodies were recovered as search and rescue teams moved in, amid fears that many more could have been swept away at one of the most popular and dramatic tourist spots in the United States.

But late on Monday, Dave Black of the National Park Service said nearly all those who were known to be in the canyon had now been found.

"There is one person unaccounted for that we know of right now," he told reporters in Grand Canyon Village, Arizona.

Black said 82 people had been rescued over Saturday and Sunday as a huge operation swung into gear and rangers had been canvassing the park's camping permit system to determine who might have been there when disaster struck.

Dave Black, an incident commander at Grand Canyon National Park, provides updates on deadly flash flooding from the canyon's South Rim, 31 August, 2026 AP Photo

"They've cross-checked between permits, license plates, any information they have, and talked to family members, made sure that they were out," he said.

Rescue efforts were hampered on Monday by more heavy rains that swept through the region, a natural part of the seasonal monsoon that frequently causes flash floods in the many creeks, gullies and washes that make up the arid landscape.

Black said better weather expected on Tuesday would help in the hunt for the one person still known to be missing, as well as any day hikers who may have been caught up in the flood. Day hikers do not require a permit to be in the canyon.

"We are still actively searching...we are absolutely holding out hope that that person is still alive," Black said.

Water pipeline damaged

The flooding damaged or destroyed 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said on Monday.

It announced water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires in areas where the lack of water might hamper firefighting efforts.

The 20-kilometre pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park's website.

The flooding also resulted in "significant impacts to infrastructure," destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said.

The Grand Canyon remained open to visitors, despite the tragedy. On Monday, dozens of people, many of them foreign tourists, huddled under umbrellas or wore rain ponchos as they stood on the South Rim snapping selfies and straining to make out the Colorado River far below.

People stand at the rim of the Grand Canyon, 31 August, 2026 AP Photo

Trails down into the canyon from the South Rim were also passable, but staff were warning of the potential dangers, with sudden squalls possible at any time.

The hike down into the wild belly of the canyon from one popular starting point takes many visitors around four hours, one staff member said, while the return journey would likely add another six.

Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments there have little capacity to absorb rain, the park's website said, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September.

World.title: Cancer and virus-free: Bats' longevity genes could hold clues for human health
World.content:
Bats are the longest-lived mammals for their size and have the ability to adapt to viruses and boost their defences. Scientists are now trying to see whether humans can learn anything from bats’ ability to resist viruses and even prevent cancer.

 

A new study published in the journal Nature looked at what these animals can teach about longevity and fighting disease. The findings reveal that the bats' ability to slow ageing and tolerate viruses is genetically linked, suggesting that the same biological 'tricks' protect them from both infections and the decay of old age

“Bats have evolved this incredible fitness capacity, this incredible ability to deal with disease and this incredible ability to be able to prevent cancer,” said Juan Manuel Vazquez, author of the study at the University of California, Berkeley.

“That means that, by understanding how bats have evolved to do all these things that other mammals haven’t, we can find completely new and unexpected ways of dealing with the normal things that cause human diseases.”

For the study, Vazquez travelled to capture, biopsy and release different species of bats. He currently has cell cultures from 259 individuals representing 32 species.

He focused on those in the Myotis genus of bats, known for having some of the most extreme adaptations for longevity and disease resistance among mammals. In this group, the Myotis brandtii (Brandt’s bat) can live up to 42 years.

How bats resist ageing and cancer

By creating high-quality genetic maps for eight different species, the researchers identified the specific biological "tricks" these animals use to survive.

One of the most important findings is that long-lived bats have evolved ways to prevent cancer. For example, the little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus) has an enhanced ability to clear out damaged cells before they can cause harm.

An example of this is a specific immune factor called PKR, as most Myotis species have evolved extra copies of this gene to fight a wider range of viruses.

A different way of fighting viruses

Bats act as zoonotic reservoirs — animals that can carry viruses dangerous to humans without becoming ill themselves. Their ability to do this is a result of a specialised evolutionary strategy known as viral tolerance.

The research found that while most mammals use "resistance" to fight viruses by attempting to eliminate the pathogen, bats have evolved high levels of viral tolerance.

They have developed mechanisms to suppress the damaging inflammation and cellular stress that would normally kill other mammals, which allows the virus to live in their bodies.

For RNA viruses, responsible for human outbreaks such as the COVID-19 pandemic, bats tend to change the number of immune genes they have and evolve extra copies to broaden their defence.

What this means for human disease

Because bats have developed natural solutions to problems like cancer and cellular decay, they provide a roadmap for understanding how these same processes might be managed in humans, the researchers said.

Vazquez noted that bats evolved to live for a long time without getting diseases, which suggests we don't necessarily need to look at diseases of ageing and diseases of infection as completely separate fields.

“We can look at these bats and try to understand how, in the same way you can improve your immune system to fight off viruses, maybe you can improve your immune system so it doesn’t decline in old age,” he noted.

“Or maybe bats can help us find ways to fight off tumors so our immune system doesn’t get tired, and that can also help us deal with other stresses of life and not exhaust our immunity.”

World.title: Heatwaves and secret emissions: Why nuclear power may not be as ‘green’ as you think
World.content:
The world stood still on 11 March 2011, when a major earthquake triggered a 15-metre tsunami that left an unforgettable scar on Japan’s east coast.

 

A series of powerful waves ripped through homes, businesses and roads – leaving more than 450,000 people homeless and killing 15,500. Alongside the chaos, the tsunami caused the meltdown of three nuclear reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, spewing out toxic, radioactive materials and forcing thousands to evacuate.

The event triggered global conversation about the safety of nuclear energy, leading several countries to plan to phase out nuclear energy or stop its expansion.

But 15 years later and the horrors of Fukushima have slowly been replaced with calls to double down on nuclear power, particularly following the war on Iran and its subsequent energy crisis. Speaking exclusively to Euronews, EU Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra listed nuclear as one of the power sources EU countries must lean on.

However, an expert from the University of Oxford has warned that new nuclear capacity will not fix today’s energy problems – urging policy makers to consider the true risks of nuclear.

“In the high‑renewables systems of Europe, the problem is increasingly not how to generate more electricity but how to access it when and where it’s needed,” says Dr Bettina Wittneben, a lecturer in Management at Oxford’s Saïd Business School and associate fellow at Pembroke College and the School of Geography and the Environment.

Is nuclear power really ‘clean’?

Nuclear energy is often touted as a clean form of energy as it is low carbon at the point of generation.

In layman’s terms, nuclear reactors can create electricity without releasing carbon dioxide or smog-forming pollutants into the atmosphere. However, experts point out that this isn’t the full picture.

“The bulky concrete structures mean that it has a large amount of embodied carbon and, of course, it is not a renewable energy as it requires the mining of uranium, bringing with it carbon costs in terms of extraction and transport,” says Dr Bettina.

“Nuclear waste disposal and decommissioning must also be factored into the carbon budget of nuclear energy generation.”

Are nuclear power plants climate resilient?

Europe was scorched by back-to-back heatwaves this summer, which experts say would have been “virtually impossible” if it weren’t for climate change. The extreme heat, combined with scant rainfall, triggered droughts across much of the continent, draining some of Europe’s biggest rivers to record-level lows.

This forced several nuclear power plants to temporarily shut off or be set to a reduced output across France, Hungary and Romania.

Nuclear requires vast amounts of water, particularly for the cooling process, and is often known as the “thirstiest power source”. According to The Nuclear Energy Institute, one nuclear reactor requires between 1,514 and 2,725 litres of water per MWh – equating to hundreds of gigalitres every year.

It’s why nuclear power plants are often built near large bodies of water. Without a constant, reliable source of water a nuclear reactor risks overheating – which could lead to serious core damage and end up releasing harmful radiation into the environment.

Coal power and hydropower also suffered during the heatwave, but a surge in solar power helped meet heightened electricity demand from cooling devices such as air conditioning.

According to energy think-tank Ember, solar output in European countries rose by up to 17 per cent on heatwave days in June and July – becoming the only major power source to perform “better than usual” during hot weather.

'Hellbrise': Nuclear is not as reliable as some say

Intermittent forms of energy such as wind and solar are often blamed for overloading Europe’s outdated energy grid.

When electricity demand outstrips supply, surplus energy is often wasted – and can lead to negative electricity prices. This is often referred to as 'Hellbrise' (hell= bright, brise= breeze) and can occur on sunny, windy days.

“This is also the narrative of fossil fuel advocates, who present fossil gas as the saviour of the baseload, or the electricity that is available when renewables fall short,” says Dr Wittneben.

“Fossil fuel sceptics point instead to nuclear power as a reliable baseload technology.”

However, the expert points out that nuclear power plants are slow and costly to turn off, which means they only “amplify” the grid’s Hellbrise challenge – rather than present a solution to it.

The EU has recognised that battery energy storage systems (BESS) are a “crucial technology” to help prevent renewable energy from being wasted or entering sub-zero pricing. The logic is that batteries can store electricity produced by renewables during the day (when consumption tends to be low) and release it to households when demand increases in the evening.

Europe installed 36 GWh of new BESS in 2025, bringing its total operational capacity beyond 100 GWh for the first time. This is enough stored energy to power around 75 million homes.

Chart showing electricity sources in Europe and the World in 2025 Ember Electricity Data Explorer, ember-energy.org

Which EU countries have become reliant on nuclear power?

Last year, the European Union generated 652TWh of electricity from nuclear, representing 23.3 per cent of the bloc’s total electricity mix.

This was more than solar (13.1 per cent) and wind (17.1 per cent) – and put nuclear as the largest share of electricity generation for 2025.

More than half of this (392 TWh) was generated in France, which has the biggest nuclear output across the bloc. In fact, France generated more than two-thirds (68.8 per cent) of its electricity from nuclear last year.

This was followed by Spain (54.1 TWh), Sweden (46.7 TWh), Finland (32.8 TWh), Czechia (31.9 TWh), Belgium (24.1 TWh), Slovakia (19.3 TWh), Hungary (16.1 TWh), Bulgaria (14.8 TWh), Romania (10.2 TWh), Slovenia (5.83 TWh) and the Netherlands (3.99 TWh).

Because European power grids are interconnected, many countries that do not have active nuclear power plants can purchase electricity generated by nuclear power from other EU countries. In 2024, France was Europe’s biggest electricity exporter – and much of this was generated from nuclear power.

But not every EU country is onboard with running nuclear power plants, particularly following the Fukushima incident.

Back in 2020, Germany generated 170 TWh of electricity from nuclear – putting it as the second largest producer in the EU. This was the year the country first passed a legal plan to end nuclear power.

Germany officially stopped using nuclear power for electricity on April 15, 2023, when it shut down its three final operating reactors.

The move was described as a “grave strategic mistake” by Chancellor Friedrich Merz – and saw the country’s reliance on polluting fossil fuels temporarily increase to bridge the gap in energy supply.

However, a recent analysis from think-tank Energy Institute found that together wind and solar generated 44 per cent of Germany’s electricity in 2025, overtaking fossil fuels by one per cent.

At the same time, coal fell from supplying more than half of the country’s electricity in 2000 to just 21 per cent last year. Experts are now hopeful that Germany will be able to wean itself off coal completely before 2038.

World.title: What are phantom scams, and why do they end with you robbing yourself?
World.content:
Phantom hacker scams, also known as phantom scams, have surged in recent years.

 

These are elaborate frauds in which criminals convince victims their money or computer has been compromised by a hacker. The scammer then pushes the victim to move their savings into a supposedly "safe" account, which is in fact controlled by the criminals themselves.

The rise of artificial intelligence, online banking and social media has fuelled the trend — more ways to pay and receive money mean more entry points for scammers to exploit.

How phantom hacker scams work

Some of the most common phantom hacker scams work in a few stages. The first one is tech support.

This usually involves a pop-up screen warning, text or call claiming that your computer or device has a virus. When you call the number provided, a person pretending to be tech support can ask you to download remote-access software.

The next phase is the fake bank alert. Another person might call you, claiming that your accounts are being hacked. Scammers may often spoof caller ID information, so you may believe that the call is from a legitimate phone number.

They may say that immediate action needs to be taken to protect your account and funds, so you need to log in right now to check your balance.

However, since they now have remote access to your device, they can watch you log in and gather your details.

The final phase is the government imposter one. This can involve a third person calling you, claiming to be from a government or law enforcement agency like the FBI or Federal Reserve.

They may pressure you to move your money into a supposedly “safe” account or direct it towards things like cryptocurrency and gold bars in order to protect it.

Some variations ask victims to download an app that supposedly speeds up fund transfers. In reality, this hands scammers remote access to the device, letting them steal money, often entire life savings, directly from the account.

The methods vary, but the underlying tactic is nearly always the same: create a sense of urgency and push victims into acting out of panic.

How to protect yourself

According to TEG Federal Credit Union, the best defence is simple: never trust unsolicited calls, texts or pop-ups about your bank account or computer. Hang up immediately if you receive one.

Never download remote-viewing software or apps at the request of someone who contacted you out of the blue.

If you suspect a scam, call your bank directly using the number on its website or on the back of your card.

No legitimate bank, tech company or government agency will ever ask you to move your savings into a "safe" account or buy gold or cryptocurrency.

How are phantom hacker scams different from phantom debt?

Unlike phantom hacker scams, which typically rely on gaining access to a victim’s money or bank account, phantom debt or zombie debt is a different type of scam. This involves scammers attempting to get victims to pay fake or expired debts.

While this was previously done through badly-written emails or unconvincing cold calls, today, scammers rely on large language models (LLMs) to write perfectly localised and highly convincing legal threats.

These debts might already have been paid off, discharged in bankruptcy or artificially inflated by shady operators.

Scammers usually pose as debt collectors and attempt to use aggressive language, fake threats of arrest or intimidation to scare victims into paying immediately.

In many cases, they may also use confusing language to explain how a debt that was previously thought to be paid off or cleared is still owed, while continuing to use intimidation and panic creation tactics to prevent victims from further digging into the mechanics.

This can especially be done to senior victims.

Scammers also leverage automated AI agents to scrape public information, build a profile on a target and use audio clips to clone voices, posing as law enforcement or bank officials.

Sometimes they may ask for crypto payments or wire transfers to settle these phantom debts.

Similar to phantom hacker scams, consumers should immediately hang up while receiving these calls, along with locking down their information and freezing payments.

They can also demand a validation letter, which real collectors in many jurisdictions are obliged to send, or block and report them.

World.title: EU needs European digital agency to close enforcement gap, experts say
World.content:
Brussels has built one of the world's densest regulatory frameworks for digital technologies. For experts, it is high time to centralise enforcement under a single European agency to overcome the fragmentation now holding it back.

 

The EU's digital rulebook spans more than 171 laws and 315 regulatory bodies — an unwieldy structure that has opened up a significant enforcement gap, leaving the bloc structurally unable to uphold its own rules.

That is the conclusion of a paper authored by Kai Zenner, head of office of MEP Axel Voss (Germany/EPP), and Maria Koomen, an independent tech and democracy analyst, who argue for the creation of a Digital Enforcement Agency.

The paper argues that streamlining enforcement is now urgent, just as Brussels has begun enforcing landmark digital laws such as the AI Act, the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA).

"Enforcement of the AI Act, DSA and DMA is ramping up, but their enforcement is split across more than 300 different EU and national bodies – many without the staff, expertise, or independence to act consistently," Koomen told Euronews.

For the authors, the European Commission — which leads enforcement of these flagship rules — is itself part of the problem, since it simultaneously legislates, enforces and evaluates while negotiating deals with foreign powers.

They point out that the EU executive is not only the bloc's most prominent digital enforcer but is also responsible for negotiating with third countries on issues such as trade and security, leaving it exposed to political pressure, or even inclined to underenforce pre-emptively.

Last year, media reports emerged that Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič had lobbied to delay an antitrust sanction against Google, for fear it could jeopardise the fragile trade truce between the EU and the US, known as the Turnberry Agreement.

For Koomen and Zenner, the combination of geopolitical capture, fragmented governance, the national interests of influential member states, and a lack of adequate resources together create an enforcement gap that leaves the EU's digital rules failing in practice.

The idea of centralising digital enforcement is not new, but has faced strong opposition in the past, with Brussels and national capitals reluctant to give up regulatory powers, and member states unwilling to finance a costly new EU body.

The paper proposes a three-step approach to overcome this resistance: starting with a short-lived cooperation forum, which would give way to a Digital Enforcement Agency in the medium term. The latter would gain fully independent status following treaty reform in the long run.

The authors argue there is a timely opportunity to act, with the Commission about to launch a broad review of EU digital legislation just as negotiations over the bloc's next long-term budget enter a crunch phase.

"A rare window is open to fix this structurally rather than patch it case by case," Koomen said. "If we miss this moment, the next opportunity will only come in seven years."

World.title: Schengen strained, solidarity broken and return hubs disputed: EU struggles again with migration
World.content:
Migration is taking center stage again in the European Union, as Brussels returns to work after a summer marked by the major crisis of recent years.

 

Over 70,000 irregular migrants entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in a single day on 30 July, more than all other irregular entries across all European borders so far in 2026, sparking a political crisis in Spain and putting other member states on alert.

The Ceuta crisis increased pressure on the EU to implement its strategy to tighten the rules for asylum seekers and speed up returns, but it also highlighted the shortcomings of the new migration rules as they face their first real stress test.

EU leaders are expected to debate the topic in October at the European Council in Brussels, the culmination of a season of heated discussions through formal and informal meetings of interior ministers and ambassadors.

Schengen in trouble

The first impact of the domino effect was on free movement within the EU.

After the Ceuta crisis, Italy reintroduced air and maritime border controls with Spain for a month, while other countries such as Denmark and Finland called for Spain to be temporarily suspended from the Schengen area, where citizens and residents have been able to move since 1985 without border checks.

Spain answered with a mirror retaliatory measure towards Italy, even copy-pasting the wording of the official notification, reintroducing border checks until 7 September. At the end of the month, both countries decided to extend the suspension for further 15 days.

And the Italian government is not the only one concerned that Schengen rules could indirectly benefit irregular movement.

In an extraordinary online meeting in Brussels in early August, EU interior ministers initiated a discussion over the future of free movement. Twenty-two governments stated that any "necessary measures" will be taken into account "to safeguard public order and address risks arising from secondary movements [of migrants]", envisaging a wider reinforcement or reintroduction of border controls.

"The Schengen system has become one of the main victims of the internal political dynamics and concerns by member states around migration," Davide Colombi, researcher on migration at Brussels-based think tank CEPS, told Euronews.

EU member states may unilaterally reintroduce temporary, ad hoc border checks at their borders for a period of up to six months — renewable up to two years — on security grounds.

Currently, nine EU countries — Germany, Spain, Italy, Denmark, Austria, the Netherlands, Poland, France and Sweden — plus Norway have temporarily reintroduced border controls, citing concerns over irregular migration or terrorism threats.

Member states started to retain their own border controls in 2015, with the so-called European refugee crisis, as the removal of internal checks within the EU is widely considered to be closely intertwined with the surveillance of external borders.

"Migration will have broad repercussions on internal movements. For the moment, the Commission is choosing diplomatic ways rather than enforcing EU law and challenging the reintroduction of border checks," Colombi said.

Related Ceuta crisis prompts EU ministers to consider internal border checks

Where is the solidarity?

Far from expressing solidarity, other EU countries accused Pedro Sánchez’s government, in the aftermath of the mass entry, of failing to sufficiently protect Europe’s external borders.

Solidarity is — on paper — one of the pillars of the new EU migration rules, which entered into force on 12 June.

The EU Migration and Asylum Pact entails a mandatory mechanism to assist the EU's frontline members, through a “solidarity pool” that defines the help countries need to offer each other for the following year. Member states have to choose among relocating a number of asylum seekers to their territory, paying a financial contribution, or financing personnel and other operational costs.

Redistribution of migrants across Europe is the most contentious point, as governments have little appetite for it and have managed to significantly reduce the numbers in the pool for 2026, asking for exemptions.

Relocations only apply to asylum seekers and people who have already been granted protection, therefore excluding most of the irregular Moroccan migrants who entered Ceuta in July, who have been or are set to be returned to their country of origin.

However, Spain is among the countries considered "under migratory pressure" because of last year's arrivals and will benefit from help this year. A total of 8,878 migrants who have applied for asylum in Spain, Italy, Greece, Cyprus and Malta will be taken in by other countries.

On the other hand, those countries will send back to frontline states the so-called "secondary movement" migrants — people who have entered the EU through a certain member state and then managed to move irregularly to another, asking for asylum there. According to EU rules, the first-entry country still has the responsibility to assess the request.

The first cracks are beginning to appear in the new solidarity system, as seven countries asked Italy to take back migrants and the Italian government invoked further compensation — which is not foreseen by EU rules — for migrants rescued at sea by NGO ships and disembarked on Italian shores.

A bilateral meeting between Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt in early September will kick off the debate on solidarity, which is set to continue at the Home Affairs Council at the beginning of October.

The crucial point will be the definition of the solidarity pool for 2027, which could see Italy and Spain on the same side, asking for more contributions from other countries after a summer of diplomatic spats between Rome and Madrid.

The uncertain future of return hubs

A key part of the EU strategy on migration concerns the return of irregular migrants, through a new regulation finalised last June and considered the strictest ever.

It introduces the possibility for member states to send people to a country with which they have no direct or indirect connection, provided that there is a bilateral agreement to set up deportation centres in the non-EU country.

These "return hubs" can be either places of transit, where a person is placed while waiting to be returned to their country of origin, or locations where a person is expected to stay with no guarantee of onward returns.

Some European governments are actively looking for partner countries, focusing on Asia and central Africa, intending to have the first partnership agreed by the end of the year, a diplomat told Euronews.

Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are working together on this project and are reportedly in talks with Uganda and Rwanda. Immigration ministers from the five countries are due to take stock of progress at a meeting in Copenhagen on 4 September.

The five-country working group could pave the way for a new model at EU level, despite criticism from civil society, operational difficulties and possible legal challenges.

"So far, it's not quite clear who is responsible for the migrants in a return hub, how long they can remain there and who monitors their conditions and provides effective remedies in case of human rights violations," Colombi said, pointing out that the EU legislation is vague on purpose to give states a free hand.

"I think there will be legal cases against the hubs once they are implemented on the ground, with a risk of a complete dismissal by the Court, as it happened with the UK-Rwanda migration scheme," he said.

World.title: Spa weekends: Where to go in Europe for a relaxing wellness escape
World.content:
Picture a getaway: rest, relaxation, rejuvenation and much-needed treatments against the backdrop of serene surroundings and no dings from urgent notifications. Sign me up, I say…

 

Hollywood has captured my sentiment in 'Spa Weekend', a new comedy film that hit big screens earlier in August.

It follows the misadventures of four lifelong friends who realise that in between juggling careers with everyday responsibilities, they lost track of taking care of themselves and each other. As burnout reaches breaking point, they all go for a – you guessed it – spa weekend.

With the trend now going beyond cinema theatres, luxury travel specialists Virtuoso reports that wellness bookings have increased by 28% year-on-year.

Now, I’m not someone who needs even an iota of convincing to indulge in spa treatments, but if you need a little push, these are the ideal European destinations where rejuvenation can easily fit into your itinerary.

A spa tour of Europe

If you're stumped on where to go for your spa weekend, you're in luck. There's actually a map of UNESCO World Heritage Sites to help you choose

The continent is home to 11 towns spread across seven countries that UNESCO has crowned as part of the “Great Spa Towns of Europe”.

According to the UN, each town has created its own "spa architecture”, pioneering a style of urban design centred on medical care as well as modern health and wellness tourism.

Out of the hundreds of spa towns across Europe, this handful were selected for their “outstanding universal value”, and they are:

Baden bei Wien, Austria

Spa, Belgium

Františkovy Lázně, Czechia

Karlovy Vary, Czechia

Mariánské Lázně, Czechia

Vichy, France

Bad Ems, Germany

Baden-Baden, Germany

Bad Kissingen, Germany

Montecatini Terme, Italy

City of Bath, UK

Europe’s top spa hotels and resorts

Even though the 11 towns above are recognised by UNESCO and, in many cases, are filled to the brim with wellness spots, Europe has myriad spas across its territories, and these are some of the best.

Finn Lough, Northern Ireland

This self-styled 'luxury hideaway' is secluded in the ancient Irish woodland on the edge of the Lough Erne lake system. The spa experience is centred around reconnecting with nature, and offerings include a soak at the Shoreline Spa, which sits on the banks of Lough Erne or a sauna session with panoramic lake views.

Lefay Resort & Spa Lago di Garda, Italy

This Gargnano property in Italy offers a “temple of wellness” which stretches over 4,300 square metres. Promising a synergy of East meets West, the treatments on offer range from Thalassotherapy, including seaweed facial purifying, to Western massages for tension relief as well as Eastern massages and rituals such as Chinese Gua Sha or Tibetan hot sponging and cupping.

AMARA, Limassol, Cyprus

The five-star AMARA Hotel in Limassol is located on Cyprus’ southern coast. Its spa hosts three-and five-day wellness retreats centred around the resort's adults-only seawater infinity pool. Away from the water, the spa also offers a range of therapies which highlight local ingredients like organic olive oil and citrus, and there are also countless rituals, therapeutic massages and facials to experience.

ZEM Wellness Clinic Altea, Alicante, Spain

For travellers looking to take the wellness element of their getaway up a notch, Alicante’s ZEM Wellness Clinic Altea features an expansive 4,000 square metre wellness and spa facility. Guests can choose from Signature treatments which spotlight Mediterranean tradition in wellbeing, to technology-based therapies which boost metabolism and promote physical recovery, as well as aquatic and manual therapies and facial treatments.

Other destinations to go for a spa weekend

Velingrad, Bulgaria

Home to more than 700 mineral springs, which are known for their healing properties, Bulgaria has seen growing interest from tourists seeking spa tourism offerings, with demand rising by 15%, according to Irena Georgieva, Bulgaria's Deputy Tourism Minister.

If your aim is to immerse yourself completely in rest and relaxation, Bulgaria Travel describes Velingrad as the “spa capital of the Balkans”. Located 130 kilometres away from the capital Sofia, and tucked away in the Rhodope Mountains, the Bulgarian town is home to some 80 springs, including the country’s largest karst spring, Lake Kleptuza.

For a thermal retreat in the pine-topped Rhodope Mountains, Velingrad’s Spa Hotel Santé’s array of rooms and apartments comes alongside various wellness offerings, including steam bathing facilities, halotherapy (salt therapy) in the salt room, as well as a Turkish bath facility.

Guests can also take their pick from the hotel’s array of pools, all filled with mineral-rich water. All pools are set to a temperature of at least 33C; the outdoor dipper pool, however, is set to 38C, and is best for quick dips. Another “dipping-style” option is the contrast pools, divided into two temperature zones, a 40C section for brief relaxation and the 18C section to stimulate blood circulation.

Hiiumaa Island, Estonia

Encircled by the Baltic Sea and a destination of natural beaches, small harbours and hiking routes, Estonia’s Hiiumaa Island is an ideal island escape.

Accessible by land, air and sea, its slow rhythm is marked by nature reserves and coastal forests of dense woodland environments, so it’s no surprise why it's a perfect “forest bathing” destination.

Between forest and sea, the Eha Retreat is earmarked to open its doors in autumn. It will be shaped around Estonia’s so-called “five seasons”, and everything here is designed to support deep rest and regenerative wellbeing.

Guests will be able to choose between a three-, five- or seven-night experience which begins with a consultation to create a personalised programme for individualised wellbeing.

The Thermal Suite invites guests to Eha’s wellness offerings, including multiple saunas, steam rooms and hydrotherapy pools within the Thermal Suite.

Eha Retreat also facilitates nature-immersive experiences, such as foraging for ingredients to learn about food as medicine, and exploring Estonian food conservation techniques, tending land, gardening, going on guided walks through its estate, as well as engaging in forest tea ceremonies.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”

World.title: AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond
World.content:
The AfD's lead candidate in the upcoming election aims to turn his small federal state into a blueprint for right-wing extremist politics across Germany.

All eyes are on Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of a state election on Sunday that could trigger a political earthquake across Germany.

Though the state is small, with a population of just 2 million — and with economic strength and life expectancy the lowest of any of Germany's 16 federal states — a victory for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could usher in the first far-right government in the history of post-World-War-II Germany.

The AfD's lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, and polls show him well in the lead. The only open question seems to be whether the AfD will be able to secure an absolute majority of the seats in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which would allow it to govern alone. This would appear to be Siegmund's only path to the state premiership, as the other parties have said they will not enter a coalition with the AfD.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Things are going well for the 35-year-old Siegmund. As he tours his state on the campaign trail, he draws crowds — even in small towns. He's often surrounded by a swarm of international journalists: from Canadian and Danish television, Swiss broadcasting, the BBC and the British magazine The Economist, alongside dozens of reporters from across Germany. Everyone wants to know: Who is Ulrich Siegmund?

The candidate was born in the small town of Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt, in 1990. He joined the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at age 19, only to leave the party five years later and join the AfD. A former perfume salesman, he cuts a dynamic and athletic figure: slim, handsome and fresh-faced.

Above all, he is cheerful — playing the role of a charismatic charmer in his public appearances. When he steps into town squares to a cheering crowd, he beams back, shaking hands and cracking jokes. Nothing about him seems forced; he visibly enjoys the campaign grind.

"I don't know when there was last such a high approval rating, even among young people," Siegmund told DW. "It's simply enormous." He speaks quickly, articulately and with practiced ease.

AfD, right-wing influencers battle for young voters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD campaign pushes policies with 'high-gloss marketing'

Even critical observers in Saxony-Anhalt can't help but admit that the AfD has all the momentum in this election.

"The AfD's campaign events run like clockwork, both logistically and in terms of political strategy," observed David Begrich of Miteinander , an organization based in the state capital of Magdeburg that fights right-wing extremism. "It is high-gloss marketing of their own policies."

But what exactly do the AfD's policies aim to achieve? To judge by Siegmund's campaign speeches, the goal is a return to a bygone era — a time before Germany viewed itself as a country of immigration, when electricity came from nuclear power plants rather than wind turbines, and when LGBTQ+ rights were not yet recognized. Siegmund wants to pursue, as he says in his campaign speeches, politics "from the people, for the people!"

Apparently, that doesn't include all the people living in the state. The AfD's "100-day immediate action plan" contains some radical policies, including a key promise to "deport from minute one" foreign nationals who have no legal right to stay, but whose presence is tolerated for humanitarian reasons, many of whom have found work and established their lives in Germany.

Germany's freedom of art under threat? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The action plan also calls for funding cuts to pro-democracy NGOs, forcing refugees to work and prioritizing a love for the German homeland over social diversity. There are significant legal doubts, however, about whether a state government actually has the authority to implement all these pledges.

Controversial figures behind the scenes

There are also doubts over the "clean" image that Siegmund has cultivated. He has not been able to escape the allegations of cronyism that have dogged the AfD, after it was reported that several of the party's state and federal lawmakers secured well-paid jobs for their friends and relatives in the offices of other AfD officials.

Siegmund himself found a position for his own father. While not illegal, the move was poorly received, even within his own party.

Then there are the people behind Siegmund, those who support him as leader of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt. According to the daily newspaper Die Welt, the group employs four former members of a now-banned neo-Nazi organization, the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend (German Youth Loyal to the Homeland). Before it was outlawed, the group openly admired Adolf Hitler's Nazism and adhered to his racial ideology, one that led to the murder of 6 million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma in the Holocaust.

German activists target neo-Nazis with trademark law To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Siegmund himself appears to have no qualms about associating with supporters who have tattoos or clothes with neo-Nazi symbols. DW observed him appearing arm-in-arm with men wearing neo-Nazi attire and sporting tattoos such as the Black Sun, a recognized symbol among neo-Nazis.

AfD wants to 'turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground'

But what would all this mean if the AfD actually did take power after the September 6 election?

"There are clear indications that if the AfD were to enter government, it would turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground for the whole country," said Begrich. "Just how far can one go in overriding the written — and perhaps even more importantly, the unwritten — rules of democratic culture in a federal state?"

For that reason, many churches, trade unions, civil society organizations and political parties have warned against an AfD victory. Begrich shares their concerns.

AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund is using social media and merchandise to push his message in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Heiko Rebsch/dpa/picture alliance

"Naturally, things will become difficult, above all, for those in society who either belong to minorities or do not fit into the AfD's ideological worldview," he said. "The social climate would inevitably shift to an authoritarian regimentation — and that poses a problem for people who need liberal openness in society as they need air to breathe."

Like many critics, Begrich believes that winning Saxony-Anhalt is only the first step for a party that wants to take over the entire country.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis guilty
World.content:
The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours in a case that had been unsolved for nearly 30 years. Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.

A Las Vegas jury on Monday found former gang leader, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, guilty of orchestrating the killing of hip hop artist Tupac Shakur, following nine days of testimony.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

Verdict reached in under three hours

It took jurors less than three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that has, up until now, been unsolved for almost three decades.

Sixty three-year-old Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.

Davis, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang, is the only person ever to have been charged in Shakur’s murder.

In closing arguments, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night.

Palal said that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but maintained that those differences showed Davis’ changing motivations and efforts to protect himself.

Palal argued that a key detail remained consistent throughout and that was that Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired.

Tupac Shakur died six days after he was shot in September 1996 Image: Kathy Hutchins/ZUMAPRESS/picture alliance

Davis, the sole surviving suspect

Davis is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac from which shots were fired. The man who prosecutors say originally gave the gun to Davis is also dead.

Police ​had long suspected Davis of involvement in Shakur's murder but could not charge him due to a lack of concrete evidence.

That was until Davis went public with his version of events in media appearances and a memoir, which along with recordings of his secret meetings with investigators, made up the bulk of the prosecution’s ​case.

Davis told the judge that he planned to appeal the verdict. He had pleaded not guilty to the single count of murder using a deadly weapon.

Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison Image: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal/dpa/picture alliance

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: US Supreme Court allows Trump ballroom project to proceed
World.content:
The ruling was backed by five of the court's six conservative justices. US President Donald Trump praised the decision in a post on his Truth Social platform.

The US Supreme Court on Monday allowed US President Donald Trump's administration to continue with the $400 million (€345 million) White House ballroom construction project for now.

The ruling was backed by five ‌of the court's six conservative justices who said that the plaintiffs in the case likely didn't have the legal right to challenge the case.

The ballroom project, hailed by Trump, has sparked controversy after the White House East Wing was torn down [FILE: May 26, 2026] Image: Joyce N. Boghosian/White House/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

Court votes 5-4 to lift lower court's order

"This Court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury," under the US Constitution, the five justices wrote in their ruling.

"Perhaps nearly any government action or project offends someone's sensibilities," they added.

Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court's three liberal-leaning justices in dissenting from the latest order, calling the construction “likely unlawful" because it hasn't been approved by Congress.

"Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers," Roberts wrote.

Trump welcomes Supreme Court ruling

"I am pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favor of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C." Trump said.

National Trust for Historic Preservation vs. Trump

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the matter after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom in the the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years.

The Trump administration had asked the nation's highest court to intervene after federal courts determined that the project needed to be halted on the grounds of it not having congressional approval.

US Justice Department lawyers previously justified the need for a secure ballroom, pointing to the July 8 missile threat against Air Force One when Trump was flown out of Turkey aboard a secret flight and other recent assassination attempts.

World.title: Poland launches sabotage probe in drone factory fire
World.content:
According to the prosecution, the fire that occurred at a drone factory 150 kilometers south of Warsaw was deliberately set.

Poland launched on Monday an investigation into a fire at a drone production factory south of Warsaw, suspecting terrorism and the involvement of a foreign intelligence service.

According to the prosecution statement, the probe had started "for participation in the activities of a foreign intelligence service directed against the Republic of Poland and for a terrorist offence, consisting of deliberately causing a fire on the premises of the WB Electronics factory using a device containing flammable materials."

The WB Electronics factory in Skarzysko-Kamienna, located 150 kilometers south of Warsaw, was reported on fire shortly after midnight Monday. The facility manufactures key components for drones.

Firefighters spent two hours containing the fire. There were no injuries in the incident.

The country's Internal Security Agency (ABW) is assisting the police with the investigation, officials said.

Poland supports Ukraine in its war with Russia

Earlier, Polish government accused Russia and Belarus of sending several agents into the country to carry out acts of sabotage.

Poland, who has been a vocal supporter of Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion into the country, has been increasing its security expenditure and military capabilities due to fears of Russian attacks.

WB Electronics, Poland's largest private defense company, is a supplier to the Polish military.

The company specializes in developing and manufacturing advanced defense technologies, including digital command and control systems, automated fire control systems, communications equipment, and modern unmanned strike systems.

World.title: Lionel Messi announces retirement from international football
World.content:
The Argentine legend announced that he will not play for the national team again, ending an illustrious international career.

Argentina legend Lionel Messi announced his international retirement on Monday.

The 39-year-old, widely considered the greatest football player of all time, won the 2022 World Cup in Qatar with Argentina, bringing the title back to the country for the first time since 1986.

The 2026 World Cup, Messi's last appearance in the world's most well-known footballing competition, ended in disappointment for Argentina after defeat to Spain in the final.

Despite being past his prime, the Argentina captain was the second most prolific goalscorer of the 2026 World Cup with eight goals, only being edged out by France's Kylian Mbappe with ten.

Messi is also second in the World Cup's all-time goalscorer list, where he is one goal behind Mbappe, with both overtaking Germany striker Miroslav Klose's 16 goals during the tournament in the US, Canada and Mexico.

Retirement comes at 'right time'

"It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul," Messi posted on his Instagram account, adding that he wrote his international retirement message two days after the World Cup final defeat to Spain.

"But I understand that it is the right time," he added.

Messi said he "always gave everything, not just in the last few years," and that he wanted to bring Argentina fans joy ​and make them "feel proud to be ​Argentine through football."

"I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — alongside my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of," he wrote, before concluding with "Vamos, Argentina!"

"I leave with the peace ​of mind ⁠and pride of having given you — alongside my ⁠teammates — ​moments we once only dreamed of," he added.

Miami contract until 2028

Messi is his country's most capped player with 207 appearances, in which he scored 125 goals, another all-time record.

With Messi as captain, Argentina also won the Copa America in 2021 and 2024.

His club career will continue at current club Inter Miami, where he has a contract until the end of the 2028 MLS season, although he did voice "serious doubts" about continuing to play football for "much longer" following the death of his father Jorge in August.

The attacker moved to the US side in 2023 from Paris Saint-Germain and after a 15-year career with Spanish giants Barcelona, with whom he won the UEFA Champions League four times and the Spanish title ten times.

Messi wanted to stay at Barcelona, but the club could not afford to keep him due to financial restrictions. This resulted in his move to Qatar-backed PSG, where he spent two years winning two league titles before moving to Miami.

World.title: Court says India must uphold Pakistan water treaty
World.content:
An international tribunal has ordered India to "observe its obligations" under a water-treaty with Pakistan.

The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague has ordered India to uphold a water-sharing treaty with Pakistan which has led to a recent increase in tensions between the two neighbors.

The PCA said New Delhi must "observe its obligations" under the treaty with on the sharing of the Indus and other rivers, which the Indian government this year sought to suspend.

In a statement, the court found unanimously found that "none of the grounds" put forward by India were justified and "concluded that the Treaty [...] remains fully in force."

The court noted that India "remains bound by the obligations incumbent upon it," particularly regarding the design and operation of "hydroelectric projects on the western rivers."

It said India's construction of hydroelectric projects on the Indus and associated rivers had to conform to the treaty.

A Pakistani government spokesman said Islamabad "welcomed" the PCA order. However, India said that it categorically rejects the order of the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

India threatens to dry out Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is the India-Pakistan water treaty?

The 1960 Indus Water Treaty governs the use of water from six rivers which originate in India but flow into Pakistan as part of the Indus basin — a resource relied on by hundreds of millions of people.

The Indus river cuts through ultra-sensitive demarcation lines between India and Pakistan in Kashmir, the Himalayan territory both countries claim.

India said in May 2025 that it was suspending its membership of the treaty after accusing Islamabad of backing a deadly attack on tourists on the Indian side of Kashmir.

India's Water Minister CR Patil said earlier this year that the government would ensure that "not a single drop of water" will flow into Pakistan.

Pakistan denies backing the Kashmir attack and has accused India of seeking to "weaponize" the precious water resource.

Islamabad has previously said it would consider any attempt to change the flow of cross-border waterways as an "act of war."
