World.title: Un proceso caro que acaba con miles de óvulos en el limbo: la vitrificación para retrasar la maternidad también tiene pegas
World.content:
La decisión de la Federación Española de Fútbol de apoyar la congelación de óvulos de las futbolistas reabre el debate sobre este procedimiento que tiene ventajas, pero también muchas aristas

La Federación Española de Fútbol está ultimando un acuerdo con una clínica de fertilidad para que las jugadoras de la selección puedan congelar óvulos, según ha adelantado a EL PAÍS, aunque no ha querido comentar los detalles de esta iniciativa. Lo recomendado es hacerlo antes de los 36 años con el fin de preservarlos en su momento de mejor calidad, para usarlos en un tratamiento de reproducción asistida cuando haya avanzado o concluido su carrera. Esta decisión, que toman aquellas deportistas que no pueden permitirse un paréntesis en ese momento, también se replica por motivos personales, profesionales y económicos en los casos de otras mujeres, y cada vez más. Pero es un debate con muchas aristas, en las que se cruzan innumerables circunstancias individuales, y que no puede entenderse como una solución milagrosa ni universal. En ese debate, hay voces que exigen a las instituciones cubrir estos procesos costosos para que el esfuerzo económico no recaiga sobre las mujeres, pero también otras que critican que, al hacerlo, se posterga además la maternidad más allá de la edad recomendada médicamente, para rendir más tiempo. Y, en todo caso, en el propio procedimiento de congelación de óvulos intervienen multitud de factores que complican la decisión: no es una solución ni barata, ni simple, ni inocua.

Más información La Federación Española ultima un acuerdo para facilitar a las futbolistas de la selección que congelen sus óvulos

En el caso de las futbolistas españolas, fueron ellas las que se lo plantearon a la federación. Pero haber congelado óvulos temprano no garantiza que en el futuro la fertilización in vitro será exitosa. Se debe informar a las mujeres de muchos matices, tanto si están considerando aplazar la maternidad desde los campos de fútbol y las pistas de atletismo, como también en oficinas, talleres, aulas o escenarios. Además de la calidad de los gametos, depende de la edad en la que decidan intentarlo, porque las complicaciones ginecológicas en la gestación también aumentan con el tiempo.

Edad y tasa de éxito

“Si congelas óvulos antes de los 36 años, multiplicas por 10 las probabilidades de que luego, cuando quieras intentarlo, realmente te quedes embarazada”, comenta la embrióloga Montserrat Boada. Y añade: “Es importante porque muchas de las personas que están preservando su fertilidad vuelven [a la clínica] a los 40″. Según Boada, jefa de Biología del Servicio de Medicina de la Reproducción en la clínica Dexeus Mujer, “el porcentaje de éxito está en un 60%, la tasa acumulada cuando se intenta con más de un embrión está por encima del 70%, y el porcentaje de niños nacidos está casi en un 52%”.

Quienes hayan vitrificado sus óvulos pueden no usarlos, porque no han querido hacerlo o ya han quedado embarazadas, pero debido a la ley vigente no pueden decidir descartarlos. Quedan en el banco de gametos hasta que dos médicos diferentes certifiquen que han concluido su edad fértil. La mayoría, de momento, no los usa. Según Boada, la tasa de pacientes que regresan para usarlos es del 30%, aunque va en aumento. Y además, hay un número importante de mujeres que recurre a óvulos de donante.

¿Cómo es el tratamiento?

En un ciclo normal se genera un óvulo. En este tratamiento de vitrificación, se receta medicación inyectable con hormonas para, durante dos semanas, estimular los ovarios y madurar más folículos, para intentar recolectar más óvulos. Después, el médico hace una punción ovárica para obtenerlos, bajo una sedación leve. Se vitrifican (una técnica de congelación rápida) y se almacenan en tanques de nitrógeno líquido.

Nicolás Prados, presidente de la Asociación para el Estudio de la Biología de la Reproducción (Asebir), explica que mejor cuantos más ovocitos puedan recolectarse, porque “es una carrera de obstáculos”. Comenta que sobreviven más del 95% de los ovocitos, pero no todos van a generar embriones y después no todos los embriones van a ser de buena calidad. Si la paciente es joven y los estudios hormonales y de reserva folicular salen bien, normalmente con un ciclo es suficiente. Si se obtienen menos de ocho óvulos, las clínicas recomiendan repetirlo para aumentar las probabilidades.

El proceso cuesta entre 2.000 y 4.000 euros, a los que se les suma el coste de los medicamentos, de entre 800 y 1.000 euros. Después, la preservación costará unos 400 euros por año. La mayoría de estos procesos se dan en el ámbito privado, porque la sanidad pública cubre exclusivamente los casos por indicación médica. Se admite en personas con posible riesgo de pérdida de su capacidad reproductiva por medicamentos o procedimientos médicos, como tratamientos oncológicos. El Partido Popular planteó en su ideario el año pasado ayudas públicas a la congelación de óvulos para las mujeres que quieran retrasar la maternidad.

¿Qué pasa con los óvulos si no se usan?

Hay tres opciones: donarlos a otra persona, donarlos para investigación científica o cesar su actividad, es decir, descongelarlos. Una de las principales críticas a la ley sobre técnicas de reproducción humana asistida de 2006 es que no pueden destruirse sin dos informes de médicos distintos que acrediten que la mujer ha terminado su período fértil. Los espermatozoides, sin embargo, sí se pueden cesar por pedido. Esta regulación es anterior a 2012, cuando se empezó a extender la preservación con la técnica de vitrificación.

“El artículo que habla de preservación de óvulos, embriones y esperma equipara el óvulo al embrión, que en su momento se hizo como para proteger a la mujer y no iba malintencionada la idea, pero un óvulo es un gameto, es como un espermatozoide, no es como un embrión que ya está fecundado y que requiere una protección mayor porque es una entidad distinta”, explica Montse.

En 2023 se vitrificaron 65.805 ovocitos, un 13% más que el año anterior, según los últimos datos disponibles de la Sociedad Española de Fertilidad (SEF), que lleva el Registro Nacional de Actividad desde 2014. La clínica debe hacer un seguimiento con la dueña cada dos años y preguntarle cómo quiere continuar. Después de dos renovaciones, si no han respondido, el centro puede tomar sus propias decisiones.

Los óvulos que se acumulan en bancos de gametos ya son un problema a resolver por el sistema. No hay cifras abiertas sobre cuántos se donan a la ciencia o a terceros. A 31 de diciembre de 2022 en España había 429.285 ovocitos almacenados (284.476 propios y 144.809 de donante), según ha respondido el Ministerio de Sanidad a una solicitud por el portal de transparencia.

¿Y con los preembriones?

Esos óvulos pueden fecundarse con esperma de una pareja o de un donante, para obtener preembriones y preservarlos. Según la misma respuesta de Sanidad, a fines de diciembre de 2022 había 791.634 congelados en el país, el 70% con más de dos años en tanques de nitrógeno. Si son de una pareja, tiene que firmar un consentimiento y se necesita de la autorización de ambos para usarlos, donarlos o cesarlos. Si el varón fallece y dejó su consentimiento, la mujer tiene permiso para usarlos durante el año posterior en España. Los embriones no caducan biológicamente: en julio del año pasado nació Thaddeus Daniel Pierce, en Ohio (EE UU), de un preembrión que estuvo almacenado 30 años.

¿Cuántos bebés nacen por año?

El 10% de los bebés en España en 2023 nacieron mediante técnicas de reproducción asistida, según los últimos datos de la SEF. Se realizaron 168.372 ciclos de fecundación in vitro y 30.464 inseminaciones artificiales. Esto dio lugar a 39.555 nacimientos, aunque el 20% de ellos se produjeron en el extranjero, fruto de tratamientos realizados a pacientes internacionales. España es centro del llamado turismo reproductivo y recibe personas de países con leyes menos flexibles.

World.title: Dolly Parton canta a Marx y Engels
World.content: El día 1 de septiembre, a toda persona de bien le brota en la boca una pipa de filósofo existencialista y una voz pesarosa que se pregunta desde el centro del pecho cómo es posible que tantísimo tiempo de la vida se vaya por el desagüe del trabajo. En 9 to 5, una de sus tres canciones más célebres, Dolly Parton resumía con una pasmosa candidez el universalísimo sentimiento de la alienación laboral que a Karl Marx tanta tinta le costó plasmar: “Trabajar de nueve a cinco, vaya forma de ganarse la vida / Lo que te pagan apenas alcanza para sobrevivir y todo son exigencias a cambio de nada / Además usan tus ideas y nunca te reconocen el mérito / Es suficiente para volverte loco si te dejas”. Vendrán los puristas y los amargados a decir que esa señora con las tetas tan grandes no conoció los horrores de las fábricas que documentó Engels y que ella por mucho que presumiese de orígenes humildes era una rubia millonaria, bastante más empleadora que empleada. No importa. Currar es un engorro y lo saben desde los tecnoligarcas que quieren darle toda nuestra faena a la inteligencia artificial hasta el presidente del Gobierno, al que le ha estado dando una pereza impresionante volver a una rutina que últimamente exige contestar preguntas muy incómodas, además de desmontar los ardides de la internacional ultraderechista. Y mientras tanto, ya nadie canta la Internacional socialista. Resulta terriblemente molesto que en un país con 19 millones de personas asalariadas solo nos pongamos a hablar de trabajo y sueldos cuando llega gente en tropel a postularse para los puestos que nadie quiere o cuando algún jefazo de la patronal nos reprocha tener que pagarnos las cotizaciones. Con tanto barullo xenófobo quizá no se hayan enterado de que desde el viernes vivimos en un país donde los jubilados pueden volver al tajo a cambio de cobrar menos pensión. Hay que prolongar a toda costa la vida laboral, no sea que de viejos tengamos tiempo para filosofar sobre el sentido de la vida.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy y los detectives desquiciados de internet
World.content:
Artículos estrictamente de opinión que responden al estilo propio del autor. Estos textos de opinión han de basarse en datos verificados y ser respetuosos con las personas aunque se critiquen sus actos. Todas las columnas de opinión de personas ajenas a la Redacción de EL PAÍS llevarán, tras la última línea, un pie de autor —por conocido que éste sea— donde se indique el cargo, título, militancia política (en su caso) u ocupación principal, o la que esté o estuvo relacionada con el tema abordado

Los mismos que saben lo que pasó en el caso Andic son los que resolvieron, antes del veredicto, el crimen de la Guardia Urbana. No es raro que con los grandes juicios mediáticos salga la Agatha Christie del Temu que todos llevamos dentro, pero en las redes los grandes sucesos dramáticos han desbarrado hasta límites desquiciados. Ya no importa si una acusada admite su crimen si internet concluye cualquier otra cosa. Es lo que está ocurriendo con el caso de Lindsay Clancy, la enfermera obstétrica que estranguló a sus tres hijos en 2023 mientras su marido hacía unos recados, intentó suicidarse tras matarlos y ha quedado en una silla de ruedas de por vida.

Poco importa que la mujer haya reconocido los hechos en el juicio que se ha desarrollado en Massachusetts. Como el proceso ha sido televisado en directo por varias plataformas, un ejército de aspirantes a detectives convertidos en creadores de contenido ha troceado la narrativa del pleito y diseccionado cada detalle para exponer sus propias teorías en TikTok. Una que ha destacado con diferencia es la que dictamina que Clancy nunca estranguló a sus hijos, sino que el caso entero debería revisarse porque el triple asesinato lo cometió Patrick, su marido. En el juzgado nadie ha puesto en duda el papel del padre de los niños, pero qué importa si Internet piensa justo lo contrario.

Un vídeo con más de 200.000 me gusta sostiene que fue Patrick porque comparando una imagen borrosa de una cámara de seguridad de la tienda a la que fue con otra de una parada de autobús mientras se cometía el crimen se ve lo que parecen unos zapatos cambiados. Otros vídeos con millones de visualizaciones insinúan que él nunca salió de su casa porque su mejor amigo se le parece mucho y podría haberle suplantado. Están los que atribuyen el triple asesinato al marido porque se ha vuelto a casar. O los que, directamente, como ha compartido con su millón de seguidores Lisa Rinna, una actriz y celebridad de Hollywood, afirman: “Lo hizo Patrick porque me han dicho que las mujeres no estrangulan”.

Las alegrías y decepciones con los detectives de las redes ya han sido narradas en documentales como A los gatos ni tocarlos: un asesino en internet o Desaparición en el Hotel Cecil. Con el juicio televisado a Clancy, el género ha llegado a una nueva era y un punto de no retorno. Aquí el delirio se ha colectivizado por motivos tan dudosos como interesados. A estas alturas de la economía de la atención, muchos estafadores buscan unos euros sabiendo que la teoría que más atrae no es la más sencilla, sino la más delirante y conspiranoica. Y nada mejor que ganarse a mujeres descreídas del sistema con conspiraciones que les darán la razón.

El caso de Lindsay Clancy, que ha abierto un interesante y necesario debate sobre la depresión posparto y las carencias estructurales en la atención a la salud mental femenina, no acabará cuando el jurado termine de deliberar. Ya se sabe que varios documentalistas están preparando un true crime sobre esta historia. Que Netflix o cualquier otra plataforma me ofrezca de aquí a unos meses un nuevo crimen de usar y tirar es algo que ya veía venir. De lo que estoy cansada es de cómo esa mirada delirante ha germinado en las cabezas de mis amigas. No falla. Las que más miedo tienen a bajar a un parking o volver solas a casa son las que más se hipnotizan con este contenido; las que se ponen podcasts de violaciones y asesinatos antes de dormir, creyendo que así aprenderán a prevenir posibles ataques y a estar alerta. Estoy harta de verlas ansiosas e hipervigilantes, siempre con el miedo en el cuerpo. Y buena parte de la culpa de ello la tienen esos que, más que detectives de sofá, son los trileros de su atención.

World.title: España dispara las compras de gas ruso a pocos meses del veto definitivo de Europa
World.content:
La escalada militar en Oriente Próximo y el bloqueo del estrecho de Ormuz han alterado los flujos de gas que abastecen a España. Esto ha llevado a los operadores a recurrir en mayor medida al suministro ruso, contra el que pesan sanciones europeas que se convertirán en un veto total a partir de 2027. Las importaciones de gas natural procedentes de Rusia han aumentado un 42% en el primer semestre del año, hasta los 37.172 gigavatios hora (GWh), según el último Boletín Estadístico de Hidrocarburos de la Corporación de Reservas Estratégicas de Productos Petrolíferos (CORES), publicado este lunes.

El aumento de las compras rusas ha permitido cubrir parte del hueco dejado por Qatar y otros proveedores de África, importantes abastecedores de gas del mercado español, aunque con un peso muy inferior al de Argelia y Estados Unidos. La escalada militar en Irán ha interrumpido el tránsito de buques gaseros por Ormuz, lo que ha dejado a España sin nuevas entregas procedentes del emirato desde el inicio de la crisis. Los datos de CORES reflejan una caída del 100% en el acumulado proveniente del país durante el primer semestre de 2026.

El contraste con 2025 muestra hasta qué punto ha cambiado el origen del suministro en apenas un año a causa de la inestabilidad geopolítica. En el primer semestre de 2025, España importó 26.208 GWh de gas ruso y las compras llegaron a caer más de un 70% interanual en los siguientes meses del año. Esa evolución apuntaba a una drástica reducción de la dependencia rusa, en línea con el cerco impuesto por la Unión Europea en represalia por la guerra en Ucrania. Pero la irrupción del conflicto en Oriente Próximo ha alterado esa trayectoria y ante la falta de cargamentos alternativos de gas natural licuado (GNL) en el corto plazo, los operadores han recurrido de nuevo al suministro del Kremlin, cuyas rutas desde el Ártico no dependen de ese paso marítimo.

Solo en junio, las compras de gas natural ruso crecieron un 68% respecto al mismo mes del año anterior, hasta unos 5.500 GWh. El repunte fue suficiente para situar a Rusia como el segundo proveedor de España durante el mes, con algo más de una quinta parte del total, solo por detrás de Argelia. El país norteafricano, que suministra buena parte del hidrocarburo a través del gasoducto Medgaz, mantuvo una distancia considerable y cubrió alrededor del 40% de las importaciones. El cambio, en cualquier caso, refleja el ajuste que está experimentando el mercado español tras la interrupción de los cargamentos procedentes del golfo Pérsico, con los operadores recurriendo a proveedores capaces de mantener sus envíos por rutas ajenas al estrecho de Ormuz.

El repunte semestral está muy condicionado por lo ocurrido en marzo, cuando España recibió el mayor volumen de gas ruso de toda la serie histórica (9.807 GWh). El estallido del conflicto entre Estados Unidos e Irán a finales de febrero desató el pánico en los mercados energéticos, lo que llevó a los operadores a asegurar cargamentos ante el riesgo de nuevas interrupciones y de precios más altos. Además, marzo fue el último mes completo en el que las empresas podían adquirir gas ruso en el mercado de corto plazo ―conocido como spot― antes de que entraran en vigor las últimas restricciones comerciales dictadas a nivel europeo contra Moscú, un factor que podría haber acelerado la compra por parte de las comercializadoras privadas para acumular inventarios a un precio más competitivo. En mayo hubo otro envío de más de 8.700 GWh, necesariamente vinculado a contratos de largo plazo, de forma que estos dos meses concentran la mitad de todo el gas ruso importado en el semestre.

La Asociación Española del Gas, Sedigas, sostiene que este repunte no es incompatible con las sanciones adoptadas por la Unión Europea. El calendario de sanciones, aclaran, hacía posible en los primeros meses del año hacer compras “al amparo de contratos a corto plazo suscritos con anterioridad a junio de 2025″. Y también “permite que los contratos de GNL a largo plazo preexistentes a esa fecha puedan ejecutarse hasta el 1 de enero de 2027″ (para el gas que llega por gasoducto a otros países comunitarios, el plazo expirará el 30 de septiembre del año próximo). Esto explica, en opinión de la patronal, “que los flujos vinculados a compromisos vigentes se mantengan o incluso se intensifiquen en toda la UE antes de su extinción normativa de forma definitiva”.

El papel de EE UU y Argelia

A pesar del creciente papel de Moscú, Argelia y Estados Unidos son los principales emisores del gas importado. España prácticamente duplicó sus compras al país norteamericano el año pasado, coincidiendo con el pacto comercial alcanzado entre Bruselas y Washington para elevar la compra de hidrocarburos estadounidenses. En lo que va de año, el flujo ha experimentado un ligero retroceso del 6% interanual, hasta los 55.790 GWh importados. Pero pese a este repliegue —motivado por el desvío coyuntural de buques metaneros hacia mercados de Asia Pacífico con primas más atractivas—, EE UU mantiene su poderío en el sistema peninsular y controla casi un tercio de todo el suministro nacional, con una cuota de mercado que ronda el 27%.

Por otra parte, Argelia continúa siendo el principal suministrador de España, aportando el 35% del gas importado en el último año. Entre enero y junio ha suministrado un total de 64.230 GWh a través del gasoducto submarino Medgaz, casi el doble de lo que ha aportado Rusia. Si a ello se suman las aportaciones de Estados Unidos y otros países, la cuota total de Moscú se mantiene en el semestre por debajo de un quinto del total (un 19,7%). Pero la patronal del gas insiste en que al mirarlo con mayor perspectiva, el peso sigue diluyéndose: “La contribución promedio del gas ruso en los últimos cinco años fue del 14,5%, pero en los últimos 12 meses ha representado un 14,4% del total importado”, señalan en Sedigas.

En la misma línea, el último informe de la compañía Enagás, participada en un 5% por el Estado, alimenta la idea de que el auge de las compras a Moscú ha sido un evento coyuntural. Según sus datos, el peso de Rusia sobre el total de importaciones pasó del 20% en el acumulado hasta junio al 18% hasta julio. La gestora y transportista de gas en España apunta a que en julio los operadores compraron a Moscú solo 2.088 GWh, la cifra más baja de todo el año y similar a los niveles observados en 2025.

Reservas y precios

Pese a la incertidumbre internacional, España afronta la crisis energética con un nivel elevado de reservas. En el caso del petróleo, el país contaba en junio con más de 15.300 kilotoneladas, un 4% más que un año antes. Esto equivale, en teoría, a poder mantener su consumo durante 101 días sin recibir nuevos suministros. La cifra se encuentra por encima del mínimo de 90 días exigido por la Agencia Internacional de la Energía, a fin de tener margen para buscar proveedores alternativos y reorganizar sus importaciones en caso de un shock negativo.

La situación es también relativamente favorable en el caso del gas. España llega a mitad de año con sus almacenes subterráneos llenos en más de un 70% de su capacidad útil, un nivel que le proporciona un buen colchón ante posibles problemas de suministro. El problema, sin embargo, se focaliza en el precio. En estos seis meses, el barril de brent, el crudo de referencia en Europa, ha experimentado fuertes oscilaciones llegando a superar los 100 dólares en mayo. Este aumento se ha trasladado directamente al coste de las importaciones españolas. En junio, el precio que pagó España por el crudo importado ―incluidos el coste del transporte y el seguro― alcanzó los 85,33 euros por barril, un 46% más que un año antes.

En este contexto, Sedigas descarta problemas de desabastecimiento físico, pero advierte de “riesgos económicos latentes”. La patronal argumenta que España opera con una robustez diferencial respecto a sus socios comunitarios gracias a “su elevada capacidad de regasificación y almacenamiento —la mayor de Europa—” y a un modelo que diversifica sus fuentes adquiriendo gas de “alrededor de 12-15 países distintos cada año”. El riesgo se sitúa en el mercado internacional de GNL, donde la competencia por los cargamentos puede elevar los precios o hacer que los buques se desvíen hacia destinos más lucrativos, trasladando esa presión a la industria española.

En cualquier caso, la capacidad de adaptación del sistema nacional permite relativizar el impacto del previsible cierre definitivo del gas ruso. Víctor Ruiz Ezpeleta, profesor de OBS Business School, considera que España no afrontaría un problema de acceso al suministro, gracias a una infraestructura privilegiada que combina la mayor red de plantas regasificadoras de Europa con el gasoducto Medgaz, que conecta directamente con Argelia. “España no tiene un problema de acceso al gas, sino de coste. El volumen que actualmente llega de Rusia puede sustituirse con GNL de Estados Unidos, Nigeria, Trinidad y Tobago o Noruega, además de aumentar las importaciones por gasoducto desde Argelia”, explica.

World.title: Rotterdam medical students offer cash to jump training queues
World.content:
Medical students in Rotterdam are offering each other thousands of euros to move up the queue for the hospital training they need to qualify as doctors amid a shortage of spaces.

The bids – one as high as €2,000, according to news website NU.nl – after the lottery system for places at Erasmus MC left hundreds of students waiting months, some more than a year, to begin.

The medicine master’s is built mostly around clinical placements in hospital departments. Each department can take a limited number of trainees, so start dates are drawn by lottery, and pulling the short straw can cost the better part of a year.

This time the draw went badly for a lot of them. Of the roughly 380 students who entered, about a quarter can’t start until autumn 2027 and 35% not until 2028, NU.nl reported, citing an email sent to students.

Richer students paying ahead

Students have bought and sold Rotterdam start dates before. Medisch Contact, a medical journal, documented the trade in 2020, when the medical faculty’s student council warned it let wealthier students buy their way ahead.

Erasmus MC told NU.nl it did not want money deciding who trains first, and said it would look at tightening the rules on swaps. It called the shortage of places temporary: extra students are graduating amid a switch to a new curriculum.

Students who wait longest can sometimes claim compensation from a university fund that covers study delays outside their control. The Netherlands is already facing a shortage of doctors, particularly neurologists.

World.title: Former CDA leader Elco Brinkman dies aged 78
World.content:
Elco Brinkman, the Christian Democrat minister and party leader whose 1994 election defeat pushed the CDA into opposition for the first time in decades, has died aged 78. He died on Monday in Leiden after a short illness, his family said.

Brinkman became minister of welfare, health and culture in 1982, aged 34, serving seven years under Ruud Lubbers.

As minister he coined the phrase “caring society”, arguing that people had grown too dependent on the welfare state. He pushed through cuts to welfare and the arts and steered a new media law that opened the Netherlands to commercial television.

He took over as CDA leader in parliament in 1989 and was earmarked as Lubbers’s successor, but his 1994 campaign collapsed after Lubbers publicly withdrew his backing. The CDA fell from 54 seats to 34, and Brinkman left national politics in 1995.

He later chaired the construction federation Bouwend Nederland and returned as the CDA’s senate leader from 2011 to 2019.

World.title: From Sting to the beach: 12 great things to do in September
World.content:
The heat has receded and autumn is almost upon us. Hanneke Sanou has a round up of ideas to keep you busy in September.

Go once more unto the beach

Scheveningen is saying goodbye to a torrid summer with Live on the Beach. Whether sodden sand or glorious sunshine, the line-up will cheer up fans of Guus Meeuwis, Suzan and Freek, Acda en De Munnik, among many others. There are four live events on four consecutive days. September 3-6. Website

Get the picture

The Fotomuseum Den Haag is mounting a retrospective of 300 photographs by Eva Besnyö (1910-2003) from its own extensive collection. It follows Besnyö’s career, from Budapest to Berlin and Amsterdam, where she arrived in 1931 and where she became part of the New Photography movement which favoured dynamism and immediacy in photography.

Besnyö, who was Jewish, had to go into hiding during the war years and was active in resistance work. Her social commitment never flagged; in the 1970s she documented the Dutch feminist movement Dolle Mina. Eva Besnyö – The Liberated Camera is on from September 5. Website

Connect the dots

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam presents a retrospective of the work of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who, it emerged last week, died on August 14 aged 97. Kusama turned her hand to everything during her long career, from painting and sculpture to performances, fashion, and literature. The show includes a new version of one of her installations executed in a characteristic black and yellow pattern, so tactile and organic, to wander round in. From September 11. Website

Drop by the Voorlinden birthday party

The Voorlinden Museum in Wassenaar is celebrating its 10th anniversary with an exhibition which combines the museum’s favourites with equally well-loved work pilfered from other collections.

The impressive line-up of Celebrating the Icons of Art includes artists Francis Bacon, Louise Bourgeois, Alexander Calder, Nick Cave, Félix González-Torres, Damien Hirst, David Hockney, Martha Jungwirth, Mike Kelley, Yayoi Kusama, Fernand Léger, Roy Lichtenstein, Henri Matisse, Annette Messager, Joan Miró, Claude Monet, Bruce Nauman, Louise Nevelson, Lygia Pape, Gerhard Richter and Bridget Riley. From September 12. Website

Catch a monument

It’s visit-a-listed-building day, or Open Monumentendag, on September 12 and 13, when the public are invited to take a peek at special buildings, some of which are off-limits for the rest of the year.

This year’s theme is Resilient heritage in turbulent times, which puts the focus on threats such as climate change and the more pedestrian, but no less urgent, lack of finances and volunteers. Some 6,000 buildings are opening their doors, including some weird and wonderful ones like riding schools and the smallest house in Groningen. September 12 and 13. Website

Play the game

How has video game technology evolved over the years, and do video games turn people into isolated weirdos, creative problem solvers, or both? Those are the questions Game On, at the NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam is trying to answer. For those who cannot be without their consoles, Super Nintendo, Atari 2600 and PlayStation 5 are on standby. Until October 26. Website

Get a load of Van Gogh(s)

Van Gogh lovers should head for the Kröller-Müller museum in Otterlo which has dusted off all 88 of its Van Goghs and put them all together in an exhibition for the first time in over 40 years. Built around faith, hope and charity, extolled in a sermon before he switched from preacher to painter as a profession, Van Gogh – All Our Paintings seeks to discover these virtues in the artist’s work. From September 15. Website

Don’t touch the art at Sonsbeek

“I don’t need a garden, I’m sharing a park” is the title of this year’s edition of the open-air art event in Arnhem’s Park Sonsbeek. The event features site-specific art, performances, film, and workshops by Dutch and international artists, including British-Ghanaian artist Larry Achiampong, whose work, wrapped in a pan-African flag, was recently vandalised. The torn flag will remain part of the work. Until October 11. Website

Climb the stairway to heaven

Soaring temperatures in June prevented Willem-Alexander from attempting the inaugural climb but now the spruced-up Kijk uit Attention, by Krijn Giezen (1939-2011), is open to the public once more. The attraction in the sculpture park of the Kröller-Müller museum consists of a path leading to stairs going up 87 metres, affording a view of the national Veluwe park. Website

Don’t miss

You still have a chance to catch the Rijksmuseum’s in-depth look at Dutch photographer Ed van der Elsken. The museum turned his private archive upside down in search of his methods and motivation, resulting in nine rooms covering 40 years of work, including the iconic Woman on a bike sticking out her tongue, which graces the Rijksmuseum, much to the surprise of the subject. Ed van der Elsken Up Close is on until September 13. Website

The run of Sting’s musical The Last Ship, fronted by the man himself, has been extended at Carré theatre in Amsterdam. Best be quick if you want to make it on board. Until September 13. Website

There is still time to catch the impressive but strangely titled exhibition Gerard van Honthorst – Different to Rembrandt at the Centraal Museum in Utrecht. Some 60 paintings and 30 drawings show the 17th-century master for who he was. Until September 13. Website

World.title: Beyond profit: Why Dutch firms want impact-driven leaders
World.content:
The Netherlands is fast becoming a testing ground for business that treats social and environmental impact as a measure of success. Its universities are adapting too: Nyenrode Business University runs an English-language Impact MBA, taught in Amsterdam and Breukelen, that builds sustainability into leadership training rather than setting it apart as a separate subject.

On April 8, 2026, the Netherlands’ National Coordinator for Sustainable Development Goals, Anna Pot, was handed a copy of the recently hashed out Impact Agenda 2030 at the Social Enterprise Government Congress in Nijmegen.

Described by the collaborative coalition of social entrepreneurs, foundations, municipal leaders, knowledge institutions and civil society initiatives that participated in its making as a “national framework for a future-proof and resilient economy”, the Impact Agenda aims to move the Dutch economy towards a system that has social and environmental metrics embedded in its core – not merely as an afterthought after profits are tallied.

“Impact is not a niche, it is a necessity,” is the message the Dutch Impact Ecosystem says it’s sending to national leaders. “And it has real economic value – for impact-driven organisations and traditional businesses alike.”

The agenda – which focusses on such themes as impact governance, procurement and finance, social and digital innovation and education and is in line with the European Commission’s Social Economy Action Plan – is just the latest national accomplishment that cements the Netherlands’ standing as a world leader in the move to sustainability and societal impact in its business sectors.

A recent report looking at how firms balance profit with impact found that of the 77 large companies the private-public consortium surveyed doing business in the Netherlands, the majority believe the initial regulatory hassles of the EU’s CSRD [Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive] are overshadowed by its long-term benefits, all while helping their businesses.

The report found that “Dutch companies are leading the way in integrating impact governance into their strategies.”

Learning laboratory

The country’s strong collaborations between businesses, government and knowledge institutions create an environment of innovation and entrepreneurship that has led professionals worldwide to increasingly choose the Netherlands to learn how businesses can create both commercial success and positive societal change.

In the Netherlands’ dynamic Dutch business ecosystem, leaders have the opportunity to put theory into practice.

New leaders

Driven by European sustainability regulations, evolving investor expectations, rapid technological developments such as AI and growing stakeholder expectations, companies today are looking for leaders who can navigate complexity rather than optimize a single bottom line.

And the country’s universities and knowledge institutions are keeping pace. Nyenrode Business University, with locations in Amsterdam and Breukelen, offers an English-language MBA program focused on creating the future leaders of this brave new business world.

Its Impact MBA was designed as a response to changing employer needs rather than as a traditional MBA program. Instead of teaching sustainability as a standalone subject, the curriculum integrates leadership, digital transformation and sustainability throughout the learning experience.

“Sustainability transitions involve long-term developments with significant short-term implications for organizations,” says Prof. Dr. Nicolas Chevrollier, Professor of Sustainability Transitions and designer of the Impact MBA. “This requires new competences, new collaborations and sometimes entirely new business models.”

Chevrollier emphasises that organizations cannot solve today’s challenges independently. Businesses increasingly operate within ecosystems involving governments, knowledge institutions, investors and civil society, meaning effective leadership depends on building partnerships rather than optimising organisations in isolation.

“Many organisations suffer from tunnel vision,” he says. “To truly innovate, leaders need to broaden their perspective.”

The Impact MBA gives tomorrow’s leaders a chance to do just that: innovation and a systems-thinking approach are embedded in its curriculum, creating business trailblazers who can balance financial and societal objectives while thinking across entire systems instead of just individual organizations.

Are you looking to develop the new capabilities needed for the profound transformations taking place in today’s business world? Then check out Nyenrode ‘s Impact MBA, available both part-time and full-time, or join one of their on-campus and online events to discover more.

World.title: Large explosion at restaurant in Utrecht
World.content:

A major explosion occurred early Monday morning at a barbecue restaurant in Utrecht, according to local broadcaster RTV Utrecht.

The blast went off at 1am at the Topkapi restaurant, shattering windows and destroying the front of the building.

No one was injured but nearby residents were evacuated as a precaution.

The restaurant was the target of another bombing in 2023. A 19-year-old from Utrecht was later convicted of the crime. According to the court, he had attempted to extort money from the restaurant’s owner.

The police would not comment on a motivation and are investigating.

World.title: Coalition budget talks still deadlocked with hours to go
World.content:
Plans to cut more than €6 billion from social security and to change the way savings and investments are taxed are in the balance, as the three coalition parties struggle to agree next year’s budget among themselves with only hours to go before it is due for review.

D66, the VVD and the CDA negotiated through the whole of Sunday and into the early hours of Monday without reaching a deal, and are still talking on Monday afternoon. The meeting at which the full cabinet has to sign off the budget, first scheduled for 11am, has been put back twice and is now set for 6pm.

Until last week, the main question was whether the minority coalition could win enough opposition votes to pass the budget. Prime minister Rob Jetten ended those talks on Friday, saying the plans would go to parliament without a majority.

That has left the coalition parties to settle the budget between themselves, and they remain divided. Jetten acknowledged on Friday that the three parties still disagree fundamentally on some key points.

What they are arguing over

Broadcaster NOS reported that two issues are holding up a deal: the box 3 tax and the planned social security cuts.

Box 3 is the tax on income from savings and investments, which the government has been trying to reform for years. The coalition’s spending plans also include cutting more than €6 billion from social security – the benefits paid to people who are unemployed, older or too ill to work.

The largest opposition party, the left-wing PRO, has made scrapping that cut a condition of its support and wants wealthy households taxed more instead. Led by Jesse Klaver, PRO already won a concession from the government this year, when it dropped a plan to raise the retirement age more quickly.

D66 and the CDA want to avoid tilting the budget too far to the right, so as to keep PRO within reach. The VVD is wary of concessions to the left that could sour its relations with the far-right JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

The coalition could pass the budget through the lower house with JA21 and SGP support, but that combination would leave it well short in the senate, where PRO’s backing offers the more realistic route to a majority.

The draft is due at the Council of State, which reviews the plans before they are presented on Prinsjesdag on September 15.

World.title: The number of English-language bookstores is on the rise
World.content:
Thanks in part to social media, the number of English-language books read in the Netherlands is increasing, and with it, the number of shops catering to those bookworms.

One in five books sold in the Netherlands is in English, according to industry monitor KVB Boekwerk. Broadcaster NOS reported that over the past four years, at least ten new English-language bookshops have opened their doors in the country, including in Tilburg, Utrecht and Amersfoort.

The increase is attributed in large part to social media, particularly the popularity of BookTok, a community of content creators making videos primarily about books.

Many bookstores now stock books popular on BookTok and have entire displays of what’s currently going viral online.

These new shops are often operated by people who came from outside of the publishing world. Daan Severijns changed course after a career in IT. He runs Books and Beans in Tilburg together with his partner Ana Maria Vallejo Perez .

“We used to philosophise about what we would like to do after retirement: run a small bookstore in a beautiful location. Then I lost my job, and the wish quickly grew into what it is today,” he told NOS.

World.title: Big cities buckling under homelessness and drugs, says Halsema
World.content:
Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has called on the government to take national action on rising homelessness, crack addiction and public disorder, warning that they are eroding quality of life in the country’s biggest cities and cannot be tackled by city authorities alone.

Speaking in an interview with Het Parool and on current-affairs programme Buitenhof, Halsema said the same pressures were affecting all four big cities – Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – and that the government was partly responsible.

“The problems in the big cities are gradually overwhelming us,” she said, calling for “major measures” from The Hague.

Amsterdam has 3,644 recorded people who cause public disorder, Halsema said, though she stressed the number of homeless people is far higher. The most recent count, in 2024, recorded more than 15,000 people in the Amsterdam region as homeless or at risk of losing their home, though the city says the true figure is higher.

“Public poverty”

The most visible problems come from a combination of homelessness and crack use, particularly in the city’s parks, which Halsema said was distressing residents and traumatising for the addicts themselves.

She said that debates in The Hague ahead of the budget focus on income and taxation, while cities are left dealing with “public poverty”: the visible result of underfunded services, the housing shortage and a strain on the mental health care system.

She wants the government to structurally improve mental health provision and overhaul rules governing foreign workers.

Foreign workers

About 1,500 of the people causing nuisance come from eastern Europe, according to Halsema, many of them foreign workers who end up losing their housing and their jobs because the two are tied together. Amsterdam organisations have previously helped hundreds return home, a significant number of them crack users.

Employers in the Netherlands are allowed to house foreign workers while deducting the cost from their wages, currently up to a quarter of the minimum wage. Former social affairs minister Mariëlle Paul ended a planned phase-out of that rule last year, a decision Halsema branded “disastrous”.

She wants the rule reversed, faster action against rogue employment agencies, and more money for shelter: of the €13 million she said was made available last year for housing foreign workers, Amsterdam received €2 million, which she said is far too little.

Sleeping outdoors

Amsterdam stopped fining people for sleeping outdoors in June last year and, like Utrecht, now wants to decriminalise it entirely. Halsema says fines only push homeless people further into debt and further from help.

Police have raised concerns about that approach. In a review by the local health service in April, officers said people were coming to Amsterdam because they were allowed to sleep outdoors there, and that police and other enforcement teams had fewer tools to steer them towards help.

With annual budget talks ongoing, Halsema said the government must act: “Enable us to make sure our city is in order and liveable.”

World.title: Fundraiser for baby orphaned by speeding driver in Polish city reaches 1 million zloty
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A fundraiser for an eight-month-old baby who survived an accident in the Polish city of Kraków in which his parents were killed by a speeding driver has reached more than 1 million zloty (€231,000). The tragedy has prompted widespread anger, with calls from residents and local politicians for the authorities to take action to deal with dangerous driving in the city. To będzie jedna z najtrudniejszych zbiórek, jakie wspólnie przeprowadzimy.💔Proszę o RT🙏 Kilka dni temu rozpędzony kierowca w Krakowie wjechał w młode małżeństwo. Mateusz i Klaudia zginęli. Ich kilkumiesięczny synek, Oliwier, trafił do szpitala. Mam dla Was dobrą wiadomość.… pic.twitter.com/R8L1xgEBPn — Damian Żurawski (@damian_zurawski) August 26, 2026 On 22 August, a married couple, Mateusz and Klaudia, both 32, were walking with their baby on Solna Street, close to the southern bank of the Vistula river, when a car driven by 26-year-old Hubert B., whose surname is masked under Polish privacy law, mounted the pavement, killing both parents. The child, eight-month-old Oliwier, survived the accident but was hospitalised. His condition is continuing to improve, reports broadcaster TVP Kraków. According to prosecutors, the car was travelling around 40 km/h (25mph) faster than the speed limit in the area. Hubert B., has been charged with unintentionally causing a fatal accident, for which he could face up to eight years in prison. “The suspect pleaded not guilty to the offence he was charged with, explaining, among other things, that the car skidded due to the uneven road surface,” prosecutors said, adding the suspect has been placed in pretrial detention. An online fundraiser set up last week to provide Oliwier “with financial security for years to come” shared the news that the baby’s condition is now stable, although “his arm and leg are in plaster”. “We can’t give Oliwier back his mum and dad,” reads the fundraiser’s description. “However, we can do everything we can to ensure he has the resources for his education and a peaceful start to adult life.” At the time of writing, the fundraiser has reached more than 1.05 million zloty, over double its initial target. There have been more than 23,300 donations so far. Meanwhile, Oliwier’s grandfather, Andrzej, told newspaper Fakt that the family had given its consent for the fundraiser and was very grateful for those who had donated. A court in Kraków has granted Mateusz’s brother custody of the child. As well as sympathy for the victims, the accident aroused anger from residents. Several hundred people attended a protest at the site, holding signs reading “How many more people must die for something to change?” and “Stop road killers”. They installed their own mock-up pedestrian crossing and speed bumps. “Such tragedies are not isolated incidents,” said the organisers, quoted by news website Interia. They cited police figures showing that Kraków had the most road accidents of all Poland’s provincial capitals in 2025. Its figure of 941 was over 100 more than in Łódź and over 250 more than in Warsaw. Local councillor Rafał Zawiślak told news website Onet that he was filing a complaint with the prosecutor’s office, saying the city authorities had been negligent, failing to respond to warnings from 2024 that the site of the accident was dangerous. Godzina ciszy w Krakowie. Mieszkańcy upamiętniają parę, która zginęła w sobotniej tragedii przy ulicy Solnej. Na miejsce przybyły tłumy. „Nie chcemy bać się chodzić po chodnikach” – apelują.@RadioKrakow pic.twitter.com/DlOn5GvyL5 — Elżbieta Raczyńska (@_eraczynska) August 25, 2026 Acting mayor Stanisław Kracik said that an inspection of the street carried out after the accident had not shown any problems with the existing signage or need for traffic-calming measures. He added, however, that the city would be installing a speed bump. “I believe that this is simply what we should do…as a kind of expression of solidarity with the victims of this tragedy,” he said, quoted by broadcaster TVN. City police said they had been monitoring and taking action about road safety issues in the district for years, but that the street in question had not previously been reported as a particularly dangerous place, with just one incident causing one injury in the five years before the fatal accident. MPs from The Left have called for tougher rules on illegal street racing, saying police currently do not have sufficient legal tools. It comes after a crash on Saturday in which four men died after their car was filmed driving at dangerously high speeds https://t.co/OSRvyPAtVA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2023 The police also claimed that Kraków is “one of the safest cities” in Poland, with 768 road accidents per 100,000 residents this year, compared to over 1,000 in some other cities. However, TVN points out that the same statistics show that, this year, Kraków has had 71 accidents per 100,000 inhabitants in which someone was injured or killed, compared to 28 in Katowice and 27 in Warsaw. Road safety in Poland has improved dramatically, with the country recording the EU’s largest decline in road deaths between 2019 and 2024. However, its overall number of road deaths in relation to population is still above the EU average. Road deaths have fallen by 35% in Poland since 2019, which is the largest decline in the EU. The improvement has come after a series of measures by the Polish authorities to improve road safety, which was previously among the worst in Europe https://t.co/kXhpXSOwH9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish student accused of planning Islamist terrorist attack on Christmas market to stand trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish student is to stand trial accused of planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market in Poland as an act of support for Islamic State. On Monday, prosecutors announced that they have filed an indictment against the 20-year-old suspect, a student at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) who can be named only as Mateusz W. under Polish privacy law. Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesman for Poland’s security services, confirmed that Mateusz W. had been “preparing a mass attack at a Christmas market, which he planned to carry out using explosive materials”. Wracamy do sprawy 20-letniego Mateusza W. – studenta Katolickiego Uniwersytetu Lubelskiego podejrzewanego o przygotowywanie masowego zamachu na jednym z jarmarków świątecznych, którego planował dokonać z wykorzystaniem materiałów wybuchowych. Do Sądu Okręgowego w Koszalinie… https://t.co/6vGPcjiDnc pic.twitter.com/seFGV8nHMz — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) August 31, 2026 The suspect was detained late last year, when details of his alleged plot and plans to establish contact with Islamic State were first revealed. He has remained in custody since then. Though the authorities have confirmed that Mateusz W. was a first-year student at KUL, a leading Catholic university that counts the late Pope John Paul II among its former students and lecturers, and that they have also searched premises in the province of Łódź, they have not revealed where his alleged attack was planned. However, prosecutors reported today that the suspect had established contacts through which he could gain access to explosive materials and devices, had looked for bomb-making instructions, and had tried to recruit others to his terrorist cause. “Mateusz W.’s actions were intended to further the policies of the terrorist organisation known as Islamic State and to seriously intimidate people with views contrary to the ideology espoused by the suspect,” wrote Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska, a spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office. In a separate statement, the Internal Security Agency (ABW) revealed that the suspect had “intended to join a terrorist organisation affiliated with the so-called Islamic State and sought people who could help him carry out this plan”. Neither the security services nor prosecutors have indicated whether Mateusz W. denied or admitted to his alleged crimes or has offered any explanation for his actions. If convicted of preparing a mass attack, he could face up to ten years in prison. Last year, after Mateusz W. was detained, Dobrzyński said that he came from a devoutly Catholic family but had become “deeply infatuated with Islam” and had “fallen in love with terrorism”. In an appeal to parents, Dobrzyński said that, “if you see your children interested in Islam, communism, or fascism, and collecting all sorts of information and items on the subject, that’s the first sign. Take care of your own children, because things can only get worse from there”. Poland has detained a man who was allegedly planning a terrorist attack on a Christmas market as an act of support for Islamic State. The suspect, a 19-year-old Pole, had become "infatuated with Islam", say the security services https://t.co/N4WDVZdlai — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 After news of Mateusz W.’s detention emerged, KUL suspended his student status. The university’s spokesman, Wojciech Andrusiewicz, said that neither fellow students nor lecturers had noticed any unusual behaviour by the suspect. World.title: Polish WWII massacre victims reburied in Ukraine at ceremony attended by officials from both countries
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The remains of 55 Poles – around half of them children – massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, many of whose bones show signs of brutal deaths, were exhumed this summer after Ukraine recently ended a moratorium on searches for tens of thousands of victims of the so-called Volhynia massacres who are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. “This is an important moment for [the victims’] families, but also the Polish state, because this funeral follows decades of waiting,” said Polish culture minister Marta Cienkowska at the ceremony in Ostrówki (Ostrovky in Ukrainian), a depopulated former village that, before the war, was part of Poland and now lies in Ukraine. “Poland has the right and obligation to speak about the crimes committed against its citizens. It has the obligation to commemorate the victims, search for their remains, and provide them with a dignified burial…We will continue this work…everywhere that the graves of the victims of the Volhynian crimes still remain.” Pogrzeb ofiar Zbrodni Wołyńskiej w Ostrówkach i Woli Ostrowieckiej Na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach na terytorium Ukrainy odbyła się uroczystość pogrzebowa 55 ofiar zbrodni dokonanej 30 sierpnia 1943 roku. W uroczystości, zorganizowanej w 83. rocznicę tragicznych wydarzeń,… pic.twitter.com/4dXPOj4m7y — Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) August 30, 2026 Others to attend the reburial included deputy Ukrainian culture minister Ivan Verbytskyi; Vitaly Skomarovsky, the bishop of Lutsk and president of Ukraine’s Roman Catholic episcopate; Piotr Zgorzelski, the deputy speaker of the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament; and former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. Karol Polejowski, the deputy head of Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which led the exhumation work, said that the presence of Ukrainian representatives “fills me with optimism for the future”. While Polish President Karol Nawrocki did not attend, one of his advisors, Jakub Banaszek, read a letter on his behalf, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will never forget those who died in agony simply because they were Poles,” wrote Nawrocki. “We will not cease our efforts to ensure that all our compatriots murdered by members of the OUN-UPA are properly buried and commemorated.” ✝️ W 8⃣3⃣. rocznicę zbrodni dokonanej przez ukraińskich szowinistów, na cmentarzu w Ostrówkach pochowaliśmy ofiary ludobójstwa na Wołyniu. 🔻🔻🔻 pic.twitter.com/5oh3uiCKX4 — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) August 30, 2026 The Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Poles were killed, were led by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which was a partisan group founded by a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) faithful to nationalist leader Stepan Bandera. They sought to ethnically cleanse areas that they saw as Ukrainian territory by wiping out other ethnic groups, in particular the large Polish population. Massacres took place in dozens of villages, including Ostrówki and the neighbouring Wola Ostrowiecka (Volya Ostrovetska in Ukrainian), where on 30 August 1943 the UPA killed over 1,000 Poles and razed the villages to the ground. Exhumations previously took place on the site of the two villages in the 1990s, and again in 2011 and 2015, uncovering the remains of hundreds of victims. However, hundreds more are believed to remain buried. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches for victims on its territory in response to the dismantling of a monument to the UPA in Poland. However, in a diplomatic breakthrough last year, it allowed them to resume, including granting permission in December for work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka. In April this year, mass graves were discovered there, with exhumations then beginning in July. Earlier this month, the IPN announced the results of that work. They uncovered the remains of 55 victims, 26 of them children (mostly under 12 years of age, with the youngest a few months old) and 20 women. In the Volhynia massacres as a whole, the majority of victims were women and children. The remains of a further 55 victims of massacres by Ukrainian nationalists during WWII have been exhumed in Ukraine. Around half were children, and most show signs of brutal deaths, including skulls pierced with farming tools https://t.co/LbLPzJcG1b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 8, 2026 The locations and conditions of the remains reveal much about the manner of their death. Most were buried “at random” without coffins, which is consistent with contemporary accounts that they were killed in a barn and then thrown into a mass burial pit. Most of the remains, in particular skulls, show signs of injuries that are also consistent with contemporary accounts, which said that victims were ordered to lie on the ground before being killed with farm tools, including hammers for slaughtering cattle. Material from the bones has been secured for genetic testing, which was recently used for the first time to identify massacre victims exhumed at another location in Ukraine last year. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 The Volhynia massacres have long been a point of tension between Poland, which recognises them as a genocide, and Ukraine, which rejects that label. The decision by Kyiv to allow exhumations to resume last year was regarded as a major step towards reconciliation. However, that process was undermined in May this year, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decided to name a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted an angry response from Warsaw, where Zelensky’s counterpart Karol Nawrocki stripped him of Poland’s highest honour. In his letter read at Sunday’s ceremony, Nawrocki warned those who “continue the tradition of Banderite ideology” that they “place themselves outside the community of citizens of the free, civilised world” and are sending “a clear sign of hostility towards Poland and Poles”. President Zelensky has signed a law establishing a national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian heroes, prompting Poland to again warn that Ukraine "will have a huge problem" integrating into the EU if it honours figures associated with massacres of Poles https://t.co/fN7Zgbovvu — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Since the crisis broke out in May, there have been efforts to reach a diplomatic solution. Last month, Zelensky pointed specifically to the exhumation work in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka as evidence that “Ukraine is doing its part to fairly establish the facts about those who were killed in those years”. Subsequently, he announced a five-point plan to alleviate the crisis, including allowing more exhumations and opening up historical archives. Poland welcomed the move but said that it would wait to see how it was implemented in practice. Earlier this month, Zelensky signed a law establishing a new national pantheon of Ukrainian heroes. Poland has warned that the inclusion of figures associated with the massacres could have consequences for Ukraine’s ambitions to join the European Union. A survey conducted this month by Rating Group, a Ukrainian research agency, which asked Ukrainians to name their country’s greatest hero found that Bandera was the fourth most popular choice, having been chosen by 11% of respondents. World.title: Poland is terrible at promoting itself – but has never had better press
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Two incidents this month have highlighted how state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad often disappoint. Yet, at the same time, the country has never had better international press. Politicians should let Poland’s successes speak for themselves, and support those already telling its story. Poles care a lot about what the world thinks of their country. Major Polish media outlets regularly devote entire articles to what Western journalists, commentators and influencers are saying about Poland. “A German showed what he saw on the streets of Poland,” read one typical recent headline by Onet, Poland’s biggest news website, which devoted an entire report to one video by a German-speaking TikToker with around 7,000 followers. One rarely sees such reports in more self-confident Western countries. Given Poland’s history, such sensitivity regarding the country’s status is not surprising. Poland was, up until the 18th century, a major European country. But, for most of the last 250 years, it has been under foreign subjugation. Only since 1989 has it been able to develop independently, and Poles are understandably keen for the world to take note of their return to the top table. Poland has emerged as Europe’s undisputed growth champion over the past 35 years. In the first part of a new series of articles and podcasts, @AlicjaPtak4 explores the reasons behind Poland's rapid economic development, and the dangers that may lie ahead https://t.co/bW3bnV7Ozn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2025 Polish politicians are also inevitably eager to capitalise on such sentiment by showing voters that they are making an effort to promote Poland abroad. The problem is that such efforts are often poorly conceived and executed – as two examples this month have shown. In mid-August, the sport and tourism ministry launched a new advertising campaign intended to attract visitors from western Europe and the United States. However, the first advert – featuring Polish football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, and actor Nikodem Rozbicki playing Fryderyk Chopin – was widely panned in Poland. Res Futura, an organisation that monitors social media sentiment, found that 85% of comments about the advert were negative. The campaign’s slogan – “Poland. More than you expected” – is negative and lacking confidence. The Polish Tourism Organisation says it is based on research showing that visitors to Poland are often positively surprised by how nice it is. Yet, while that is undoubtedly true, it does not mean it is a good idea to try to attract potential tourists by focusing on their low expectations. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The video also has no narrative, with the creators seeming to think that showing famous faces will be enough. Rubik does not speak a single word, while Eisenberg says only “Poland” and Lewandowski “More than you expected”. The film itself does nothing to show that Poland is more than anyone expects. In fact, its depressingly colourless palette and focus on Warsaw’s Stalinist Palace of Science and Culture actually reinforce (false) stereotypes of Poland as grey, dull and post-communist. The country has so many interesting and colourful places that could have been showcased instead. The advert is also a wasted opportunity to tell a story about the film’s stars, especially Eisenberg, who has reconnected with his family’s Polish roots, produced a critically acclaimed movie set in Poland, and last year obtained citizenship. Instead, Chopin dominates the film, but his dialogue is incoherent. When he says, “Warsaw is where my heart is”, almost no potential visitors would understand that this is a reference to the real Chopin’s heart being transported from Paris, where he died, to Warsaw, where it is now entombed in a church. Not long after that advert launched, another controversy emerged around a state official, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, who had been appointed only weeks earlier by the government to lead the promotion of Poland. It quickly transpired that a report she had authored last year on creating a national brand – and which appeared to have played a big part in her getting the new job – contained significant errors, questionable methodology, and bizarre language. Many parts showed signs of being AI-generated. Mróz-Gorgoń, who has now resigned, insists that the report was the genuine product of work by her and her team at Marka Polska (Brand Poland), a think tank she leads. However, that is not particularly reassuring given the report’s content. Many parts are simply obvious: at the end of the 26-page text, the three recommendations for the government are to “develop a coherent, long-term national branding strategy”, “invest in promotional campaigns in key markets”, and “coordinate between ministries and other entities”. Other sections are very strange, such as noting that “Germany does not build its brand on the Holocaust”. But perhaps the most telling aspect is that, although the introduction claims it is “a comprehensive report on building…a coherent, long-term branding strategy in the international arena”, the document focuses entirely on how Poles themselves view their own country (its title is even A Self-Portrait of the Poles). It includes no research into what foreigners know or think about Poland and what could interest or attract them. While any national branding exercise should of course take account of the views of the native population, it is clearly incomplete without research into the target of such a campaign, the outside world. Yet that is sadly typical of many state-led efforts to promote Poland, which focus more on pleasing a domestic audience – the voters that politicians want to keep happy – than on being truly outward looking. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland's brand abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing major errors, bizarre language, and signs of being generated by AI https://t.co/9fpfzFCFuI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 It should be noted that such failings are nothing new. Successive governments have been responsible for botched efforts to promote Poland. The uninspiring slogan “Poland. More than you expected” has been used since 2021. A previous one, “Polska. Spring Into”, launched in 2014, was simply bizarre and quickly disappeared. In 2016, the former Law and Justice (PiS) government established the Polish National Foundation (PFN), which was pumped full of money from state-owned companies and tasked with promoting Poland abroad. Instead, it focused much of its efforts on domestic activity, often intended to support PiS’s political agenda. The work it did do internationally was often of questionable efficacy, such as spending millions on buying a yacht, naming it “I Love Poland”, then attempting to sail it around the world (before it ended up breaking down and getting stuck in port). A senior official under the former PiS government has been charged over alleged misspending of funds. The case relates to a campaign in 2017 that used money meant for promoting Poland abroad to instead advertise PiS's judicial reforms domestically https://t.co/tH64Bekhec — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 15, 2026 Yet, despite woeful state-led efforts to promote Poland abroad, the country has in recent times been enjoying a soaring international reputation. Western media have been full of articles about the country’s economic success; about how not only are Polish emigrants returning from the UK, but many Brits are moving to Poland too; about how Poles are becoming major buyers of property in Spain; about how companies with roots in Poland, such as InPost and ElevenLabs, are pioneering their industries. Social media feeds are full of influencers extolling Polish cities, with their safe, clean streets; the beauty of Polish nature, with its mountains, lakes and beaches; and the sense of dynamic development that you can feel as soon as you set foot in the country. Last weekend,@thetimes reported on how Brits are moving to Poland. This weekend, on how Poles are replacing Brits as property owners in Spain. pic.twitter.com/IDDdDlluTE — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) June 21, 2026 This positive publicity is largely organic – it is the product of Poland’s own actual successes, not of artificial efforts to create an image of success. It is generated from the bottom up, not from the top down. While the state can play a role – for example, by arranging visits for foreign journalists and influencers and supporting media and institutions that are already telling Poland’s story – it would be better for politicians to focus on creating the conditions for those successes, rather than concocting cockeyed schemes to promote them. World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
