World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Main image credit: Andrzej Romański/UMK

World.title: Polish president’s office criticises government for rejecting hosting of allied nuclear weapons
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. A dispute has emerged between Poland’s government and the office of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over whether Poland would be willing to host allied nuclear weapons. Deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski announced on Thursday that Poland wants to participate in the US-led NATO nuclear sharing programme, but without actually hosting warheads. That prompted criticism from Nawrocki’s senior foreign policy aide, Marcin Przydacz, who says Poland should host such weapons. Jedno zdanie wiceszefa MON wystarczyło, by wywołać polityczną burzę wokół kwestii broni jądrowej w Polsce. Paweł Zalewski stwierdził w Kwaterze Głównej NATO w Brukseli, że Polska nie chce głowic nuklearnych na swoim terytorium. Kilka godzin później zareagował szef MON Władysław… pic.twitter.com/EqjTPKqidg — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) August 28, 2026 Zalewski met on Thursday with Elbridge Colby, US under secretary of defence for policy, at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels. Afterwards, he was asked by reporters if an expanded future US military presence in Poland might include nuclear weapons. “No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory,” replied Zalewski, quoted by broadcaster TVN. The minister added that Poland still wants to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme. However, he said that this could be achieved without hosting the weapons themselves. Those remarks triggered criticism from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. Former PiS defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak said that refusing to host warheads “in practice means renouncing participation in nuclear sharing”. “Poland should strive for full participation in nuclear sharing,” added Błaszczak. “This is not a matter of Poland possessing its own nuclear weapons, but of strengthening NATO’s nuclear deterrence on the eastern flank.” Criticism also came from other sources, including retired Brigadier General Stanisław Koziej, who served as head of the National Security Bureau (BBN) of former President Bronisław Komorowski, who is an ally of the current government. Koziej called Zalewski’s announcement “an incomprehensible strategic mistake in the field of deterrence”. He said that, to deter Russia, Vladimir Putin must know that there is the possibility Poland could host nuclear weapons. Chęci nie odstraszają. Odstraszają realne zdolności – własne i sojusznicze. A przede wszystkim takie, o jakich użyciu sami decydujemy. To elementarz, który warto przypomnieć https://t.co/Nc3xXnA7bU — Paweł Zalewski (@ZalewskiPawel) August 27, 2026 Late on Thursday, Zalewski commented on the controversy. He rejected Błaszczak’s claim that refusing to host warheads would effectively exclude Poland from nuclear sharing. “We want to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme without wanting the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland,” he wrote. “Thanks to our efforts, NATO has opened up precisely such a possibility.” In response to Koziej, Zalewski argued that “intentions do not deter, real capabilities do…above all, those whose use we ourselves decide upon”. Meanwhile, defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also weighed in, declaring that “Poland remains strongly interested in participating in the NATO nuclear sharing programme” and is also “conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in a European nuclear protective umbrella”. Kosiniak-Kamysz did not, however, comment on the issue of Poland potentially hosting warheads. Rozwiewając wszelkie wątpliwości: Polska jest niezmiennie zainteresowana udziałem w programie NATO Nuclear Sharing. Prowadzimy także rozmowy na temat propozycji uczestnictwa w europejskim nuklearnym parasolu ochronnym. Stanowisko naszego rządu jest w tych kwestiach… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) August 27, 2026 On Friday morning, Przydacz, who is the head of President Nawrocki’s International Policy Bureau (BPM), joined the criticism of Zalewski, calling his comments “bizarre, absurd and completely inconsistent with what Poland has been saying so far and what the policy of the Polish state is”. “Both the presidential palace and the executive branch of the government have so far supported Poland joining the nuclear sharing programme as part of its deterrence policy,” he continued. Przydacz added that “it is not true” the country wants to participate without actually hosting warheads. “Poland also wants to have warheads on its territory,” he said. Nawrocki, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump, has made clear his support for Poland seeking a nuclear sharing arrangement with the United States. But it remains unclear exactly what the government’s plans are. Earlier this year, Poland entered discussions with France over the extension of the French “nuclear umbrella” over Europe. Later, however, Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated that Poland would not want to actually host French nuclear-armed aircraft. Both last year and this year, Tusk has also hinted that Poland could seek to develop its own independent nuclear deterrent. However, Colby made clear that the US would “strenuously oppose” European countries such as Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian states seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has regularly clashed with the government, including vetoing a record number of laws. However, the two sides have sought to present a more united front on issues of national security. The United States would “strenuously oppose” Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian countries seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons, says a senior Pentagon official. World.title: Prague Philharmonic Could Begin Construction in 2028. New Visuals Reveal Design
World.content:
Prague has taken another step toward building the long-planned Vltava Philharmonic.

The Prague Development Company (PDS) submitting an application for planning permission and new visualizations revealing the project in greater detail.

The application covers not only the Philharmonic building but also the surrounding public spaces, transport infrastructure and connections to the existing metro, tram, road, cycling and pedestrian networks.



If the permitting process stays on schedule, the city expects to receive the necessary approval in the first quarter of 2027. A tender for the construction company would then follow, with building work potentially starting in the first quarter of 2028.

The project is planned for the Bubny-Zátory district, near the existing Vltavská metro station. The new cultural complex is expected to be completed in 2033, when trial operations could begin.

The building was designed by Danish architecture studio BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group, which won an international competition in May 2022. Preparation of the detailed permit documentation began in 2025.

The complex will have three underground levels and six floors above ground. It will contain five music halls, creative spaces, restaurants and other facilities.

The project is also intended to provide new premises for the Prague Symphony Orchestra FOK and music collections belonging to the Municipal Library of Prague. The Czech Philharmonic is also expected to gain additional facilities, addressing the limitations of its current premises.

Construction could start in early 2028

The current estimated cost of the Philharmonic building is around CZK 12.33 billion, including equipment but excluding VAT. The surrounding infrastructure and public spaces are expected to cost an additional CZK 5 billion, also excluding VAT.

World.title: Tiny Steps, Big Milestones: What Really Matters When Toddlers Start Preschool
World.content:
For a one-year-old, starting preschool is not about learning letters or sitting through lessons.

It is about feeling safe without Mum or Dad nearby, discovering the joy of playing alongside other children, and slowly gaining the confidence to explore the world independently. At Tiny Tots in Prague, these small everyday moments are at the heart of the programme.

A favourite toy clutched tightly in one hand. A cautious look back at Mum or Dad from the classroom door. Perhaps a few tears (from either side).

For families with children aged one or two, the first experience of leaving a little one in someone else’s care can feel like a very big step.

And for the child, it is one too.



At this age, development happens through moments that can look almost insignificant to adults: reaching for a spoon without help, joining another child in play, recognising a familiar song, saying a new word, or feeling comfortable enough to wander a little further away from a trusted adult.

These are precisely the moments that Tiny Tots, a programme for children aged 1–2 at Nessie English Preschool, part of Park Lane International School, is designed to encourage.

Before learning comes feeling safe

For very young children, a good first preschool experience begins with something much more fundamental than an academic curriculum: trust.

“Parents often want to know how their child will cope with separation, whether we can follow the rhythm they are used to at home and, above all, whether their child will really be seen as an individual,” says Catalina Gonzalez-Got, who leads the Tiny Tots programme.

Catalina knows the feeling from both sides. An early-years educator with international experience, she is also a mother herself. Becoming a parent, she says, gave her a much deeper understanding of how emotional it can be to entrust a young child to somebody else for the first time.

That is why settling in is treated as a process rather than a test that a toddler is expected to pass on day one.

Some children may quickly become curious about their new surroundings. Others need more time, reassurance and proximity to a familiar adult before they are ready to explore.

Both are perfectly normal. The goal is to allow each child to find that confidence at their own pace.

For toddlers, play is serious business

Adults sometimes separate “playing” and “learning”. Toddlers do not.

When a child squishes playdough between their fingers, listens to a story, sings along to a familiar song, explores the garden or watches another toddler build something, they are constantly learning.

They are practising movement and coordination. They are discovering cause and effect. They are learning how to communicate, negotiate space with other children, manage emotions and make choices.

Tiny Tots therefore follows a play-based approach inspired by the English Early Years Foundation Stage framework, with activities designed around the developmental needs of one- and two-year-olds.

There are no miniature school desks or pressure to perform.

Instead, children encounter language, movement, music, creative activities, sensory experiences, stories and outdoor play as a natural part of their day.

The programme keeps the class to a maximum of eight children, allowing teachers to pay close attention to individual personalities, routines and developmental stages.

English without the flashcards

The same philosophy applies to language.

At one or two years old, learning English does not mean memorising vocabulary lists. Children absorb language through relationships and repetition: hearing the same words during snack time, listening to songs, following simple instructions, sharing a picture book or hearing an adult describe what is happening during play.

Tiny Tots provides an English-language environment, giving children regular, natural exposure to the language throughout their day.

Catalina, who raises her own child in a multilingual family, sees communication as something that should grow out of connection rather than performance.

Toddlers often understand far more than they can say, she explains. What matters is creating a positive environment in which language is associated with people, experiences and emotions that make sense to the child.

Learning to do things “all by myself”

Anyone who lives with a toddler knows how powerful those words can be.

Between one and two, children increasingly want to try things independently — even when the result is a spoon on the floor, mismatched shoes or a task that takes considerably longer than if an adult simply did it for them.

Tiny Tots gives children safe opportunities to practise that emerging independence while knowing that an adult is close by when they need help.

The milestone may be eating more independently, choosing an activity, joining a group song, approaching another child or simply becoming comfortable enough to explore a new corner of the room.

For a toddler, these are significant achievements.

And independence does not mean pushing children away from adults. In fact, the opposite is often true: children are more willing to explore when they know they have a trusted person to return to.

A small community for Prague’s smallest residents

For international families in particular, early-years programmes can provide something else that is easy to overlook: a sense of community.

Many parents raising children in Prague live far from grandparents, siblings and the wider family network that might otherwise form part of everyday life.

A nurturing preschool environment can therefore become more than somewhere a child spends part of the day. Familiar teachers, other children and their families can gradually become part of the support network that makes a new city feel more like home.

Tiny Tots is based at Nessie English Preschool in Prague 5, in a quiet residential setting with its own garden. The programme combines experienced early-years teachers, personalised attention and structured routines with plenty of room for children simply to play, discover and be little.

Because at one or two years old, success does not need to look impressive.

Sometimes it is a child who cried at the door last week walking in happily today.

Sometimes it is making a first little friend.

Sometimes it is a new word, a messy painting, a favourite song or the confidence to let go of a teacher’s hand and go exploring alone.

Those tiny steps are exactly where the big journey begins.

Tiny Tots at Nessie English Preschool is designed for children aged 1–2 years. Families interested in the programme can arrange a visit to the Prague 5 campus to see the environment and meet the team.

Enrolment for the 2026/27 school year is now open.

World.title: Wine Harvest Festivals in Prague in September: The Full Guide
World.content:
Every September, Prague celebrates vinobraní, the traditional wine harvest festival marking the end of the grape season.

Visitors can look forward to concerts, dance and theatre performances, food stalls, and tastings of young wine and the seasonal favorite burčák (partially fermented grape juice). The festivals are family-friendly, offering children’s theatre, horse rides, folk craft demonstrations, competitions, and workshops.



Here is an overview of the main wine festivals in Prague in 2026:

Vinohrady Wine Harvest Festival

September 11–12, 2026, 10:00–21:00

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad

Facebook

Winemakers from across Europe — Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Romania, Serbia, Ukraine, and Poland — will join Czech and Moravian producers.

Alongside wine, expect a wide range of food: sausages, cheeses, potato spirals, langoše (fried dough with toppings), and traditional Wallachian cakes (frgály). The festival also offers live music and a children’s zone with a playground, carousel, and creative workshops. Admission is free.

Wine Harvest at Prague Castle

September 5–6, 2026, 11:00–18:00

Royal Garden & Ball Game Hall, Prague Castle, Hradčany

hrad.cz

Set in the historic Royal Garden of Prague Castle, this festival features tastings of Czech and Moravian wines, sparkling wines, fresh grape juice, burčák, and high-quality local produce. The program includes folk ensembles, historical fencing, and family activities.

Entry to the garden is free; a tasting glass costs 120 CZK.

Grébovka Wine Festival

September 18, 2026 (14:00–20:00) at náměstí Míru

September 19, 2026 (13:00–20:00) at Havlíčkovy sady (Grébovka Park)

Facebook

Organized by Prague 2, the Grébovka Festival is one of the city’s largest and most popular wine events. Set in Havlíčkovy sady (often described as a hidden gem of Vinohrady), the festival offers wine tastings, culinary specialties, live music, dance performances, and a cultural program celebrating wine traditions. Families can enjoy workshops, theatre, competitions, and children’s activities.

St. Clare’s Vineyard Harvest Festival

September 12–13, 2026

Prague Botanical Garden, Fata Morgana greenhouse, Troja

botanicka.cz

Hosted at the St. Clare’s Vineyard in the Prague Botanical Garden, this festival is renowned for its carefully made burčák, produced from handpicked grapes. Guests can sample varietal wines, cuvées, and brandies from this rare Prague vineyard, along with wines from leading Czech and Moravian producers. Guided cellar tours, food stalls, live music, and terrace dancing complete the program.

Troja Wine Harvest Festival

September 13, 2026, 11:00–20:00

Gardens of Troja Chateau, Prague 7

Facebook

Held in the baroque Troja Chateau, this festival combines wine tastings from Czech, Moravian, and international producers with burčák, traditional food, and live music. Children’s activities include games, workshops, and a kids’ zone. Admission is free.

St. Wenceslas Wine Festival

September 28, 2026, 12:00–18:00

Villa Richter & St. Wenceslas Vineyard, Prague Castle

Facebook

Taking place in the historic St. Wenceslas Vineyard, the oldest in Bohemia, this festival is steeped in legend — St. Wenceslas is said to have planted and harvested vines here for sacramental wine. Visitors can enjoy wines from leading Czech and Moravian wineries, sample burčák, and take in panoramic views of Prague’s Old Town.

17th Malá Strana Wine Festival

September 19, 2026, 13:00–22:00

Kampa Park, Malá Strana

Set along the Vltava River in Kampa Park, this festival celebrates the traditions of the Horňácko region in South Moravia. Expect cimbalom music, folk dancing, local wines, burčák, homemade sausages, and slivovice (plum brandy). Craft stalls and lively performances bring a taste of Moravian countryside to the heart of Prague. Free entry.

Vinobraní na Náplavce

Tents selling wine and burčák from Czech producers will be located on the Rašínovo nábřeží embankment (between the railway bridge and the Vyšehrad rock). The festival will also offer snacks that pair perfectly with wine. Organizers have prepared live music and several different wine competitions for guests, including a corkscrew competition, blind tasting, flavor identification, and more.

September 25 and 26, 2026, from 1:00 PM to 9:30 PM;

Price: 100 CZK (includes a glass tasting glass)

World.title: Czechia Spent CZK 19 Billion on COVID Vaccines and Used Less Than Half
World.content:
The Czech Republic has spent roughly CZK 19 billion on COVID-19 vaccines since 2020, but fewer than half of the 41 million doses supplied under its pandemic-era procurement agreement were ultimately used in the country.

More than 18 million doses expired and had to be destroyed, representing a value of about CZK 8 billion.

A further four million doses were donated to other countries, according to information provided by the Czech Ministry of Health in response to a request from the Czech Technical Committee.



For the 2026-27 vaccination season, around 900,000 doses will be available in the country. By comparison, fewer than one-third of that number was administered during the previous season. The vaccination season runs from September through the end of August the following year.

Demand for COVID-19 vaccination has fallen sharply since the initial rollout. More than 15 million doses were administered during the first year vaccines were widely available. A year later, demand had fallen to roughly one-fifth of that level. Between 2022 and 2023, interest dropped by more than 80 percent, followed by further declines of about one-third in subsequent years.

Only about 1,500 doses had been administered by July 26 this year. Most vaccinations, however, take place during the autumn months.

The low demand has contributed to substantial vaccine waste. When the original purchases were made, authorities faced considerable uncertainty over how the pandemic would develop, how many booster doses would be required and how many people would seek vaccination.

Maintaining sufficient supplies was considered necessary in case the epidemiological situation deteriorated.

The Czech Republic is now considering a different approach to future procurement. The Ministry of Health is negotiating with vaccine manufacturers, health insurance companies and medical organisations over supplies and financing for the 2027-28 season. The talks are taking into account both the expected demand and the cost-effectiveness of vaccination.

World.title: Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools — Nearly One in Five in Prague
World.content:
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.

According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.

Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.

Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.



The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.

The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.

Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.

The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.

Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School

Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.

Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.

This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

World.title: Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
World.content:
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.

McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.

The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.



Burgermeister prepares Czech debut

One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.

The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.

Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding

Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.

The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.

Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.

Five Guys adds another international brand

The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.

The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.

Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.

Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.

The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.

Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities

The expansion is not limited to international companies.

Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.

The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.

World.title: Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
World.content:
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.

Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.

At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.



The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.

The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.

The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.

How the Champions League league phase works

The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.

Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.

The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.

The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

World.title: MINT Market Returns to Prague’s Náplavka with More Than 130 Local Brands
World.content:
MINT Market returns to Prague’s Rašín Embankment on Sunday, September 6, bringing more than 130 independent brands and makers to the Vltava riverbank.

From 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., visitors can browse a wide selection of independent fashion, jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations and original accessories, with many of the products made by small Czech and Prague-based businesses.



The popular design market is also known for its relaxed atmosphere, food stalls and chill-out area. Admission is free, and the riverside venue is fully accessible. The event is suitable for visitors of all ages.

MINT Market has been supporting independent and local creators since 2010.

Over the past 16 years, the project has grown from a small market into a nationwide platform, hosting more than 450 events in over 20 Czech cities and bringing together a community of more than 1,500 designers and makers.

For visitors, the September event offers a chance to discover products that are often made locally and in small quantities, while meeting the people behind the brands directly.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The best design markets in CZ (@mintmarket.cz)

“Supporting small and local brands has been one of the core ideas of our project from the very beginning,” says MINT Market organizer Lenka Šašková.

“We provide creators with a place where they can showcase their products and meet their customers, because nothing can replace a personal meeting.”

The full list of vendors and further information about the September market can be found on the MINT Market website. Updates are also available through the Facebook event and Instagram.

World.title: Internal documents show Orbán-linked politician and businessman had unlimited power over Hungary’s public media
World.content:
Hungarian public media chiefs are filing a police complaint over alleged unlawful management practices in previous years, the press office of the operator, Duna Médiaszolgáltató, said on Monday.

Orbán-linked politician ‘steered Hungary’s public media’

Internal letters, statements and other documents uncovered during a review of the then operator, the Media Services and Asset Management Fund (MTVA), reveal details of the political surveillance of the public media and the role played by Attila Várhegyi, a Fidesz-linked politician and businessman, in directing the organisation, the statement said.

According to the statement, the public media was effectively managed by Mr Várhegyi, who had been contracted as an adviser. He assumed the powers of media executives, making decisions on content, staffing and financial matters. “In many cases, those in charge of the institution did not even dare to make a decision without his consent,” it said.

The 20 August broadcast of the renewed Hungarian public media. Source: Facebook/Közmédia

Link between politicians and public media

The statement also suggested that Mr Várhegyi acted as a link between the political leadership and the public media, conveying the wishes of government ministers and Fidesz politicians.

“Várhegyi’s conduct clearly shows that the public media, which is legally required to be independent of political influence, was in fact under close political control,” the statement said.

According to the statement, not only was Mr Várhegyi’s informal influence unlawful, but so were “the benefits he accepted”.

If you missed: Why is it a problem if Péter Magyar decides who can lead Hungary’s public media?

For years, for example, the public media provided him with a driver, who was employed as an event organiser “to conceal the truth in official documents”.

PM Orbán (left) and propaganda minister Antal Rogán (right). Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Mr Várhegyi also held weekly meetings with public media executives, at which “director general Dániel Papp and other leaders informed him about even the smallest matters”, consulted him on planned decisions and acted on his instructions, the statement said.

The document added that Mr Várhegyi had received a monthly salary of HUF 3.5 million since 2023.

Owner of Hollóháza porcelain brand

Mr Várhegyi owns 100 per cent of the shares in Hollóháza Porcelain Manufacturer, a world-renowned Hungarian brand that he bought in 2020. He paid HUF 175 million for the company at the time.

New chapter may begin in history of public service media on 20 August

World.title: PM Magyar: Hungary has met all conditions to access frozen EU funds
World.content:
Hungary has met all the European Union’s requirements to access “thousands of billions” of forints in EU funding, “in line with its commitments and by today’s deadline”, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Facebook on Monday.

“Now the funds from Brussels are welcome to arrive,” Magyar said, thanking everyone who had contributed to the Government’s efforts. Hungary has reportedly completed the measures required to unlock around €10 billion from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility, while a total of €16.4 billion in previously frozen EU funds is at stake.

Magyar talks about a more constructive role

Hungary had become a more constructive player within the European Union under the new Government, Magyar said at the Bled Strategic Forum. “But that does not mean that we would not defend Hungarian interests every minute of every day,” he added.

PM Péter Magyar and FM Anita Orbán in Bled, Slovenia. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Magyar also spoke of the need to strengthen the EU’s political leadership, improve its competitiveness and harness the potential of Central European co-operation. He said Hungary was ready to play a more constructive role in the European Union than it had in the past.

‘We have come for our money’

“It is not a great challenge to be more constructive than we were before,” he remarked.

Magyar stressed that the Prime Minister’s duty was to represent the interests of the Hungarian people, just as every EU member state was required to defend its own interests.

If you missed: Hungarian Parliament clears fiscal reforms to unlock additional EU funds

Recalling his first meeting with Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Brussels, Magyar said he had made Hungary’s position clear: “We have come for our money.”

Photo: Anadolu/Dursun Aydemir

He described negotiations over €16.4 billion in Hungarian EU funds, which had been frozen for three or four years, as smooth. According to Magyar, Hungary gained access to the money within a single day, although the European Commission is expected to assess the country’s compliance with the agreed milestones before funds are disbursed.

Hungary set to launch EUR 5.5 billion railway upgrade as development plan gets green light

Featured image: illustration. Facebook/Péter Magyar

World.title: Péter Magyar in Bled about crisis management, budget deficit, EU affairs, illegal migration, regional cooperation
World.content:
Hungary’s government has already solved several crisis situations since coming to power in May, Prime Minister Péter Magyar told the Bled Strategy Forum in Slovenia on Monday, adding: “I am proud of my government.”

He cited the energy supply crisis due to extreme weather conditions as an example, saying that the solution was provided by “a huge, unprecedented cooperation.” He also said that while his government had inherited a significant deficit, they have managed to shrink it by 2.5 billion euros.

PM Péter Magyar and FM Anita Orbán in Bled, Slovenia. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Straightforward dialogue

A straightforward dialogue is crucial when it comes to resolving problems facing the European Union, Magyar said. Concerning the fight against illegal migration, Magyar said “it is hard to explain to Hungarians why Hungary receives unfair treatment in Brussels.”

Under a European court ruling, Hungary has to pay a significant amount a day “just because we protect the common EU borders … this is not fair,” he said, adding that border control was “one of the most important tasks” of EU member states.

Tisza government ‘more constructive’ than predecessor

The Tisza government is “more constructive than its predecessor in the EU, but it does not mean that we would not promote the Hungarian interest day and night,” the prime minister said at the Bled Strategy Forum on Monday.

The European Union needs to focus on such issues as economic cooperation and competitiveness, he said. “It is not too late for change … we need to decide if the EU just wants to survive or win,” he said, adding that the two ways required two different approaches.

He said “the latter is still not the goal” in Brussels, but added that central Europe “must work to become a winner” and highlighted the importance of regional cooperation.

Regional cooperation important for Hungary, FM Anita Orbán highlighted

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán underscored the importance of regional cooperation ahead of the Bled Strategic Forum, which begins on Monday. Hungary’s security, competitiveness, transport and energy connections, and the European integration of the Western Balkans all depend on how well the country can cooperate in the region, Orbán said in a post on Facebook.

If you missed – Péter Magyar’s government promises a new era for Hungarian schools: should pupils and teachers be celebrating?

The minister is attending the forum in Slovenia, which she described as “one of the most important foreign policy meetings in central and south-eastern Europe”, where political and diplomatic leaders gather to discuss the region’s most pressing issues.

She said the Bled Strategic Forum had “tangible stakes” for Hungary. Orbán said she would discuss regional cooperation with her counterparts on Monday and hold several bilateral meetings.

The 21st Bled Strategic Forum, which begins on Monday, will focus on Europe’s future, European Union enlargement, European security, and the Western Balkans. The two-day event will bring together heads of state and government as well as foreign ministers from central and south-eastern Europe, EU commissioners and economic and policy experts.

New home-building programme in Hungary may reshape property market

World.title: Another Budapest city centre district may ban Airbnb – referendum on the horizon
World.content:
Buda Castle District council is launching a poll on short-term rentals (Airbnbs), allowing residents’ views to inform decisions on future regulation, the council told Hungarian news agency MTI.

Mayor wants a vibrant and attractive residential district

The issue is particularly timely because the statutory moratorium on registering new short-term accommodation will expire at the end of the year. The council must therefore decide what rules should apply in District I, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Short-term rentals are a particularly significant issue in District I, one of Budapest’s main tourist destinations, especially in and around Buda Castle. Short-term rentals generates tourism revenue, but residents’ associations and property owners have also raised a number of concerns about such rentals.

Buda Castle District: operating short-term rental(s) here can be a gold mine for families, companies. Photo: PrtScr/Youtube

“There are markedly different arguments and interests at stake in the debate, and all of them deserve consideration. As mayor, I believe it is right that we should not make decisions over the heads of the people who live here,” László Böröcz said, according to the statement.

The Fidesz mayor added that the council wanted to preserve Buda Castle as a vibrant and attractive residential district, while recognising that tourism and short-term rentals are important to many people and local businesses.

Buda Castle district may ban Airbnb

Residents aged 18 or over who have a permanent address in District I will be eligible to take part in the poll. They will be asked two questions.

The first will ask whether they support a complete ban on Airbnb. The second will ask whether, if Airbnb were not banned, they would support the council imposing conditions on the provision of short-term accommodation.

Airbnb restrictions in Budapest could deter tourists

In response to a question from MTI, the council said that District I currently has more than 400 licensed private accommodations and other properties, typically operated as commercial businesses.

The first Budapest district to ban Airbnb rentals was the capital’s 6th district following a referendum, which had a very low turnout.

Locals against the ban of new short-term rentals in Budapest’s 6th district. Photo: Facebook/Magyar ApartmanKiadók Egyesülete

Airbnb bust continues in Budapest: another district joins the regulations

World.title: Man in life-threatening condition after huge fall near Budapest’s Chain Bridge
World.content:
A man is in a life-threatening condition after plunging on to the paved embankment beside the Danube in central Budapest, near the Pontoon entertainment venue.

Accident near popular Budapest riverside venue

The serious accident took place in the early hours of Sunday near the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. The man, believed to be aged about 40, fell on to the embankment paving and was taken to hospital by ambulance with severe injuries, Telex wrote.

Both Pontoon and the police issued statements about the incident. The venue stressed that the accident had not occurred on its premises.

Pontoon said the accident occured in a public space. Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

“The incident did not take place within the area of Pontoon’s open-air hospitality venue, but further away, in a public space,” it said.

According to Pontoon, the man’s fall was preceded by a fight. The venue said members of the group involved had also used pepper spray. It did not, however, provide further details of what happened during the fight or the circumstances in which the man fell on to the embankment.

Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

Police opened an investigation

The venue said it had offered immediate assistance after the accident, helped secure the scene and co-operated with the authorities. It added that, to its knowledge, the responding authorities had not linked the incident to Pontoon’s operations.

The Budapest Police Headquarters confirmed that it had received several reports at about 1.23am on August 30 that a man had fallen on to the paved embankment near the Pest end of the Chain Bridge. Officers who arrived at the scene gathered information, while paramedics took the injured man to hospital.

Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

If you missed: Bus and car crash at Budapest’s Astoria leaves nine injured, woman in life-threatening condition

Police have opened an investigation on suspicion of the criminal offence of disorderly conduct committed by a group, in an effort to establish the full circumstances of the incident. Investigators have questioned witnesses and seized CCTV footage.

Pontoon said that the investigating authorities were best placed to provide an authoritative account of the precise details, adding that the venue fully supported efforts to establish what had happened.

The venue is in the heart of Budapest’s city centre, so the police will probably be able to find out what happened exactly. Photo: Facebook/PONTOON

Source of all photos: Facebook/PONTOON

World.title: Domestic mosquitoes spread African virus linked to serious illness as first Hungarian case diagnosed
World.content:
The case was diagnosed in the 33rd epidemiological week of 2026, with laboratory tests by the National Public Health and Pharmacy Centre confirming the infection. An epidemiological investigation found that the patient had not travelled abroad before falling ill, meaning the infection is considered to have been acquired in Hungary.

Virus behind exotic disease is active in Hungary

The case is particularly noteworthy because last year’s first locally acquired infection in Hungary was identified as early as the 31st epidemiological week. The latest infection therefore once again indicates that the virus is present in the country’s mosquito population, Szúnyogmonitor wrote.

The West Nile virus’s natural cycle takes place primarily between birds and the native and widespread Culex mosquito. Humans and horses are known as ‘dead-end hosts’: they can become infected but generally do not pass the virus on.

The infection often goes unnoticed. Most human cases are asymptomatic. When symptoms do develop, they may include fever, headache, muscle pain, malaise and other flu-like symptoms. In rarer cases, however, the virus can attack the nervous system, causing encephalitis or meningitis, severe neurological symptoms and, in extreme cases, death.

It can be fatal: these groups face the greatest risk

Fatal cases are not unknown in Europe. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), 1,112 locally acquired infections and 97 deaths were recorded across 14 European countries in 2025. The situation was particularly serious in Italy, where 72 of 779 cases proved fatal – a mortality rate of almost 10 per cent.

The greatest risk is faced by older people and those whose immune defences are weakened by an underlying medical condition. Most infected people, however, recover from the illness without serious consequences.

The Hungarian case should therefore prompt heightened vigilance rather than panic. Mosquitoes play a key role in the virus’s emergence in Hungary, making the continuous monitoring of mosquito populations and the pathogens they carry particularly important. There are no vaccines or specific treatments for the virus.

Multiple deaths in Europe

In the Netherlands, an infection causing West Nile fever was detected in August for the first time in seven years. The country’s public health institute said at the time that about 80 per cent of people infected with the virus showed no symptoms. However, roughly 1 per cent developed neurological complications, chiefly people over 50 and those with weakened immune systems. In rare cases, the infection can prove fatal.

The agency advised people to wear long-sleeved clothing, use insect repellent and keep mosquitoes at bay with bed nets and window screens.

If you missed: A curious experiment reveals why Hungary is fighting a losing battle against a mosquito invasion

But on August 26, the Hungarian news agency MTI reported that the first person in the Netherlands had died from West Nile fever, in the province of Utrecht. The only detail released about the victim was that they were elderly. At the time, two further cases were known to have been acquired within the country. Another patient being treated in hospital for West Nile virus was also reportedly elderly, according to the Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant. Earlier, a woman had died after contracting the infection while travelling in south-eastern Europe.

This is hardly surprising: reports last week said that further West Nile virus infections had been recorded in Serbia and Croatia, while North Macedonia was facing the most serious outbreak in the region.

According to figures released last week by the ECDC, Albania, Austria, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Kosovo, the Netherlands, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia and Spain have reported cases this year.

ECDC: Hungary, among other countries, facing a growing threat from mosquito-borne diseases

World.title: Documents revealed: how former Economic Minister Márton Nagy splashed public money on luxury and private jets abroad
World.content:
While not a single hope, plan or promise Márton Nagy made as economic minister concerning economic growth appears to have materialised, the minister seems to have been more than willing to spend public money – both at the time and in retrospect, inexplicably – on luxury accommodation and private jets. All the while, Hungary was enduring one of the most severe bouts of inflation in its history.

Ministry releases inexplicable figures

Documents released in response to a freedom-of-information request by the Ministry for National Economy and its legal successor show that tens of millions of forints in public money were spent on the minister’s travel and accommodation between 2023 and 2026. The figures suggest that these were not merely expensive trips: in several cases, both the choice of hotel and the mode of transport are difficult to justify.

Márton Nagy speaking as Hungary’s Economy Minister at the CPAC 2024 conference in Budapest. Photo: Facebook/Alapjogokért Központ

The documents reveal that Márton Nagy travelled on official business to 51 cities in 32 countries between 2023 and 2026, spending a total of 115 nights abroad. Accommodation cost 51.9 million forints in total, amounting to an average of 451,000 forints per night, according to 24.hu.

That figure is striking enough in its own right. According to figures from Hungary’s Central Statistical Office, the country’s net median salary was 438,000 forints in July 2026. In other words, an average night abroad for Márton Nagy cost more than a Hungarian employee took home in an entire month, hvg.hu reports.

The most extravagant spending

The detailed expenses include even more eye-catching items. In September 2025, two nights at The Stafford in London cost 1.8 million forints, while three nights at Copenhagen’s Hotel Sanders came to 3.8 million forints – approximately 1.2 million forints per night. Two nights at the Botanic Hotel in Antwerp were charged at 980,000 forints.

Illustration. It seems that Márton Nagy loved to spend public money on luxury accommodations…

The choice of hotel does not appear particularly restrained, either. According to the figures, the delegation regularly stayed at hotels belonging to international luxury chains such as Four Seasons, Mandarin Oriental, Ritz-Carlton and Waldorf Astoria. In Antwerp, Márton Nagy stayed several times at the same luxury hotel, despite having an official programme in Brussels. He did the same in Zagreb, where he stayed in accommodation on the Adriatic coast, and in the Far East.

Public money for private jets

The use of private aircraft substantially inflated the cost of the trips. A journey from Paris to Davos in January 2024 cost 39.7 million forints, of which the private jet alone accounted for 30 million. According to HVG, private aircraft were also used for destinations that could easily have been reached by commercial flights.

… and private jets. Photo: depositphotos.com

The 2024 trip to South Korea is particularly noteworthy. Márton Nagy and his seven-member delegation also visited Jeju Island, one of South Korea’s most popular resorts, often described as the Hawaii of Korea. The official purpose of the visit was listed as “strategic partner consultations”, yet the documents provided do not make clear how many days the minister spent on the island or what his specific programme there involved. The delegation’s accommodation, however, cost slightly more than 1 million forints for five days.

How Márton Nagy grew wealthy under the Orbán government

An investigative series by Válasz Online, published in three parts (HERE, HERE and HERE), suggests that Márton Nagy has accumulated considerable wealth in recent years through economic interests linked to his family and its business network. According to the publication, his brother, Szilárd Nagy, has played a particularly important role, as has the circle of lawyers he operates, which over the years has received a lot of public money through commissions from numerous state-owned and state-backed companies.

Válasz Online’s analysis found that contracts awarded by at least 80 state-linked entities were connected to this network. In the case of 34 companies, it identified specific contracts worth at least 8.2 billion forints. According to Márton Nagy’s own asset declaration, he has owned a 89-square-metre flat in Budapest’s District II since 2014. He bought it while serving as a central-bank executive, with the National Bank of Hungary providing financial assistance towards the purchase.

Luxury property and asset managers

The family’s property holdings are considerably more substantial, however. His wife owns a stake in a 168-square-metre luxury flat in District II, estimated to be worth roughly half a billion forints, the larger share of which belongs to Szilárd Nagy. She also has an interest in a property in Vászoly worth approximately 150 million forints. A bank mortgage of 447 million forints was registered against the luxury property in Buda, but according to Válasz Online, it was repaid within just four or five months.

If you missed: Was a EUR 275 million fraud uncovered in connection with Gondosóra emergency alert device for the elderly?

Another important figure in the family’s business network is Péter Fenyvesi, who was previously involved in managing Szilárd Nagy’s property assets and later became head of Trustify Investment Fund Management. The private-equity funds managed by Trustify received substantial amounts of state capital, Válasz Online reports. Trustify Impact I, for example, was allocated 35 billion forints through a state capital programme, while a bank loan backed by a state guarantee was also used to finance the fund’s contribution.

The funds have acquired interests in a range of ventures, including property developments around Lake Balaton, an office building in Buda, energy and technology companies, and solar and wind farms. Their investments include a property project in Zánka that was previously state-owned.

Taken together, the three Válasz Online investigations point to a network linking state positions, family business connections, legal commissions, property holdings and private-equity funds operating with substantial public money. Through this network, Márton Nagy appears to be connected – directly or through his family – to assets and business interests of considerable value.

Horror over Paks II NPP overpricing: did Orbán-linked and Tisza-affiliated businessmen and politicians pocket the cash?

World.title: Video, photos: Hungarian man who evaded FBI for years and wanted for crimes against kids tracked down
World.content:
A 48-year-old Hungarian man arrested in Győr and wanted by the authorities over child pornography has been extradited to the United States, the National Bureau of Investigation of Hungary’s Rapid Response Police told police.hu on Monday.

Hungarian man handed over to the FBI

According to the statement, US authorities had been pursuing multiple proceedings against the man for several years over the possession of child pornography, after videos of that nature were found on electronic devices seized from him.

The Hungarian had been on the run for four years, prompting speculation that he may have sought refuge in Hungary. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) asked the Hungarian authorities for help in tracking him down at the beginning of this year.

He was eventually arrested in Győr on March 17, when it emerged that he had lived in the city for two years.

Photo: police.hu

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court ordered his extradition detention on March 18, after which the Hungarian justice authorities ordered his extradition.

Photo: police.hu

In the early hours of August 28, Hungarian police officers handed him over to representatives of the US authorities at Budapest’s Liszt Ferenc International Airport. The defendant is being taken to Florida before being transferred to a correctional facility. The US proceedings against him can therefore continue while he remains in custody, the statement said.

Photo: police.hu

If you missed: FBI alert leads Hungarian police to arrest British fugitive wanted for 20 years, court makes questionable decision – video

World.title: Romanian Language Day celebrated simultaneously in Romania, Moldova and Ukraine
World.content:
Romanian Language Day was celebrated for the first time simultaneously in Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine, according to a message posted by Romanian president Nicușor Dan on Facebook on Monday, August 31.

The president said that “protecting the rights of Romanians everywhere and promoting our language and culture remain essential objectives of the Romanian state beyond its borders.” He also highlighted the importance of the Romanian language. “We are united by this valuable bond of the Romanian language, which anchors us in history and opens our future,” the head of state said.

Nicușor Dan ended the message with a greeting addressed to those who speak, write and keep the Romanian language alive: “Happy Romanian Language Day and happy Romanian Language Day to all those who speak it, write it and keep it alive!”

In the Republic of Moldova, Romanian Language Day has been marked on August 31 since 1990. In Romania, Romanian Language Day has been officially celebrated since 2013, following the adoption of the law establishing August 31 as a day of celebration. Ukraine is officially marking Romanian Language Day for the first time in 2026. The decision was made through a decree signed by Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy on March 12.

Celebrations in Romania

Aside from the Romanian head of state, numerous public bodies, officials, and personalities mentioned the event within the country. Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted in a message that “promoting the Romanian language abroad is a mission with a permanent mandate.”

The institution noted that “August 31 is therefore also the symbol of the defeat of artificially fabricated formulas such as the ‘Moldovan language’, which does not exist de jure,” the message posted on the MFA’s Facebook page says.

According to the cited source, “today, Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine are more cohesive, demonstrating that we bring unity through a vector of communication, language and culture, in a period marked by an unjust and illegal war that should never have taken place on the European continent.”

The US embassy in Romania marked the day in a video posted on Facebook.

Events and celebrations were moreover organized throughout the country for Romanian Language Day. To mark the event, president Nicușor Dan decorated the National Institute for Oriental Languages and Civilizations in Paris and university professor Alexandru-Daniel Mardale, head of the institute’s Romanian Language Department, on the occasion of Romanian Language Day. The decorations were in appreciation of the outstanding merits in promoting the Romanian language in the French Republic, and for the contribution to deepening bilateral relations and strengthening the Romanian-French dialogue.

Romanian Language Day in Moldova

In Moldova, the Romanian Language Day has a special significance, as the country was long subjected to a process of Russification before the fall of the USSR, of which it was a part. In 1989, following pressure exerted by tens of thousands of people gathered at the first Great National Assembly, Romanian was proclaimed the state language of the Moldavian SSR and the Latin script was restored. In 2023, Moldova recognized Romanian as its national language.

Romanian Language Day was marked in Chisinau, Moldova’s capital, throught the fourth edition of the Great National Dictation and other cultural events. The former brought together more than 3,500 participants from across the country. This year, participants had to transcribe a fragment from the work of the late Gheorghe Urschi, the beloved actor, director, playwright and humorist, nicknamed the “king of humor” in the Republic of Moldova.

Present at the Dictation, Moldovan prime minister Vasile Tofan spoke about the importance of the Romanian language, as well as the sacrifices of those who fought for the return to the Latin script and the recognition of the Romanian language in the Republic of Moldova. He paid tribute to those who fought for the Romanian language and national identity and paid a price for this.

“The Romanian language survived here despite the Soviet occupation, the foreign alphabet that was imposed on it and the enormous pressure of the Russian language in education, administration and public life. It survived because it could not be removed from people. It was the language spoken at home, the language of grandparents, the language of songs, the language in which people shared their joys and sorrows. It was in the marrow of this nation,” the Moldovan prime minister said, cited by Agerpres.

“The Romanian language should not be a barrier; it should be a bridge. Knowing the Romanian language means the possibility of fully participating in the life of this country; it means access to education, work, culture, institutions, the possibility of speaking to one another and building the same society together,” he added.

Moldovan president Maia Sandu also sent a congratulatory message on the occasion of Romanian Language Day, highlighting the role of the Romanian language in preserving the identity and memory of generations.

“The Romanian language is part of our being. [...] Today we can speak it freely, without fear. All the more, we have a duty to take care of it. And, above all, to pass on to our children the love for the Romanian language, just as we received it from those who came before us. Let us leave them this precious heritage: a living language, beautifully spoken, in which they can tell their stories, sing their doinas and express their longing. Happy Romanian Language Day!” Maia Sandu said.

Romanian Language Day in Ukraine

Romanian Language Day was marked for the first time in Ukraine on Saturday, August 29, in Chernivtsi, in the southern part of the country.

Representatives of the Romanian authorities, the Romanian diplomacy in Ukraine, as well as the Romanian community in the Chernivtsi region laid wreaths at the statue of Taras Shevchenko and the statue of Mihai Eminescu in the city center. Candles were also lit at the Heroes’ Memorial in Chernivtsi’s Central Square, according to Digi24.

The event was attended by Romania’s ambassador to Kyiv, Victor Micula, Romania’s consul general in Chernivtsi, Irina Loredana Stănculescu, State Secretary at the Ministry of Culture Diana Băciuna, president of the Iași County Council Costel Alexe, as well as the military governor of the Chernivtsi region, Ruslan Osipenko, and president of the Chernivtsi District Council, Mykola Guitor.

Later, the Romanian officials held a meeting with the leaders of the Romanian community at the National Palace.

Back in March, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree establishing Romanian Language Day in Ukraine. “To develop mutual understanding, mutual respect and cooperation in Ukrainian-Romanian relations, encouraging intercultural dialogue, taking into account the preservation of identity and developing the linguistic and cultural identity of Ukrainian citizens, I decree: Romanian Language Day is hereby established in Ukraine, to be celebrated annually on August 31,” the decree said.

radu@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Julien Viry|Dreamstime.com)

World.title: Social Democrat leader Sorin Grindeanu says party ready to form Romania’s next government
World.content:
The Social Democratic Party (PSD) is ready to form a new government around itself, including a minority administration, party leader Sorin Grindeanu announced on Monday, August 31. However, the party will not support any governing formula in which it does not participate, he said following a meeting of the PSD National Political Council in Sinaia.

“PSD is ready to support a functional government and assume the formation of a government around itself, including a minority government, but only on the basis of a clear program with precise objectives, deadlines, financing, and assigned responsibilities,” Sorin Grindeanu said, as quoted by News.ro.

“To be unequivocal, PSD will not support any governing formula of which it is not part,” he added.

Romania has been governed by a caretaker administration since the Liberal-led government of interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan was dismissed in a no-confidence vote in early May.

The Social Democrats had withdrawn from the previous governing alliance before joining the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) in passing the motion. Forming a new majority remains difficult, as the National Liberal Party (PNL) and Save Romania Union (USR) have repeatedly ruled out joining another government that includes PSD.

PSD, meanwhile, has said it would not accept PNL leader Ilie Bolojan as a member of a future cabinet.

On Monday, Sorin Grindeanu said PSD would first negotiate the objectives of a future administration and discuss its political structure, government positions, and allocation of responsibilities only if those priorities are accepted.

“Romania must restart its economy. Our goal is to protect purchasing power, stop fiscal experiments, and relaunch production in Romania,” he said.

PSD has proposed a two-year political agreement built around ten priorities to parties willing to help form a parliamentary majority. These include energy and natural resources, the national defence industry, reindustrialization, improved tax collection before the introduction of new taxes, reforming state costs, wages linked to productivity, education and healthcare, irrigation and rural development, strategic investments, and defending Romania’s interests within the EU and NATO.

Grindeanu said each measure included in the agreement should have identified financing, a deadline, a responsible institution, and a publicly available performance indicator. Progress would be assessed after the government’s first 100 days and again by a final evaluation deadline.

Any breaches of the agreement would be formally reported, technically assessed, and subjected to a 15-day mediation period.

Romania’s constitutional, European, and transatlantic orientation would remain non-negotiable, the PSD leader added.

Last week, interim prime minister and PNL leader Ilie Bolojan confirmed that his party will not vote for a government with PSD ministers and warned that if negotiations on a new government remain deadlocked, Romania may head towards early elections. However, he added that the odds of early elections are rather slim.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

World.title: Romanian billionaire Daniel Dines publishes book about AI written with help of AI
World.content:
Daniel Dines, founder of Romanian-American software robots and artificial intelligence company UiPath (NYSE: PATH), has launched a book about AI, which he wrote with the help of AI chatbots ChatGPT from OpenAI and Claude from Anthropic.

Daniel Dines is the founder and Chief Executive Officer of UiPath, a global leader in business orchestration and automation. In the early 2000s, Dines spent five years at Microsoft in Seattle, working on SQL Server Agent. In 2005, he returned to Romania, his home country, and from his apartment started the company that would become UiPath. The company is now a leader in business orchestration and automation.

In his book, Dines, 54, draws on his experience to “outline a new operating model for the company of the future.” He examines one of the most important questions facing business leaders: “As AI becomes capable of taking over more and more intellectual work, how should companies rethink the way they work without giving up responsibility, control and human judgment?”

The Romanian self-made billionaire sets out to “offer business and technology leaders a practical framework for exploring the role that responsibility, control and human judgment will play in the company of the future, built by orchestrating AI agents, automation and people,” according to a UiPath statement sent to Romania Insider.

Dines describes the book as an accessible guide for leaders trying to understand a rapidly changing AI landscape. “You will learn more about AI in four hours than you have learned in the past year,” Daniel Dines promised.

Dines' book, The Work That Remains/What Remains to Be Done When Machines Do the Rest, can be downloaded for free in PDF format from the UiPath website.

The book is available in English and Japanese in digital format starting August 27, followed by a limited print edition on September 22.

World.title: Romanian authorities inaugurate new PNRR-funded medical centers in Cluj-Napoca, Târgu Mureș
World.content:
Interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan and other officials attended the inauguration of the new cerebrovascular pathology and neurosurgery center within the Cluj County Emergency Hospital on Saturday, August 29. Another medical center was inaugurated on Monday, August 31, in Târgu Mureș, central Romania. Both projects were completed with EU-backed PNRR funds.

The new center is able to provide modern services in the field of neurosurgical pathologies, has an area dedicated to imaging investigations, and is equipped with equipment for neurosurgical and neurovascular investigations and treatment. The center, built in Cluj, has six operating rooms for neurosurgical procedures, 105 beds, of which 26 are intensive care beds, the Romanian government said in a press release.

The facility was financed from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, which ended on August 31, and from national funds and was badly needed, according to the head of the executive, since most serious cases in the Transylvania region are treated in Cluj-Napoca.

“I am here for this great city, Cluj-Napoca, a locomotive of Romania's development, for the people here,” the interim prime minister also said at the inauguration of the Cerebrovascular Pathology and Neurosurgery Center in Cluj-Napoca.

Bolojan thanked the doctors and medical students in the city. “I am grateful to them for what they do in our medical system, Cluj being one of the strongest centers from this point of view,” he said.

Cluj County Council president Alin Tișe avoided delivering any message at the inauguration event of the new medical center, amid a spat with the prime minister. Instead, Cluj-Napoca mayor Emil Boc was alongside Bolojan, delivering an extensive message about the PNRR-funded investment carried out in Cluj-Napoca with the government's support.

“The new hospital, the Cerebrovascular Pathology and Neurosurgery Center, was built from scratch,” Boc said, emphasizing that the investment secured through the PNRR amounts to more than EUR 50 million. “Cluj's medical sector is richer as of today. Richer with a new hospital, with more than 100 beds and state-of-the-art technology for doctors and patients,” he added.

The new facility has 79 beds for neurosurgery and neurology patients, 26 intensive care beds for neurosurgical and neurovascular pathologies, 6 operating rooms for neurosurgical procedures, and a 70-square-meter hybrid room, a modern imaging area equipped with a 3 Tesla MRI, multislice CT and angiograph, among others.

The Cluj mayor further emphasized that the hospital will become “a new landmark of Romanian medicine.”

The Cluj-Napoca County Emergency Clinical Hospital is one of the first six Class I medical units in Romania, alongside the county hospitals in Constanța, Iași, Târgu Mureș, Timișoara and the Central Military Hospital, the government also said.

New medical facility in Târgu Mureș

Alongside the Cerebrovascular Pathology and Neurosurgery Center in Cluj-Napoca, Romanian authorities also inaugurated the Emergency Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases and Transplant (IUBCvT) in Târgu Mureș on Monday, August 31. The facility was valued at over RON 770 million, out of which roughly RON 500 million came from the EU-backed National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The facility has 214 beds for inpatients and five beds for day hospitalization, surgery rooms equipped to a top technological level, as well as modern spaces dedicated exclusively to investigation, treatment and intensive care (ICU) activities.

The new institute is equipped with state-of-the-art equipment, while the structure and equipment of the new rooms were specifically designed to reduce the risk of nosocomial infections.

Also present at this inauguration, the Romanian prime minister highlighted that Romania was unable to fully take advantage of the PNRR funds.

“In healthcare, we started with a PNRR budget of more than EUR 2 billion and, through successive cuts, we reached just over EUR 1 billion, which means that the money was not lost, but went to other areas where it could be spent. And this means that from 19 hospitals, after the PNRR was rearranged in 2023, we ended up completing eight,” Bolojan said, cited by Agerpres.

At the same time, the interim prime minister spoke about the need to simplify procurement procedures and partnerships with local authorities.
