World.title: Association: While mistrust of AI high, 3 out of 4 firms still use it
World.content:
The Estonian Marketing Association (Eesti turundajate liit) noted cost savings is not always the main driver, but whatever the reasoning, AI should remain a tool and not an end in itself.

Supermarket Maxima runs around 300 campaigns a year which make use of AI. Its sales and marketing manager Jaanika Terasmaa said the technology allows ad agencies to bring hot ideas to meetings. "The agency comes to every meeting with a live idea, because it has been able to make quick clips of what a new advertising campaign could look like," Terasmaa told "Aktuaalne kaamera".

In any case, if agencies have been using AI, this has not been detrimental to campaigns, she went on.

"Unfortunately, or fortunately, an advertising agency is made up of people, so we don't recognize that from the price list, but we have been seeing better and more interesting quality in the content," Terasmaa added.

AI-created Ad on a billboard. Source: ERR

Kent Raju, creative director at Kala Ruudus, an advertising agency, said AI should remain a tool, not a final product. "We don't start by writing a command, but rather come up with an idea which is right for the brand," he said.

He criticised the use of AI for more simple tasks, such as restaurant menus, and which can be quite obvious. "I feel bad looking at the waste of artificial intelligence – material where restaurant menu pictures are taken with AI – for what purpose? You can take a real picture of real food, but it came with AI and it seems like the wrong choice."

Musician Mikk Saar said AI has created ads for events he has been a part of which have had defects, such as distorted faces or incorrect text, and he now wants to be consulted before ads get run. "A party won't be canceled, but if the poster is made with AI and everything is distorted, I won't be sharing it on social media – which means the organizer loses out. It doesn't match my brand image."

In any case, old‑fashioned advertising seems to be making a comeback. "It's become very popular to put out an ad and show that you actually made it," said Anniken Haldna, CEO of the marketing Association. This fact can get as many views as the ad itself, she added

The growing use of AI in advertising has also raised concerns about authenticity and trust. Studies cited by the association suggest that consumers are nowadays generally sceptical of AI‑generated ads, while experts warn that overuse could lead to a greater spread misinformation, as well as damaging companies' credibility. Creative professionals say the human perspective remains essential, with AI best employed as an aid rather than a replacement for human creativity.

World.title: School year opens with hundreds of students still waiting for placement
World.content:
As of Monday, 575 young people who finished basic school this spring still do not have a new school place registered in the Estonian Education Information System. The lists continue to change constantly, as some students decline the places offered to them, after which those places are offered to the next candidates.

The situation is especially tense in the capital. "There really aren't many free places in Tallinn," said Krista Keedus, head of education management at the Tallinn Education Department. "Estonian‑language high schools have completed their admissions and all places are filled," she added.

Tallinn's municipal high schools currently do not have the capacity to add more places, due to both space limitations and a shortage of teachers, Keedus said.

"There is no immediate plan to create additional places," she noted, pointing to the need to wait for the final data on needs and available places on 10 September.

The filling of school places is also strongly affected by the influx of residents from neighboring municipalities, as nearly 27 percent of students admitted to Tallinn's 10th grades for the new school year are not residents of the capital.

Tallinn's municipal high schools currently do not have the capacity to add more places. Source: Anna Aurelia Minev/ERR

Although high school places in Tallinn are full, there are still available study places at Tallinn Applied College and the technology college Tehno Tallinn. Keedus encouraged students without a place to consider vocational education: "Our vocational education is not only vocational training — it is also vocational secondary education." "They could at least try continuing their studies there first, and if it truly doesn't suit them, then look again for a gymnasium place," she said.

Places in preparatory studies — intended for students with weaker final results — were also filled already in the summer. Discussions are currently underway with the Ministry of Education about creating additional places based on need.

The final deadline for local governments to offer solutions to students in need is 1 November, but officials are already trying to contact young people now to understand why they have ended up without a school place.

"It is of course sad if young people haven't managed to secure a school place by 1 September and cannot start their school year," Keedus said. "But that doesn't mean starting later — a few days or even weeks — would be impossible. Their learning opportunities are certainly not locked," she added.

Keedus also pointed out that in previous years, the number of young people who ended their education after basic school was similar or slightly smaller, although monitoring was incomplete before the study obligation was introduced.

"The ministry has monitored each year how many young people do not reach the next level of education, and that number has usually been around 400–500," Keedus said.

"Previously, this was not a legal problem. It was, however, a problem for the young people and for Estonia as a whole, because those who continue their education have better chances of coping in life — which is why the study obligation was established. Until now, this issue wasn't directly on the table, because young people had the freedom to go to work, for example, and therefore we did not conduct this kind of ongoing monitoring at the start of the school year," Keedus explained.

World.title: 'Even If...' campaign assures sexual assault survivors help is available
World.content:
A new Estonian campaign is reminding survivors of sexual violence that they can seek free, 24/7 help even if they lack the words or don't remember everything.

The Social Insurance Board's (SKA) "Even If..." campaign highlights the free, round-the-clock assistance and care available at dedicated sexual violence crisis centers (SAKs) across Estonia.

It addresses three common reasons survivors may hesitate to seek help: "Even if no one saw," "Even if you don't remember everything," and "Even if you can't find the right words."

"After experiencing sexual violence, your memories may be patchy, and you may feel confused, angry, ashamed or guilty," said Kai Part, a gynecologist at the Tartu University Hospital (TÜK) center. "These are normal trauma responses to an abnormal event."

No police report or referral needed

Estonia's sexual violence crisis support centers are free and open 24/7 to anyone who has experienced sexual violence or suspects they may have, regardless of age or gender.

The sooner someone seeks help, the better, but it's still worth coming to a crisis center even after changing clothes, showering or waiting some time before deciding to seek help.

No referral or police report is required, and minors can also seek help independently.

Sexual violence crisis centers offer medical examinations, evidence collection, pregnancy prevention, STI testing and treatment, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and counseling.

The centers will also help people access further psychological and other help, and provide support if a victim chooses to contact the police.

"People can decide for themselves what help they want to receive," Part said. "That can also be the beginning of healing — when they can once again decide what happens to them."

Patient at a psychiatrist appointment. Photo is illustrative. Source: Sigmund/Unsplash

Five centers across the country

Annika Silde, head of violence victims services at SKA, emphasized that anyone can become a victim of sexual violence, regardless of age, gender or background.

"You don't have to prove what happened or explain why you reacted a particular way in order to seek help at a SAK," she said. "The responsibility always lies with the perpetrator."

Sexual violence crisis centers operate at five hospitals across Estonia: West Tallinn Central Hospital (LTK), Tartu University Hospital (TÜK), Pärnu Hospital, Ida-Viru Central Hospital (IVKH) in Kohtla-Järve and Kuressaare Hospital in Saaremaa.

In 2025, 268 people sought help at the centers, including 106 minors. Women accounted for 95 percent of those seeking help.

SKA's "Even If..." campaign runs in public and online through September 13.

More help available

If you have experienced, are experiencing or think you may be experiencing domestic abuse, domestic violence or sexual violence, or are otherwise in crisis, help is available.

In case of emergency, call 112. Estonia's five sexual violence crisis centers (SAKs) are open 24/7 in Tallinn, Tartu, Pärnu, Kohtla-Järve and Kuressaare. On-call psychiatric care can also be reached by phone 24/7 in Tallinn at +372 617 2650, in Tartu at +372 731 8764 and in Pärnu at +372 447 3281. The Eluliin emotional support hotline is open daily from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. in Estonian (+372 655 8088) and in Russian (+372 655 5688). Another emotional support hotline is available every day from 10 a.m. to midnight in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 123. The Ohvriabi victim support hotline is available 24/7 in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 006. The child helpline is also open 24/7 in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 111.

World.title: Pioneering Estonian curling duo Kaldvee and Lill split after 11 years
World.content:
The duo, who won silver at the 2024 World Championships and were named Estonian Team of the Year the same year, made history as the first Estonians to compete in mixed doubles curling at the Olympics, which they did in February this year at the at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics.

"We played together for 11 years — it's a very long and successful collaboration. We are both very proud of what we achieved," Lill told ERR. "The decision didn't come easily. We met several times and discussed what to do, as we always do after an Olympic cycle. This time we decided to go our separate ways, but we are both staying in curling."

Lill outlined just how extraordinary their sporting journey had been, starting from training in a Soviet-era munitions plant. "What we did is quite impossible — you come from an old Soviet rocket factory and make it to the Olympics," he said with emotion. "Against all the odds, we made it happen. I'm deeply proud of that."

Asked if he had any regrets, Lill said: "Every athlete feels they could have done better. We are ambitious people and always aimed high. We gave our maximum and achieved great results."

Lill will continue in the mixed doubles, partnering with Karoliine Kaare, his life partner. Kaldvee is to captain an all-new new Estonian women's team. "There were options — not too many, we are in Estonia after all," Lill joked. "With Karoliine, we decided it was worth trying. You never know how a new team will work, so we'll give our best and see what happens."

Kaldvee is at the helm of a young and talented women's team with Czech coach Jakub Bareš already on board. Lill was buoyant about the team's prospects. "Marie is Estonia's most experienced curler," he said. "She has captained the national team before. She will lead a young and talented team, preparing for the European Championships and the B‑division World Championships."

Lill and Karoliine Kaare. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"If I ever leave curling, I want the sport to be in a better place than when I started. It would be sad if we just walked away and didn't pass on what we've learned," he reflected.

The Lill-Kaare new sporting pairing's immediate goal is to qualify for the World Championships in January. "First we need to qualify from Estonia," Lill said. "November will see who gets to represent Estonia."

In an Instagram post, the duo wrote: "One chapter ends but the journey continues! From an old Soviet missile factory to the Olympics. Against all the odds, we made Estonian curling history."

Kaldvee and Lill placed 10th at the 2026 Winter Olympics.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate increases against Iraqi dinar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar experienced an increase on Monday in both Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,541.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,540 Iraqi dinars on Sunday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,545 Iraqi dinars and 1,535 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate increased, fluctuating between 1,541.5 and 1,541 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraqi judiciary sentences kidnapper of US journalist to 15 years in prison
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Central Criminal Court sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim, a member of the Iran-backed group Kataeb Hezbollah, to 15 years in prison under the country’s anti-terrorism law for kidnapping US journalist Shelly Kittleson on March 31.

Kittleson was kidnapped during the daytime on Saadoun Street in central Baghdad. Armed gunmen pushed her into a silver vehicle, while another getaway car crashed during the escape. Iraqi security forces intercepted the crashed car and arrested Lazim.

The US journalist was kept hostage for more than a week when Kataeb Hezbollah freed her in early April ahead of a US-Iran ceasefire.

Kittleson, who has extensively covered the Middle East for publications like the BBC and Politico, expressed her gratitude to the Iraqi justice system on X and affirmed her right to seek compensation.

This decision marks a rare court step against a major, Tehran-aligned armed group in Iraq.

The verdict comes at a critical time for Iraq’s new government, led by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, which is under intense pressure from Washington to disarm pro-Iran militias and place all weapons under strict state control.

The effort to disarm Kataeb Hezbollah has pushed Iraq into a severe security and political crisis, as the group has rejected the government’s disarmament mandates and vowed to expand its military arsenal.

World.title: Iraq discusses oil and gas development with BP, ConocoPhillips
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair and representatives from British Petroleum (BP) and Texas-based ConocoPhillips discussed on Monday the development of Iraq’s oil and gas industry.

The meeting held in Baghdad included BP’s Iraq director Zaid al-Yasiri, Nader Zaki, Ariel Flores, and ConocoPhillips representative William Arnold, as well as senior Iraqi officials in the oil sector.

The discussions addressed strategic advancements to maximize the utilization of Iraq’s hydrocarbon resources, optimize field development, and upgrade extraction technologies, according to a statement cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The Iraqi Oil Ministry activated in early August its Kirkuk oilfield contract with BP, a project aiming to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day to a peak target of 420,000 barrels per day.

The deal expands crude extraction while capturing associated gas to eliminate gas flaring and provide fuel for power plants.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major step in Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

ConocoPhillips has agreed to purchase a 42 percent share in BP’s Kirkuk project, boosting its position in Iraq by redeveloping four key oil resources in the northern Iraqi province.

ConocoPhillips Chairman Ryan Lance said that the investment aligns with the company’s conservative approach by offering access to a big, high-quality, and long-life resource base while needing very little expenditure.

The agreement represents another initiative by Iraq to attract foreign investments and boost production from its aging oil assets, as well as to strengthen partnerships with prominent global energy companies.

World.title: India to receive first Iraqi oil shipment in five months
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – India is preparing to receive its first shipment of Iraqi oil in five months, a development reflecting the return of Iraq’s crude oil flows to one of Asia’s largest oil markets, despite ongoing shipping challenges across the Strait of Hormuz.

India’s Bharat Petroleum expects to receive the shipment within the next few days. The tanker carrying Iraqi oil has already passed through the Strait of Hormuz and arrived in Fujairah, UAE, for a ship-to-ship transfer, according to Reuters.

Bharat Petroleum’s Chief Financial Officer, Vetsa Ramakrishna Gupta, said that the company secured a vessel to load the Iraqi shipment and transport it to Fujairah. There, the oil will be transferred from ship to ship before reaching the company’s refineries.

These arrangements reflect the efforts of Asian refiners to find flexible logistical solutions for securing crude oil at a time when transportation cost, insurance, and tanker availability have become crucial factors in determining the viability of purchasing shipments from the Gulf region.

The Indian company typically requires around two million barrels of Iraqi oil per month, making a consistent supply from Baghdad crucial to meeting its refinery’s crude oil needs.

Bharat Petroleum has not disclosed the name of the vessel used to transport the shipment but stated that the ship’s owner agreed to load the crude and proceed to Fujairah for a ship-to-ship transfer.

Iraq is one of the countries most affected by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, given that a significant portion of its oil exports depend on ports located on the Arabian Gulf.

World.title: Iraq exports 21 million barrels of fuel oil through Syria
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s fuel oil exports through Syria have seen a significant increase since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran on February 28.

Iraqi oil flows via neighboring Syria are part of alternative routes for the country’s oil shipments to global markets following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Total Iraqi fuel oil exports transported via Syria reached 21.4 million barrels between March and the end of August 2026.

This step is part of Baghdad’s continuous efforts to establish alternate export channels amid shipping disruptions via the Strait of Hormuz, the country’s primary maritime trade artery, which led to unprecedented challenges to the oil industry.

Iraqi fuel oil began flowing overland through Syrian territory after the Iraqi state-owned oil marketing company (SOMO) reached deals to transport approximately 650,000 tons per month (approximately 4.7 million barrels) to be stored at the Baniyas port before being shipped to global markets.

Iraqi fuel oil shipments via Syria increased rapidly between March and the end of August 2026.

Iraq’s fuel oil exports through Syria were 254,000 barrels in March, 686,000 barrels in April, 3.86 million barrels in May, five million barrels in June, 5.65 million barrels in July, and 5.91 million barrels in August.

World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq imported approximately 90,000 tonnes of potatoes valued at $52.4 million in 2025, according to specialized agricultural market data from IndexBox, highlighting a structural gap in domestic agricultural supply chains and food security planning.

Economic researcher Ali Karim Idheeb stated on Monday, August 31, 2026, that trade volumes across core vegetable crops demonstrate that domestic output remains vulnerable to seasonal volatility, regional price shocks, and supply disruptions.

Trade Figures and Regional Sourcing

2025 Potato Import Totals: ~90,000 tonnes with an aggregate import value of $52.4 million.

Primary Source Markets: The Iraqi market relies predominantly on regional agricultural exporters, led by Iran, Egypt, and Turkey.

Price Transmission Factors: Consumer prices in Iraqi wholesale markets are directly influenced by freight logistics, climate shocks affecting export yields, and input pricing within supplier countries.

Economic Opportunity: The $52.4 million import bill represents capital that could be retained within the domestic economy through targeted investments in post-harvest cold storage, yield optimization, and certified seed propagation.

World.title: CBI: Iraq’s domestic public debt reaches 106T dinars in H1 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s domestic public debt surged to 106.072 trillion IQD (approximately $80.97 billion) by the end of June 2026, up from 103.179 trillion IQD at the end of May, according to official financial data published by the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) on Monday, August 31, 2026.

The monthly jump of 2.893 trillion IQD caps a broader upward trajectory over the first half of the year, with total domestic liabilities expanding by 15.557 trillion IQD from 90.515 trillion IQD recorded at year-end 2025.

The portfolio of domestic debt instruments reflects a heavy concentration of central bank obligations alongside government securities and commercial borrowing:

Ministry of Finance Claims to CBI: Rose to 67.499 trillion IQD by end-June (up from 63.199 trillion IQD in May), representing the largest individual liability component.

Direct Loans: Stood at 18.964 trillion IQD.

Government Bonds: Reached 10.867 trillion IQD.

Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Totaled 8.742 trillion IQD.

World.title: Integrity Commission halts 550-dunam land auction in Anbar, saving 19B dinars
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Federal Commission of Integrity announced on Monday, August 31, 2026, that it has successfully halted the fraudulent sale and auction procedures of a prime 550-dunam state-owned real estate parcel in Anbar Governorate, preventing the squandering of over 19.25 billion IQD (approximately $14.7 million) in public funds.

According to an official statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the operation was executed by a field investigation unit from the Commission’s Anbar Investigation Office as part of its ongoing oversight of state-owned properties nationwide.

Field investigators conducted comprehensive on-site audits and cross-referenced documentation across the State Real Estate Department in Anbar, the Urban Planning Directorate, and the City Organization Division at the Ramadi Municipality Directorate:

Location & Unauthorized Sale: The 550-dunam plot is situated within the master plan designated for the future urban expansion of Ramadi. It had been auctioned and sold to an individual buyer without obtaining statutory municipal approvals from the Ramadi Municipality Directorate.

Severe Undervaluation: The official appraisal committee at the Anbar State Real Estate Department had valued the property at just 25.09 million IQD per dunam, resulting in a total sale price of 13.75 billion IQD.

Market Discrepancy: The Commission’s field investigators analyzed land coordinates and comparable market pricing, referencing the General Commission for Taxes’ benchmark guidelines. They determined that the actual market value stands at 60 million IQD per dunam, bringing the true aggregate value to 33.00 billion IQD.

Total Prevented Loss: The fraudulent undervaluation represented a direct financial deficit of 19,250,000,000 IQD against the state treasury.

World.title: Uttarakhand CM's intervention ensures medical aid for ailing child

UTTARAKHAND: Uttarakhand Chief Minister

has intervened to secure urgent medical aid for an eight-year-old boy suffering from a lifelong debilitating health condition.

This comes after the Chief Minister visited a local food stall in Lohiahead, where the boy's father shared their struggle.

World.title: CJP’s proposed march on Sep 5 an attempt to create lawlessness before Brics: PIL in SC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to pass any interim orders on two PILs, including one by a retired police officer, seeking deferment of Cockroach Janata Party âs proposed march on Sep 5 by alleging that it is intended to create lawlessness ahead of Sep 12-13 BRICS summit in Delhi to deter participation of world leaders.

When the petitioners questioned how such a march from the India Gate to the Police Headquarters can take place without permission, A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said there are two issues â one relates to law and order and the other to policy relating to permission to protest marches.

âLet the stakeholders talk to them. As of now we have no reason to doubt that everyone would act and behave in a very responsible manner and in a peaceful and lawful manner.

Right now, there is no compelling reason for us (the court) to presume that any wrong will happen. It is for the law enforcing agencies to ensure law and order while acting in accordance with law,â the CJI-led bench said.

Appearing for one of the petitioners, advocate Syed Rizwan Ahmed said given the BRICS summit, till date no application seeking permission has been given to the authorities. In West Bengal, the previous govt did not give permission to so many protest rallies and the organizers had to move the HC for permission.





Why does CJP, an unregistered entity not follow the same process? Are they above law, he asked.

âGod forbid another mishap, may not be by CJP, but by some mischievous elements take place, it will be covered by international media and deter participation of the foreign country leaders in BRICs,â he apprehended.

The bench said, âAll these factors are to be considered by some other quarters, not by us. There is nothing we can say right now.

If something untoward or alarming happens, then file an application before us, provided the issue falls for determination in judicial domain.â

The bench issued notice to the Centre on the two PILs, asked them to supply copies to the SC-constituted High-Powered Committee headed by retired SC judge R Subhash Reddy as well as the office of the solicitor general and posted these for hearing on Sep 10 along with petitions on July 20 incidents during protest march to Parliament, which turned violent resulting in alleged police excesses, injuries to protesters and security personnel and damage to public and private properties.

When Ahmed asked whether CJP is above law and its processes, the bench said, âThese are issues which are to be taken care of by the law and order enforcing agencies. It is their responsibility to maintain law and order. We expect both sides â protesters and law enforcing agencies - to respect, honour and follow the law of the land.â

SC said it has referred a host of issues to the HPC, which is expected to give recommendations one after the other on them.

When Ahmed persisted for a hearing on Sep 3 ahead of the proposed march, the bench said the petitioner must approach the Centre and Delhi police on the issue of absence of permission for the march. âLet them consider it,â it said.

âThere is no organized or identified group before us so that we can request them,â the bench said. Ahmed said that is another problem as CJP has no registered office where notice can be served. Can such an unorganized body hold the capital of the country to ransom, he asked.

World.title: 'A particular issue': Penguin India on impasse over Sonia Gandhi memoir
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Penguin Random House India on Monday said publication of Sonia Gandhiâs memoir in India had stalled after the publisher and the authorâs representatives reached an âimpasse over a particular issue.

â The publisher also firmly denied that any external pressure had influenced the decision.

Penguin India said the disagreement emerged during its normal editorial review of Belonging: A Journey of Love, which it had been keen to publish.

The clarification came amid a growing political controversy over the memoirâs India publication, after Alfred A Knopf, the US-based imprint of Penguin Random House, announced that the book would be released worldwide on November 10.

While Congress leaders have raised questions about possible governmental pressure and freedom of expression, Penguin India said the disagreement was strictly part of the editorial process.

âOn some, they agreed to changes and on others, we accepted the authorâs position. Unfortunately, and ultimately, an understanding could not be reached on a particular issue,â the publisher said.

PRHI spokesperson Pallavi Narayan said the publishing house had been âreally keenâ to bring out the memoir, describing it as âa hard-won acquisitionâ.





âWe feel it is important for us to correct certain misrepresentations regarding the forthcoming memoir 'Belonging'. This is a book that we at Penguin Random House India, were really keen on publishing as it was a hard-won acquisition,â Narayan said in an exclusive statement to PTI.

The publisher said the manuscript had gone through its ânormal editorial processâ, during which several points were raised and discussed with the authorâs representatives.

Some proposed changes were accepted, while on other matters Penguin India accepted the authorâs position.

It was ultimately the unresolved issue that brought the publication process to a halt, according to PRHI. The authorâs team subsequently informed the publisher that they did not wish to proceed with the publication, a decision the publishing house said it respected.

At the same time, Penguin India rejected suggestions that the impasse was the result of intervention from outside the publishing process.

âSince the content of the book is confidential and under embargo, there was no external pressure whatsoever,â the publisher said.

PRHI declined to reveal the nature of the disputed issue, citing its contractual obligations and commitment to author confidentiality.

âSince we are bound by an agreement, and author confidentiality is paramount to us, we will not divulge details of what led to the impasse,â the publisher said.

The publishing house also defended its decision to scrutinise the manuscript, saying editorial assessment, questioning, fact-checking and recommendations were part of its responsibility as a publisher.

âAs publishers, it was its âresponsibility and dutyâ to critically assess a manuscript, ask questions, make recommendations and exercise its independent editorial judgement,â Penguin India said.

The controversy intensified after reports that Penguin India had backed out of publishing the memoir following disagreements over editorial changes.

Former Rajasthan chief minister Ashok Gehlot alleged that pressure had been put on Penguin India to remove sections concerning Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the RSS and Chinaâs occupation of Indian territory during the Modi government.

The memoir is expected to offer a rare account of Gandhiâs life, covering her childhood in post-war Italy, her marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family, the assassination of her husband and former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, and her subsequent entry into politics.

World.title: SC: Externment orders cannot be passed routinely, require reasons
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Holding that forcing a person to stay out of a city or district affects freedom guaranteed by the Constitution, SC on Monday ruled that a govt cannot pass an externment order routinely and must pass a reasoned order to justify such harsh measures.

A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed an externment order passed by Raigarh district magistrate directing a person to remove himself from the district and contiguous districts for one year. The order was passed against him as multiple criminal cases were pending and the district authority apprehended that his presence would create further problems in the area and nearby districts.

âAn order of externment directly impinges upon valuable fundamental freedoms guaranteed to a citizen and, therefore, cannot be made as a matter of routine.

Further, merely because multiple criminal cases have been filed against a person would not, ipso facto, be a ground for ordering externment,â the bench said.

Before exercising such power, the DM is required to arrive at a bona fide and informed subjective satisfaction that circumstances warrant such an extreme measure and externment is necessary, it said.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The bench said the authority is not expected to render a judgement as a court of law but the order must nonetheless disclose, at least in broad terms, the reasons for such satisfaction.





âThe existence of objective material and a discernible nexus between such material and the conclusion reached are indispensable safeguards against arbitrary exercise of power,â it said.

Quashing the order under Chhattisgarh Rajya Suraksha Adhiniyam, SC said the externment order fell short of statutory requirement. âThe order does not indicate the material on the basis of which such conclusion was reached. No reasons are forthcoming to demonstrate why the third respondent (Raipur DM) considered the situation grave enough to necessitate the appellantâs externment,â it said.

World.title: JNU’s Barak Hostel: Built for northeast students but houses only 12% from the region
World.content:
In 2014, a brutal racial assault on a student from Arunachal Pradesh in Delhi triggered many protests and much soul-searching on problems faced by people from the northeast region living and studying in the rest of India. A panel formed to study their concerns and suggest solutions and measures noted the need for dedicated accommodation for them. Citing it as a positive feature, it talked about how a hostel dedicated to students from northeast was being planned at the Jawaharlal Nehru University.

(

The new hostel has indeed come up, more than 10 years later, after much delay. The plaster peeling off and the cracks on the walls of a facility built at a cost of more than ₹28 crore are only a few of the unkept promises, though. The most glaring one is that Barak Hostel houses only 12% of students from the northeastern States today, according to the student president of the hostel, Hrishikesh Talukdar.

Join THEdge LinkedIn group

Taniam and the committee

Nido Taniam was an 18-year-old first-year student from Arunachal Pradesh studying in a college in Delhi who died following a brutal racial assault in the national capital.

He was in Lajpat Nagar on January 29, 2014, when he stopped at a local shop to ask for directions. Some men reportedly made remarks about his hair and hurled racial slurs at him. A confrontation ensued, and Taniam was allegedly assaulted by a group of men who beat him with sticks. He was taken to the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in Delhi, where he died the following day. According to the autopsy report submitted by the Delhi Police, Taniam suffered nine internal and external injuries, including injuries to his head, lungs and face, which caused his death.

Taniam’s death, and the protests that followed, brought a fresh attention to the discrimination, hostility and insecurity experienced by people from the northeast outside the region.

In its aftermath, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), in February 2014, constituted the Bezbaruah Committee, headed by M.P. Bezbaruah, then a member of the North Eastern Council (NEC), a statutory advisory body constituted under the North Eastern Council Act, 1971. The committee was tasked with examining the concerns of the people from the northeast living in different parts of the country.

Among the concerns noted by the committee was the need for safe and adequate accommodation. In its report, the committee referred to a proposal for a 500-room facility at the JNU. It noted that the university authorities were ready to implement the project and recommended that it be sanctioned immediately.

But it took several years for that recommendation to acquire a physical form. The Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) agreed to fund the project, following the signing of an MoU between JNU and the NEC. At that time, the Aam Aadmi Party was in power. The agreement provided ₹28.30 crore for the project, with 75% of the hostel’s seats to be reserved for students from the Northeast region and the remaining 25% for students from other parts of the country.

In July 2017, Dr. Jitendra Singh, then Minister of State for Development of North Eastern Region (Independent Charge), laid the foundation stone for what would eventually become Barak Hostel on the JNU campus.

A press release issued at the time stated that the NEC was funding 100% of the construction, at a cost of ₹28.30 crore. The hostel was expected to be completed within three years and accommodate 400 students - 200 boys and 200 girls. Of these, 320 seats were to be available to students from the northeast and 80 to students from the rest of the country.

The hostel was eventually completed in 2024, but remained unoccupied for another year, with the university citing shortage of staff. It was then virtually inaugurated by Union Home Minister Amit Shah on April 7, 2025. On the same day, JNU’s current Vice-Chancellor Santishree D. Pandit conducted the ribbon-cutting ceremony to formally open the hostel.

Main promise not kept

Barak Hostel was conceived as more than a building providing beds and rooms. It was conceived as a dedicated space for students from a region whose experiences of discrimination and exclusion had prompted the government to promise a safer and more inclusive university environment. Almost a decade after the foundation stone was laid, however, questions surrounding Barak Hostel extend beyond the promise of inclusion.

On the very day of the Vice-Chancellor’s opening ceremony in 2025, the North East Students’ Forum (NESF) organised a silent protest outside Barak Hostel. During the protest, JNU Vice-Chancellor Santishree D. Pandit was heard saying in a video that there would be no reservation for students from the northeast in the hostel. The video, recorded by protesting students, is on YouTube.

Today, as of August 2026, the hostel houses 420 students, but only 53 of them are from the Northeast, barely 12%, Mr. Talukdar said. The original mandate was 75% reservation.

Students from JNU’s NESF have repeatedly raised the issue with the university administration. They have approached the Dean and Vice-Chancellor, filed Right to Information (RTI) applications, and held protests, seeking clarity on the hostel’s and government’s original mandate. Yet, they say, the issue remains unresolved.

More problems

And while the dispute over whom the hostel was built for continues, another question has emerged: the infrastructure itself. Almost a decade after its foundation stone was laid, and barely two years after construction was completed, Barak Hostel is already showing visible signs of deterioration.

Moss has appeared on its walls; balconies and washrooms face waterlogging; toilet seats are broken; doors broken; Wi-Fi is inadequate; and the hostel has no mess facility, say students.

The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), which The Hindu has accessed, stated that JNU would assign the work to public works agencies, including the Delhi State Public Works Division, for civil and electrical works. The State Public Works Division is a key operational unit of a State Public Works Department (PWD), responsible for the planning, design, construction and localised maintenance of public infrastructure.

An RTI was filed by Hrishikesh Talukdar, who is also the Assam State representative of NESF, seeking information on the non-operationalisation of the mess. In its reply dated July 30, 2026, the JNU administration said that it had first approached the Ministry of Education (MoE) on February 24, 2025, seeking financial assistance of ₹2.15 crore as annual recurring expenditure, along with a one-time grant of ₹50 lakh, to operationalise the mess. The proposal included expenditure for cooks, helpers, sanitation workers, security guards and other staff required to run the hostel and mess.

In the RTI reply, JNU said the MoE responded on March 19, 2025, and subsequently forwarded the university’s proposal to the University Grants Commission (UGC) for examination and appropriate action. However, the RTI reply does not clarify whether any funds were eventually sanctioned or released. JNU also said that no specific deadline had been fixed for opening the mess, and that there had been no meeting exclusively between the JNU and the MoE on the issue.

The funding issue also extends to Wi-Fi facilities at the hostel. On June 10, 2026, JNU’s Dean of Students, Professor Manuradha Chaudhary, wrote to the DoNER seeking a one-time grant of ₹2.69 crore for installing and operationalising Wi-Fi at Barak Hostel. The university said its Communication and Information Services (CIS) had prepared an estimate for the infrastructure, but the facility could not be installed due to a lack of funds.

JNU also cited a joint visit to the hostel on March 10, 2026, during which a Monitoring Committee, including officials from the MHA and DoNER, had recommended that DoNER consider supporting the WiFi installation. However, according to the Barak Hostel Committee’s August 3 representation to the Vice-Chancellor, DoNER subsequently rejected the funding request.

The NESF then questioned the rejection, pointing out that the minutes of a JNU meeting dated March 11, 2026, had recorded that DoNER should be approached for funding for both the mess and WiFi. The students have now sought clarification from the university on both funding proposals: whether the UGC sanctioned or released funds for the mess, what components were approved, and, if funds were provided, why the mess remains non-operational; and why DoNER rejected the WiFi proposal despite the earlier recommendation to consider funding it.

In its latest representation to the MHA, the NESF raised concerns over the 75:25 allotment ratio of the hostel. The letter mentioned that rooms had been allotted to non-northeastern students and, in some cases, even to non-students, while legitimate applications from northeastern students seeking accommodation had been rejected. In the same letter the NESF also highlighted the hostel’s non-operational mess, absence of WiFi connection, inadequate sanitation and dustbins, lack of recreational and sports facilities, water leakage and other maintenance and structural issues - It urged the monitoring committee to intervene with the JNU administration.

The Hindu reached out to the JNU administration, student helpdesk and Dean of Students through publicly available email addresses and phone numbers seeking the university’s response to concerns raised by hostelers of Barak Hostel. The queries covered the non-operational mess facility and the status of funds sought for it, the availability of Wi-Fi and the status of funding sought from the DoNER, concerns regarding hostel allotments, and grievances related to the infrastructure at the hostel. At the time of writing this article, the university had not responded to the queries. The article will be updated if and when JNU responds.

World.title: Nepal flash floods aftermath LIVE: Over 11,000 rescued as government intensifies search operations
World.content:
At least 16 helicopters have also been deployed for search-and-rescue operations in the areas affected by the deadly Himalayan flood, National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) spokesperson Shanti Mahat said.

More than 11,000 people have been rescued so far, he said, adding that the government has intensified search and rescue efforts in the flood-hit areas.

ALSO READ | Nepal disaster, a grim reminder to rethink preparedness | Data

Over 22,000 security personnel, including those from the Nepal Army, have been mobilised for the operations, Mahat said.

Catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border has killed hundreds and left thousands more missing. Rescuers in Nepal are racing to free hundreds of workers thought to be trapped in hydropower site tunnels that were buried in mud.

The number of Indian nationals rescued in the wake of the devastating flash floods stands at 158, the Ministry of External Affairs said, as India stepped up its relief and rescue efforts in coordination with Nepalese authorities.

World.title: PM Modi lauds 7.8% growth ‘despite wars, instability’; asks people not to buy gold ‘unless necessary’
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated the people on India’s 7.8% GDP growth in the April-June quarter, crediting the nation’s resolve and efforts for the achievement. He also requested people not to buy gold and to shun foreign holidays and weddings to preserve foreign exchange reserves.

“Since the 2020 COVID pandemic, there has been no stability anywhere, but India has progressed well,” said PM Modi in an Instagram post.

He said that the country achieved this milestone despite wars and conflicts across the globe. “We have to maintain the speed of our growth, and for that, we must become self-reliant,” PM Modi said. He credited the growth to the country’s policies, intentions and people’s strength.

“Certain people in India have been trying to spread negativity, falsehood,” he accused. “But we progressed well despite all that.”

He asked people to be ‘vocal for local’ by shunning foreign holidays and weddings. “Unless necessary, do not buy gold,” he said.

“If we continue to stress on Swadeshi, self-reliance, we will present our youth with a developed India in the 100th year of Independence,” the Prime Minister said. “Our hard work will fulfil the youth’s dreams; let’s not hold back.”

The growth in India’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) stood at 7.8% in the April-June 2026 quarter (Q1 FY27), quicker than the 6.9% recorded in Q1 of last year, but slower than the 8.6% of the January-March 2026 quarter.

Mr. Modi in May 2026, issued a seven-point austerity appeal to citizens to conserve foreign exchange and protect the economy amid energy and oil crises caused by the West Asia conflict.

World.title: Delhi SIR documents differ on categorisation of voters left out
World.content:
Among the documents published by the office of the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) on Monday, two — the minutes of a meeting between Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and booth-level agents (BLAs), and a media statement — placed 47.56 lakh voters whose names had been left out of the draft roll in five categories: ‘absent’, ‘shifted’, ‘dead’, ‘duplicate’ and ‘others’.

A third document – ASDD list - also published on Monday and containing details of the voters left out for the citizens to check “the reasons for the names left out”, however, classified them under only four categories: ‘permanently shifted’, ‘untraceable/absent’, ‘dead’ and ‘already enrolled’. These are the enumeration forms (EFs), which as per the Delhi CEO, were uncollectable/did not return to the BLO. The reasons were to be shared as per EC rules.

The discrepancy is significant because official documents — including the detailed list of uncollectable forms with the reasons, shared with political parties, as part of the minutes — and an earlier press statement from the CEO’s office identify ‘others’ as a category comprising electors who did not submit or refused to submit their enumeration forms EFs and who were marked as ‘EF refused’. According to a senior official, around 2.5 lakh such voters were identified during the enumeration phase. However, in the press statement shared on Monday, the office of Delhi CEO put combined figures for voter names removed as “absent/shifted/others” at 43.32 lakh.

Delhi draft electoral roll out: How to check your name

An analysis of the ASDD list of names removed from all 14,947 polling booths by The Hindu found no separate category for ‘EF refused’. Instead, all names were categorized in four categories, including the ones who refused the EF, contradicting other official records. This is even as the lists shared with the political parties, which are not machine readable but scanned documents, after completion of enumeration phase mentions names under the fifth category – the others for “EF refused”, raising questions over how the reasons were changed for such voters in the final ASDD list — marking them either absent/untraceable or shifted.

As per rules, an elector is marked “absent” or “shifted” if verified to have shifted to a different state/UT or not present at the registered EPIC address during door-to-door verification visits by the area BLO. The officer is required to visit at least three times and paste a notice incase of absent voters. Importantly, BLO could only make changes in the voter’s EF status and the reasons for uncollected forms during the enumeration phase on the BLO app and the draft roll is only compiled after all EF data, including uncollectable is shared with political party appointed BLAs.

For instance, in Tughlaqabad Extension part of Sangam Vihar constituency, 15 electors were recorded as ‘EF refused’ in the list shared with the political parties in the minutes of the meeting dated August 17, the last day of the enumeration phase, beyond which no changes were allowed. The minutes were signed by BLOs and BLAs of the BJP and AAP.

In Monday’s ASDD list, however, one of these 15 electors was categorised as ‘shifted’, while the remaining 14 were shown as ‘untraceable/absent’. Similar contradictions were found in other records in manual comparison of the list shared with minutes undersigned by the area BLO and BLAs and the final ASDD list published.

In New Delhi’s five parts of Mandir Marg, reasons for 56 voter names and in Basant Lane part for 87 voters not included in the draft roll is mentioned ‘EF refused’ in the list compiled after compeltion of enumeration phase, per the minutes of meetings. For the same voters name, in the ASDD list published, it’s either absent or shifted. The examples go on, as not a single voter name is recorded in the final list of excluded voters for the ‘EF refused’ reason.

When reached for comment on how these changes were made, marking voters’ names who earlier ‘refused EF’ under absent/shifted after deadline for verification was over, the CEO’s office did not respond. The office has also refused to share constituency wise details of reasons for draft stage deletion, or individual breakup of total figures under the categories listed by them.

As per The Hindu’s analysis, a total of 31.59 lakh voters is marked “permanently shifted”, and 11.73 lakh as “untraceable/absent”. Another 2.82 lakh as “deceased” while 1.41 lakh as “already enrolled.”

World.title: Delhi draft electoral roll out: How to check your name
World.content:
The draft electoral roll for Delhi was published on August 31, 2026, after the completion of the Special Intensive Revision or SIR, which began on June 20 and culminated on August 17.

As many as 47.7 lakh electors out of the 1.45 crore of the national capital’s voters were excluded in the draft roll. They are now considered as people who may have moved or died; are covered under duplicate entries, or for “other” reasons have now been marked “uncollectible” and will eventually have their names struck off. However, a system for inclusion has also been outlined.

Also Read: Supreme Court and the SIR exercise

Delhi’s Chief Electoral Officer has said that those excluded can file their claims till September 30 through Form 6 with supporting documents. The final voter roll will be published on November 4.

How to check your name on Delhi’s draft electoral roll?

There are three ways to check your name on the draft roll. Open Election Commission’s voter services websitethat lists the three ways:

Search by EPIC

• Select desired language

• Fill in your Electoral Photo Identity Card (EPIC) Number and State (NCT of Delhi)

• Enter captcha and search

Search by details

• Select your State (NCT of Delhi) and desired language

• Fill in your name and relative’s name. This should be the same as what you filled in the SIR form earlier.

• Enter your date of birth, age, and gender

• Select your district and Assembly constituency

• Enter the captcha and search

Search by mobile

• Select your State (NCT of Delhi) and desired language

• Enter captcha and search

What happens if your name is not on the draft electoral roll?

If a person’s name is not present on the electoral roll, they can use the ‘Claims and Objections’ process to dispute this missing entry.

Here are the steps:

Step 1. Visit https://voters.eci.gov.in/searchInSIR/S2UA4DPDF-JK4QWODSE to cross-verify your historical registration details. There are two ways to do this. The first is the ‘Search by Elector Details’ option and the other is the ‘Search in last SIR E-Roll’ option. If this does not show up your name, then proceed to the next step.

Step 2: Go to the Election Commission of India’s voter website and use the sign-up option to register with an active mobile number and an email ID (optional).

Step 3: Once logged in, click on New Voter Registration or Form 6.

Complete the lineage declaration by giving yours or your parents’ historical voter roll details. Filling these details are mandatory.

Step 4: One needs to provide supportive documentation for online claim verification. The documents that are required are:

Age/Identity Proof: Aadhaar card, passport or PAN card

Delhi Address Proof: Recent electricity bill, water bill or bank passbook that show your current residence

Step 5: Submit the form and save the instantly generated reference ID

This ID can be used to track in real-time the status of your claim to be included in the roll.

One can also use the Voter Helpline App to file the dispute. It is available on Google Play Store and Apple App Store.

Last date for inclusion of name in SIR exercise

The last date for the inclusion of one’s name by submitting a claim is September 30, 2026.

World.title: Can India build a strategic fuel system? | Explained
World.content:
The story so far:

West Asia-related disruptions have exposed a vulnerability in India’s energy-security system. India can import large quantities of crude oil, LNG and LPG, but its ability to store, transport and release these fuels during a prolonged disruption differs sharply by fuel. India already operates underground strategic crude-oil storage and two underground LPG caverns, but has no operating underground natural-gas storage facility.

Commercial LPG prices hiked by ₹10 per cylinder, ATF hiked by ₹6.28/litre

Against this background, the government is considering a decade-long strategic-fuel programme that would add about 28 MT of crude-oil storage, 9 MT of LNG storage and 4 MT of LPG storage. Reuters reports that the proposed reserves are intended to provide nearly two months of crude and LNG demand and about six weeks of LPG demand. The programme remains under consideration and should therefore be treated as a proposed target, not committed capacity.

How much storage does India have today?

India’s position varies considerably by fuel. For crude oil, Phase I of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve provides 5.33 MT of underground capacity, with actual storage of about 3.37 MT, or roughly 63-64% utilisation, across Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur. A further 6.5 MT has been approved under Phase II at Chandikhol and Padur.

However, execution on the Chandikhol project remains protracted amid ongoing land acquisition requirements and finalisation of commercial PPP frameworks.

LPG has a much smaller underground footprint. The Visakhapatnam and Mangaluru caverns together provide about 0.14 MT of capacity. A proposed 4 MT strategic reserve would therefore represent roughly a 30-fold increase in underground LPG capacity.

Natural gas presents the largest storage gap. India currently has no operational underground gas-storage facility. Its gas-security system instead depends on domestic production, LNG imports, import terminals, commercial inventories and pipelines.

These figures also highlight an important distinction between storage capacity and inventory. A facility has a physical capacity, but the fuel it holds can vary. Not all inventory is necessarily immediately accessible either. During a crisis, the critical measure is therefore not simply how many tonnes can be stored, but how much fuel is available and at what withdrawal rate it can reach consumers.

What does the proposed 9 MT of LNG storage mean?

LNG is particularly prone to confusion because India already has substantial LNG import and regasification infrastructure. A regasification terminal can receive LNG and convert it into natural gas, but its regasification capacity does not constitute strategic inventory.

LNG is stored as a cryogenic liquid at around –162°C, requiring specialised insulated tanks and boil-off gas management. Underground gas storage is different: LNG is first regasified and the resulting natural gas is injected into a depleted reservoir or cavern.

The PNGRB–ICF study provides a useful but narrowly defined stress test. Its 2030 scenario examined how much additional LNG infrastructure would be required to supply priority consumers for 20 days under stress conditions. It estimated a requirement of about 0.56-0.6 MT of LNG equivalent, achievable with roughly eight additional LNG tanks. The combined cost of the tanks and the associated strategic inventory was estimated at around $1 billion. This was a scenario-specific estimate, not an assessment of India’s overall strategic LNG requirement.

The proposed 9 MT strategic inventory is an order of magnitude larger. Against the ICF projection of roughly 58 MT of annual LNG imports, 9 MT represents about 56 days of imports — hence the description of approximately two months of LNG import cover. It does not mean two months of India’s total gas consumption.

The difference is important. A 0.6 MT requirement addresses a 20-day priority-sector stress scenario; 9 MT represents a much broader strategic objective of buffering India against prolonged LNG-import disruption. The associated investment would therefore be substantially larger.

Does all the gas have to be stored as LNG?

No. India could eventually use a portfolio of surface LNG tanks and underground natural-gas storage.

Additional LNG tanks would hold inventory directly at import terminals. A separate proposal from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas would require LNG import terminals to maintain storage capacity 10% above their normal operating requirement, with the additional capacity available to the government during supply or price disruptions.

For longer-duration requirements, depleted oil and gas reservoirs, which account for 74% of global working gas volume, could provide much larger volumes of underground gas storage. Salt caverns offer different advantages: faster injection and withdrawal and the ability to cycle inventory more frequently, potentially making them useful for shorter-duration balancing.

But a depleted field cannot simply become a storage site because production has ended. Reservoir characteristics, cap-rock integrity, pressure behaviour, existing wells, cushion-gas requirements and pipeline connectivity must all be assessed. India’s sedimentary basins — including Krishna, Godavari, Cambay, Mumbai Offshore and Rajasthan — offer potential locations, but moving from geological potential to usable storage requires subsurface investigation, site selection, engineering, construction, testing, filling and pipeline integration.

Salt caverns face a similar qualification process. Rajasthan’s salt-bearing formations have been investigated for solution-mined caverns, but suitability depends on depth, thickness, purity, geometry, groundwater and mechanical properties.

Can India scale its crude and LPG experience?

Crude is the most mature component. India already operates underground crude caverns and has developed the associated engineering capabilities. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve illustrates the scale possible with salt caverns, with authorised capacity of 714 million barrels across 60 caverns. But the U.S. system works as an integrated network of caverns, pipelines, marine terminals and refineries. Storage is therefore fundamentally an infrastructure system, not simply an underground space.

LPG is technically proven in India but presents a much larger scaling challenge. A proposed 4 MT reserve would require a substantial network of new caverns or other storage facilities, together with import terminals, pipelines, pumping systems and bottling infrastructure.

The Mangaluru cavern illustrates the complexity. Underground construction requires geological and hydrogeological investigation, rock-mechanics analysis and groundwater management, particularly where work takes place alongside operating surface facilities. Scaling the system would require sustained capabilities in geophysics, geomechanics, tunnelling, reservoir engineering and project execution.

What happens if the fuel cannot reach India?

Because energy security relies heavily on maritime logistics, including vulnerable chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and long-distance routes from the U.S., India is proactively diversifying both its import sources and shipping capabilities. To reduce reliance on foreign vessels, State-run oil refiners and the Shipping Corporation of India plan to invest $1.5 to $2 billion in a joint venture to acquire 59 ships. Simultaneously, Indian Oil is expanding sourcing through new 2027 agreements with Algeria and increased U.S. purchases, while exploring direct stakes in Very Large Gas Carriers to secure greater control over its supply chain.

What about pipelines?

Pipelines provide the final link between imported or stored fuel and inland consumers. PNGRB has recently authorised approximately 1,800 km of new LPG pipelines across six States, involving investment of around $0.7 billion. These pipelines improve connections between supply sources and inland markets and reduce dependence on road movement, but they do not themselves add strategic storage. Their value lies in improving deliverability.

The same principle applies to natural gas. Underground storage is useful only if it can inject into and withdraw from the gas grid at the required rate. LNG tanks are useful only when regasification and downstream pipelines can move the gas. LPG caverns require connections to bottling and distribution systems.

Who pays for the strategic reserves?

The reported $42 billion programme, which has yet to be confirmed by the government, combines infrastructure CAPEX with the cost of purchasing and maintaining strategic fuel inventories. Reuters reported that more than half could go towards storage infrastructure, with the balance used to purchase and fill the reserves. Financing would be a challenge and the government shot down reports that a cess would be charged to pay for the reserves.

The financial obligation does not end with construction. Billions of dollars of fuel would need to be purchased, financed and maintained. Stocks released during a crisis would then have to be replenished, potentially when commodity and freight prices are higher. The policy therefore needs to establish who owns and finances the inventory, minimum stock obligations, emergency-release authority, and who bears replenishment and price risk. A commercial-cum-strategic model could reduce the public burden, provided commercially used capacity remains available during emergencies.

Is storage enough to make India energy-secure?

Building 41 MT of combined storage is only part of the equation. A strategic reserve is effective only if India can seamlessly access fuel, transport it inland, and replenish stocks after a release.

Ultimately, energy security relies on an integrated framework: reserves buy time, shipping brings the next cargo, pipelines deliver fuel inland, and governance dictates emergency execution. The ultimate test of India’s strategic fuel programme will be its ability to coordinate all these elements simultaneously when a crisis hits.

(The author is an Energy and Emerging Technologies expert)

World.title: Park your car over your open well
World.content:
For many apartment residents in Chennai, an open well may sound like something from another time — a structure with a parapet wall, a pulley and a bucket. With space at a premium, keeping one may seem impractical. But an open well does not necessarily mean giving up a parking spot or valuable open space. With the right design, it can be built below ground, allowing vehicles to pass over it while the well continues to collect rainwater and recharge groundwater.

This is what N. Ramshankar, an executive member of The Rain Centre, has done at the Rain Centre in Adyar. An old open well that once had only about two feet of water now holds around 16 feet after rooftop rainwater was directed into it with minimal filtration.

Sekhar Raghavan, director, The Rain Centre, weighs in about this open well on the premises of the Rain Centre: “Unless I open the lid, you will not even know that there is an open well below.” Such wells can even be incorporated into driveways or parking areas, Sekhar says, provided they are kept away from structural columns. “You can have your open well within your stilt car parking,” says Sekhar. The minimum space required for the well, according to him, is about 3.25 feet in diameter.

“We were afraid in the initial days. We were wondering whether an open well can be closed and whether it will accumulate gas and all that. An engineer told us, ‘Don’t make that mistake, nothing will happen.’ He even set up a vent for us,” says Ramshankar. The parapet wall was subsequently removed and a slab was placed at floor level. “We demolished the parapet wall of the well and then we put a slab on it, at the floor level. Now we have vehicles going on top of it,” he says.

The benefit has not been limited to saving space. The quality of the water has also improved. “The TDS has also been diluted from almost 850 to now 400,” he says.

For Ramshankar, the value of an open well lies in what it can provide while also being replenished. Open wells generally tap the shallow aquifer, around 25 to 30 feet below the ground and, at most, about 40 feet. Unlike the deeper hard-rock aquifer tapped by borewells, this shallow groundwater can be replenished more easily through rainwater harvesting. Rooftop rainwater can be directed into an existing well, replenishing the water and helping dilute salts and TDS.

Sekhar Raghavan says open wells generally tap the shallow groundwater layer, which can be replenished through rainwater harvesting.

“During monsoon, your open well will have a lot of water, and a couple of months thereafter. So, start tapping it. Then during summer months, go to your borewell,” he says. For an apartment, this can also translate into a reduction in dependence on tanker water.

Keeping the tankers away

At Hiranya Apartments in Raja Annamalaipuram, resident Raghunandan Ranganathan says the open well was never shut, even though three borewells had been installed and two were later closed. “This open well is what is giving us a lot of water,” he says.

The apartment already had rainwater-harvesting infrastructure, including percolation wells. But during heavy rain, water would collect in the compound and flow out through the gates onto the road. The residents then sought Sekhar Raghavan’s help.

“We made these collection pits at every gate and diverted the water to the percolation pits, which in turn were feeding the well,” says Raghunandan. Over time, the system changed the quality and availability of water in the apartment.

“Builders often do not make use of the open wells available on a property. Instead, they tend to shut them down and install borewells. I am not able to understand the logic behind this.”

Making use of the monsoon

At Bayview Apartments in Besant Nagar, the open well has been in use since the apartment was built around 1989-90. “We are using an open well. Generally, during the rain, mainly after the Northeast Monsoon, it fills up,” says resident K. Sangameshwar.

The apartment also has two borewells and a Metro Water connection. During the rainy season, residents use more of the open well and borewell. Rainwater from the terrace is directed towards the ground, with parts of the system leading close to the open well. The complex also has rainwater-harvesting pits in its open areas. “So all these go into the well, and from the well, I think it slowly percolates into the groundwater,” says Sangameshwar.

Unlike the well at The Rain Centre, the Bayview well remains above ground, with a cover and mesh over it. It shows that there is no single way for an apartment to retain an open well. It can remain visible in an open space, or it can be covered and integrated into a driveway or parking area.

For apartment residents, then, the question may not be whether there is enough space for an open well. It could be whether the space already available can be put to better use — above the ground for parking, and below it for water.

World.title: Madras Day 2026: alone with the timepieces at tiny Peer & Sons in Mylapore
World.content:
On that part of Kutchery Road, where the Buckingham Canal flows sluggishly under a bridge, S. Shakil Ahmed operates from a shop smaller than a niche in a dovecote. The shop was once larger, recalls Shakil, but as the owner reclaimed a part of it for another enterprise, it shrunk to its present dimensions. But this small shop still catches the eye for its wall displays: clocks, either demode or delectably antique, depending on the eye beholding them. Another eye-catching feature is the enseigne above the entrance that announces the enterprise as Peer & Sons. When quizzed about the name and its homonymic alignment with the iconic P. Orr & Sons on Mount Road, Shakil sounds a tad amused as he offers a reply: obviously, when they see this shop, they know the two are galaxies apart. But when they hear the name ‘Peer & Sons’ over the phone, they would be confused for a split second. And the name was not carefully chosen to evoke that iconic shop, remarks Shakil, just to reflect that it was started by his father S.K. Peer.

S.K. Peer had opened this shop in 1963 and continued in the saddle till his demise in 2008. Shakil relishes reminiscing about the unquestioning obedience with which he followed in his father’s footsteps, not in 2008 but way back in 1991 when the senior was at the height of his prowess as a mender of timepieces and he was just a school student. Shakil joined his father as his understudy in 1991, right after finishing his Class X board exams.

“I did not even wait for my results,” he says with a faint laugh at the memory.

“If my father asked for something, it was always a yes,” states Shakil, his decision driven by a straightforward logic: if his father needed him at the shop, that was reason enough to be there.

He observes that for parents to get a ‘yes’ from their children today, they would have to first answer a gazillion ‘whys’. Shakil, who has three children, two girls and a boy, all of them falling within the Gen Z bracket, is at peace with the current generation’s questioning mindset as they are spoilt for choice in terms of career options, and have information at hand to suss those careers out.

Hands-on training

What began as an attempt to help his father in this metier, turned into a deep-rooted passion for mending the keepers of time. Watching his father repair watches and clocks, he was fascinated by the work, the patience it demanded and the power one felt when they got the timepiece ticking again. He was actively trained in this craft by his father, and Shakil proudly admits the way he repairs timepieces is rooted in that hands-on training.

To the question, if he has ever regretted not having taken a different career path, Shakil’s answer is a ‘no’, but he qualifies it by admitting that on rare occasions, the thought has crossed his mind. That thought most likely occurred during the pandemic and in recent times, on account of Metro Rail work at the Luz Corner (where Kutchery Road meets Luz Church Road meet) restricting access to his shop. That thought gets counterbalanced by his awareness of the benefits of being one’s own boss.“If there is a function, I can attend it without prior leave complications; if I want to travel, I can take a few days off and do so,” he smiles.

He has commendably built a livelihood just by the practice of the craft of repairing timepieces, has managed to give his children good and meaningful education (the two daughters are in college and the son in school).

After his father’s death in 2008, Shakil has been running the shop in a veritable one-man show spending that vast chunk of his waking hours (that is, from 10.a.m. to 9p.m.), sitting hunched over timepieces, peering at them through a magnifying eyepiece. The punch-in punch-out time is sometimes longer: during the pandemic, he began taking delicate and major repairs home, a habit that has stuck with him ever since. His workbench has witnessed everything from a Seiko to a 1960s Omega; and also those ornate tall, weight-driven pendulum clocks, colloquially called grandfather and grandmother clocks depending on their height and size. His customer base includes collectors of antique clocks. He accepts every timepiece that comes his way, from the grand to the commonplace. Repairs of antique clocks can soak up considerable time.

Availability of spare parts can sometimes pose a challenge. When unable to find spare parts, he has fashioned them himself, says Shakil. But obviously, there is a limit to what you can fashion yourself; the sustainable option is to have dealers who can hand them over to you. On a normal day though, he sources spares from dealers. He also buys old clocks to salvage those parts that are in working order.

Now, the question that stares at any enterprise sustained by successive generations. Would the next generation take the baton from Shakil and continue the legacy started by his father S.K. Peer? His children might likely choose different fields, and Shakil admits the possibility of the business continuing through them being thin. For now, Shakil remains at his bench, turning back time by getting old timepieces ticking again. And he luxuriates in the sweet sound of a timepiece ticking and sounding back to life.

(Celebrating Madras Day (August 22), Resilience Series tracks old markets and enterprises in the city that are under the shadow of a major civic infrastructure work but are soldiering on with inimitable poise.)

World.title: Dubai property no longer safe haven
World.content:
KARACHI: The Gulf war has curbed the outflow of black money from Pakistan to Dubai, while funds already invested are returning and being diverted into property in the country, according to sources in the property and currency markets.

Thousands of Pakistanis have invested hundreds of millions of dollars in Dubai, particularly in property. Pakistan was identified twice as the second-largest foreign investor in Dubai property. It was widely believed that black money created in Pakistan had a safe haven in Dubai and was a catalyst for property price hikes there.

“About $60 million in illegal (or black) money is created in Pakistan per month and has been invested in Dubai, but this has now stopped,” said All Pakistan Builders Association Chairman Hassan Bakhshi.

Currency dealers said the situation has reversed, with black money in Dubai stuck and recovery difficult due to the ongoing war.

Pakistanis struggle to recover investments as black money fuels Karachi property rally

“The higher remittances from Dubai reflect that Pakistanis are sending back their liquid assets to Pakistan,” said a currency dealer. The war has changed Dubai’s appeal as a destination for investment and tourism.

Inflows from Dubai have increased. The impact is that illegal money being created in Pakistan has once again diverted towards the property business.

“Property prices in Defence went up 50-60 per cent after the Gulf war started. Since the title of the Defence property is safe (meaning no double filing or fake dealing), most of the money is going towards the area,” said Mr Bakhshi.

Not only was black money going to Dubai, but many tech companies had also shifted there before the war because of a hurdle-free business environment. They were also moving abroad due to frequent internet connectivity issues and excessive interference from the tax authorities.

Thousands of Pakistanis were using Dubai as a third country and conducting legal business with countries such as India and Bangladesh. Now they are stuck and trying to recover their investment from Dubai, as the war-like situation still prevails.

Currency dealers said that once the situation normalises, hundreds of millions of dollars would return to Pakistan from the Gulf, as Dubai has lost the confidence of foreign investors.

Mr Bakhshi also endorsed reports that Pakistani investors were trying their best to recover their investments from Dubai, but property prices in the war-affected country have fallen to a minimum level.

Property dealers said that prices in Pakistan have started to increase after the war, and trading has also increased. Both buying and selling have increased due to improved liquidity.

“The government is also taking measures to boost the construction industry, and the rebound in property prices was the result of this effort. The property prices in other areas of Karachi have increased in the range of 20 to 25pc,” said Karim Dad, a property dealer.

Published in Dawn, September 1st, 2026

World.title: Schools closed in Rawalpindi as heavy rain lashes twin cities
World.content:
RAWALPINDI: Heavy rain lashed Rawalpindi and Islamabad on Tuesday morning, inundating low-lying areas, raising the water level in Leh Nullah and prompting the district administration in the garrison city to announce a holiday for educational institutions.

The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) said that the water level in Leh Nullah had risen to 29 feet at Kattarian and 23.5 feet at Gawalmandi.
