At the national meeting in Ganzhou, officials discussed new data that revealed a shift: almost a third of the 361 couples who married in Shicheng County in the first half of this year reportedly paid no bride price — in contrast to years past, when bride price was expected.

In some Shicheng County villages, the rejection of high bride prices has been enshrined in local rules and customs, reportedly cutting total wedding costs to about one-fifth of what they used to be. “Red and white” councils, or hongbai lishihui — named for the colors that represent weddings and funerals — have been established to “step in” to correct excessive spending on bride prices.

Changxi village in the county has also promoted lower costs for weddings in general, ensuring that wedding banquets are kept under 680 yuan per table.

The villagers have also developed a consensus that bride prices should be kept at either 3,600 or 6,900 yuan — considered lucky in Chinese culture as “six,” or liu, is a homophone of “smooth,” and “nine,” or jiu, is a homophone of “a long time,” symbolizing a long marriage.

Shicheng also offers rewards to couples and their parents who do not spend vast sums on bride prices. Such families can apply for a card granting them access to discounts on wedding banquets, discounted business loans, free entrance to local attractions, and free pregnancy checks. Over 1,000 cards are said to have been issued this year.

“The card is not just about money; it’s an honor,” Lai Hua, deputy director of Shicheng Civil Affairs Bureau, told domestic media. “We want people who support the new customs to feel recognized, rewarded, and proud.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Wrapped bundles of cash given as bride prices in Sinan County, Guizhou province, Feb. 22, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018964/For China’s Gen Z Investors, Patriotism Meets Portfolio Math
World.title: For China’s Gen Z Investors, Patriotism Meets Portfolio Math
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018964/For China’s Gen Z Investors, Patriotism Meets Portfolio Math
World.content:
Huang Jiarui knew she’d beaten the odds when she secured 1,000 shares in CXMT’s IPO, one of China’s leading memory-chip makers and a key player in the country’s push to build its own chip industry. The allotment rate was just 0.47%.

On July 27, CXMT debuted on Shanghai’s STAR Market, the exchange’s Nasdaq-style board for tech companies. Its shares opened at 49.5 yuan ($6.93) — nearly six times the 8.66-yuan offer price. Huang sold immediately.

“Short-term moves are driven by emotion and money flow,” the 28-year-old told Sixth Tone. “The profits were already good, so I’ll wait for the price to fall back before buying again.”

Huang, who works in the financial industry in the country’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has long favored tech stocks, from Chinese battery makers to Nvidia and Tesla. In April, she began shifting more attention back to China, drawn by advances in chips, AI, and manufacturing. “In tech right now, it’s either China or the U.S.,” she said.

Asked how much those considerations influence her decisions, Huang puts the combined weight of “patriotism” and “confidence” in China at about 30%. She says they also make her willing to pay a premium for Chinese tech even when valuations look stretched.

Even so, about 80% of Huang’s portfolio remains in U.S. tech, with the remaining 20% evenly split between China and South Korea. “China’s tech sector has only been gaining ground since 2024,” she said. “The U.S., by contrast, has three decades of history to look back on.”

That mix of enthusiasm and caution is increasingly visible among a growing cohort of younger Chinese retail investors entering the market.

Lu Xiaomeng, an associate professor of finance at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said older investors tended to get information from financial news and account managers. Younger investors now open their phones to a stream of market data, influencers’ opinions, and AI analysis.

Investors born in the 1990s and 2000s accounted for more than 45% of the 27.44 million new A-share accounts opened in 2025, according to Shanghai Stock Exchange data. Separate research by Ping An Securities and the Hurun Research Institute found that investors under 30 made up about 30% of all investors, roughly double their share before September 2024.

Lu said companies such as CXMT can appeal to younger investors for reasons beyond returns. Buying shares in chipmakers and other hard-tech companies, she said, can also be a way to back industries they see as important to China’s development.

“The capital market can carry ideals,” Lu said, “but in the end, price is what counts.”

Crash course

When Huang began trading in college, she saw the stock market as a place to test what she was learning as a finance major. She quickly found that textbook models offered only so much help once real money was involved.

“Technical indicators such as moving averages and mean reversion can be helpful,” she said. “But in the end, it’s often instinct and psychological resilience that really count.”

In February, Huang bought a leveraged Nasdaq-100 exchange-traded fund (ETF) designed to magnify the index’s daily gains and losses threefold. She held on as it fell in March and, by May, had made more than $20,000. Her biggest loss came from a Hong Kong-listed AI concept stock, where she lost more than HK$40,000 ($5,100).

Over time, Huang became less convinced that active trading could consistently give her an edge. She said whatever advantage she gained over passive investing did not seem large enough to justify the time and effort she was putting in.

She still follows the market closely. Huang swaps financial news and stock ideas with her parents in a family group chat, follows financial influencers, and joins online trading groups. She also treats the mood in those groups as a signal in itself. “When everyone is excited, it’s time to reduce positions,” she said. “And when everyone is in despair, it’s time to add.”

On the popular lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, the topic “My Stock Trading Diary” has drawn nearly 3.9 billion views and over 37 million discussions. Users post about wins and losses, exchange lessons from trades, and sometimes frame investing as something larger than making money.

Some posts frame trading as a way to improve their financial circumstances; others treat it almost as a form of self-discipline. One user wrote that trading had not made him rich, but had made him want less and pay more attention to geopolitics and the chip industry.

Losses are documented just as openly. One investor who said he had lost 600,000 yuan traced his progression from denial at 150,000 yuan down, to desperation at 250,000, to delusion at 500,000, and finally resignation at zero: “Oh well, waking up to nothing.”

Shi Donghui, a finance professor at Fudan University, said the shift online has lowered the barriers to trading: investors can open accounts, check prices, find information, and place trades from their phones.

“This change has directly pushed up trading frequency,” he said. “Market correlation has increased, and short-term news can easily sway young people’s trading decisions.”

Lower barriers have also brought less experienced investors into the market, Shi said, including university students with little financial training. Easier access to information and trading, he argued, does not necessarily lead to better investment decisions.

“Big data’s targeted recommendations make it easier to create information bubbles,” Shi said. “Young people can easily be trapped by a single point of view.”

Zhang Yixuan began trading in 2019, just after turning 18. A personal finance documentary first persuaded her to start managing her money early. She began with funds, then opened a stock account after growing frustrated with the delays involved in buying and selling them.

“At the time, I had no strategy and was buying almost randomly,” Zhang said. One stock she picked was later delisted after being flagged as high risk.

She never studied a formal trading method, instead piecing together what she knows from finance books, documentaries, and videos on streaming platform Bilibili. Trading now takes up about four hours of her workday, and stocks account for roughly 60% of her liquid assets.

Unlike Huang, Zhang’s money is concentrated in non-ferrous metals and power utilities rather than domestic tech.

On July 29, after the STAR 50 — an index tracking major companies on Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR Market — had fallen sharply, she began buying an ETF that tracks it. She bought in several batches and sold around July 31 as soon as the position turned profitable. Because she does not know the tech sector well, she said, she kept the position small.

“If there’s a chance to make money, I take it,” she said. “It has nothing to do with being optimistic about the sector.”

Shi said younger investors can amplify short-term moves in fashionable sectors but are unlikely to change the market’s longer-term cycles. Previous booms in solar, liquor, and electric vehicles followed much the same pattern, he said. Sustained gains ultimately need to be supported by company earnings.

Zhang has no regular circle of trading friends and rarely discusses investment ideas with others. She follows information across several online platforms but is wary of simply following influencers.

“It’s your own money,” she said. “In the end, you have to decide for yourself.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018949/Study Linking Solar Farms to Bird Loss Draws Scrutiny in China
World.title: Study Linking Solar Farms to Bird Loss Draws Scrutiny in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018949/Study Linking Solar Farms to Bird Loss Draws Scrutiny in China
World.content:
Solar farms reduce bird diversity, a Chinese study published last week in the international, peer-reviewed journal Science, announced. But the country’s scientific community has contested the reliability of its birdwatching data and the significance of its statistical findings.

The study, published Aug. 21, was led by researchers at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, in collaboration with other researchers from China, Vietnam, and the United States.

Examining 2,344 Chinese counties from 2014 to 2023, it found that cutting carbon emissions may come at the cost of protecting biodiversity, as birds’ cropland and grassland habitats are converted for solar projects.

China has been expanding solar power to meet its targets of peaking carbon emissions by 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality by 2060. By 2024, solar facilities covered an estimated 4,520 square kilometers of land and are projected to make up nearly 45% of the country’s electricity generation by 2060.

“The research is not against solar expansion but rather offers policy recommendations on how to do it better,” Li Shanjun, one of the study’s corresponding authors and a professor at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, told Sixth Tone.

The authors suggested developing solar projects in areas where solar panels cause lower ecological impact, such as in deserts; promoting phased rollouts rather than sudden large-scale expansion; and assessing ecological recovery beyond vegetation density, as they found uniform vegetation inferior for housing bird habitats.

However, experts from the China Ornithological Society said “flaws” in the study’s bird observation data could undermine its conclusions, according to a Tuesday article published on the society’s official WeChat account. The academic group includes ornithologists from universities, research institutes, and conservation organizations nationwide.

The crowdsourced dataset from the China Birdwatching Record Center contained missing bird counts, erroneous records, and reporting differences driven by the growing popularity of birdwatching, the Society wrote.

Among the issues, over 40% of the over 500,000 reports collected during the nine years recorded the presence of species, indicated using the number “1.” However, the Society noted that this is commonly used as a placeholder when the observer did not enter a count, rather than that only one bird was seen, making the data unreliable.

The analysis also said the data had not been properly cleaned. One record from 2015, for example, reported over 2 billion little egrets at a single location. The record was retained in the dataset, contributing to bird totals “beyond a reasonable range.”

Meanwhile, the original study may have removed some migratory waterbirds’ records at wintering sites as statistical outliers, as they recorded tens of thousands of birds at a given location, “potentially underestimating true bird diversity,” the analysis said.

The analysis also noted that birdwatching records surged between 2021 and 2023 amid a growing birdwatching boom in the country, just as authorities were introducing significant solar policies. This, it argued, makes it difficult to determine whether changes in biodiversity data were driven by increased birdwatching or photovoltaic development.

Chinese ecologists generally agree that amid cutting carbon emissions, biodiversity can be protected through careful planning, Ma Zhijun, deputy director of the China Ornithological Society and a co-author of the analysis, told Sixth Tone. Ma is also a professor at Fudan University’s School of Life Sciences.

Such planning means avoiding key wildlife habitats when building solar, wind, and other renewable energy facilities, Ma said.

He added that the “easy availability” of birdwatching datasets has led researchers without a background in bird ecology to use them without “fully understanding their limitations.”

“This paper is a typical example of the problem,” he said. The analysis recommended cross-checking data from different sources and cleaning datasets before using them to assess large-scale changes.

A separate statistical analysis of the study’s data also found that birdwatching duration — where longer sessions correlate with more species detected — had a significantly greater effect on measured bird diversity than solar policy.

That analysis, published Sunday, was conducted by Lai Jiangshan, an ecology professor at Nanjing Forestry University, and Zhang Shuang, an associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

“This (comparison of birdwatching duration and solar policy) was not reflected in the Science paper, meaning its conclusion is not statistically supported,” Zhang told Sixth Tone.

Li, one of the Science paper’s corresponding authors, responded that the two measures were “not comparable” and that the comparison was not informative for policymaking.

“Policy variables typically account for only a small share of variation in environmental outcomes,” he said. “But policies remain among the few tools people can actively change.”

Li also rejected any suggestion that the team had concealed metrics, noting that the full data and code used to run the statistical models were publicly available. Regarding the birdwatching data, he said the findings were tested using different statistical methods, and outliers were removed.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Solar panels cover the mountains in Anshun, Guizhou province, Aug. 4, 2024.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018941/After ‘Sleep No More,’ What’s Next for Chinese Immersive Theater?
World.title: After ‘Sleep No More,’ What’s Next for Chinese Immersive Theater?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018941/After ‘Sleep No More,’ What’s Next for Chinese Immersive Theater?
World.content:
After 2,670 performances, the immersive theatrical production “Sleep No More,” co-produced by Shanghai Media Group and pioneering British theater company Punchdrunk, will conclude its 10-year run at the McKinnon Hotel in Shanghai on Aug. 30.

When it opened in Shanghai a decade ago, the production wowed local theatergoers with its novelty and impact. Audience members donned white masks and entered a dimly lit building where they could move freely between rooms: following Macbeth, searching for the witches, or wandering the corridors piecing together clues. No one could see the complete story, but “missing out” was part of the experience.

A decade on, immersive theater has blossomed across China, appearing in theaters, scenic areas, museums, shopping malls, and former factories. There are even purpose-built theatrical theme parks. “Unique Henan,” for example, in the suburbs of Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, features 21 performance spaces and nearly 1,000 actors performing almost 700 minutes of material each day. Visitors can spend an entire day exploring the park and still see only a fraction of what it offers. Meanwhile, “Unique Dream of Red Mansions” in Langfang, in the northern Hebei province, takes the classic Chinese novel “Dream of the Red Chamber” as its theme, with four large theaters, eight smaller ones, and 108 interconnected immersive spaces. Its daily performances total more than 800 minutes.

Was all this brought about by “Sleep No More”? Yes and no.

In traditional theater, the theatrical world is confined to the other side of the stage, while the audience sits in darkness and watches a carefully framed reality. This model came under scrutiny in the 20th century. Avant-garde theater pioneers, including Antonin Artaud, Jerzy Grotowski, Peter Brook, and Richard Schechner, reexamined the body, space, presence, and the relationship between audiences and performers. Schechner, in particular, developed the concept of “environmental theater,” emphasizing that a theatrical event encompasses not only performers and text but also the audience, sensory stimuli, architecture, and other elements of the performance space. Modern theater has since continued to seek ways to move audiences beyond fixed seats and into cities, rivers, markets, and historical settings, making space part of the work itself.

Such practices are nothing new in Chinese theater. From 1932 to 1937, playwright Xiong Foxi went to Ding County in Hebei as part of a movement to popularize theater in rural China. His productions integrated stage scenery with the real sky and surrounding forest, while audiences crossed the fourth wall to participate directly in the performance.

Since the early 2000s, director Wang Chaoge’s pioneering “Impression” and “Encore” series have reshaped the spatial aesthetics of China’s cultural tourism performances through large-scale live productions. They took theater beyond the proscenium arch and into outdoor landscapes, familiarizing audiences with expansive, panoramic, and interactive performances. “Encore Pingyao,” which premiered in 2013 in Pingyao, in the northern Shanxi province, went further by dispensing with the traditional stage entirely. Audiences walked through streets, courtyards, and indoor spaces alongside the actors.

“Sleep No More” was therefore by no means the starting point for immersive theater in China. Long before its arrival, Chinese audiences were already familiar with shared spaces, physical participation, and collective rituals. Nevertheless, it marked an important watershed. It gave Chinese theater practitioners an internationally influential model: a mature, replicable, sustainable, and long-running production. By combining free movement, multiple narratives, repeat viewings, and word-of-mouth recommendations, it demonstrated that audiences were willing to pay for highly personalized live experiences.

Before “Sleep No More,” even China’s grandest immersive productions were generally guided by their creators, with audiences moving through history as a group. It gave individuals greater agency, allowing each person to follow different characters and leave with an incomplete but unique story. These approaches represent two important strands in Chinese immersive theater: one emphasizes group movement, local history, and collective memory, while the other focuses on individual choice, free exploration, and fragmented narratives. Both, however, make the performance environment part of the show, place audiences and performers in the same space and time, and allow them to experience together a theatrical event unfolding “here and now.”

Over the past decade, many Chinese productions have emerged between these two approaches. Theater has moved beyond the traditional stage into public squares and parks, forests and lakesides, warehouses and factories, and historical sites. Its forms range from parades in theme parks and rituals at village temple fairs to farmers singing together in fields or an individual quietly grieving in a museum before onlookers.

Chinese immersive theater has not simply imitated “Sleep No More.” Instead, it has converged with China’s established traditions of live performance, experiential theater, and cultural tourism, gradually forming a distinctly local style. At destinations such as “Unique Henan” and “Unique Dream of Red Mansions,” theater has expanded from a single work into an entire cultural attraction. Productions of different scales and formats coexist, while architecture, landscapes, dining, and travel all become part of the experience.

This form of theater draws on China’s rich resources of local history, classic literature, and cultural heritage, while also being closely linked to urban renewal, scenic-area development, and destination tourism. Compared with Western immersive productions, which tend to emphasize individual exploration and unfamiliar experiences, Chinese productions more often combine historical resources, collective viewing, and large-scale spaces.

Yet the proliferation of such productions has also exposed problems. A bigger space does not necessarily mean deeper immersion. Enormous scale can accommodate more narratives, but it can also allow architectural spectacle to overshadow the drama. Likewise, local culture can provide rich material, but it can also be compressed into a handful of easily recognizable symbols.

Now that “immersive” has become a ubiquitous cultural label, perhaps we theater practitioners need to reconsider a fundamental question: Why do we need immersion?

Immersion is not the purpose of theater, but a way of establishing a relationship between the audience and the work. It shortens not only the physical distance between audiences and performers but also the psychological distance between audiences and characters, environments, history, and real-life situations. Audiences should enter a theatrical space for the novelty of “being there” as well as to better understand the characters’ environment, the pressures they face, and why they make particular choices at a particular time and place. Physical presence is only the starting point. Meaningful immersion moves from presence to understanding, and then to empathy, identification, or reflection.

As the boundaries of spatial spectacle continue to expand, the future value of immersive theater in China should not be measured by architectural scale or technological sophistication. Instead, it should be judged by whether it can transform space into narrative and the audience’s presence into understanding.

At its best, immersive theater is not about temporarily transporting audiences to another world but about ensuring that the characters, history, and culture they encounter remain with them after they leave, creating connections with their own lives. In this sense, even as “Sleep No More” ends its Shanghai run, its influence on contemporary Chinese theater will continue.

(Header image: A promotional image for “Sleep No More.”From @SleepNoMore上海 on Shanghai)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018953/Hundreds Still Missing After Deadly China-Nepal Border Mudslide
World.title: Hundreds Still Missing After Deadly China-Nepal Border Mudslide
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018953/Hundreds Still Missing After Deadly China-Nepal Border Mudslide
World.content:
On Monday, Zhao Jianing rode his motorcycle through the Gyirong border checkpoint under clear skies, inching past export trucks and lines of BYD vehicles as traffic backed up along the China-Nepal border. He recalled seeing at least a dozen uniformed workers at their posts.

Two days later, a massive surge of water, mud, and debris descended from the Nepali side of the Himalayas and tore through the border area at around 11 a.m. Wednesday. Funneled through a steep valley toward southwestern China’s Xizang Autonomous Region, the torrent swept away police posts and buried the Gyirong checkpoint.

Surveillance footage from outside the checkpoint showed muddy floodwaters surging above the border gates and engulfing the area within seconds as people fled. Aerial footage from state broadcaster CCTV later showed the border zone blanketed in mud, with no buildings visible.

By Thursday, three people had been confirmed dead and 558 remained missing in Gyirong County on the Chinese side, while two people had been rescued. Across the affected area, at least 273 people were dead and 1,384 remained missing.

China’s Ministry of Water Resources told CCTV that a landslide dam had formed upstream, creating a lake containing an estimated 2 million cubic meters of water. The lake was already overflowing, and another 3 million cubic meters were expected to channel into it over the next three days, raising the risk that the dam could fail.

The threat further complicated rescue efforts already hampered by damaged roads and communications infrastructure.

Xizang activated its highest-level emergency response, deploying military transport aircraft, more than 800 firefighters, and armed police officers to the area. Central authorities also allocated 220 million yuan ($30.7 million) for disaster relief, recovery, and reconstruction.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang arrived in the mudslide-hit area of Gyirong Township on Thursday to oversee rescue and relief efforts, state news agency Xinhua reported. He visited on behalf of President Xi Jinping and met rescue workers and people displaced by the disaster.

Wang Qian, an official with the Shigatse military sub-command, told CCTV that the edge of the mudslide was about 2.5 kilometers from the Gyirong checkpoint, where mud was nearly 1.5 meters deep.

Gyirong is Xizang’s largest land port and a major gateway for trade and travel between China and Nepal. As of June 23, the checkpoint had recorded more than 100,000 entries and exits this year, up 12.85% from the same period in 2025.

Crossing into Nepal two days earlier, Zhao, a 26-year-old motorcyclist from Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, remembered the checkpoint as busy but ordinary, with clear skies, lines of export vehicles, and workers directing traffic.

One of those workers, a uniformed man Zhao estimated to be in his 30s, had briefly argued with him over his speed.

After seeing footage of police posts being swept away, Zhao said he kept thinking about the encounter. “I never imagined that just one or two days later, everything would be gone,” Zhao told Sixth Tone. “It happened so fast. I think he probably had no chance to escape. I feel really guilty and upset.”

The road on the Nepalese side beyond the checkpoint was extremely difficult to navigate, he said. In some places, the mud was “as deep as half the length of an arm,” he said, forcing him to use both feet to keep the motorcycle moving. His shoes even came off.

“The cliff was on the right and the muddy road was on the left. I could barely ride. I thought I was going to die there,” he said.

No official investigation has established the cause of Wednesday’s disaster, but several experts said preliminary evidence points to a possible high-altitude ice-rock avalanche originating from a tributary of the Donglin Tsangpo River in Nepal.

Fan Xuanmei, director of the State Key Laboratory of Geohazard Prevention and Geoenvironment Protection at Chengdu University of Technology, told Southern Weekly that a high-altitude mass of ice and rock may have destabilized and collapsed before rapidly descending into the valley.

As it moved downstream, the mass could have mixed with water and scraped loose material from the valley floor, Fan said, expanding into a much larger flood and mudslide. Such a mechanism would differ from a conventional glacial-lake outburst flood.

The terrain may have amplified the destruction. Yi Shaoliang, an expert at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development based in Nepal, said the enormous volume of water may have struck hard rock formations on the opposite side of the Lhende River, generating powerful turbulence and redirecting the flow toward buildings at the Chinese checkpoint, according to Southern Weekly.

The border corridor has faced destructive flooding before. In July 2025, a flood destroyed the Friendship Bridge linking China’s Gyirong Port with Rasuwa Fort in Nepal. Research across the Himalayan region has linked warming to expanding glacial lakes and greater instability in high mountain environments, though experts cautioned that Wednesday’s disaster may have followed a different mechanism.

Kang Shichang, director of the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Chengdu, told domestic media that if an upstream ice-rock avalanche were detected quickly enough, downstream communities could theoretically receive about 20 minutes of warning.

In the remote Himalayan valleys around Gyirong, however, limited monitoring and the speed of such events can leave little time between detection and disaster.

Additional reporting: Jiang Xinyi; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A landslide-dammed lake near Gyirong Port in Gyirong County, Xizang, Aug. 27, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018944/Eye of the Storm: Viral Podcaster Breaks Silence Over Plagiarism Scandal
World.title: Eye of the Storm: Viral Podcaster Breaks Silence Over Plagiarism Scandal
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018944/Eye of the Storm: Viral Podcaster Breaks Silence Over Plagiarism Scandal
World.content:
“Every time fishermen head out to sea, they have to face the uncertainty of the ocean. When a storm hits — you can only head back to port.”

Zhuge Yiyang, an essayist and podcaster better known online as Zhong Shu, stares lost in thought from the pier at Jiaoshan Fishing Port Town, part of Wenling City in the eastern Zhejiang province.

Facing her own storm, she’s returned home.

In early August, the 29-year-old rode a wave of global fame after a viral interview with British-American filmmaker Christopher Nolan about his latest blockbuster, “The Odyssey.” Yet things quickly came crashing down when she was accused of plagiarism, sparking widespread criticism.

In the wake of the controversy, almost all of Zhuge’s public appearances in China were canceled. Yet on Aug. 18, she agreed to meet with reporters from Jiefang Daily in her hometown, taking in the alleyways, docks, and fish markets she frequented as a child.

In her own words

Zhuge has released three episodes of her hit podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer” since the plagiarism accusations emerged, discussing Shakespeare and Plutarch. The show has more than 970,000 subscribers on the Chinese podcast platform Xiaoyuzhou.

While she acknowledges that she draws on media reports and international podcasts, she firmly denies copying any content.

“When I talk about the Canadian election, for example, I’ll read reports from the American and Canadian media, and compile that information into an episode. I’m not a journalist,” says Zhuge, who is currently studying toward a Ph.D. in political philosophy at Boston College in the United States. “A lot of my information I get from listening to overseas podcasts.”

Yet the claims against her have drawn intense public scrutiny. On Aug. 19, business news outlet Caixin removed from its website a recent column Zhuge wrote on universities dealing with student use of artificial intelligence. This came after several online users remarked on the column’s similarity to a piece published in The Atlantic magazine in May. (Editor’s note: Sixth Tone can verify that the first two paragraphs published on Caixin closely match The Atlantic’s first two, as well as parts of its third.)

Until now, Zhuge has refused to respond publicly to the plagiarism accusations, preferring instead not to get involved in the “maelstrom of online harassment.”

“I don’t know how to respond. … There’s no point in trying to clarify things at a moment like this,” she says. “People have claimed that I stay up every night deleting comments. I haven’t deleted a single comment. I do want to find out who is really behind all this, who is pulling the strings, but there’s simply nothing I can do.”

For her most recent podcasts, Zhuge says she wrote the script on a plane, without referring to any materials. But when the episodes were released, people began claiming that specific passages had been plagiarized.

“Some people have set up a website that lays out what they claim are examples of ‘article spinning,’ word by word. I’ve looked at it. The English and Chinese don’t match; not a single example is a word-for-word translation,” she says. “There are some passages from sources that I haven’t even read, and they don’t correspond to the material they are being compared with.”

(Sixth Tone has listened to several episodes highlighted on the website and noted multiple instances where Zhuge’s scripts closely match content from overseas podcasts. In not all instances does she credit her source.)

“Once this started circulating online, my comment section began getting hundreds of comments every hour, many of them mentioning this website,” Zhuge adds. “This is the storm I’m going through.”

So is that why most of her upcoming public appearances have been canceled?

“That has nothing to do with any of the conjecture,” she insists. “I canceled (the events) a long time ago, but the organizers only announced it recently. These events had already been called off before this wave of controversy.

“Some of my elderly relatives aren’t in good health, and with the controversy surrounding me online, I’ve also been feeling emotionally drained. So I wanted to come back and spend more time with them.”

Humble beginnings

Zhuge is no stranger to criticism. In the past, she’s been branded arrogant and condescending, particularly for repeatedly calling Wenling “uncultured” on her podcast.

However, she insists the term isn’t derogatory, but rather an objective fact. With a strong tradition in commerce, the people of Wenling are more interested in pursuing wealth than reading or academic pursuits, she says. As a result, being “uncultured” is inevitable.

“When I was growing up, there was only one Xinhua Bookstore (a state-owned chain), and almost everything it sold was study materials,” Zhuge recalls.

She says speaking bluntly is also common among Wenling people. Her grandmother, for example, alternates between telling her she is “as fat as a pig” and “as skinny as a refugee.” She believes this way of speaking has influenced her own manner of expression, making her come across at times as blunt or even offensive.

“People in big cities wouldn’t talk like this, but no one here thinks there’s anything wrong with it — it’s simply the truth.”

After finishing elementary school, Zhuge left Wenling for a boarding school in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang. She later completed high school and university in the U.S., when she eventually began her career as a translator, writer, and podcaster.

She often refers to herself as a “small-town girl,” yet critics argue that Zhuge uses her background as a “shield” to justify her arrogance, saying that her “manufactured persona” hardly fits with someone who attended the elite Groton School in Massachusetts, U.S.

“I don’t think coming from a small city is something to be ashamed of,” Zhuge says, “nor do I think it means you’ve overcome some kind of hardship or that you have to prove something to people from big cities.”

However, her origins did have an impact when she arrived at Groton at age 15. The few Chinese students at the school were from first-tier cities like Beijing and Shanghai. Through them, Zhuge says she was exposed to an “elite discourse” she had never encountered before.

“I’ve never deliberately constructed any persona, but I know that there’s been a change — not intentional; my circumstances were simply different back then,” she says.

Zhuge was living in the U.S. when she first rose to prominence on Zhihu, China’s Quora-like platform, writing on political theory. Later, she began posting on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, about the meals she cooked for her husband and the books they were reading, as well as podcasting about her academic research.

“Then I went through a divorce, racked up a large amount of legal fees, and spent a period living a fairly miserable life,” she says. “At this point, the narrative online changed, and I became this ‘strong, independent woman.’ But I still cook, I still enjoy cleaning, I still post about sports. I’m still very happy — the only difference is that I no longer have a husband.”

But after her interview with Nolan went viral, Zhuge says she no longer felt as comfortable posting about her daily life, as it could be easily misinterpreted.

“For example, my father has a softshell turtle, and we often visit the nearby stream to catch fish and shrimp to feed it. I’d posted about that before, only now people were saying I was trying to construct a persona,” she says. “There seems to be a stereotype about intellectuals — people think it’s OK for me to hold events in big cities, but I shouldn’t go back to my hometown. But that’s my life.”

What lies ahead

Standing by the Jiaoshan pier, Zhuge begins reminiscing about her childhood. She would often visit the harbor with her parents on weekends, sometimes sailing out on a small fishing boat.

Today, the dock is dominated by larger, more advanced vessels. Yet the fishermen must still brave the same rough sea, never knowing whether they will return with a lucrative haul or be forced back to shore by high winds.

For Zhuge, this is the fundamental element of coastal life: You never know what will come — you can only eat what there is to eat.

“That’s what life by the sea is like. When the winds and waves come, you can’t go out to sea, and you never know when a storm will hit,” she says. “When I was going through my divorce, that’s how I comforted myself: this is just the stormy sea of life.”

The legal proceedings in 2024 consumed a great deal of time, money, and energy, affecting her Ph.D. studies. It was around this time that she began podcasting more frequently.

“I wanted to speak out on a public platform, and a podcast is a place where you can talk for 40 minutes and still be well listened to,” Zhuge says, adding that she has no interest in fame or wealth — she simply eats what there is to eat. “If I wanted to make money, I definitely wouldn’t be podcasting.”

However, the popularity of “Monologues of a Committed Observer” has helped her foster connections with Chinese media outlets and publishers, eventually leading to her being asked to translate works by the philosophers Hannah Arendt, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and Plutarch. The income has alleviated some of the financial burden from her divorce.

In the face of the online storm, she is now considering whether to halt the podcast entirely. “I’m seriously considering giving it up,” Zhuge says. “Maybe tomorrow I’ll decide I’m done, and quit. I don’t have a team, so I don’t have to force myself to keep going. That’s my advantage here.”

Reported by Yu Liang, Zhu Lingjun, and Zhou Liya.

A version of this article originally appeared in Jiefang Daily. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from Zhou Liya and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018948/Who Let the Dogs In? Chinese Universities Open Dorms to Pets
World.title: Who Let the Dogs In? Chinese Universities Open Dorms to Pets
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018948/Who Let the Dogs In? Chinese Universities Open Dorms to Pets
World.content:
A growing number of Chinese universities are allowing student pets both on campus and in university dormitories, drawing online support and sparking sharp debate over the safety, equity, and cost of campus pet ownership.

This past weekend, both Shanghai Lida University and Kunming City University in the southwestern Yunnan province announced on their official WeChat accounts that they would now allow student pets on campus. At least five other universities across China — mostly private institutions with pet-related programs — have also rolled out similar policies since Monday.

Previously, Chinese universities did not allow pets in dorms or on campus — not even to visit. With the recent policy shifts, that is now changing.

The new policies come amid China’s booming pet industry and the advancement of related professional training and services. According to the 2026 China Pet Industry White Paper, the consumer market for dogs and cats in urban areas reached 312.6 billion yuan ($43.2 billion) in 2025, up roughly 4% from the previous year. The market is expected to surpass 400 billion yuan by 2028.

On Saturday, Kunming City University announced that students can now bring dogs, cats, rabbits, hamsters, and legally permitted exotic pets to campus. Banned dog breeds — such as pit bulls and Rottweilers — and “pets that pose health risks” are not allowed, however.

The university plans to roll out pet-friendly dormitories, a pet daycare center, and partner with professional institutions to establish an on-campus pet health station. Faculty and students from the university’s School of Pet Technology will also regularly offer free pet health checkups and consultation services, the university said.

Campus-wide amenities will include waste bags, water stations, and fenced play areas, with most outdoor spaces except cafeterias open to pets. Per-semester pet registration and vaccine checks will also be implemented.

A dedicated fund will support stray animal rescue and student volunteer work, while “pet companionship therapy” will be available to help students relieve stress.

Online, users hotly contested the new policies, with supporters arguing that pets provide important emotional comfort for students far away from home, helping to alleviate loneliness and stress in academic and daily life. Many voiced approval of the universities’ detailed regulations, such as providing centralized pet care facilities and pet-friendly dormitories separate from other student housing.

Others questioned whether the new policies would infringe on other students’ rights, pointing to issues such as allergies, noise, and safety.

A university student in Shanghai who had previously secretly kept a cat in her dormitory told Sixth Tone that the new rules — which require pets to be housed in dedicated pet-boarding facilities and ban them from dorms — are “no different from not being allowed to keep a cat at all.”

Her roommate, surnamed Chen, instead called the new policy a “very loving move” that shows the school is “warm and humane.”

“While it doesn’t meet most people’s needs, I think it’s a good first step that will spark discussion and encourage other schools to follow suit and make better policies in the future,” she told Sixth Tone.

Wu Qi, founder of Shanghai-based animal therapy nonprofit Paw for Heal, said the core challenge of keeping pets on campus is balancing companionship needs with public safety and collective rights.

“(Universities need to) respect (pet owners’) companionship needs while protecting students with allergies or a fear of animals,” he told Sixth Tone.

Wu advised restricting pets on campus to certain zones and recommended implementing a registration system so that students bear responsibility in the event of pet-related disputes. He also recommended that universities have clear protocols for removing animals when necessary.

He noted, however, that owning a pet as a university student has its own educational value, teaching responsibility and pet knowledge, while also cultivating empathy.



Additional reporting: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

World.title: Nepal rescuers reach remote areas, electricity restored nearly a week after devastating floods
World.content:
DISASTER. Members of the Nepal Army head back after collecting the bodies that were washed away by flash floods and a mudslide, in Narayani River, Chitwan, Nepal, August 31, 2026.

About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts, while Prime Minister Balendra Shah says over 11,000 people have been rescued across the affected region

KATHMANDU, Nepal – Nepali rescuers built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue close to 300 trapped workers, nearly a week after devastating floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.

About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts, while Prime Minister Balendra Shah said over 11,000 people have been rescued across the affected region and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.

At least 939 people have been killed in the destruction, Shah said in a late-night social media post.

“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” he said.

“The government understands the immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to support them through this suffering and help them return to normal life through rehabilitation.”

Rescue teams had managed to restore road networks to Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected districts, facilitating rescue operations and distribution of relief material, Shah said.

A glacier collapse triggered a deluge of ice, rock and mud which swept through the impoverished nation’s border region with China, posing a massive challenge for Nepal’s six-month-old government.

Police official Bipin Regmi said a search team recovered 24 bodies from a house in Betrabati village in Nuwakot district.

“We are reaching new areas and recovering bodies,” Regmi told Reuters.

Aid worth more than $42 million had poured into the country after the disaster, Shah said, and the government expected the contributions to increase.

Neighbors India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, were helping with rescue efforts, including building bailey bridges to reach remote affected areas.

Rescue efforts focus on hydropower stations

Shah said 279 workers had been rescued from hydropower projects so far where authorities estimated that close to 1,000 people were trapped.

Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night as workers watched. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.

There has been a boom in hydropower projects in Nepal since the turn of the century as the mountainous country sought to take advantage of its Himalayan water resources to address chronic domestic power shortages and exploit prospects for selling electricity to southern neighbour India.

Hydropower projects in Nepal’s mountains need tunnels to carry water through the steep terrain, allowing developers to exploit the sharp elevation drop between Himalayan rivers and powerhouses to generate electricity.

China blames global warning

Shah said the catastrophic event signaled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces.

“The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” Shah said in his post.

Last week’s flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming,” China’s state broadcaster said on Monday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sony, Warner Music sue Anthropic over songs used in AI training
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. The Anthropic logo, a keyboard, and a robotic hand are shown in this illustration created on June 5, 2026.

Sony and Warner say Anthropic pirated hundreds of song lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson, and hundreds of other artists to train Claude to respond to human prompts

The music publishing branches of Sony Music and Warner Music have sued Anthropic in California federal court for allegedly misusing their copyrighted song compositions to train its Claude AI models.

Sony and Warner said in the complaint, filed on Friday, August 28, that Anthropic pirated hundreds of song lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson, and hundreds of other artists to train Claude to respond to human prompts.

The lawsuit is the latest in a wave of cases brought against tech companies by copyright owners including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets over the use of their work to train AI systems. Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and earlier this year over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training, in lawsuits that are still ongoing.

Anthropic became the first AI company to settle one of the disputes last year, when it paid $1.5 billion to resolve a class action from a group of authors.

“Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” Sony and Warner said in their complaint. “And $1.5 billion is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering 2-trillion-dollar valuation.”

“This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts,” an Anthropic spokesperson said on Monday. The spokesperson also said that the company will defend itself “robustly” and that AI training makes fair use of copyrighted material, citing the judge in the authors’ case against it.

Spokespeople and an attorney for Sony Music and Warner Music did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the case on Monday.

The complaint alleges Anthropic illegally obtained the publishers’ lyrics and sheet music through torrent downloads to train Claude, and that Claude can reproduce copyrighted lyrics “verbatim” when prompted.

Sony and Warner also said Anthropic used their lyrics to teach Claude to “generate vast quantities of purportedly ‘new’ AI-generated song lyrics, which compete with Music Publishers’ legitimate copyrighted works as harmful market substitutes.”

The labels are seeking damages of up to $150,000 for each infringed copyright and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] What’s left for the Philippines’ Left?
World.content:
The revolution has become a war of attrition against history itself

For more than half a century, the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) has been promising a revolution. Today, I find myself asking: what exactly is left to revolutionize when history has already rendered judgment on the ideology behind it?

At its height, the CPP’s armed wing, the New People’s Army (NPA), reportedly commanded more than 25,000 armed fighters across the archipelago. It was an insurgency that the Philippine state could not dismiss, but that’s no longer the organization confronting us today.

Government figures say all 89 guerrilla fronts that existed at the beginning of the Marcos administration have been dismantled. By August 2025, authorities estimated that only about 785 armed NPA members remained, with roughly 780 firearms operating in small, dispersed units.

I hesitate to call what remains an army. An army seeks to defeat another army, capture territory, and ultimately seize political power. What we see today are armed remnants capable of ambush, extortion, and intimidation, but apparently incapable of mounting anything resembling the revolution promised by the CPP in 1968.

The revolution has become a war of attrition against history itself.

We note its political decline, too. Makabayan mounted an ambitious Senate campaign in 2025. Not one candidate won, while the broader movement’s party-list representation contracted.

Various shades

This does not mean every Filipino identified with the Left has become irrelevant. Social democrats, labor activists, environmentalists, Akbayan, and the CPP-aligned national-democratic movement are not interchangeable.

Akbayan, after all, topped the 2025 party list elections. My argument concerns the revolutionary Maoist Left and the worldview that continues to orbit around it.

Nowhere is its intellectual predicament more obvious to me than in its opposition to EDCA (Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement) and, more recently, Pax Silica.

EDCA is a 2014 military pact between the Philippines and the US, which allows US forces rotational access to designated military bases in the country, pre-positioning of equipment, and infrastructure construction, even as the Philippine maintains complete ownership and sovereignty over all sites.

Pax Silica, meanwhile, is a US-led global alliance launched in December 2025 to protect global supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, and critical minerals among allied nations, primarily to counter China’s tech dominance.

According to Left-leaning groups, these foreign partnerships enhance geopolitical risks for the Philippines. EDCA is transforming our country into an American military outpost and giving Americans access makes us a target. Washington is using Manila to contain China. Philippine sovereignty is supposedly being surrendered to another imperial power and local development is being sacrificed for foreign security interests.

These allegations deserve a debate. No military agreement should escape scrutiny. Concerns for the environment, indigenous rights, and Philippine sovereignty surrounding Pax Silica should not be simply shrugged off.

Parroting Beijing?

But listen carefully to the larger narrative. The perspective begins sounding remarkably similar to Beijing’s.

China has repeatedly argued that expanded EDCA access undermines regional stability and drags the Philippines into America’s confrontation with China. Parts of the Philippine national-democratic Left make essentially the same strategic argument.

I’m not alleging collusion. But there is a more interesting question about the resistance to EDCA that needs to be answered. Why are supposedly opposing ideological camps repeatedly arriving at positions producing the same strategic outcome: weakening Philippine-American security cooperation precisely when China is pressing its expansive claims in the West Philippine Sea?

What about the opposition to Pax Silica?

The Philippines joined the US-led initiative in April. New Clark City is being positioned as a hub for AI, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, and secure technology supply chains. The proposed development covers roughly 1,620 hectares, with BCDA projecting eventual investments of $40 billion to $70 billion and more than 130,000 jobs.

Those are projections, not guarantees, and the government should be required to prove them.

But Pax Silica’s strategic purpose is unmistakable. The United States and its partners want technology and critical-mineral supply chains less dependent on China. The Philippines wants to climb those same supply chains rather than remain primarily an exporter of labor and low-value commodities.

And once again, elements of the Philippine Left are marching against it.

The ideological ancestors of today’s Philippine Maoists once looked toward Mao Zedong’s China as proof that a communist revolution could transform an impoverished Asian society. Yet modern China became an economic superpower only after dismantling much of Mao’s economic system.

Beginning in 1978, Deng Xiaoping’s China opened itself to foreign investment, introduced market incentives, and loosened collectivized agriculture, eventually becoming one of capitalism’s greatest manufacturing platforms. China’s economy subsequently grew around 9% annually for decades, while close to 800 million people escaped extreme poverty.

China did not accomplish that by becoming more Maoist. It achieved economic success by becoming less so.

Vietnam offers another uncomfortable exhibit. Its Doi Moi reforms that began in 1986 moved the country toward markets, private enterprise, foreign investment, and international trade. Vietnam remained communist politically, while retreating from orthodox communist economics. The Soviet Union, too, disappeared in 1991.

Communism’s greatest historical humiliation was not simply that its enemies defeated it. Its surviving practitioners had to abandon much of its economics to survive.

So that while Filipino Maoists continue fighting American imperialism as though history stopped during the Vietnam War, communist Vietnam, for example, welcomes American investment.

The revolutionaries have somehow become more doctrinaire than the revolution that inspired them.

Meanwhile, American bases in Subic and Clark disappeared more than three decades ago. Today, Chinese vessels confront Filipino vessels in waters over which the Philippines possesses sovereign rights.

Yet much of the revolutionary script remains unchanged: America is the imperialist; capitalism is exploitation; foreign investment creates dependency; and security cooperation with Washington constitutes surrender.

An ideology that cannot adjust to a changing reality eventually stops being a logical tool for truth. It becomes dogma.

The NPA may still possess guns. Its remnants can still kill and intimidate. The government must therefore continue treating them as a security threat until armed resistance ends.

But I no longer see an advancing tide of the revolution, only its vestiges.

Perhaps the supreme contradiction of the Philippine communist movement is that, after more than half a century of armed struggle and generations sacrificed for a revolution, its greatest adversary turned out to be neither the Armed Forces, the United States, nor capitalism.

It is history.

Time moved on. The revolution did not.

World.title: ChatGPT, Reddit, Roblox to adhere to EU’s ‘very large platform’ rules
World.content:
ROBLOX. A boy poses for a photo while holding a game pad in front of a screen displaying the logo of the US children's gaming platform Roblox, in this illustration taken December 8, 2025.

ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox have four months to comply with additional obligations following their designation

BRUSSELS, Belgium – The European Commission on Monday said ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox will need to adhere to the EU regulations for very large online platforms and search engines.

The services have declared that they reach at least 45 million monthly users in the EU.

This qualifies them for the “very large” designation under the bloc’s Digital Services Act, the Commission said.

ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox have four months to comply with additional obligations following their designation.

This includes assessing and mitigating risks of illegal content being disseminated through their platforms. They also need to mitigate the negative effects on minors, and on the physical and mental wellbeing of users.

Very large platforms and search engines also need to limit risks for fundamental rights, electoral processes and public security.

The Commission can supervise compliance with the DSA and will get investigative powers to assess functionalities behind the services.

AI-system ChatGPT qualifies as an online search engine under the DSA.

Gaming platform Roblox and discussion-based platform Reddit qualify as online platforms, as they enable users to disseminate third-party content to the public. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos wants P4.58-B confidential funds for 2027 — almost half of proposed OP budget
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address at the House of Representatives on July 27, 2026.

Observing the long-held tradition of parliamentary courtesy, the House appropriations committee approves the proposed budget of the Office of the President

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang is seeking over P10.158 billion for 2027 — an amount that’s just over a third of its current 2026 budget and over two-thirds of its 2025 budget.

The dramatic drop between 2026 and 2027 is because spending for the Philippines’ chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) was lodged under the Office of the President (OP), and is broken down based on the various agencies involved in the preparations related to hosting different meetings and the summits under the regional grouping. The 2025 budget had also included allocations for ASEAN chairmanship preparations.

“We are asking for less while remaining fully prepared to do more,” Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, a former legislator himself, said during the OP’s budget briefing before the House committee on appropriations on Tuesday, September 1.

The OP budget, as usual, was not subjected to scrutiny at the committee level because of the long-standing tradition of extending “institutional and interbranch courtesy” to the OP as a co-equal branch. Scrutiny of the OP’s budget, if any, usually only begins at the plenary level.

House Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio pointed out that over half of the OP’s budget, some P4.58 billion, is allocated for confidential expenses. Tinio, and later impeachment spokesperson House Assistant Minority Leader and Representative Renee Co, opposed the observance of parliamentary courtesy, citing public interest in the use of public, including confidential, funds.

Tinio noted that the OP’s confidential funds use should be scrutinized the same way that Vice President Sara Duterte’s past confidential funds use is being scrutinized, both in the public and before the impeachment court.

Within less than 16 minutes after Recto’s briefing, legislators from both the minority and majority voted to waive questions on the OP budget at the committee level, citing parliamentary courtesy. This was after a motion was made to terminate the hearing, with only five panel members voting in the negative.

At 10:29 am, the committee hearing for the OP’s budget officially ended, which means less than an hour had passed between the start of Recto’s briefing and the OP budget’s approval.

Priorities

But what exactly are Marcos’ priorities for 2027 under his own office?

Based on the National Expenditure Program for 2027, some P4.58 billion is allocated for confidential expenses (P2.25 billion), extraordinary and miscellaneous expenses (P20.77 million), and intelligence expenses (P2.31 billion).

Confidential and intelligence funds (CIF) have been under the spotlight of late, especially in the context of erstwhile Marcos ally Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial.

The proposed OP CIF for 2027 is slightly lower — by a few million pesos — than in 2026.

The OP also wants over P1 billion for local/foreign missions and state visits, the same amount Marcos had asked in recent years. That budget covers both Marcos and his delegations’ trips overseas for official and working visits, and for hosting state visits in the country.

After the vote to terminate the hearing, legislators manifested either their opposition to the waiving of questions or unequivocal support for Marcos and the OP. Panel senior Vice chairperson Bataan 2nd District Representative Albert Garcia assured lawmakers as well as civil society organizations that their queries and concerns would be relayed to the OP by the time the plenary deliberates on its proposed budget. – Rappler.com

World.title: Archaeological dig challenges story of 1903 battle in Lanao del Sur
World.content:
University of the Philippines-School of Archaeology's Leee Anthony Neri presents the archological report on Kota Kalawi in Lanao del Sur.

The findings prompt a reevaluation of the accepted narrative surrounding the Battle of Kota Kalawi, raising questions about the historical accuracy of the events attributed to the US military campaign in Mindanao

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – For decades, the Battle of Kota Kalawi has stood in the historical record as a bloody encounter between American forces and Meranaw defenders along the shores of Lake Lanao. Now, an archaeological excavation is challenging that account, raising questions about one of the most consequential episodes attributed to the US military campaign in Mindanao.

At the presentation and turnover of the Kota Kalawi Archaeological and Historical Project on August 24 at the Lanao del Sur Provincial Capitol, project team leader Leee Anthony Neri, dean of the University of the Philippines’ School of Archaeology (UPSA), delivered this assessment: the battle was a “historical hoax” written by Americans in the 20th century.

Neri said the archaeological dig, commissioned by the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage (BCPCH) and conducted by a team from UPSA from July 29 to August 19, 2024, showed no evidence that the purported Battle of Kalawi ever took place.

This was the first formal archaeological excavation in Lanao del Sur. The project was a collaboration among the UP School of Archaeology (UPSA), Mindanao State University-main campus and Mindanao State University-Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT), organized by the BCPCH.

ILLUSTRATE. A reconstruction of Kota Kalawi in Lanao del Sur. courtesy of Leee Anthony Neri

“Of the six trenches we dug on the Kota Kalawi site, we found only a single bullet and no evidence of bullet penetration on the North Wall from the purported machine gun fire or mortar fire,” Neri noted. “There’s also simply no space within the kota (earthen/stone forts) to accommodate a hundred defenders.”

“Archeologically, this does not support the historical narrative,” Neri stressed.

Iligan historian Ricardo Jorge Caluen said the excavation was the first formal archaeological re-examination of the accepted narrative surrounding the Battle of Kota Kalawi.

“Neri’s assertion is therefore a bold challenge to the traditionally-accepted events of the battle that could alter its historiography,” Caluen said. “It is difficult to challenge findings of archaeology that are based solely on material evidence.”

American account

The American account dated June 30, 1903 was written by American Brigadier General Samuel S. Sumner, commander of the Department of Mindanao, and included as Appendix II in the Annual Report of Major General George W. Davis, United States Army commanding Division of the Philippines from October 1, 1902 to July 26, 1903.

According to Sumner’s report, the Battle of Kota Kalawi – often referenced alongside the Battle of Bacolod Grande – was a violent clash that took place at Bacolod Grande from April 6 to 8, 1903, and at Kalawi on April 9, along the shores of Lake Lanao. Kalawi is also spelled Calahui in the American account.

At the time of the battle, then-captain John J. Pershing, who later commanded the American Expeditionary Forces (AEF) on the Western Front during World War I, was newly promoted as commander of Camp Vicars, overseeing the early American pacification campaigns in the Meranaw and Iranun areas surrounding Lake Lanao.

The defensive fortifications, or kota, served as vital strongholds during local resistance against foreign invaders around Lake Lanao. Built strategically on plateaus and along the shores of the lake to control movement and trade, they were constructed with heavy timber, stone, earth and bamboo, and often bristled with sharp bamboo spike pits (surung) and high walls. Defenders used indigenous blades such as the kris and kampilan, along with swivel cannons called lantakas.

Sumner described Kota o Panondiongan as “the strongest fort in Mindanao.” Based on his account, the Americans’ superior firepower, including machine guns, mountain artillery and mortars, gave US forces a decisive advantage over traditional Meranaw defenses.

The American field expedition was led on the ground by Pershing, commanding roughly 700 soldiers composed of four companies from the 27th Infantry, three troops of the 15th Cavalry, and two mountain artillery batteries.

Sumner recounted that American forces surrounded the earthen walls of Kota o Panondiongan, with initial bombardments from Vickers-Maxim mountain guns countered by traditional Meranaw lantakas (brass cannons). He wrote that the US tightened the siege using 3.6-inch mortars, dropping shells directly into the fort. Despite a water-filled moat and heavy fire from hidden loopholes, Meranaw defenders repeatedly drove back infantry advances and rejected all offers of surrender.

Relentless artillery fire, based on the account, breached the front wall, allowing US forces to overrun Kota o Panondiongan. Supposedly, a quick body count taken in the still-burning fort showed 30 Moro warriors dead on the top floor, with one American killed and 14 wounded.

The following day, April 9, 1903, the Americans supposedly bombarded Kota Kalawi with mortars and Maxim-Vickers machine guns. Sumner claimed the Meranaw defenders abandoned their positions after suffering 23 casualties.

TEAM. Members of the Kota Kalawi archeological project team in Lanao del Sur. courtesy of Leee Anthony Neri

For over a century, the American account has shaped the history of Kota Kalawi. But the archaeological findings merely showed a single bullet, and no physical evidence of the intense exchange of gunfire and artillery described in Sumner’s report.

The findings have raised questions about what really happened at Kota Kalawi in 1903 and prompted a closer examination of the account that for generations was seen as established history. – Rappler.com
