World.title: SCO economic agenda aligns with Uzbekistan's growth priorities
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 1. Uzbekistan is seeking to leverage its position within the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) to strengthen trade and investment ties, enhance transport connectivity, and expand cooperation in emerging areas such as digital technologies and artificial intelligence. With SCO member states already accounting for a substantial share of Uzbekistan’s investment and international freight flows, the organization has assumed increasing importance in the country’s efforts to deepen regional economic integration and diversify access to foreign markets.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev arrived in Bishkek to participate in the SCO Council of Heads of State meeting and the SCO Plus format on August 31–September 1. The summit is expected to adopt the Bishkek Declaration marking the SCO’s 25th anniversary, alongside documents addressing economic cooperation, transport, artificial intelligence, environmental protection, and other areas.

For Tashkent, the timing is particularly relevant as several of its priorities within the organization are moving toward more concrete forms of cooperation. Uzbekistan has advanced initiatives related to transport corridors, investment mechanisms, industrial cooperation, critical minerals, energy, and digitalization, reflecting its efforts to utilize the SCO as a platform for addressing practical constraints on economic expansion. The key question for Uzbekistan, therefore, is how effectively the organization can facilitate connectivity, capital flows, and technological cooperation that directly support the country’s development objectives.

Uzbekistan is becoming increasingly integrated with SCO economies

The scale of Uzbekistan's economic ties with SCO members provides a strong economic rationale for deeper cooperation within the organization. According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, investment from SCO countries reached $17.5 billion in 2025, with China accounting for about $13 billion, Russia $2.6 billion, Kazakhstan $870 million, Iran $265 million, India $247 million, Kyrgyzstan $197 million and Tajikistan $196 million. China therefore represented roughly 74% of investment from SCO members, while Russia accounted for almost 15%, highlighting both the depth of Uzbekistan's economic links with the two largest SCO economies and the concentration of capital flows within the group. This concentration creates an incentive for Tashkent to broaden the investment base by making it easier for companies and financial institutions from other SCO countries to participate in Uzbek projects.

Uzbekistan has increasingly promoted mechanisms aimed at achieving this, including an SCO investment forum, an electronic business portal and networks of venture companies and funds. The SCO Investment and Business Forum held in Bishkek on June 24-25 brought these priorities together, with discussions covering investment, trade, industrial and technological cooperation, artificial intelligence, e-commerce and industrialization. The emerging approach is therefore centered on creating channels through which existing economic ties can generate a wider range of investment and business connections, rather than relying predominantly on bilateral capital flows from the largest SCO economies.

Transport remains the most important economic priority

For Uzbekistan, transport connectivity has a particularly strategic importance because the country is landlocked and depends on transit through neighboring states to access major external markets. The importance of SCO countries to Uzbekistan's logistics network is already substantial. According to Uzbekistan's Center for Transport and Logistics Development Studies, international freight transportation between Uzbekistan and SCO member states increased by 40%, or 9 million tons, over five years, reaching 33.5 million tons in 2025.

SCO countries account for around 80% of Uzbekistan's international freight transportation, with the largest volumes involving Russia, Kazakhstan, China and Kyrgyzstan. Uzbekistan's Ministry of Transport estimates that freight transportation with SCO members could reach 47 million tons by 2030. This implies an additional increase of about 13.5 million tons, or 40%, from the 2025 level by the end of the decade.

The figures demonstrate why transport cooperation has become one of the central elements of Uzbekistan's SCO agenda. One of the most important projects is the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which could strengthen Uzbekistan's connection with China and create an additional east-west route through Central Asia. At the same time, Tashkent has promoted transport links southward through Afghanistan toward Pakistan and the ports of the Indian Ocean. The development of these east-west and north-south corridors could expand Uzbekistan's access to external markets, reduce transport costs and strengthen the country's position as a regional logistics hub.

For Tashkent, however, the benefits of greater connectivity extend beyond transit revenues. More efficient transport links can improve the competitiveness of Uzbek exports and make the country more attractive to manufacturers seeking access to multiple markets. The SCO could support this process by improving coordination between national transport systems, including through harmonized customs procedures, digital documentation, border-crossing processes and transportation standards. Such coordination could help reduce bottlenecks along cross-border routes and increase the economic value of infrastructure projects already being developed across the region.

Tashkent wants to move from trade toward industrial cooperation

Uzbekistan's economic objectives within the SCO increasingly extend beyond increasing the volume of trade. Tashkent has been advocating the development of reliable production and logistics chains, mutual investment and deeper industrial cooperation. At the 2025 SCO summit in Tianjin, Mirziyoyev proposed several mechanisms, including a Regional SCO Center for Critical Materials, an SCO Energy Consortium, a network of venture companies and funds, and an electronic portal for business contacts and investment promotion.

The critical-materials initiative is particularly relevant to Uzbekistan's industrial strategy. The proposed center would facilitate cooperation in modern technologies for the extraction and deep processing of mineral resources. For Uzbekistan, greater participation in regional processing chains could help shift the country's role from a supplier of raw materials toward a producer of higher-value products. This distinction is important for the country's long-term growth. Investment in mining alone can increase export revenues, but investment in processing, metallurgy, chemicals, and related manufacturing can generate wider industrial effects, including technology transfer, skilled employment, and the development of domestic suppliers.

Cooperation with SCO members could therefore support Uzbekistan's efforts to integrate its mineral resources into broader regional value chains. The same principle applies to industrial localization. Uzbekistan can use its expanding domestic market, relatively large labor force and improving industrial base to attract production projects aimed at serving not only the Uzbek market but also neighboring Central Asian and other SCO markets.

Finance could provide another layer of support

The proposed SCO Development Bank is another initiative with potential relevance for Uzbekistan. SCO Deputy Secretary-General Sohail Khan said in May that consultations on establishing the bank had begun, describing it as a potential institution for financing joint projects and strengthening the organization's financial architecture. The issue was also discussed at the July meeting of SCO foreign ministers in Cholpon-Ata, where member states noted progress in consultations on the proposed institution, particularly in connection with investment, infrastructure and transport-logistics projects.

For Uzbekistan, an SCO financial institution could provide an additional source of long-term financing for infrastructure and industrial projects involving several member states. The potential value is particularly significant given the scale of infrastructure investment required to expand transport networks, electricity generation, industrial capacity and digital infrastructure. At the same time, the Development Bank would complement rather than replace existing financial institutions.

Uzbekistan already works with the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Islamic Development Bank and other international institutions. The country's 2025 presidential address specifically highlighted continued cooperation with these institutions on infrastructure modernization, sustainable energy and transport. The proposed SCO mechanism could therefore be most useful for projects with a clear regional component, particularly those requiring coordination and financing across multiple SCO countries.

The same applies to discussions on increasing the use of national currencies in mutual settlements. Wider use of local currencies could eventually reduce transaction costs and dependence on third-country currencies, although the effectiveness of such arrangements will depend on the development of financial markets, currency convertibility and settlement infrastructure.

Energy cooperation could support Uzbekistan's growing electricity needs

Energy represents another area where SCO cooperation could have a direct economic relevance for Uzbekistan. The country is facing rising electricity demand while simultaneously expanding generation capacity, renewable energy and transmission infrastructure. Against this backdrop, discussions within the SCO on energy security, efficiency, infrastructure protection, renewables and the proposed SCO Energy Consortium are aligned with Uzbekistan's own investment priorities. A regional mechanism could facilitate cross-border investment, technology transfers and greater coordination in electricity generation and transmission, particularly as Central Asian countries seek to develop complementary energy resources.

The economic implications extend beyond energy security. For Uzbekistan, a more coordinated regional energy system could support industrial expansion by improving the availability and reliability of electricity for manufacturing, data centers and other energy-intensive activities. This could become increasingly important as the country seeks to attract investment into higher-value industries and digital infrastructure. In this context, energy cooperation within the SCO could serve not only as a mechanism for coordinating energy projects, but also as part of the infrastructure base supporting Uzbekistan's broader industrial and technological development.

Digital cooperation is becoming a new dimension of Uzbekistan-SCO ties

The recent engagement between Uzbekistan and the SCO Business Council indicates that technology is becoming a more substantive component of Tashkent's economic agenda within the organization. At an August 11 meeting, IT Park Uzbekistan and the SCO Business Council discussed investment in Uzbek IT startups, digital infrastructure, data centers and R&D, including projects involving electronic mapping, government platforms, and transport and healthcare information systems. The sides also considered integrated projects combining computing capacity, energy supply and operational infrastructure. For Uzbekistan, such cooperation could help address one of the key requirements of its digitalization strategy: moving from the expansion of basic digital services toward the development and export of technology-intensive products.

Access to SCO markets and investors could give Uzbek technology companies additional opportunities to scale beyond the domestic market, while investment in data centers and R&D could strengthen the infrastructure needed to support AI and other advanced technologies. This direction is consistent with Mirziyoyev's earlier proposal to establish a New SCO Economic Dialogue focused on digitalization, artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology and other emerging sectors. The growing focus on these areas suggests that Uzbekistan is seeking to use the SCO not only to facilitate traditional trade and infrastructure cooperation, but also to connect its technology sector with a broader pool of capital, markets and expertise.

Uzbekistan's SCO strategy complements its multi-vector economic policy

Uzbekistan's expanding role within the SCO is taking place alongside an active effort to diversify its external economic partnerships. Tashkent continues to deepen relations with China and Russia while expanding economic ties with India, the European Union, Türkiye, the Gulf states, South Korea, Japan and other markets. The latest example is India, with the two countries agreeing on August 31 to raise bilateral trade to $5 billion by 2030 and expand cooperation in energy, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, electronics, machinery and agriculture. Bilateral trade reached $598.1 million in the first half of 2026, while Indian investment and loans for fixed-capital projects in Uzbekistan amounted to $225.9 million. The agreements also cover areas such as healthcare, education, tourism and environmental protection, demonstrating that Tashkent's diversification strategy extends well beyond traditional goods trade.

This approach gives the SCO a specific place within Uzbekistan's broader economic architecture. The organization brings together several of the country's major economic partners, including China, Russia, India and Iran, while providing access to additional markets in Central and South Asia. At the same time, Uzbekistan is developing economic and transport links outside the SCO, including connections through the Caspian Sea and the Middle Corridor, as well as routes toward Afghanistan, Pakistan and the Persian Gulf. The SCO can therefore complement Uzbekistan's multi-vector strategy by providing a multilateral framework for coordinating selected cross-border projects, while Tashkent retains the flexibility to pursue bilateral partnerships and alternative trade routes with countries outside the organization.

What Uzbekistan brings to the SCO

The relationship is also important from the perspective of what Uzbekistan contributes to the organization. With its large domestic market, expanding industrial base, growing technology sector and central position within Central Asia, Uzbekistan represents a significant potential market for SCO companies and investors.

Its geographic position also gives it a role in several potential transport corridors connecting China with Central Asia and, further south and west, with the Caspian Sea, South Asia and the Middle East.

Uzbekistan's economic development therefore gives it an interest in strengthening regional connectivity, while its market and industrial potential give other SCO members an incentive to support such initiatives.

This creates a degree of mutual interest around infrastructure and trade that can exist even where member states have different geopolitical priorities.

Bishkek could advance Uzbekistan's economic agenda within the SCO

The Bishkek summit comes at a point when several of the initiatives promoted by Uzbekistan are moving through different stages of discussion. The summit agenda is expected to include documents on the economy, transport, artificial intelligence, environmental protection and other areas.

For Uzbekistan, several developments will be particularly relevant.

The first is the future of the SCO Development Bank and broader financial mechanisms for regional projects.

The second is the development of transport cooperation, including measures to improve customs procedures, digital logistics and the interoperability of transport systems.

The third is the proposed Energy Consortium and cooperation on renewable energy and regional energy infrastructure.

The fourth is industrial cooperation, particularly critical minerals, processing and localization.

The fifth is digitalization, including artificial intelligence, data infrastructure, R&D and technology investment.

The outcome of these initiatives will determine the practical scope of Uzbekistan's economic engagement with the organization in the coming years.

Outlook: Uzbekistan is seeking practical value from the SCO

Uzbekistan's approach to the SCO increasingly reflects the country's broader economic priorities. The objective is to improve connectivity, attract investment, integrate domestic companies into regional and global value chains, expand exports, and gain access to new technologies.

The organization can support these goals through several complementary mechanisms: transport coordination can reduce logistical barriers; financial institutions can provide additional capital; industrial cooperation can facilitate localization and deeper processing; energy cooperation can strengthen infrastructure; and digital initiatives can help Uzbek technology companies reach larger markets.

The scale of existing economic interaction suggests that the potential is significant. SCO member states already provided $17.5 billion in investment to Uzbekistan in 2025, while freight transportation with SCO countries reached 33.5 million tons and accounted for roughly 80% of Uzbekistan's international freight traffic. At the same time, the most important opportunities for Uzbekistan are likely to come from greater coordination of existing economic activity rather than the creation of entirely new economic relationships.

The country already has strong bilateral ties with China, Russia and other SCO members. The added value of the organization can therefore come from connecting these relationships through common transport standards, investment mechanisms, production networks and digital infrastructure. In this context, Uzbekistan is positioning the SCO as an additional layer of its economic strategy — one that can help connect its bilateral partnerships and regional initiatives into a broader framework. For Tashkent, the long-term value of the SCO will ultimately be measured by its contribution to lower transport costs, greater investment, stronger industrial capacity, expanded exports, and access to technology. The current trajectory suggests that Uzbekistan will continue pushing the organization toward precisely these practical economic objectives.

World.title: The number of patients stuck in Qld hospital beds has climbed to 1,400
World.content:
Queensland's health minister has again heaped pressure on the Commonwealth to address rising numbers of patients stuck in hospital beds.

There were more than 1,400 people in the state's hospitals in April waiting to be discharged to an aged care or NDIS placement, around three-quarters of those older patients.

That was up from just over 1,100 a year earlier. It's estimated bed block costs Queensland more than $3 million daily.

Health minister Tim Nicholls said funding for the cohort, labelled 'stranded Australians', rested with the federal government.

Tim Nicholls has raised the issue ahead of a meeting of health ministers later this week. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"Queenslanders deserve a health system that delivers, not one that leaves people stuck in a hospital bed, stranded, stuck and waiting for support.

"We're meeting our responsibilities. It's time for the Commonwealth to meet their responsibilities, and until they do, we'll continue to hold them accountable.

"It is about the dignity of older Australians. It is about ensuring that they receive the respect and the care that they deserve towards the latter end of their lives."

The stoush comes ahead of a meeting of health ministers on Friday, with the issue expected to be at the forefront of discussion.

Around three-quarters of 'stranded' hospital patients are older people. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

A spokesperson for the Commonwealth said it had attempted to provide a stopgap solution to bed block earlier this year.

"During hospital funding negotiations, the states told us older long-stay patients were the biggest issue when it came to the hospital system.

"In response, our government proposed a ringfenced $2 billion for aged care services as part of the agreement, but states and territories rejected that offer, instead choosing to direct that funding into their hospital systems."

Urgent call for funding uplift

Australian Medical Association Queensland president, associate professor Erica Gannon, said bed block had a massive ripple effect across the health system and called on the Commonwealth to do more.

"There is a flow-on effect to those patients who are needing to come in through frontline services in our emergency departments.

"That will impact on ramping, and the care needs of ongoing ED patients."

She added there was a health impact for those people stuck in hospitals.

AMA Queensland president Erica Gannon says long-term hospital exposure can be distressing for patients. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"It is certainly distressing for those patients who are in hospital for a prolonged period of time.

"It can be a noisy environment and distressing for those dementia patients, not to mention their exposure to hospital-acquired infections."

'Dismal' figures

Mr Nicholls claimed Queensland was "ground zero" for stranded Australians.

In one case, he said a patient had been in hospital awaiting discharge for more than 1,000 days, and another 15 people were stranded for more than 700 days.

Of particular concern was a net increase of just 26 residential aged care beds to the system in the year to June 2025 in Queensland.

Just 26 residential aged care beds were added to the system in Queensland last financial year. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

"This is a dismal amount. Only a 0.06 per cent actual increase in the number of beds available in Queensland," Mr Nicholls stated.

Shadow Attorney-General Meaghan Scanlon said while she would encourage the Commonwealth to continue investing in aged care, it should be in partnership with the state government.

"They've delayed hospitals all across the state. They need to take responsibility as well.

"At the moment, they're prioritising the construction of a stadium over hospitals."

World.title: Teenager found guilty of stabbing murder of Melbourne teen Oscar Hamilton
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy has been found guilty of the daytime stabbing murder of Melbourne teenager Oscar Hamilton at a suburban shopping centre.

The teenager's Supreme Court trial heard Oscar was hanging out with his girlfriend and two other friends at Woodgrove Shopping Centre in Melton West in September 2024 when he was stabbed three times by another teenager.

The culprit, who was aged 15 when he carried out the killing, stared straight ahead as the jury delivered its verdict after two hours of deliberation.

The boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had pleaded guilty to manslaughter, but prosecutors rejected the plea and pressed on with a murder trial.

He pleaded not guilty to the murder charge on the basis he did not intend to kill or seriously hurt Oscar.

Oscar Hamilton was spending time with friends at the Woodgrove Shopping Centre when he was fatally stabbed. (ABC News)

Prosecutors argued the motive for the attack was an unproven allegation that Oscar had sexually assaulted the killer's ex-girlfriend, which Oscar had denied.

"This is not the tragic consequence of a fight between two boys," prosecutor Erin Ramsay said.

"This was a targeted attack."

But defence lawyers for the teenager disagreed.

"This was a young person who had clearly lost the ascendancy in terms of the pushing and shoving, who has produced a knife in response … something he accepts he should never have done," defence lawyer Richard Edney said in his closing address.

There were audible gasps in the courtroom as the verdict was delivered, with Oscar's family wiping away tears and comforting each other.

The boy will be sentenced at a later date.

World.title: Man found guilty of creating sexualised deepfake images of Brisbane students
World.content:
A man who created and distributed sexualised deepfake images of current and former Brisbane high school students and staff has been found guilty of more than a dozen charges.

Last week Antonio Rotondo pleaded not guilty to 17 offences at the beginning of his Brisbane District Court trial.

This included 11 counts of stalking, five counts of distributing intimate images and one count of distributing child exploitation material.

After deliberating for several hours, a jury returned a guilty verdict on all charges.

Antonio Rotondo is charged with 11 counts of stalking and five counts of distributing intimate images. (ABC News)

During his trial, the court heard details about the 56-year-old's offending, which took place in September 2023 whilst he was living in the Philippines.

Using a website, he digitally altered publicly available photographs of several women and girls to remove their clothing or replace it with lingerie.

Rotondo then sent the images, including one of a 13-year-old girl, via email to her school and various other recipients.

He also emailed similar altered photographs of women who had participated in a Brisbane Fashion Week event, to another woman involved in the same event.

More than a dozen images included in the emails were also uploaded to a website.

Rotondo was arrested a month later after he travelled to the Gold Coast.

Rotondo told police it was 'funny'

In his police interview, which was played to the jury, he admitted to sending the emails and uploading the images online.

When asked why he did it, he told officers because it was "funny" and described it as a "hobby".

He also claimed you "cannot stop deepfakes" and given the software to create them exists, they must be "acceptable to a percentage of community".

In order to find him guilty of some of the charges, the jury needed to determine the offending caused distress to the complainants.

Man pleads not guilty to making deepfake images A jury has heard a man accused of making sexualised deepfake images of former Brisbane high school students and staff told police he did it because it was "funny".

Rotondo, who represented himself during the trial, told jurors during his closing address there was reasonable doubt some had suffered serious emotional harm as they had never viewed them.

"They didn't see that image so it's not possible for them to have a psychological problem with that image," he said.

Rotondo also said there was a lack of evidence he controlled the website.

The jury heard numerous complainants describe the impact of the images in police interviews, with one woman saying she was "very distressed".

Another woman told police she felt "extremely violated" and her "trust is gone" in general society.

"I've since significantly self-censored how I show up, how I present publicly," she said.

Rotondo was remanded in custody ahead of his sentencing hearing tomorrow.

World.title: 'I punched him in the head': Body-cam footage from Town Hall protest emerges
World.content:
Body-worn camera footage from the controversial Town Hall protest has emerged showing NSW Police officers apparently boasting about striking a protester, as the state's police watchdog investigates what became the most complained-about incident in its history.

The footage, which has been widely shared on social media, captures an officer telling colleagues: "I f***ing pumped that c***.

"And then I punched him in the head when he was down," he continues. "I saw that," a female colleague responds, laughing.

The officers can be seen walking down George Street as they disperse protesters following the anti-Herzog rally in Sydney in February.

Police actions during the Town Hall protest became the subject of intense public scrutiny and saw hundreds of complaints lodged to the state's police watchdog.

Videos filmed by protesters and members of the public circulated widely online at the time, however this is the first-known body-worn camera vision to emerge publicly.

An NSW Police spokesperson said the force was aware of the video but could not comment because of an ongoing investigation by the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission (LECC).

More than 800 people have complained to the police watchdog about the actions of officers. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

In May, LECC Chief Commissioner Peter Johnson told an NSW parliamentary inquiry the watchdog had received more than 800 complaints about police conduct at the rally, which was the "greatest number of complaints on one topic in the commission's history".

The new footage was posted online by several pro-Palestinian accounts, including former Greens candidate Hannah Thomas, who sustained a serious eye injury after being struck by a police officer during a separate protest.

It is unclear how the body-worn camera footage was obtained, however it was understood to have formed part of recent court proceedings involving a protester arrested at the rally.

It has been viewed online more than 240,000 times.

Do you know more? If you have any information about a story, contact Amy Greenbank at greenbank.amy@protonmail.com or amygreenbank.01 on Signal.

Video referred to police watchdog

The footage is among several videos and images of police that night being poured over by the LECC. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

In the aftermath of the February protest, NSW Premier Chris Minns rejected calls for an independent inquiry into police actions.

"I'm not going condemn the police for doing what we asked them to do, to keep the public safe. I'm not going to throw police under the bus" he told NSW parliament at the time.

New police altercation video A new video filmed by a bystander and shared with ABC NEWS Verify shows the full minute before two police officers began punching a protester, shedding light on the beginning of the altercation.

NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson has referred the body-worn camera footage to the LECC as "evidence of misconduct" by NSW Police.

"This footage shows the attitude of the police that night and should result in an immediate suspension and investigation of the officers involved," she said in a statement.

The LECC's investigation, called Operation Makalu, is expected to hold public hearings into the matter in the coming months.

World.title: Materials to rebuild homes after disaster rise by 70 per cent in five years, report finds
World.content:
The cost to build a home in Australia has risen almost 30 per cent in five years, with the price of some construction materials going up by as much as 70 per cent, according to a new report.

Prices have risen most steeply in Queensland and northern Australia, where it now costs 44 per cent more to build a home than it did in 2021, the report from the Insurance Council of Australia found.

Between 2022 and 2026, insurers received 400,000 claims to repair or rebuild homes damaged in declared events, costing $11.3 billion.

Materials most needed after a natural disaster have gone up in cost the most, with roof tiles up more than 70 per cent — more than three times the rate of inflation — and windows, plasterboard and concrete prices increasing upwards of 37 per cent.

In the past five years, in Queensland alone, insurers have repaired or replaced more than 240,000 homes. (ABC News: Sophie Johnson)

Insurance Council Australia (ICA) chief executive Andrew Hall said inflation was driving up costs, and people's premiums with it.

"In states like Queensland, where quite often it's severe storms that impact a home, those things that need replacing immediately are the things that are costing the most, that all goes into the calculation when we're looking at the cost of an insurance premium," he said.

Meanwhile, as extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, Australia is repairing nearly as many homes as it is building new ones.

In 2025, declared events damaged 145,392 homes. Nationally, 172,657 new homes were built.

In the past five years, in Queensland alone, insurers have repaired or replaced more than 240,000 homes.

Andrew Hall says the insurance sector is competing for the same workers and materials as builders to repair damaged houses. (ABC News: Craig Hansen)

"These are homes that are already existing which means we're competing with the same sector that's trying to deliver new homes to meet the housing challenges," Mr Hall said.

It's set up a "double whammy" where insurers vie with builders for materials and trades, he said.

Queenslanders warned about 'disaster chasers' targeting storm-hit homeowners Home owners in storm-hit parts of Queensland are being warned about “disaster chasers” targeting vulnerable residents.

"Not only are we trying to meet the affordability and accessibility challenge, we're at the same time competing for the same builders and materials to repair existing housing stock."

The report recommends Australia builds more resilient homes, and stop homes being built in high-risk areas.

"Future-proofed" homes would stop resources for new buildings being diverted for repairs, Paula Jarzabkowski, Professor in Strategic Management at the University of Queensland said.

Instead of rebuilding "like for like" repairs need to make a home safer and more likely to withstand severe weather, she added.

Paula Jarzabkowski says there needs to be a focus on building future-proofed homes. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"At a time when we should be building more homes and we know that, we're having to go backwards and rebuild existing homes," Professor Jarzabkowski said.

"If we weren't rebuilding that 150,000 perhaps we could have put those resources into building the housing stock for tomorrow.

"We need to build that housing stock in a way that is future-proofed. Let's not build tomorrow's buyback today."

World.title: Is Marnus Labuschagne finally out of luck?
World.content:
For a period of 23 Tests, Marnus Labuschagne was statistically the luckiest batter in Test cricket.

He had more genuine chances dropped or missed than any other batter from his debut up until the end of the 2021/22 Ashes series. He was more often than not able to turn those reprieves into significant scores.

In more recent times, it's been slim pickings. In fact, it's been 23 Tests since his last century, dating back to the fourth Ashes Test at Old Trafford in 2023.

He's been left out of the ODI squad travelling to take on Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month. The right-hander has only missed five of Australia's last 56 ODIs, raising questions about his future in the Test side.

"We're still very much working through what that Test squad looks like, but I can say we separate out those formats," chair of selectors George Bailey told reporters when unveiling the ODI squad.

"He has played some really important one-day cricket for us; at his best that looks a certain way, but the way that squad and team is structuring up there just wasn't space for him."

If you break down Labuschagne's career into the period before his last Test ton and the period since, there is somewhat of a trend: his luck has seemingly run out.

The 2023 Ashes series in England was the last time Marnus Labuschagne made a Test century. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Looking at only genuine chances missed by opposition teams — dropped catches, missed stumpings, opposition teams not reviewing a decision that would have seen him dismissed, or wickets on a no ball — he was given a reprieve 25 times from 75 innings where he faced at least one ball.

That's a chance every three innings from his Test debut in 2018 to his most recent hundred back in 2023.

Across his first 20 Tests he scored six centuries and 12 fifties, earning him a batting average of 62.15. If, in that time, he had been taken at the first opportunity, that average drops to 46.50.

In the 2019-2021 World Test Championship cycle, Labuschagne played 13 Tests and scored the most runs of any other batter in the world. He finished that period with 1,675 runs at an average of 72.82. Across the 23 innings he was required to bat in, he was afforded 12 chances, or one every 1.92 innings.

When you compare that with Steve Smith in the same period, he was given a reprieve four times, which equates to one every 5.5 innings. Smith was still able to score 1,341 runs in that WTC cycle, which highlights Labuschagne's ability to capitalise when given the opportunity.

In fact, his entire Test career has been based on it.

Labuschagne's luck was a key feature of his game in his early Tests, with his ability to capitalise on opportunities given to him by opposition mistakes. (AP: Rick Rycroft)

Labuschagne made his Test debut in 2018 due to the bans handed down to Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft after the sandpaper incident the last time Australia's Test team toured South Africa.

That put him in the frame for the 2019 Ashes squad and, after a red-hot Smith was hit in the neck by a Jofra Archer bouncer at Lord's, Labuschagne got his next chance as the first concussion substitute in the history of international cricket, courtesy of a rule introduced the month before the series started.

In the next Test in Leeds, Labuschagne was dropped on 14, 42 and 60, and England failed to review an edge that would have been given out when he was on 35. He went on to make 80.

That series, including that fortunate knock of 80 at Headingley, cemented his spot in the side, with Usman Khawaja the unfortunate one to make way when Smith returned, a decision that left Khawaja on the outer for three years.

His ability to turn a reprieve into a significant score was a hallmark of his early Test career. Labuschagne's maiden Test century came against Pakistan at the Gabba in 2019 when he scored an impressive 185 off 279 balls. Pakistan fans might still be ruing the fact he was dropped by Asad Shafiq on 33 that same innings.

Labuschagne made a habit of scoring big runs when given a reprieve by the opposition. (AAP: David Mariuz)

In that WTC cycle alone, if he had been taken at the first opportunity, his batting average would drop to 55.68, which would have had him ranked 11th in the world.

It's not just his luck that's seemingly run out; it's his ability to capitalise on it.

From that first Ashes series to his last Test century, Labuschagne was able to turn missed opportunities into scores of 50 or more on nine occasions, including five hundreds.

Since that last century, he has been afforded only four reprieves, and the most he's added to his total is 18 runs.

Loading...

He was briefly dropped from the side after failing to impress as a makeshift opener in last year's World Test Championship final, missing Australia's tour of the West Indies. But, after only three Tests out of the side, he came back in for the 2025/26 Ashes and has remained in the team since.

When you compare that to the likes of Jake Weatherald, who has been in and out of the Test squad with questions around his form, Labuschagne has not just been given chances by opposition fielders; he's also been given them by the Australian selectors.

With an important series against South Africa on the horizon and his omission from the ODI squad, all eyes now look to see if his luck really has run out.

World.title: 'Next moment the most important' for Longmuir's dominant Dockers
World.content:
The Fremantle Dockers may be just three wins from claiming the club's first-ever AFL premiership, but coach Justin Longmuir has dismissed suggestions he will be using that as motivation heading into the finals.

The 2026 version of the Dockers is comfortably the best-performed team in the club's history when it comes to the home-and away season.

Fremantle won 19 of its 23 games to race away with the minor premiership, earning the right to host Hawthorn in a qualifying final at Perth Stadium on Thursday night.

Murphy Reid (left) will return for the Dockers against the Hawks after recovering from a groin knock. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos )

It has seen excitement build among the Freo faithful, who are hopeful this could be their year, having made just one grand final since the club entered the AFL in the 1995 season, losing to the Hawks in 2013.

But throughout this year's campaign, Longmuir has urged his players to stay in the moment and focus on more immediate tasks, and he insisted thinking about the ultimate goal is not what would get the job done.

'I'm only human': Fremantle star Jackson dreaming of Dockers' maiden flag Luke Jackson has already been to the top of the AFL mountain and now, with Fremantle just three wins from a maiden premiership, the man known as 'Dogga' is desperate to get there again.

"I just don't feel like we need to [lean into it]. If there's someone at the footy club that doesn't see that carrot, well then you're probably in the wrong game, right?" he said.

"All our players know what's on the line, and we just need to make sure that we use whatever motivation that gives us to give it all to your next moment.

"Everyone feels it in different ways … some players will see it as a stimulus and some players will maybe see it as a distraction, and we'll work through that.

"Everyone sees pressure as different things and we've done some work on that, and it's all about staying in the moment.

Hawks forward Nick Watson will be one man the Dockers are keen to keep a close eye on. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition.

"We've just got to make sure that we give our best to each moment, and the next moment is the most important one."

Fast start wanted

Much of the talk in the build-up to Thursday's game has focused on the Dockers' home-crowd advantage, after they rode the Wharfie Time rallying cry to come from behind to win their last clash against Hawthorn at Perth Stadium.

But Longmuir is hopeful they will not have to rely on the fans to overcome another slow start.

Fremantle got up in Wharfie Time against the Hawks in round nine, but hope they will not need it this week. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

"They're not going to get us over the line if we're not playing good footy, so we've got to give them something to cheer for, and it needs to be from the start," he said.

Key defender Brennan Cox will miss Thursday's match through injury, but Fremantle is set to welcome back the likes of Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and the retiring Sam Switkowski.

Hawthorn is at virtually full strength for the clash, with only two players unavailable on its most recent injury list.

The Hawks enjoyed a comfortable win over West Coast at Perth Stadium in their final game of the home-and-away season.

World.title: Police charge man with alleged serious assault of two-month-old baby
World.content:
Detectives have charged a 33-year-old man following a prolonged investigation into the assault of a two-month-old baby boy in southern Queensland.

Police said the Toowoomba Child Protection Investigation Unit has been investigating the alleged assault since January 2025.

The baby boy was taken to Warwick Hospital with life-threatening injuries last year, according to police.

After an 18-month investigation, police arrested the 33-year-old man in Harristown on Saturday and charged him with serious child harm offences.

The man, who is known to the child, was charged with one count of grievous bodily harm, assault occasioning bodily harm, and failing to provide the necessities of life.

The man was given bail and is due to appear in the Toowoomba Magistrates Court on September 15.

Police investigations into the alleged assault remain ongoing.

World.title: ‘Give them something to aspire to’: The Swans mantra behind undefeated run
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans ‘Give them something to aspire to’: The Swans mantra behind undefeated run Frances Howe September 1, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Inside the Sydney Swans AFLW locker room in Coffs Harbour on Saturday, coach Colin O’Riordan gave a routine pre-game pep talk. He began by warning his team about getting complacent after winning their first two games of the season, instructed them to lookout for their teammates, but finished by telling them to play not just for this game, but for the bigger picture. “There’s someone in the stand or there’s someone on TV looking at you, aspiring to be you,” he said. “Let’s give them something to f---ing aspire to later on today.” Swans coach Colin O’Riordan speaks to his players during the round three AFLW match between Sydney and St Kilda in Coffs Harbour. Getty Images The talk worked. The Swans AFLW team won their third consecutive game on Saturday, making them one of four undefeated teams this season, beating St. Kilda 38-15. Their success follows what has been a troubling time for the club off the field.



On August 19, five Swans AFL players – James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were stood down for breaching club standards for their actions earlier that week including drinking, staying out late and bringing women back to the team hotel. A separate police investigation into an alleged sexual assault is ongoing. Back in Sydney for training on Tuesday, and in front of a slightly smaller crowd of reporters than the past few weeks, O’Riordan said he was proud of his team’s performance amid the increased attention. “I’m loving this group. Their ability to show resilience in tough moments, whether it’s on-field or off-field, is something I’m incredibly proud of,” he said. “And again, I’m a broken record for saying this, but I have immense pride for every single person, staff, and players in our program. I just think the way they conduct themselves on and off the field is incredible, and they’re incredible ambassadors for the club.” But the women’s team’s culture, and O’Riordan’s insistence on playing for the next generation, predates Saturday’s talk, and any scandal.



Related Article Sydney Swans Dropping the body armour: How the Swans AFLW team united amid crisis ”I think as a player, and I talk from experience, you don’t realise the impact you have on the next generation,” O’Riordan said. “Something I’ve really noticed since I’ve taken over the job is you see girls coming up to the likes of Chloe [Molloy] and Zippy [Fish], Mon Ham [Montana Ham], Ally Morphett, you saw it after the game. You see them wanting their autographs, and they know who they are, and they want to be these people. “I think at times you get stuck in your head that you’re playing for you … or you’re playing for the coach. You’re actually not. You’re playing for the next generation of young female athletes who want to aspire to be something. “Whether you like it or not, you are the role model, and that comes with a level of responsibility, and it’s just leaning into that a little bit to make them realise that you are actually pretty special, and what you’re doing is pretty cool.” Sydney’s AFLW team will look to extend their streak when they play the Western Bulldogs in Melbourne on Saturday.

World.title: More house price pain to come, warns nation’s biggest lender
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices More house price pain to come, warns nation’s biggest lender Shane Wright September 1, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s biggest home lender has warned property prices will continue to fall until well into next year, led by steep falls in Sydney and Melbourne that could be even worse if the Reserve Bank delivers another interest rate rise to quell inflation. Before the June quarter national accounts, which are expected to show the economy barely growing despite resilient household spending, the Commonwealth Bank on Tuesday said it expects Sydney dwelling prices to fall 11 per cent this year and Melbourne to drop 10 per cent. The nation’s biggest home lender is tipping house prices to continue falling all the way until April next year. Joe Armao Figures released by analytics firm Cotality on Tuesday showed national dwelling values down for a fifth consecutive month in August. About $40,000 was wiped from the median value of homes through winter as high interest rates, the federal government’s property tax changes and poor affordability combined to hit the market. So far this year, dwelling values have fallen by 6.7 per cent in Sydney and by 6.3 per cent in Melbourne. Other capitals are still up on where they finished last year but are now falling.



Commonwealth Bank senior economist Trent Saunders said the market was deteriorating faster than expected, forcing a downgrade to the bank’s outlook for the market. Related Article Property prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter The bank has sliced its forecasts for each capital city, with Sydney likely to experience a peak-to-trough fall of 13 per cent and Melbourne 12 per cent by April next year when values are expected to stop falling. The Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth markets, which had been holding, are also expected to be either flat or show a small fall this year. A recovery through the second half of next year is expected to lift prices in almost every capital by around 2 per cent through 2027. The key factor is interest rate settings, with the CBA expecting the Reserve Bank to lift rates by November before starting to cut in May next year.



“The interest rate outlook has also moved against the housing market,” Saunders said. “We still expect the downturn to eventually run its course. Falling prices should improve affordability and increase the rental yield, drawing some buyers back into the market. ” Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused the government of failing to deal with inflation as the key factor in the fall in house values. “The Albanese active inflation agenda that is forcing the hand of the RBA is killing home values,” Wilson said. “Australian families already struggling to pay their bills are now sitting at the kitchen table watching the value of their biggest asset, their family home, fall through the floor.”



The Property Council’s group executive for policy, Matthew Kandelaars, said the government’s planned changes to the tax treatment of trusts would also harm the market. “Family-owned and mid-tier builders do much of the heavy lifting on housing supply. The proposed trust tax risks hitting exactly those businesses the government is relying on to help deliver 1.2 million homes,” he said. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics confirm the government is falling further behind its target of 1.2 million new homes by the end of the decade. Building approvals fell by 3.6 per cent in July, with approvals for new houses slipping by 4.2 per cent. The single largest drop was 5.5 per cent in Queensland. Despite the fall in July, overall approvals are still 9 per cent up on the same time last year. On the more stable trend measure, which takes out monthly statistical noise, approvals are at their highest level in five years. Approvals of units and apartments are at their highest level since 2018.



Over the past year, almost 210,000 homes have been approved for construction. To meet the 1.2 million target, there needs to be about 250,000 properties green-lit for construction each year. Separate figures released by the bureau on Tuesday highlight the overall sluggishness of the economy. Trade and government spending figures suggest that Wednesday’s national accounts will show economic growth easing back from 2.5 per cent to around 2 per cent. The only bright spot remains household spending, although that is facing headwinds from higher interest rates and ongoing inflation. The war against Iran and the volatile nature of the Trump administration are also changing Australians’ spending habits. For the first time since COVID, June quarter travel by Australian tourists for the European and American summers fell as oil prices and security issues through key Middle East transit hubs pushed up the price of long-distance flights.



There was a near-20 per cent drop in trips to Britain and Ireland, a 16 per cent fall to north-west European nations such as Germany and a 19 per cent tumble in visits to southern and eastern European destinations. Australians also shunned trips to the USA, with visits down by 12.6 per cent in the quarter despite the Australian dollar appreciating against its American counterpart. Instead, they headed for Canada with visits up 18.5 per cent to a record 39,000. Outside of travel, the surge in oil prices meant the nation imported a record amount of petrol and diesel in the quarter. In original terms, the value of fuel imports jumped by 62 per cent, or $9 billion.



That high-priced oil also meant motorists imported a record number of EVs and hybrid vehicles. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up Karl Quinn Updated September 1, 2026 — 3:48pm ,first published 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ray Martin will come face to face with an AI-driven deep fake version of himself in a bid to understand the threats and opportunities posed by the rise of artificial intelligence in Ray Martin is Misinformed. The documentary is one of the highlights of the slate unveiled in SBS’ annual upfront presentation — a showcase of its most eye-catching (and ad-friendly) content of the year ahead — in Sydney on Tuesday. The broadcaster also announced that it has secured the rights to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which will be staged in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. This follows the record-breaking ratings for this year’s tournament, which was watched, the network claims, by 8 million Australians. “For almost 50 years, SBS has been the spiritual home of the world game,” said managing director Jane Palfreyman. “Football has always reflected the Australia we are, and the Australia we aspire to be, a nation shaped by many cultures, communities, and stories. That’s why the FIFA World Cup on SBS matters. Because when SBS is doing its job well, Australia sees itself a little more clearly. I can’t think of a time when that has mattered more.” Joseph Maxwell, the network’s head of factual, said that in the Ray Martin-fronted documentary “we actually create Ray-I, an AI version of Ray, and by the end of the show you cannot tell who’s Ray and who’s Ray-I.”



Ray Martin will meet an AI version of himself. Will he know which is which? SBS “It’s pretty unsettling for Ray at certain moments. The model grows; it starts off not sounding like him and by the end, you feel you’re in the room with two Rays. It’s got his voice, it’s got his pauses. They say AI can’t have a sense of humour, but it certainly picks up some of his tone and playfulness by the end.” The show is not merely an exercise in what’s possible, Maxwell adds. It’s a meditation on what the fact that it is possible means — especially for the notion of truth in reporting. “Ray’s entire world has been journalism, and now journalism is under threat like it’s never been before. And Ray-I in some ways represents that threat. But in some ways it represents a solution, too.” Related Article Streaming This Emmy nominee is a star in America. At home in Australia, no one knows his name Maxwell highlighted a number of other notable documentaries in the slate, including Dan Goldberg’s Bondi, a “minute by minute” account of the events of December 14, 2025 from the perspective of those who were there.



“This has got no narration; it’s all told by the people who were there,” says Maxwell. “And it paints a broader portrait of antisemitism, a broader portrait of social cohesion, a broader portrait of multicultural Australia.” Similarly confronting is 2.6 Seconds, a four-part documentary series about the killing of Kumanjayi Walker by Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe in 2019. Marking the directorial debut of Darren Dale, co-founder of production powerhouse Blackfella Films, the series has all the marks, Maxwell says, of being a “channel-defining” commission. “It’s a proper, landmark, premium true-crime show that reveals something really fascinating about Australia, doesn’t tell you what to think, but allows you to explore the evidence, explore the story,” he says. “And I think we will be holding this up as the kind of show that only SBS does – really distinctive, really bold and absolutely gripping.” Samuel Johnson presents Homeless 300, a new documentary series for SBS. Alone Australia will be back, and again the contestants will have to try to survive in the Arctic Circle. It will be in a different location to the season currently airing, and they’ll be going in later, so the harsh winter conditions will begin to bite earlier. But the biggest change will be that this time they’re allowed to hunt.



The Sami people’s sacred animals will not be on the menu, though. “There will be no reindeer harmed in the making of this show, I guarantee you that,” says Maxwell. “There are birds they can hunt, there are other animals they can hunt. But I can’t really reveal too much because the cast don’t know the details yet.” If Alone is all about people who opt to sleep rough in pursuit of a big cash prize, Homeless 300 will look at the plight of those who have no choice in the matter. Presented by Samuel Johnson, the show takes its name from the fact that 300 Australians are turned away from homeless shelters each night. And it’s a subject that resonates deeply with the Gold Logie-winning actor. Related Article Emmys Two Emmy nods and a fridge full of Tim Tams – meet the Aussie staging pop culture’s biggest moments “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a presenter so angered by the society in which we live,” says Maxwell. “He’s out there looking at this issue, and he’s just absolutely gobsmacked and asks us, ‘What as a nation can we do, and how did we get to this place?’”



The three-part series marks a return to the topic SBS explored with Filthy Rich and Homeless back in 2017, but from a fresh angle. “And the sad thing is that issue has not changed,” says Maxwell. “The show is very much looking at solutions as well as the problems.” If the SBS slate is rich in hard-hitting factual content – including a series in which Marc Fennell revisits the Hilton Bombing of 1978, and sits down with Evan Pederick, the man who confessed to the act, was jailed for it, but whose testimony was later deemed unreliable – it is noticeably thin on locally produced scripted content. The network announced just three commissions for its Digital Originals program, which has previously produced The Tailings and this year’s Logie-winning Homebodies. Ethan Hawke plays Lee Raybon, a self-styled “truthstorian”, in The Lowdown. The new series are adventure drama Mangrove Mansion, supernatural First Nations story Pretty Deadly and a social media comedy about feuding friends, Tantrum. But with a combined running time of just three hours, the slate does little to allay concerns about the parlous state of Australian drama and comedy on free-to-air television.

World.title: Alan Jones trial as it happened: Former broadcaster’s 2GB colleague Ray Hadley gives evidence of conversation with complainant ‘C’, reveals he gave police statement about Jones in 2024
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and thank you for reading our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

If you’re just joining us now, it has been a short day of evidence. Former 2GB heavyweight Ray Hadley, a longtime colleague of Alan Jones, started giving evidence in the trial after 2pm.

Ray Hadley departs the Local Court in Sydney on Tuesday. Dominic Lorrimer

A legal issue arose that resulted in his evidence being paused about an hour later. Here are the key parts of his testimony so far.

Hadley said complainant “C” told him in 2019 that Jones had “put his hand on my c--- and kissed me” on a number of occasions some years earlier.

“I asked him if he was homosexual, and whether he was consenting to it,” Hadley said. “He broke down and cried and said, ‘no, I hated it. I’m not homosexual’.”

Hadley said he comforted “C” during the conversation and told him it was not his fault. He offered to take the complainant to the police, he said, but “C” had insisted he did not want to do this because Jones was “too powerful”.

Hadley told the court that author and journalist Peter FitzSimons, a journalist at The Sydney Morning Herald, had been investigating allegations against Jones and that he facilitated a phone call between “C” and FitzSimons in 2019.

At this stage, the complainant’s identity was kept secret from FitzSimons and the allegations were not reported, the court has heard.

In 2023, the Herald’s chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont spoke to “C”, the court heard, and his allegations were published in an anonymised form. Hadley agreed he discussed the article on air.

The hearing resumes at 10am tomorrow, and Hadley’s evidence will continue at some stage after that.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 22 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent spanning six complainants and a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the allegations.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: US Army’s top civilian leader resigns as it grapples with two wars
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US Army’s top civilian leader resigns as it grapples with two wars Helene Cooper and Greg Jaffe September 1, 2026 — 3:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, the service’s top civilian leader, who has clashed repeatedly with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the removal of key combat-tested army leaders, has handed in his resignation to President Donald Trump, administration officials say. Driscoll’s resignation on Monday was expected, but it comes at a tumultuous time, as the military’s largest service faces its busiest period since the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. Army air defence soldiers are playing the leading role in defending American troops in the Middle East from increasingly sophisticated Iranian missile attacks. Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll (centre) found himself increasingly at odds with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth (centre right) and his boss, President Donald Trump. Bloomberg via Getty Images The army’s command in Europe is also providing critical intelligence and other support to Ukraine as it fights to hold off a larger Russian force. In the meantime, Hegseth has initiated a series of firings and feuds that have left the army essentially rudderless as it struggles to deal with the threat posed by cheap, deadly drones and missiles that have pounded US bases in the Middle East.



Related Article Trump's White House Pete Hegseth is hollowing out the US Army at the worst possible time Driscoll met Trump in person to hand in his resignation and discuss the current state of the army, said one official, who, like others in this story, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues. The army has not had a chief of staff, the service’s top officer, since Hegseth fired General Randy George without explanation in April, and there are no signs that he is close to filling the position, officials said. Hegseth has forced out at least three senior officers who had been viewed as potential successors to George. Now, the army will also be without a civilian leader, at least until Trump appoints a new army secretary. The resignation of Driscoll, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, comes as the midterms approach, and it may be difficult to get a replacement confirmed soon.



Hegseth has indicated that he would like to see Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, in the job. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell is Hegseth’s pick to replace Driscoll, but could face opposition in the Senate. Department of Defence Parnell served as an officer in Afghanistan, but his tenure as the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson has been buffeted by controversy. Parnell recently fired three journalists at Stars and Stripes, a federally funded but independent news organisation. The journalists sued the government last week, claiming that the Pentagon had fired them in retaliation for writing about the worsening conditions on the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which was recently deployed in the Middle East. Parnell also led an effort to restrict reporters’ access within the Pentagon. The moves prompted The New York Times to sue the Pentagon on the grounds that the policy violated the First Amendment.



Parnell withdrew from a Senate race in November 2021 after a judge ruled that his estranged wife should have primary custody of their three children in a case in which she accused him of spousal and child abuse. The order was later vacated, and Parnell has shared custody with his wife for several years, a Pentagon official said. Related Article US politics Pete Hegseth’s wife and her ‘bonkers’ hands-on role in the Pentagon Parnell, who spoke at the 2024 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, where Trump was nearly assassinated, had a strong relationship with the president, officials said. But senior administration officials said Parnell would probably struggle to be confirmed by the closely divided Senate. Driscoll, a 40-year-old army first lieutenant, was until recently seen as a potential candidate to replace Hegseth if he decided to step down or fell out of favour with Trump. He garnered more support on Capitol Hill than Hegseth, who has a combative relationship with the Democrats and even some Republicans on the key House and Senate committees that oversee the Pentagon.



Driscoll, in contrast, was viewed by many in Congress as one of the few Trump administration Pentagon officials who could work with lawmakers in both parties, two congressional aides said. While Hegseth has tried to limit direct communications between military officials and lawmakers, Driscoll has responded to requests from Republicans and Democrats alike in the armed services committees, the aides said. Driscoll was once seen as a potential successor to Hegseth as defence secretary. Getty Images During Driscoll’s nomination hearings, Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed him to commit to allowing the army to repair its own equipment instead of sending it back to defence contractors. Months later, Driscoll did so, putting the policy, known as “right to repair”, in place and earning a rare plaudit for a Trump administration official from a Democratic lawmaker (and one who had voted against his nomination).



But Driscoll told Trump that he was frustrated with Hegseth’s removal of so many proven army leaders and his blocking of the promotions of a number of colonels who had worked for people he did not like, two officials said. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Norway’s rapist prince freed from house arrest to attend late king’s funeral
World.content:
WorldEuropeNorway Norway’s rapist prince freed from house arrest to attend late king’s funeral Nick Squires September 1, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rome: The disgraced son of Norway’s new queen will be allowed to leave house arrest despite a recent rape conviction so that he can attend the funeral of the late King Harald V. King Harald died on Friday at the age of 89. His son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon VIII. King Haakon’s wife, who has had a troubled time in recent years, became Queen Mette-Marit. Marius Borg Høiby, back right, was also allowed to attend the transfer of King Harald’s coffin through the royal palace to the palace chapel on Monday. Ole Berg-Rusten/Pool NTB via AP Her son, Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from a relationship before she married King Haakon, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being found guilty of committing two rapes. He is serving his sentence under house arrest with an ankle tag while awaiting a new trial after he appealed against the conviction.



Norwegian police said on Monday (Oslo time) that Høiby would be allowed to leave house arrest to go to the funeral of the late king on September 9. Related Article Royalty The princess and her ‘monster’ son: A royal family faces a moral reckoning Høiby was previously granted permission to visit King Harald in hospital before his death last week. “The public prosecutor deemed that there were grounds to grant the requests for leave submitted by Høiby in connection with the death,” said Oda Karterud, a police prosecutor. “Leave has been granted.” In addition to the two counts of rape, Høiby was convicted of 32 other charges, including violence towards a former partner. He was acquitted of two other rapes.



The 29-year-old was also allowed to attend the transfer of the king’s coffin through the royal palace to the palace chapel on Monday. His mother, the new queen, joined the procession, making her first official appearance since assuming the title. Marius Borg Høiby and his mother Mette-Marit in 2022. AP King Haakon will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday (Oslo time). Among the challenges he faces will be repairing the image of the monarchy after his wife’s past association with paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein, and the rape conviction of his stepson.



Queen Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye following a lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. Related Article Updated

Royalty King Harald’s death at 89 ushers in new era for Norway Norwegians paid tribute to the late king at the weekend, laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived on Friday from the hospital. Tens of thousands of people attended memorial services in churches and cathedrals across the country. As crown princess, Mette-Marit apologised earlier this year for her friendship with Epstein and said she had been “manipulated” by the disgraced financier and sex offender.



She said she had no idea that Epstein was a predatory abuser of teenage girls and young women, insisting that she never witnessed anything illegal. The close friendship between the two was revealed in the Epstein files, released by the US Department of Justice. Norwegians paid tribute to the late king at the weekend, laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace. Rune Hellestad/Getty Images King Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since mid-August, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. He faced mounting health problems in his final years and scaled back his official duties. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
