World.title: Australia news LIVE: Second Australian found alive after Nepal floods; NSW man Michael Keats among Nepal dead; Trump vows to ‘hit Iran hard’ as Middle East tensions escalate
World.content:
An Australian missing in the Nepal flooding disaster has been located in Tibet, China by DFAT officials.

“We’re incredibly thankful another Australian, who had been unaccounted for, has now been found,” Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement.

“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”

She said finding a second person alive, who for privacy reasons has not yet been identified, was welcome news, but the government remained realistic about the ongoing search efforts.

“Around 4000 people remain missing across the affected areas, and the conditions facing search and recovery teams are extremely challenging,” she said.

“Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed, and many areas are still difficult to reach. As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow.”

It follows Cara Severino being found a few days ago.

World.title: Melbourne records its warmest winter on record, as bushfire season looms
World.content:
Melbourne has officially recorded the warmest winter since records began in 1855, with a mean temperature of 12.8 degrees – just above the 2013 record of 12.7 degrees. On Tuesday, the first day of spring, Melbourne reached a top of 23 degrees – well above the average September maximum of 17.3 degrees – before forecast showers in the evening. Melbourne residents enjoy the late winter sun in Moonee Ponds. LUIS ENRIQUE ASCUI Winter weather records show warm conditions extended up the eastern seaboard, smashing temperature records.



Sydney experienced its warmest winter in 167 years of records, according to Weatherzone meteorologist Ben Domensino, and Sydneysiders can expect the warmest start to spring in more than 50 years, with temperatures predicted to reach between 24 and 27 degrees this week. Temperatures are also expected to soar in Brisbane over coming days, potentially reaching 33 by Thursday and staying within a few degrees of that maximum at the weekend. Scarlett Keast basking in the sun on the first day of spring in Fitzroy Gardens. Simon Schluter Domensino attributes the immediate cause to a large high-pressure system passing over southern Australia that is allowing a hot air mass to build up over the country’s interior and north-west, spilling towards the east and south. He said the mean seasonal temperature for this winter stood at 15.27 degrees – about 2.25 degrees above the long-term winter average – and was on track to beat the previous record of 14.95 degrees set in 2013.



Temperatures have been elevated by a lack of strong cold fronts and east-coast lows, which in turn had an impact on the snow season. A person enjoying the balmy weather at Flagstaff gardens on Monday. Ruby Alexander Snow resorts in Victoria and NSW closed early this year after a season of low snow cover, which also led to the value of Thredbo alpine resort being written down from $292 million to $143 million. “I grew up skiing at Selwyn snowfields and remember having to dig our front doors out at Cabramurra,” said Mia “Miff” Rennie, a member of the advocacy group Protect Our Winters.



“That’s now a thing of the past. I have seen firsthand how quickly our winters are changing and how quickly we need to respond so future generations can continue to experience the magic of winter that I grew up with.” The broader cause of the warmer weather is climate change. Australia’s area-averaged mean temperature in July was 1.14 degrees above the 1961-90 average, the warmest since 2023. All states and territories had above-average mean temperatures in July. Tasmania and Queensland were within their top seventh- and 10th-warmest July months on record since 1910, respectively. Western Europe enters autumn having been battered by a rolling series of heatwaves and its hottest ever June and July period.



The Mediterranean Sea has been supercharged with so much heat that it is expected to keep regional temperatures higher than average over coming months, prompting warnings of increased flood risk in some countries. “September and October are the Mediterranean’s flash-flood season: the sea is at its annual warmest after three months of heating and the first cold troughs arrive overhead,” Ioanna Vergini, founder of the forecasting platform WFY24, told Euronews Earth. Related Article Visual story

Floods A terrifying roar, then came the fury of the flood: How disaster unfolded in Nepal Over the northern summer, 634,022 hectares of land burnt across the EU, more than double the long-term average, prompting the evacuation of more than 300,000 people and shattering heat records. In the United States and Canada, wildfires burnt at least 25 per cent more land than the 10-year average and more than double the land area decades ago.



Scientists are exploring how the thawing of permafrost may have contributed to the landslide and flood disaster that cost thousands of lives in Nepal and China last week. The most intense El Nino event so far recorded is brewing in the Pacific Ocean, charging waters with intense heat that will be released into the atmosphere over coming months, potentially leading to even higher temperatures in Australia this summer and next. The European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service reported last month that the highest sea-surface temperatures ever recorded for July in oceans outside the polar regions were recorded in July. This, it said, was partly driven by the looming El Nino, which is expected to contribute to one of the most dangerous bushfire seasons since Black Summer.



Australia’s bushfire chiefs last month warned of increased bushfire risk among parts of Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia, northern and south-eastern NSW, south-east Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, and large parts of the Northern Territory. But the higher-than-usual temperatures experienced in Australia over winter and forecast for spring are unlikely to have yet been significantly altered by the El Nino, according to Professor Mark Howden, director of the Australian National University’s Institute for Climate, Energy and Disaster Solutions. “What’s going on in Australia [so far] fundamentally is the underlying temperature increase due to climate change.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: ‘Give them something to aspire to’: The Swans mantra behind undefeated run
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans ‘Give them something to aspire to’: The Swans mantra behind undefeated run Frances Howe September 1, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Inside the Sydney Swans AFLW locker room in Coffs Harbour on Saturday, coach Colin O’Riordan gave a routine pre-game pep talk. He began by warning his team about getting complacent after winning their first two games of the season, instructed them to lookout for their teammates, but finished by telling them to play not just for this game, but for the bigger picture. “There’s someone in the stand or there’s someone on TV looking at you, aspiring to be you,” he said. “Let’s give them something to f---ing aspire to later on today.” Swans coach Colin O’Riordan speaks to his players during the round three AFLW match between Sydney and St Kilda in Coffs Harbour. Getty Images The talk worked. The Swans AFLW team won their third consecutive game on Saturday, making them one of four undefeated teams this season, beating St. Kilda 38-15. Their success follows what has been a troubling time for the club off the field.



On August 19, five Swans AFL players – James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were stood down for breaching club standards for their actions earlier that week including drinking, staying out late and bringing women back to the team hotel. A separate police investigation into an alleged sexual assault is ongoing. Back in Sydney for training on Tuesday, and in front of a slightly smaller crowd of reporters than the past few weeks, O’Riordan said he was proud of his team’s performance amid the increased attention. “I’m loving this group. Their ability to show resilience in tough moments, whether it’s on-field or off-field, is something I’m incredibly proud of,” he said. “And again, I’m a broken record for saying this, but I have immense pride for every single person, staff, and players in our program. I just think the way they conduct themselves on and off the field is incredible, and they’re incredible ambassadors for the club.” But the women’s team’s culture, and O’Riordan’s insistence on playing for the next generation, predates Saturday’s talk, and any scandal.



Related Article Sydney Swans Dropping the body armour: How the Swans AFLW team united amid crisis ”I think as a player, and I talk from experience, you don’t realise the impact you have on the next generation,” O’Riordan said. “Something I’ve really noticed since I’ve taken over the job is you see girls coming up to the likes of Chloe [Molloy] and Zippy [Fish], Mon Ham [Montana Ham], Ally Morphett, you saw it after the game. You see them wanting their autographs, and they know who they are, and they want to be these people. “I think at times you get stuck in your head that you’re playing for you … or you’re playing for the coach. You’re actually not. You’re playing for the next generation of young female athletes who want to aspire to be something. “Whether you like it or not, you are the role model, and that comes with a level of responsibility, and it’s just leaning into that a little bit to make them realise that you are actually pretty special, and what you’re doing is pretty cool.” Sydney’s AFLW team will look to extend their streak when they play the Western Bulldogs in Melbourne on Saturday.

World.title: More house price pain to come, warns nation’s biggest lender
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices More house price pain to come, warns nation’s biggest lender Shane Wright September 1, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s biggest home lender has warned property prices will continue to fall until well into next year, led by steep falls in Sydney and Melbourne that could be even worse if the Reserve Bank delivers another interest rate rise to quell inflation. Before the June quarter national accounts, which are expected to show the economy barely growing despite resilient household spending, the Commonwealth Bank on Tuesday said it expects Sydney dwelling prices to fall 11 per cent this year and Melbourne to drop 10 per cent. The nation’s biggest home lender is tipping house prices to continue falling all the way until April next year. Joe Armao Figures released by analytics firm Cotality on Tuesday showed national dwelling values down for a fifth consecutive month in August. About $40,000 was wiped from the median value of homes through winter as high interest rates, the federal government’s property tax changes and poor affordability combined to hit the market. So far this year, dwelling values have fallen by 6.7 per cent in Sydney and by 6.3 per cent in Melbourne. Other capitals are still up on where they finished last year but are now falling.



Commonwealth Bank senior economist Trent Saunders said the market was deteriorating faster than expected, forcing a downgrade to the bank’s outlook for the market. Related Article Property prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter The bank has sliced its forecasts for each capital city, with Sydney likely to experience a peak-to-trough fall of 13 per cent and Melbourne 12 per cent by April next year when values are expected to stop falling. The Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth markets, which had been holding, are also expected to be either flat or show a small fall this year. A recovery through the second half of next year is expected to lift prices in almost every capital by around 2 per cent through 2027. The key factor is interest rate settings, with the CBA expecting the Reserve Bank to lift rates by November before starting to cut in May next year.



“The interest rate outlook has also moved against the housing market,” Saunders said. “We still expect the downturn to eventually run its course. Falling prices should improve affordability and increase the rental yield, drawing some buyers back into the market. ” Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused the government of failing to deal with inflation as the key factor in the fall in house values. “The Albanese active inflation agenda that is forcing the hand of the RBA is killing home values,” Wilson said. “Australian families already struggling to pay their bills are now sitting at the kitchen table watching the value of their biggest asset, their family home, fall through the floor.”



The Property Council’s group executive for policy, Matthew Kandelaars, said the government’s planned changes to the tax treatment of trusts would also harm the market. “Family-owned and mid-tier builders do much of the heavy lifting on housing supply. The proposed trust tax risks hitting exactly those businesses the government is relying on to help deliver 1.2 million homes,” he said. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics confirm the government is falling further behind its target of 1.2 million new homes by the end of the decade. Building approvals fell by 3.6 per cent in July, with approvals for new houses slipping by 4.2 per cent. The single largest drop was 5.5 per cent in Queensland. Despite the fall in July, overall approvals are still 9 per cent up on the same time last year. On the more stable trend measure, which takes out monthly statistical noise, approvals are at their highest level in five years. Approvals of units and apartments are at their highest level since 2018.



Over the past year, almost 210,000 homes have been approved for construction. To meet the 1.2 million target, there needs to be about 250,000 properties green-lit for construction each year. Separate figures released by the bureau on Tuesday highlight the overall sluggishness of the economy. Trade and government spending figures suggest that Wednesday’s national accounts will show economic growth easing back from 2.5 per cent to around 2 per cent. The only bright spot remains household spending, although that is facing headwinds from higher interest rates and ongoing inflation. The war against Iran and the volatile nature of the Trump administration are also changing Australians’ spending habits. For the first time since COVID, June quarter travel by Australian tourists for the European and American summers fell as oil prices and security issues through key Middle East transit hubs pushed up the price of long-distance flights.



There was a near-20 per cent drop in trips to Britain and Ireland, a 16 per cent fall to north-west European nations such as Germany and a 19 per cent tumble in visits to southern and eastern European destinations. Australians also shunned trips to the USA, with visits down by 12.6 per cent in the quarter despite the Australian dollar appreciating against its American counterpart. Instead, they headed for Canada with visits up 18.5 per cent to a record 39,000. Outside of travel, the surge in oil prices meant the nation imported a record amount of petrol and diesel in the quarter. In original terms, the value of fuel imports jumped by 62 per cent, or $9 billion.



That high-priced oil also meant motorists imported a record number of EVs and hybrid vehicles. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up Karl Quinn Updated September 1, 2026 — 3:48pm ,first published 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ray Martin will come face to face with an AI-driven deep fake version of himself in a bid to understand the threats and opportunities posed by the rise of artificial intelligence in Ray Martin is Misinformed. The documentary is one of the highlights of the slate unveiled in SBS’ annual upfront presentation — a showcase of its most eye-catching (and ad-friendly) content of the year ahead — in Sydney on Tuesday. The broadcaster also announced that it has secured the rights to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which will be staged in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. This follows the record-breaking ratings for this year’s tournament, which was watched, the network claims, by 8 million Australians. “For almost 50 years, SBS has been the spiritual home of the world game,” said managing director Jane Palfreyman. “Football has always reflected the Australia we are, and the Australia we aspire to be, a nation shaped by many cultures, communities, and stories. That’s why the FIFA World Cup on SBS matters. Because when SBS is doing its job well, Australia sees itself a little more clearly. I can’t think of a time when that has mattered more.” Joseph Maxwell, the network’s head of factual, said that in the Ray Martin-fronted documentary “we actually create Ray-I, an AI version of Ray, and by the end of the show you cannot tell who’s Ray and who’s Ray-I.”



Ray Martin will meet an AI version of himself. Will he know which is which? SBS “It’s pretty unsettling for Ray at certain moments. The model grows; it starts off not sounding like him and by the end, you feel you’re in the room with two Rays. It’s got his voice, it’s got his pauses. They say AI can’t have a sense of humour, but it certainly picks up some of his tone and playfulness by the end.” The show is not merely an exercise in what’s possible, Maxwell adds. It’s a meditation on what the fact that it is possible means — especially for the notion of truth in reporting. “Ray’s entire world has been journalism, and now journalism is under threat like it’s never been before. And Ray-I in some ways represents that threat. But in some ways it represents a solution, too.” Related Article Streaming This Emmy nominee is a star in America. At home in Australia, no one knows his name Maxwell highlighted a number of other notable documentaries in the slate, including Dan Goldberg’s Bondi, a “minute by minute” account of the events of December 14, 2025 from the perspective of those who were there.



“This has got no narration; it’s all told by the people who were there,” says Maxwell. “And it paints a broader portrait of antisemitism, a broader portrait of social cohesion, a broader portrait of multicultural Australia.” Similarly confronting is 2.6 Seconds, a four-part documentary series about the killing of Kumanjayi Walker by Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe in 2019. Marking the directorial debut of Darren Dale, co-founder of production powerhouse Blackfella Films, the series has all the marks, Maxwell says, of being a “channel-defining” commission. “It’s a proper, landmark, premium true-crime show that reveals something really fascinating about Australia, doesn’t tell you what to think, but allows you to explore the evidence, explore the story,” he says. “And I think we will be holding this up as the kind of show that only SBS does – really distinctive, really bold and absolutely gripping.” Samuel Johnson presents Homeless 300, a new documentary series for SBS. Alone Australia will be back, and again the contestants will have to try to survive in the Arctic Circle. It will be in a different location to the season currently airing, and they’ll be going in later, so the harsh winter conditions will begin to bite earlier. But the biggest change will be that this time they’re allowed to hunt.



The Sami people’s sacred animals will not be on the menu, though. “There will be no reindeer harmed in the making of this show, I guarantee you that,” says Maxwell. “There are birds they can hunt, there are other animals they can hunt. But I can’t really reveal too much because the cast don’t know the details yet.” If Alone is all about people who opt to sleep rough in pursuit of a big cash prize, Homeless 300 will look at the plight of those who have no choice in the matter. Presented by Samuel Johnson, the show takes its name from the fact that 300 Australians are turned away from homeless shelters each night. And it’s a subject that resonates deeply with the Gold Logie-winning actor. Related Article Emmys Two Emmy nods and a fridge full of Tim Tams – meet the Aussie staging pop culture’s biggest moments “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a presenter so angered by the society in which we live,” says Maxwell. “He’s out there looking at this issue, and he’s just absolutely gobsmacked and asks us, ‘What as a nation can we do, and how did we get to this place?’”



The three-part series marks a return to the topic SBS explored with Filthy Rich and Homeless back in 2017, but from a fresh angle. “And the sad thing is that issue has not changed,” says Maxwell. “The show is very much looking at solutions as well as the problems.” If the SBS slate is rich in hard-hitting factual content – including a series in which Marc Fennell revisits the Hilton Bombing of 1978, and sits down with Evan Pederick, the man who confessed to the act, was jailed for it, but whose testimony was later deemed unreliable – it is noticeably thin on locally produced scripted content. The network announced just three commissions for its Digital Originals program, which has previously produced The Tailings and this year’s Logie-winning Homebodies. Ethan Hawke plays Lee Raybon, a self-styled “truthstorian”, in The Lowdown. The new series are adventure drama Mangrove Mansion, supernatural First Nations story Pretty Deadly and a social media comedy about feuding friends, Tantrum. But with a combined running time of just three hours, the slate does little to allay concerns about the parlous state of Australian drama and comedy on free-to-air television.

World.title: Alan Jones trial as it happened: Former broadcaster’s 2GB colleague Ray Hadley gives evidence of conversation with complainant ‘C’, reveals he gave police statement about Jones in 2024
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and thank you for reading our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

If you’re just joining us now, it has been a short day of evidence. Former 2GB heavyweight Ray Hadley, a longtime colleague of Alan Jones, started giving evidence in the trial after 2pm.

Ray Hadley departs the Local Court in Sydney on Tuesday. Dominic Lorrimer

A legal issue arose that resulted in his evidence being paused about an hour later. Here are the key parts of his testimony so far.

Hadley said complainant “C” told him in 2019 that Jones had “put his hand on my c--- and kissed me” on a number of occasions some years earlier.

“I asked him if he was homosexual, and whether he was consenting to it,” Hadley said. “He broke down and cried and said, ‘no, I hated it. I’m not homosexual’.”

Hadley said he comforted “C” during the conversation and told him it was not his fault. He offered to take the complainant to the police, he said, but “C” had insisted he did not want to do this because Jones was “too powerful”.

Hadley told the court that author and journalist Peter FitzSimons, a journalist at The Sydney Morning Herald, had been investigating allegations against Jones and that he facilitated a phone call between “C” and FitzSimons in 2019.

At this stage, the complainant’s identity was kept secret from FitzSimons and the allegations were not reported, the court has heard.

In 2023, the Herald’s chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont spoke to “C”, the court heard, and his allegations were published in an anonymised form. Hadley agreed he discussed the article on air.

The hearing resumes at 10am tomorrow, and Hadley’s evidence will continue at some stage after that.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 22 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent spanning six complainants and a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the allegations.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: US Army’s top civilian leader resigns as it grapples with two wars
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US Army’s top civilian leader resigns as it grapples with two wars Helene Cooper and Greg Jaffe September 1, 2026 — 3:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, the service’s top civilian leader, who has clashed repeatedly with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the removal of key combat-tested army leaders, has handed in his resignation to President Donald Trump, administration officials say. Driscoll’s resignation on Monday was expected, but it comes at a tumultuous time, as the military’s largest service faces its busiest period since the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. Army air defence soldiers are playing the leading role in defending American troops in the Middle East from increasingly sophisticated Iranian missile attacks. Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll (centre) found himself increasingly at odds with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth (centre right) and his boss, President Donald Trump. Bloomberg via Getty Images The army’s command in Europe is also providing critical intelligence and other support to Ukraine as it fights to hold off a larger Russian force. In the meantime, Hegseth has initiated a series of firings and feuds that have left the army essentially rudderless as it struggles to deal with the threat posed by cheap, deadly drones and missiles that have pounded US bases in the Middle East.



Related Article Trump's White House Pete Hegseth is hollowing out the US Army at the worst possible time Driscoll met Trump in person to hand in his resignation and discuss the current state of the army, said one official, who, like others in this story, spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues. The army has not had a chief of staff, the service’s top officer, since Hegseth fired General Randy George without explanation in April, and there are no signs that he is close to filling the position, officials said. Hegseth has forced out at least three senior officers who had been viewed as potential successors to George. Now, the army will also be without a civilian leader, at least until Trump appoints a new army secretary. The resignation of Driscoll, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, comes as the midterms approach, and it may be difficult to get a replacement confirmed soon.



Hegseth has indicated that he would like to see Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, in the job. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell is Hegseth’s pick to replace Driscoll, but could face opposition in the Senate. Department of Defence Parnell served as an officer in Afghanistan, but his tenure as the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson has been buffeted by controversy. Parnell recently fired three journalists at Stars and Stripes, a federally funded but independent news organisation. The journalists sued the government last week, claiming that the Pentagon had fired them in retaliation for writing about the worsening conditions on the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which was recently deployed in the Middle East. Parnell also led an effort to restrict reporters’ access within the Pentagon. The moves prompted The New York Times to sue the Pentagon on the grounds that the policy violated the First Amendment.



Parnell withdrew from a Senate race in November 2021 after a judge ruled that his estranged wife should have primary custody of their three children in a case in which she accused him of spousal and child abuse. The order was later vacated, and Parnell has shared custody with his wife for several years, a Pentagon official said. Related Article US politics Pete Hegseth’s wife and her ‘bonkers’ hands-on role in the Pentagon Parnell, who spoke at the 2024 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, where Trump was nearly assassinated, had a strong relationship with the president, officials said. But senior administration officials said Parnell would probably struggle to be confirmed by the closely divided Senate. Driscoll, a 40-year-old army first lieutenant, was until recently seen as a potential candidate to replace Hegseth if he decided to step down or fell out of favour with Trump. He garnered more support on Capitol Hill than Hegseth, who has a combative relationship with the Democrats and even some Republicans on the key House and Senate committees that oversee the Pentagon.



Driscoll, in contrast, was viewed by many in Congress as one of the few Trump administration Pentagon officials who could work with lawmakers in both parties, two congressional aides said. While Hegseth has tried to limit direct communications between military officials and lawmakers, Driscoll has responded to requests from Republicans and Democrats alike in the armed services committees, the aides said. Driscoll was once seen as a potential successor to Hegseth as defence secretary. Getty Images During Driscoll’s nomination hearings, Senator Elizabeth Warren pressed him to commit to allowing the army to repair its own equipment instead of sending it back to defence contractors. Months later, Driscoll did so, putting the policy, known as “right to repair”, in place and earning a rare plaudit for a Trump administration official from a Democratic lawmaker (and one who had voted against his nomination).



But Driscoll told Trump that he was frustrated with Hegseth’s removal of so many proven army leaders and his blocking of the promotions of a number of colonels who had worked for people he did not like, two officials said. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Norway’s rapist prince freed from house arrest to attend late king’s funeral
World.content:
WorldEuropeNorway Norway’s rapist prince freed from house arrest to attend late king’s funeral Nick Squires September 1, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rome: The disgraced son of Norway’s new queen will be allowed to leave house arrest despite a recent rape conviction so that he can attend the funeral of the late King Harald V. King Harald died on Friday at the age of 89. His son, the crown prince, immediately became King Haakon VIII. King Haakon’s wife, who has had a troubled time in recent years, became Queen Mette-Marit. Marius Borg Høiby, back right, was also allowed to attend the transfer of King Harald’s coffin through the royal palace to the palace chapel on Monday. Ole Berg-Rusten/Pool NTB via AP Her son, Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from a relationship before she married King Haakon, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being found guilty of committing two rapes. He is serving his sentence under house arrest with an ankle tag while awaiting a new trial after he appealed against the conviction.



Norwegian police said on Monday (Oslo time) that Høiby would be allowed to leave house arrest to go to the funeral of the late king on September 9. Related Article Royalty The princess and her ‘monster’ son: A royal family faces a moral reckoning Høiby was previously granted permission to visit King Harald in hospital before his death last week. “The public prosecutor deemed that there were grounds to grant the requests for leave submitted by Høiby in connection with the death,” said Oda Karterud, a police prosecutor. “Leave has been granted.” In addition to the two counts of rape, Høiby was convicted of 32 other charges, including violence towards a former partner. He was acquitted of two other rapes.



The 29-year-old was also allowed to attend the transfer of the king’s coffin through the royal palace to the palace chapel on Monday. His mother, the new queen, joined the procession, making her first official appearance since assuming the title. Marius Borg Høiby and his mother Mette-Marit in 2022. AP King Haakon will take the oath to Norway’s constitution on Tuesday (Oslo time). Among the challenges he faces will be repairing the image of the monarchy after his wife’s past association with paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein, and the rape conviction of his stepson.



Queen Mette-Marit has been largely absent from the public eye following a lung transplant in June. She was diagnosed in 2018 with pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive disease that damages and scars lung tissue. Related Article Updated

Royalty King Harald’s death at 89 ushers in new era for Norway Norwegians paid tribute to the late king at the weekend, laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived on Friday from the hospital. Tens of thousands of people attended memorial services in churches and cathedrals across the country. As crown princess, Mette-Marit apologised earlier this year for her friendship with Epstein and said she had been “manipulated” by the disgraced financier and sex offender.



She said she had no idea that Epstein was a predatory abuser of teenage girls and young women, insisting that she never witnessed anything illegal. The close friendship between the two was revealed in the Epstein files, released by the US Department of Justice. Norwegians paid tribute to the late king at the weekend, laying flowers, writing cards and lighting candles in front of the royal palace. Rune Hellestad/Getty Images King Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since mid-August, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. He faced mounting health problems in his final years and scaled back his official duties. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

An Australian missing in the Nepal flooding disaster has been located in Tibet, China by DFAT officials.

“We’re incredibly thankful another Australian, who had been unaccounted for, has now been found,” Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement.

“It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.”

She said finding a second person alive, who for privacy reasons has not yet been identified, was welcome news, but the government remained realistic about the ongoing search efforts.

“Around 4000 people remain missing across the affected areas, and the conditions facing search and recovery teams are extremely challenging,” she said.

It follows Cara Severino being found a few days ago.

World.title: Melbourne records its warmest winter on record, as bushfire season looms
World.content:
Melbourne has officially recorded the warmest winter since records began in 1855, with a mean temperature of 12.8 degrees – just above the 2013 record of 12.7 degrees. On Tuesday, the first day of spring, Melbourne reached a top of 23 degrees – well above the average September maximum of 17.3 degrees – before forecast showers in the evening. Melbourne residents enjoy the late winter sun in Moonee Ponds. LUIS ENRIQUE ASCUI Winter weather records show warm conditions extended up the eastern seaboard, smashing temperature records.



Sydney experienced its warmest winter in 167 years of records, according to Weatherzone meteorologist Ben Domensino, and Sydneysiders can expect the warmest start to spring in more than 50 years, with temperatures predicted to reach between 24 and 27 degrees this week. Temperatures are also expected to soar in Brisbane over coming days, potentially reaching 33 by Thursday and staying within a few degrees of that maximum at the weekend. Scarlett Keast basking in the sun on the first day of spring in Fitzroy Gardens. Simon Schluter Domensino attributes the immediate cause to a large high-pressure system passing over southern Australia that is allowing a hot air mass to build up over the country’s interior and north-west, spilling towards the east and south. He said the mean seasonal temperature for this winter stood at 15.27 degrees – about 2.25 degrees above the long-term winter average – and was on track to beat the previous record of 14.95 degrees set in 2013.



Temperatures have been elevated by a lack of strong cold fronts and east-coast lows, which in turn had an impact on the snow season. A person enjoying the balmy weather at Flagstaff gardens on Monday. Ruby Alexander Snow resorts in Victoria and NSW closed early this year after a season of low snow cover, which also led to the value of Thredbo alpine resort being written down from $292 million to $143 million. “I grew up skiing at Selwyn snowfields and remember having to dig our front doors out at Cabramurra,” said Mia “Miff” Rennie, a member of the advocacy group Protect Our Winters.



“That’s now a thing of the past. I have seen firsthand how quickly our winters are changing and how quickly we need to respond so future generations can continue to experience the magic of winter that I grew up with.” The broader cause of the warmer weather is climate change. Australia’s area-averaged mean temperature in July was 1.14 degrees above the 1961-90 average, the warmest since 2023. All states and territories had above-average mean temperatures in July. Tasmania and Queensland were within their top seventh- and 10th-warmest July months on record since 1910, respectively. Western Europe enters autumn having been battered by a rolling series of heatwaves and its hottest ever June and July period.



The Mediterranean Sea has been supercharged with so much heat that it is expected to keep regional temperatures higher than average over coming months, prompting warnings of increased flood risk in some countries. “September and October are the Mediterranean’s flash-flood season: the sea is at its annual warmest after three months of heating and the first cold troughs arrive overhead,” Ioanna Vergini, founder of the forecasting platform WFY24, told Euronews Earth. Related Article Visual story

Floods A terrifying roar, then came the fury of the flood: How disaster unfolded in Nepal Over the northern summer, 634,022 hectares of land burnt across the EU, more than double the long-term average, prompting the evacuation of more than 300,000 people and shattering heat records. In the United States and Canada, wildfires burnt at least 25 per cent more land than the 10-year average and more than double the land area decades ago.



Scientists are exploring how the thawing of permafrost may have contributed to the landslide and flood disaster that cost thousands of lives in Nepal and China last week. The most intense El Nino event so far recorded is brewing in the Pacific Ocean, charging waters with intense heat that will be released into the atmosphere over coming months, potentially leading to even higher temperatures in Australia this summer and next. The European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service reported last month that the highest sea-surface temperatures ever recorded for July in oceans outside the polar regions were recorded in July. This, it said, was partly driven by the looming El Nino, which is expected to contribute to one of the most dangerous bushfire seasons since Black Summer.



Australia’s bushfire chiefs last month warned of increased bushfire risk among parts of Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia, northern and south-eastern NSW, south-east Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, and large parts of the Northern Territory. But the higher-than-usual temperatures experienced in Australia over winter and forecast for spring are unlikely to have yet been significantly altered by the El Nino, according to Professor Mark Howden, director of the Australian National University’s Institute for Climate, Energy and Disaster Solutions. “What’s going on in Australia [so far] fundamentally is the underlying temperature increase due to climate change.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: 'Very few' middle tier staff understood the gravity of reports into Mt Maunganui landslide risks
World.content:
A Tauranga City Council manager says "very few" people understood the gravity of reports into the risk of landslides at Mt Maunganui.

Elected officials and staff met on Tuesday to discuss the council's response to Paul Davison KC's report that said information showing a risk to life from a landslide was received, filed, discussed, forwarded, and then left.

He found the risk was known decades before six people died in a landslide on January 22 2026.

They were Lisa Maclennan, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler, Måns Loke Bernhardsson, Sharon Maccanico, and Max Furse-Kee.

Deputy mayor Jen Scoular asked staff about "media responses" that the chief executive and leadership team did not know abut the risks.

Chief executive Marty Grenfell told RNZ that no senior staff saw those reports.

"These reports were never escalated to a point where anybody at a senior level within the organisation could provide guidance, direction, and ensure that they were appropriately managed," he told Checkpoint.

Scoular questioned what was being done to help "middle tier staff" escalate information.

"Escalation of a risk requires that you understand it, that you know what your escalation requirements are, and that you feel psychologically safe to do so," general manager of strategy, partnerships and growth Reneke van Soest said.

"The first step there is actually recognising the hazard. People received reports but very few actually understood the gravity of what was said in those reports. That means we haven't appropriately helped our staff understand these things."

RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

She said risk assessment, identification and training is one of the recommendations to implement, but there's also elements of culture and systems.

"Staff with the benefit of hindsight are deeply affected by what happened."

Davison found the failure was not the fault of any one person, it was the failure of a system that enabled an identified risk to life to remain unowned, un-escalated and unmanaged.

"The central conclusion of this review is sobering in its simplicity. This was not a hazard that was unknown, hidden, or beyond the reach of foresight.

"For more than two decades, one competent consultant after another identified the landslide hazard to the campground, located it on the very slope that failed, and explained - sometimes in stark terms - what the consequences of a landslide occurring could be."

Davison said his recommendations are directed at building a single accountable ownership of every risk to life.

The council has committed to implementing all of the recommendations, which it said was "embedded in a broader program of organizational transformation focused on culture, risk management, governance, systems and processes".

World.title: Meningococcal case confirmed at Rosmini College on Auckland's North Shore
World.content:
Health New Zealand has confirmed a Rosmini College student has been diagnosed with meningococcal disease.

In a statement to the school, Health NZ said there was also one prior suspected case, notified in July.

There were no close contacts in the school community from either case, it said.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

"The National Public Health Service has undertaken the appropriate public health follow-up, with close contacts identified and offered treatment and support.

"We are investigating any links between the two students but the risk to the school community is considered low.

"To protect patient privacy, we are unable to provide any further details."

It comes weeks after Waikato young woman Kyla Te Wano Greensill died from the disease.

Her parents said at the time that she had become unwell with what first appeared to be flu-like symptoms and did not have symptoms commonly associated with meningococcal disease like sensitivity to light.

Health NZ Waikato medical officer of health Dr Kate Meerkerk had previously said the disease was more common in children, teenagers and young adults.

"It is important that people know the symptoms and seek medical attention early if they are concerned," she said

Symptoms can include fever, headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light and confusion.

The first symptoms of meningococcal disease may seem like the flu or a cold, but the symptoms will usually get worse quickly, with some people suddenly becoming very unwell, sometimes in just a few hours.

Dr Meerkerk said the meningococcal B vaccine was free for babies and children under five years old.

World.title: Hundertwasser Art Centre pleas for return of stolen sculpture 'no questions asked'
World.content:
Sculpture stolen from Hundertwasser Art Centre by bicycle Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

An outdoor sculpture has been stolen from the Hundertwasser Art Centre in Whangārei and if returned the gallery says there'll be no questions asked.

Police said the outdoor sculpture Tiori Toru has been missing for about a week and was removed from the centre's grounds at about 3.15am on Monday 24 August.

The wooden sculpture made by local artist Karin de Beer is approximately 1.4m x 600mm and is inlaid with glass birds.

Hundertwasser Art Centre director Joost de Bruin told Checkpoint the centre's outdoor sculpture exhibition had six sculptures.

De Beer's work is made of pohutukawa wood, he said.

"So it's a wood slab that was mounted onto a rock and that rock was concreted to the ground. Now the pōhutukawa slab has been taken, the rock was still there when we found it and somebody somehow managed to get the slab off the rock."

There was some footage from cameras around the town basin where the centre is located, he said.

"And we actually saw that the individual who stolen the slab was pretty quick and managed to detach it from the rock and then took off with it under their arm on a bike."

The person appeared to be pretty savvy and managed to evade some areas where there were cameras, he said.

On that basis de Bruin said they thought that it appeared to be a premeditated theft and that the person had done some prior research.

De Bruin said he did not know why someone would steal such an artwork because it would likely be difficult to sell because people would recognise it.

"It is an artwork we've received a lot of positive feedback on, the public really liked it because it is glass inside pohutukawa wood and it represents three different bird species, perhaps this person just really liked it for themselves, but of course that makes everybody else pretty sad about what has happened."

"[Karin de Beer is] pretty sad that the artwork is gone because for her it is an opportunity to show case her art to the wider public and that opportunity's now been taken away from her."

De Bruin wanted anyone who might know where the sculpture is to arrange for it to be returned.

"If it is dropped off here at the Hundertwasser Arts Centre we will happily receive it with no questions asked, we would just be happy to have it back."

World.title: MBIE head Nic Blakeley's position now 'untenable' - Labour
World.content:
The Labour Party has toughened its stance on chastened ministry head Nic Blakeley, saying his position is now untenable.

Parliament's Privileges Committee last week found the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) in contempt, ruling that Blakeley, as chief executive, and a former colleague had "deliberately misled MPs" about the status of a bungled multi-million dollar IT project.

At the time, Labour leader Chris Hipkins stopped short of calling for Blakeley to face further punishment.

But in a fresh statement - published almost a week later - Labour MP Phil Twyford said Blakeley's position was "untenable".

"Nic Blakeley must be accountable for his actions," he said.

Twyford said the finding of the Privileges Committee must not be treated as "business as usual".

"Parliament must be able to hold the Executive and public service to account, and that requires truthful and accurate information.

"This is about maintaining public confidence in our democratic institutions. When a senior public servant misleads Parliament, there must be accountability."

The call is a step up from Labour's position just last week and that of the Privileges Committee itself.

Labour MP Phil Twyford says the finding of the Privileges Committee must not be treated as "business as usual". RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The panel of MPs - including two from Labour - was scathing of Blakeley's conduct but did not recommend any further consequences: "We intend that our findings will be of sufficient consequence on their own."

Speaking then, Hipkins told reporters the ruling was "incredibly disappointing".

But asked whether he wanted to see more punishment, Hipkins suggested that was not necessary.

"I think the finding in itself will send quite a few reverberations through the public sector," he said.

The committee's ruling prompted Blakeley to offer his resignation to Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche, but it was turned down.

Roche said he took several factors into account when weighing that decision, including that Blakeley had been fresh into his job and had unreservedly apologised for his actions.

In a statement last week, Blakeley said the committee's findings were "extremely serious" and he was committed to rebuilding trust.

"I accept responsibility for this failure. Accountability rests with me. Parliament, Ministers and the public are entitled to expect better from MBIE.

"My focus now is making sure a failure of this nature does not happen again."

During a select committee appearance in March, Blakeley was asked about the progress of a biometric upgrade programme but failed to disclose that the project had already been cancelled.

In its findings, the Privileges Committee said officials would have known their incomplete answers would leave MPs with a false impression.

"The limited manner in which the ministry answered questions... was intentional," it said.

"We find that the ministry deliberately misled the Education and Workforce Committee and, in doing so, committed a contempt."

The report said it was "alarming" that neither of the senior public servants were aware they could have requested to provide evidence in private or secret.

"We wish to be very clear: officials appearing before select committees have an absolute obligation to tell the truth. Being truthful, responsible, and acting in good faith is the very essence of public service.

World.title: Maritime NZ launches investigation after worker dies at Wellington port
World.content:
Maritime NZ has launched an investigation into the death of a worker at Wellington's harbour port.

It said the death on Tuesday morning was the first at a major port since 2022.

Logistics company C3 said it was "deeply saddened" to confirm that one of its employees had died following an incident.

"This is a tragic event and our priority is supporting the employee's family, his colleagues and others, including those who attended the scene, during this incredibly difficult time," it said in a statement.

Do you know more? email mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

CentrePort chief executive Anthony Delaney said it was advised of the fatal incident at the port this morning involving a worker for an independent stevedore.

He said the company was working with C3, police, and Maritime NZ as the safety regulator.

Police said it was advised around 7:20am on Tuesday of a death at a facility in Pipitea.

"Enquiries into the specific circumstances are ongoing," a spokesperson said.

It is unclear how the worker died.

A spokesperson for Maritime NZ said the investigation into the tragic incident would be thorough.

"Any death at work is incredibly sad and we take all incidents very seriously.

"This death is also particularly difficult given this is the first death at a major commercial port since 2022 and given the significant work done over the past four years by the sector to improve safety and reduce harm."

The Maritime Union's national secretary Carl Findlay said the death was a tragedy.

He said the worker was not a member, but all port workers were devastated by a death in the workplace.

"We offer our sympathy and support to family, friends and workmates of the deceased."

World.title: 'The smell of death': Son tells trial how he found his father dead and mother missing at Ellerslie home
World.content:
It was the smell of death that made Chi-Ho Ricky Kwok suspect his father was dead.

His next question was where was his mum.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li was on trial for the murders of Fuk Fu Joseph Kwok and his wife, Mei Han Chong, in their home in Auckland's Ellerslie in 2023.

He's also charged with conspiring to murder someone else, who cannot be named.

A jury in the High Court at Auckland heard harrowing evidence about the night Ricky Kwok went to check on his parents, and found his dad dead and his mum missing.

Lok Fung Lorrence Li is on trial. Nick Monro

Kwok, an only child, told the court his parents would come to Hamilton where he lived on a regular basis.

The Kwok's were meant to visit their son for Joseph's birthday, shortly before a trip to Hong Kong, but never arrived.

Just after 1pm, Kwok grew nervous, calling them to no avail.

Kwok, who followed his theatre nurse father and midwife mother into a career as a vascular surgeon, said it was "extraordinary unusual" for his mother not to pick up.

"I was very concerned," he said.

Kwok alerted the police and asked for a welfare check.

He was worried his parents had been involved in a car crash on their way to Hamilton, after WhatsApp messages weren't able to reach his parents phones.

He made the decision to drive to Auckland to check himself.

The home cordoned off in 2023. (File photo) RNZ / Nick Monro

Arriving in Auckland, Kwok saw his parents car was missing from their driveway when he arrived.

Inside the Celtic Crescent house, Kwok found a body - his father.

It was then his medical training kicked in.

"As I approached towards that area, which was technically the area just beside the dining table, there was this smell," Kwok told the court.

"Medically, I would describe it as melena, essentially the smell of rotting blood, fermented blood."

Kwok knew not to touch the body, something he'd also learned from his medical training and watching "too much CSI dramas".

He did however check for a pulse, which he could not find.

"On top of that, the reason why I suspected that he was dead was because he had that smell of death that, again, working in the profession, you know when someone's been dead for at least a couple of hours," Kwok said.

"There's a certain rotting smell associated with that."

It was then, Kwok's mind shifted.

"My first fear was, dad's gone, but where's mum?" he said.

"Especially because there was no reply when I was calling out for her."

Kwok searched the house but could not find his mother.

"My medical instinct was that he was dead already but mum was missing and she was hopefully still alive but perhaps unconscious for whatever reason," he said.

"You can't save the dead, but you can save the living."

When he couldn't find his mother, he called the ambulance and police.

Fuk-Fu Joseph Kwok and Mei Han Chong with their son. Supplied / NZ police

The operator asked if he needed an ambulance, and it was then Kwok checked for the signs of death.

He had already checked for a pulse, and could not see signs of breathing, but had not checked his father's pupils.

Kwok lifted a jacket and bloody towel that had been covering his father's face.

He was asked by Crown prosecutor Alysha McClintock if he could recognise his father.

"Battered, bruised, bloated," Kwok said.

Soon after, he went to the front neighbour's property to see if they had heard anything.

They invited him inside, and made him a hot chocolate as he waited for police to arrive.

Jurors hear details of 'minor traffic incident'

In the afternoon, the court heard from Zhihui Zhong who had been in the car in December 2022 when Li first encountered Fuk-fu Joseph Kwok.

It was the Crown's case that the alleged murders stemmed from the accident, after the Kwok's address was given to Li as part of proceedings in the Disputes Tribunal.

Zhong told the court he had hired Li as a part-time driver.

Giving evidence through an interpreter, Zhong said he and Li travelled from the Auckland CBD to a motel in Greenlane on the evening of December 30th.

As they exited the motorway, another car bumped into them. The cars stopped, and Li got out to speak to the other driver.

Zhong said an older man had gotten out of the other car.

The other driver wanted to report the crash to police, as did Li, he said.

Zhong described the collision as small, adding he never got the damage to the vehicle fixed.

He was asked by Li's lawyer Paul Dacre KC if Li appeared angry at the crash.

Zhong said no.

"My understanding is, it was not a big issue, because both of them exchanged their information," he said through the interpreter.

Dacre KC asked Zhong to confirm how he had described Li to the police.

"'Mr Li is a very kind person, if I needed help with anything he'd be willing to help'," Dacre quoted.

"'He was nice person who would never get angry about anything'."

"Yes" Zhong replied.

Li was told by Kwok's insurance that he was at fault, and the issue was taken to the Disputes Tribunal.

As part of the process, Kwok had asked if his address could be kept confidential.

The court heard from the service manager for Auckland Disputes Tribunal at the time, Glenn Adkin who said that request had been refused.

Constable Robert Lawrence, who investigated the Disputes Tribunal matter, told the court the reason was that there were no real safety reasons or concerns.

"He didn't ask for Mr Li's address so he didn't see why Mr Li should have his address," Lawrence said.

Jurors were told in the Crown's opening Li recieved the Kwok's address earlier on the same day he and alleged co-conspirator Shu Man Poon had planned to kill Li's former landlord, who's identity is supressed.

Poon had earlier pleaded guilty to his part in the killings and was sentenced last year.

Alleged co-conspirator had warned police prior to killings

Earlier on Tuesday, the court heard from an officer in charge of the investigation, detective senior sergeant Lisa Anderson.

She gave jurors an overview of their investigation, how they picked up two people on CCTV going into the Kwok's house, and tracked those individuals until they had a clear image of who they were.

Police found Shu Man Poon, the man who was charged and subsequently pleaded guilty to his role in the Kwok's death, in Hamilton.

It was information from him that led police to find the Kwok's missing car, as well as Mei Han Chong's body which had been dumped on the city's North Shore.

She was asked by one of Li's lawyers, Paul Dacre KC, about Poon going to the front desk of a police station, two months prior to the killing.

The court had heard Poon went to the Auckland city police station where he told them he owed Li $7,000 and that Li said he'd erase the debt if Poon helped kill his former landlord.

Poon told staff he had been trying to deter Li from the plan, but felt the only way out was to commit suicide.

"I was aware that he had come to the front counter to report that he was feeling pressured to engage in a homicide of his friend's landlord or ex-landlord," Anderson said.

World.title: ACT overtakes National for large political donations
World.content:
RNZ is tracking the money flowing to the parties this election year and where it is coming from.

In an update on Tuesday 1 September it was revealed the tally of donations of $20,000 and above tipped over the $6 million mark to $6.2m.



ACT has edged in front of National in the rolling tally of donations after banking $100,000 from tech entrepreneur Brian Cartmell.

ACT also received donations from Craig and Shayne Greenlees, Andrew Bagnall and Jonathan Ayling.

ACT’s total of $2m in large donations now exceeds what it raised in the same way in 2023.

Here’s where things stand across all parties for declared donations of over $20,000.

When the donations made to the parties in the governing coalition are combined, the spread looks as below.

Who are this election's big donors?

The following donors have given $100,000 or more so far in 2026.

Not all donors are individuals. Companies, trusts and unions also give to political parties. The chart below shows the split between organisational and individual giving over $20,000 for each party.

In the 2023 election, unions gave $335,000 to Labour. National received no donations from unions, but did receive more than $1m from businesses.

Farah Hancock looks into political donations Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Exploring the data in the below chart shows where donors have focused on a single party or donated to more than one party.

Each line represents a donor with wider lines indicating larger amounts.

How the money grew

Donations of $20,000 and more made from the start of the year are captured on the below chart.

If someone makes numerous donations under $20,000, once the cumulative total tops $20,000 it must be declared.

How much bigger could the donation pot grow?

The below chart shows the 2023 annual total of donations over $20,000, compared to the current 2026 total.

Some who donated in 2023 haven't given more than $20,000 so far in 2026 to the same party. The table below identifies who these donors are.

Each row represents a party. A donor may appear more than once if they gave to multiple parties in 2023.

The following donors haven't donated before 2026.

How we analysed the data

All original data comes from the Electoral Commission website. RNZ's analysis normalises names which may appear more than once, but with different treatment. For example a John Smith and J Smith with the same address are updated to both be John Smith. In some instances where people have given individually as well as jointly their names are collated. If Joan Smith had the same address as John Smith and had donated individually, as well as made a joint donation with John Smith, the name is updated to John and / or Joan Smith.

Donation dates are taken from the "date received by party" information. In some cases one donation entry will consist of several donations made over time. The date received is the date on the donation return and should be the date the total donated by the donor tipped over $20,000.

World.title: House buyers have 45 percent more choice
World.content:
House buyers now have 45 percent more homes to choose from than they did three years ago, Realestate.co.nz says.

It says there are just under 33,000 homes for sale on its website, and there were 8000 new listings in August, up 11.8 percent from three years ago. The number of new listings was down 5.1 percent year-on-year.

Chief executive Sarah Wood said some of the increase was because sales had slowed while listings continued.

"This is a combination of more properties coming to market and the rate at which they're selling through has slowed over time and that has led to a stock build-up."

She said changes like the reduction in the brightline test from 10 years to two might also have encouraged more investors to sell.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

She said at the peak of the property market, after Covid lockdowns, there were only about 12,500 home listed for sale.

"But historically in the seven years I've been working here, they've been sitting more around the 25,000 mark...33,000 is definitely on the higher side but they have been sitting higher now for a couple of years," Wood said.

The average asking price was $849,362, on a national basis.

Wood said that was less than $28,000 below where it was in 2023.

"It's been three years of relatively flat asking prices ... people are waiting for the next correction but what I think we've found is our new normal."

Coromandel and Marlborough had the largest percentage drops in new listings in the month.

Realestate.co.nz said it would take 26 weeks to clear the current stock of listings at the current are of sale, 56 weeks in Coromandel, 48 in Northland, 49 on the West Coast and only 15 in Canterbury.

World.title: Cats coach speaks for first time since club's concussion fine
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists he is unsure if Jake Kolodjashnij will play for the Cats again following the club's concussion saga.

Speaking for the first time since Geelong was fined $140,000 for failing to officially let the AFL know about the concussion waiver in Kolodjashnij's contract, Scott kept it brief.

The dual premiership coach referred back to the club's response and was adamant he had stayed out of dealings about Kolodjashnij's future.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

If the defender does play it will almost certainly be at VFL level, with the club premiership favourites to win the second-tier competition.

"I've been really conscious to separate myself from this," Scott said about Kolodjashnij.

"This is one of those situations [where] if I could help, I would.

"But I'm told, and I believe independently, that I just wouldn't be any assistance, so I just don't get in the way."

The penalty was $100,000, plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

"Hand on heart, I don't really even know the facts, so I'm certainly not going to be swayed by people who understand the facts less than I do," Scott said.

"So my go-to is that I just support the club's position … whether some people accept that wholeheartedly, that's something you can ask them privately.

"But the club's position is, it's best for us to say, 'OK we acknowledge certain aspects, and we're keen to move forward.'"

After having the pre-finals bye, Geelong will face red-hot Carlton in an elimination final at the MCG on Friday night.

Speaking on Monday, experienced midfielder Tom Atkins denied the saga was a distraction for the Cats as they aimed to win their fifth premiership this century.

AAP

World.title: Sharks want to play their home NRL finals match at their home ground
World.content:
Cameron McInnes would not be surprised to see the NRL deny Cronulla a home final at Shark Park, warning players were now used to head office making rule changes "at the drop of a hat".

Out of form on the eve of finals, the fifth-placed Sharks are nevertheless guaranteed to host a week-one elimination match against one of South Sydney, North Queensland or Newcastle.

But the finals suitability of dilapidated Shark Park, the NRL's lowest-capacity regular venue at 15,000 seats, has been a discussion point in recent years.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

The NRL pockets ticket sales from finals games so would take a financial hit from hosting in the shire rather than the Sydney Football Stadium or Stadium Australia, which each have more than twice the capacity.

Shark Park has been deemed unfit for use in week two or three of the finals, but hosted week-one finals matches in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

The NRL is unlikely to publicly confirm venues until after round 27 finishes this Sunday, and told clubs in the pre-season it had the discretion to determine where finals games were played.

The possibility of playing elsewhere did not sit well with England-bound McInnes, who could be playing his last game at Shark Park against Melbourne this Saturday.

"I was under the impression the rule was if you earn a home semi, whether you're first or second, or fifth or sixth, you get to play it at your home. Our home is Shark Park," he said.

"I don't know if that was a rule change that they can just put in, but then again, the NRL changes rules all the time.

"Rule changes just happen at the drop of a hat now, don't they? So as a player, you just have to adapt."

The league most recently trialled a change to the kick-off rule in Melbourne's defeat of Brisbane last week, having introduced six-agains, 20/40 kicks, two-point field goals and captain's challenges since the start of the decade.

The NRL has also made less prominent changes to its trainer and interchange policies in that time, as well as reverting to one on-field referee per game.

"How much do you need to change? I understand at the end of the day, it's entertainment, I get it," McInnes said.

"But it's like someone's constantly sitting there going, 'The game's going really well, but now let's change something else'."

Inconsistency around ruck infringements was most dismaying to veteran McInnes, who sympathised with the league's match officials.

"When you bring that [six-again rule] in, I get it, to speed the game up and have the speeds to score long-range tries with fatigue, but it also creates an inconsistency in the game," he said.

"[It's] hard for the refs, isn't it? Because it's so subjective.

"If someone gets hit in the face and is offside, that's clear as day, but with the six-agains, it's just sort of a lottery."

AAP

World.title: Former rival says Nick Kyrgios's drug ban 'pretty much expected'
World.content:
Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drug use.

Kyrgios was banned earlier this month after he revealed he tested positive for cocaine in June when he was in Spain to play at an event.

The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected.

Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting 10th-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.

The former world number three, who had a famously contentious relationship with Kyrgios, said he was surprised the suspension did not come sooner.

"I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it," Tsitsipas said.

"So, what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, 'Here we go'. I kind of expected it, to be honest."

Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022 , when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple of shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a "bully".

Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt "helpless and alone", though added that "none of that excuses what I did".

Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas.

"I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that," he said.

"I'm not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I'll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviours that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.

"So, when I saw it, I was like, 'Well, pretty much expected, to be honest'. I am surprised it came so late, though."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Messi's legendary run for Argentina almost never happened after heartbreak
World.content:
Lionel Messi's retirement from the Argentina national side brings down the curtain on one of world football's most storied international careers.

The records and achievements of Messi are stuff of legend, and his status in international sport is reserved for only the very greatest of their craft.

Messi was denied the perfect finish to his Argentina career in July, defeated in a thrilling FIFA World Cup final by Spain that went to extra time.

But the loss in New Jersey only denied the fairytale finish, and did not diminish the legend that Messi created for himself, or the legacy that he has left among his people.

But the love and admiration of his people, the two Copa America wins, and the 2022 FIFA World Cup triumph, which brought Argentina back to the pinnacle of world football and raised Messi to the legendary status of fellow countryman Diego Maradona, almost never happened.

Legend at Barca, struggles with Argentina

Messi has been on top of world football for two decades, winning the coveted Ballon d'Or as the world's best player a staggering eight times.

From 2004 to 2021, he won 10 La Liga titles, seven Spanish Cups, seven Spanish Super Cups, four Champions Leagues, three UEFA Super Cups and three FIFA Club World Cups with Barcelona.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

In a legendary 2012, he scored 91 goals in all competitions, a record haul for a calendar year, and slotted 50 goals in the 2011-12 La Liga season.

Trophies, accolades, love and admiration grew and grew for the Barcelona great, but success for Argentina was not forthcoming.

Coming through the ranks, Messi led Argentina to a Youth World Championship in 2005 and the Olympic medal at the Beijing Games in 2008.

But in the very big tournaments, trophies were harder to come by.

When Messi made his senior debut for Argentina in 2005 against Hungary, the South American giants had not won a trophy since the 1993 Copa America.

Messi's final tears As the champion wept on the pitch after the World Cup final defeat, Argentina may well have wondered with trepidation what life will look like in the post-Messi era.

Messi's Argentina senior debut was nothing to write home about either, sent off after less than a minute on the pitch for elbowing an opponent.

But Messi overcame that infamous beginning to establish himself as a star, and the hope of a nation that Argentina could return to the top of South America, and the world.

What followed was a string of bitter disappointments.

Argentina made the final of the Copa America in 2007, but was soundly beaten 3-0 by arch rival Brazil.

At the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa, Messi failed to score at the tournament as Argentina exited at the quarterfinal stage.

Argentina was then knocked out again at the quarterfinal stage, this time at the 2011 Copa America, by eventual winner Uruguay.

These were bitter disappointments for Argentina and Messi, but the pain was about to increase, and it led to the great man announcing he did not want to be part of it anymore.

Three years, three finals, three painful defeats

Heading into the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, it had been 21 years since Argentina's last major trophy.

But the blue and whites marched into enemy territory intending to claim international football's greatest prize, and doing it in the backyard of their greatest rival.

Loading...

Argentina won all three group games — over Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iran, and Nigeria — to top the group, beat Switzerland 1-0 in extra time, and finally won a quarterfinal by defeating Belgium 1-0.

A scoreless semifinal against the Netherlands, finalists in 2010, went to penalties, where Argentina won 4-2, including a successful spot kick from Messi.

But the joy ended there.

In a major final for the first time in seven years, Argentina faced a German side that had just humiliated Brazil 7-1 in the semifinal.

Like all of Argentina's games to that point, the game was tight and tense. It went to extra time, but the strike of German Mario Götze sealed Germany's triumph.

A photograph of Messi looking at the World Cup trophy after the defeat, captured by Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily in China, became the defining image of Messi for years.

Lionel Messi walking past the FIFA World Cup trophy after defeat in the 2014 final. (Supplied: Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily via X)

The heartbreak only continued for Messi and Argentina.

The Copa America was held in 2015 and 2016, with Argentina reaching the final both times and losing to Chile each time.

Both finals ended scoreless and went to penalties. Messi converted his penalty, the only Argentinian player to do so, in the 2015 defeat, but the great man missed his spot kick in 2016.

The pain of the 2016 final defeat was too much for Messi, who announced he was retiring from Argentina.

"For me, the national team is over," he said after the loss to Chile in 2016. "I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion."

"It's been four finals, I tried.

"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over.

"I think this is best for everyone. First of all for me, then for everyone.

"I think there's a lot of people who want this, who obviously are not satisfied, as we are not satisfied reaching a final and not winning it."

World football was that close to never seeing Messi reach the heights he would achieve.

Six-week retirement, 10 years of legacy building

When Messi announced on Sunday, June 26, 2016, that he would no longer play for Argentina, he ended what was by any other measure a magnificent international career.

He had made 113 appearances, scored 55 goals and led his country to four major finals.

But the absence of a trophy was not good enough — not for someone as great as Messi.

On July 10, the world watched Cristiano Ronaldo lift an international major trophy as Portugal won the 2016 Euros.

On August 12, Messi announced that he was back.

What followed after his six-week retirement is, on its own, one of the greatest international careers ever forged.

Messi would add another 94 caps to his name, score another 70 goals, and more importantly, end Argentina's trophy drought.

And Messi didn't just win one major trophy for Argentina; he won four.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia was another familiar quarterfinal exit for Argentina, but it was the precursor to an era of success.

Argentina finally broke through to win the Copa America in 2021, and they did it against Brazil, in Brazil.

Lionel Messi was thrown into the air in celebatrion after Argentina ended a 28-year trophy drought. (Getty Images: MB Media)
